News.title: Hairy Biker Si King reveals he still speaks to late co-star Dave Myers
News.content:
Proper Home Cooking is Si King’s first solo cook book since the death of his Hairy Bikers partner, Dave Myers - and this is one instance when fans should judge the book by its cover. Si says: “My book is a bit of a love letter to comfort food.”

And while Dave, sadly died from cancer in 2004, aged 66, his influence is still very much present. Si, 60, says: “I talk to him quite a lot. When I'm in the kitchen, I'll go, ‘you all right, mate?’”

The nation took the pair to their hearts when they teamed up in 2004 and they became a regular TV double act, with their unique blend of cooking and fun. Si says: “You take people that you've loved and lost with you. You can move on, but they move on with you.

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

Mary Berry's Christmas Pudding recipe READ MORE :

“Dave always used to say, ‘oh, let's just give it a go.’ And then I used to go, ‘well, what's the worst thing that could possibly happen?’ It’s dangerous advice. But it was bloody fun, that's the thing. Now, I only have myself to think about. It's a very different space and place. It's taken quite a lot of adjustment. It's definitely a time of change.”

View 4 Images The Hairy Bikers: Si King and Dave Myers (Image: SCU)

Determined to respect Dave’s legacy and that of the Hairy Bikers, Si - who has three grown up children with his ex wife Jane King - says his book is stuffed full of easy to prepare recipes. Now a grandfather-of-two, the cook - whose son Dylan's a chef, while James is a restaurateur and another son, Alex, is a tree surgeon - says his recipes also strike out against ultra-processed food.

Si, who is dating Staffordshire-based designer and property manager Caroline Witcomb, says: “I've tried to keep recipes down to how long it would take for the oven to heat up and to cook chicken nuggets - 40 mins or less.

“What I'm actually saying is that if you have a choice, try doing this instead of eating ultra-processed foods. If you don't have a choice, then feed your kids whatever you can get your hands on. I have been in that position and that's exactly what I did.”

He hopes his book will encourage families to sit down together for dinner, saying: “Eating together is the glue that binds a family. Those that eat together and play together, stay together. Bon appetit!”

Frying pan pizza

View 4 Images Si King's Frying Pan Pizza

Serves 6-8

500g 00 or pizza flour, plus extra for rolling

2 tsp instant yeast

1½ tsp salt

2 tbsp olive oil

Up to 300ml tepid water

Pizza sauce:

1 tbsp olive oil

3 garlic cloves, crushed

400ml passata

1 tsp dried oregano

A large sprig of basil

Salt and black pepper

Topping:

400g mozzarella cucina or 2 balls of fresh mozzarella, sliced

Extra topping ideas:

Broccoli

Sliced mushrooms

Ham

Salami

Crumbled sausage

Cherry or sliced tomatoes

Olives

Anchovies

Capers

Grilled aubergine or courgettes

Sliced chillies

First make the dough. Put the flour into a bowl with the yeast and mix thoroughly before adding the salt. Add the olive oil and work in up to 300ml of tepid water, adding it gradually until you have a slightly sticky dough. Leave to rest for half an hour, then turn out on to a floured work surface and knead until soft and pliable – this will probably take about 10 minutes. Of course, you can do all of this with a dough hook on a stand mixer if you have one. Put the dough back into the bowl and cover with a damp tea towel. Leave to stand for 1–2 hours until puffy and doubled in size. Divide the dough into 6 rounds. At this point, you can leave the dough in the fridge until you need it. Otherwise, leave to prove again for at least another half an hour. To make the sauce, heat the olive oil in a saucepan and add the garlic. Cook for a minute, then add the passata, oregano and basil. Season with salt and pepper. Bring to the boil, then turn the heat down to a simmer and leave to reduce by a third until a little thicker. When you are ready to cook the pizzas, roll the dough rounds out to a size that will fit an ovenproof skillet or frying pan. Heat the pan and the grill. Put the pizza round on the frying pan, then, working quickly, spread over a small ladleful of the pizza sauce and top with a few slices of mozzarella and any toppings you want to use. Cook until you can tell that the dough is setting – you will see it start to dry out around the edges and carefully check that it is lightly browning underneath. Transfer to the grill and cook for a further 2–3 minutes or until the cheese is bubbling. Repeat to make the rest of the pizzas.

TIP: Get to know this basic recipe, then be creative and top with what suits your family. I’ve listed some examples of toppings but the possibilities are endless, so choose what you fancy. The dough is quick to make but if you’re really pushed for time you can buy pizza bases at the supermarket and add your own toppings. Use whichever type of mozzarella you prefer – the dry sort sold for cooking, often labelled ‘cucina’, takes less time, but the fresh tastes better and has a better stretch. So down to your preference.

Aubergine & potato curry

View 4 Images Si King's Aubergine & Potato Curry

Serves 4

2 tbsp olive oil

1 onion, thickly sliced

400g new potatoes, halved

2 medium aubergines, cut into chunks

15g root ginger, grated

4 garlic cloves, grated or crushed

1 tsp cumin seeds

1 tsp coriander seeds

1 tbsp curry powder (a chilli/paprika one works best)

200ml vegetable stock or water

4 medium tomatoes, cut into quarters

3 tbsp yoghurt

Handful of chopped spinach (frozen is fine)

A squeeze of lime juice, if you have it

Salt and black pepper

To serve:

A few green chillies, sliced

Coriander leaves

Flatbreads (shop-bought)

Heat the oil in a large flameproof casserole dish. Add the onion and potatoes and sauté until the potatoes are lightly browned. Stir in the aubergines, then the ginger, garlic, spices and curry powder and season with salt and pepper. Pour in the vegetable stock or water and bring to the boil. Simmer for 10 minutes or until the aubergines and potatoes are just about tender, then add the tomatoes. Continue to cook until the tomatoes have softened and have started to collapse. Add the yoghurt, gently swirling the dish around so the yoghurt spreads through the curry, then stir in the spinach until wilted. Heat through for a minute. Taste for seasoning and adjust to your liking, then add a squeeze of lime juice, if using. Serve garnished with the chillies and coriander and with some flatbreads on the side.

*Proper Home Cooking by Si King is out now (Seven Dials, £25).

News.title: RUSSELL MYERS 'Break in at Anmer Hall should be a wake-up call for the entire Royal Family'
News.content:
Protecting the royals has never been an easy job, but a break in at Prince and Princess of Wales’ country home brings every worry and concern ever held by the royal family into the spotlight.

Intruders breaching Anmer Hall, the Norfolk home of the future King and Queen, on the King's own Sandringham Estate, is not only a gross invasion, it is a matter of national security.

In a month's time the entire senior royal family will gather at Sandringham for Christmas. The King and Queen, the Prince and Princess of Wales and their children will all be on the same Norfolk estate, on dates everyone knows. On Christmas morning they will walk to St Mary Magdalene Church past crowds who have queued since dawn. The royals enjoy welcoming hundreds of locals and well wishers there in the spirit of Christmas. After recent events this now could be under threat.

The questions need answering before Christmas. How did the intruders get in? How quickly did anyone respond? What has changed since Shaw Farm? And what will be different when the family walks to church on Christmas morning?

View 4 Images Police are investigating a reported burglary at Anmer Hall, on the Sandringham Estate (Image: Getty Images)

The catalogue of recent security breaches makes stark reading.

On Christmas Day 2021, Jaswant Singh Chail climbed into the grounds of Windsor Castle with a rope ladder and a loaded crossbow and told a protection officer he was there to kill the Queen. He was jailed for nine years under the Treason Act.

In October 2024, masked thieves drove a stolen truck through a security gate on the Windsor estate and stole vehicles from Shaw Farm while the Waleses slept at Adelaide Cottage nearby.

View 4 Images Prince William, Prince George, Prince Louis, Princess Charlotte and Catherine, Princess of Wales (Image: Getty Images)

In May this year, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor was allegedly confronted by a man in a balaclava while walking his dogs near his Sandringham home. A man denies the charges and is due to stand trial next month.

Anyone who has ever been at the hands of callous burglars will know the feeling of devastation that comes with your home sanctuary being sullied.

The Princess of Wales recovered during her cancer treatment and where the family filmed the video marking the end of her chemotherapy. William, Catherine and the children were fortunately at their family home, Forest Lodge in Windsor. But it's a home the heir to the throne uses all the time, and for a royal protection team that has to be one of the worst breaches there could be.

View 4 Images A police officer following a reported break in at the Prince and Princess of Wale's country home in Anmer, Norfolk (Image: Getty Images)

The estate covers 20,000 acres of open countryside with public roads running through it. It's now home to Andrew Mountbatten Windsor - the disgraced former prince who lives in exile at the King’s expense - the Waleses' retreat and the King's Christmas base. Now it has seen two incidents in six months. Yet protection there still seems to be arranged house by house.

Then of course, far from Prince Harry seemingly shouting into the abyss regarding his own security issues, surely now his points, heavily made across the judiciary and the countless broadcast interviews he pops up in, must be taken into account.

Alleged stalkers have been detained at their Montecito home. Harry, Meghan and her mother were caught up in what his spokesman called a near catastrophic car chase in New York, if such an incident can exist in the city.

But in London last year, a woman known to Harry's team as a fixated individual reportedly got within feet of him twice. Since the family moved back to Britain in August, Archie and Lilibet have had to leave their first school after two days because security couldn't manage the school run. Weeks later, two photographers were seen looking into the grounds of their new school.

Is it any wonder Harry is pleading for round-the-clock protection? For six years he has argued that being born royal makes you a target for life, and he has been mocked for it. Yet the evidence keeps piling up. Andrew has lost his titles and his public role, and he still had a protection officer with him that night. Harry has a wife and two young children at school in this country and relies on private bodyguards. The body in charge of royalty protection (Ravec) agreed in September to review his case and Meghan's. They are still waiting.

Questions will no doubt be asked but the answers need to cover off whether the royal family, who also work for us and represent our country at home and abroad, are not only being protected, but whether wholesale changes need to be implemented immediately.

News.title: Takeaway owner used children as young as 12 to flood seaside town with cocaine
News.content:
Takeaway owner used children as young as 12 to flood seaside town with cocaine

Gang leader Cole Muir - who sold cocaine around Lancashire - used school age children in his criminal enterprise which had links to Dubai

View 8 Images Cole Muir, 28, ran a drugs gang in Blackpool that used children (Image: Lancashire Police / SWNS)

A takeaway owner who ran a drug dealing gang used children as young as 12 in his criminal enterprise in Lancashire which also had links to Dubai.

‌



‌



Cole Muir, 28, was the ring leader of a criminal group called 'Dial A Bag' who supplied cocaine in Blackpool and around the Fylde coast for over a year. Officers from Lancashire Police made the shocking discovery that school children were involved in the gang’s activities after a 12-year-old was seen on CCTV buying up a top-up card for a phone used for the ‘Dial A Gram’ line, which it was initially known as. When officers visited a house, a teenage girl, 17, dropped a bag containing 212g of cocaine from a window.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

‌



8 View 8 Images Keiran Gibson, 29, of Wetherby Avenue, Blackpool, was jailed for four years. (Image: Lancashire Police / SWNS) 8 View 8 Images Katrina Allen, 45, of Ennerdale Road, Blackpool, was jailed for 12 years. (Image: Lancashire Police / SWNS)

Police say individuals who delivered drugs were encouraged to work harder with the promises of new cars and places to live if their targets were met.

‌



The gang used their mobile phone line to push the class A drug across the Blackpool, a court was told.

Eight members of the crew - including Muir - appeared at Preston Crown Court this week, where they were sentenced to a combined total of 81 years and seven months.

‌



Officers from the Targeted Crime Team in Blackpool launched an investigation after an Audi driven by Mr Muir was stopped outside a takeaway on Dickson Road which he owned.

A phone seized from a passenger inside the car was examined, and officers found incoming messages about bulk drug dealing.

‌



The number the messages were sent from was saved in the phone as 'Dial A Gram'.

8 View 8 Images Connor Gardener, 32, of Anderson Street, Blackpool, was jailed for eight years and six months. (Image: Lancashire Police / SWNS) 8 View 8 Images Curtis Crothers, 32, of Staining Road, Blackpool, was jailed for 15 years (Image: Lancashire Police / SWNS)

‌



Muir’s phone was also examined and showed him to be extensively involved in street-level and mid-level supply of cocaine.

‌



He was supplied with drugs in bulk by Dubai-based kingpin Harry Warner, 32, until July 2025, after which Warner took charge of the group’s business.

Evidence gathered during the investigation linked the various group members to roles in the supply of cocaine.

‌



It found the group had supplied drugs between early January 2025 and late January 2026.

Police began making arrests in Blackpool for the conspiracy in late January. Body cam footage shows Mr Muir being arrested.

‌



Warner was arrested at Manchester Airport in May, having flown back to England from Dubai.

Eight members of the crew - seven men and one woman - appeared at Preston Crown Court for a two-day sentencing hearing which concluded on November 20.

‌



8 View 8 Images Keiran Gibson, 29, of Wetherby Avenue, Blackpool, was jailed for four years. (Image: Lancashire Police / SWNS) 8 View 8 Images Declan Reilly, 23, of no fixed address, was jailed for 13 years. (Image: Lancashire Police / SWNS)

‌



They had all pleaded guilty at previous hearings to conspiracy to supply Class A controlled drugs.

Cole Muir, 28, of Bela Grove, Blackpool, was jailed for 20 years. Curtis Crothers, 32, of Staining Road, Blackpool, was jailed for 15 years. Declan Reilly, 23, of no fixed address, was jailed for 13 years.

‌



Katrina Allen, 45, of Ennerdale Road, Blackpool, was jailed for 12 years. Connor Gardener, 32, of Anderson Street, Blackpool, was jailed for eight years and six months.

David Winstanley, 42, formerly of Westmorland Avenue, Blackpool, was jailed for four years and three months. Keiran Gibson, 29, of Wetherby Avenue, Blackpool, was jailed for four years.

‌



Lewis Mason 27, of Webster Avenue, Blackpool, was jailed for three years and six months. Also before the court was Daron Warner, 27, of Midgeland Road, Blackpool, who was given a two-year suspended sentence and 150 hours unpaid work in the community. He had pleaded guilty to conspiracy to supply Class A controlled drugs.

View 8 Images David Winstanley, 42, formerly of Westmorland Avenue, Blackpool, was jailed for four years and three months (Image: Lancashire Police / SWNS)

‌



Rachael Higgin, 50, of Midgeland Road, Blackpool, who was given a 12-month suspended sentence and a £600 fine. She had pleaded guilty to assisting an organised crime group.

Harry Warner, of Midgeland Road, Blackpool, will be sentenced in December for his involvement in the conspiracy.

‌



Det Insp Fiona Jackson of the West Targeted Crime Team, said: “These people were involved in the supply of large amounts of cocaine in Blackpool over a lengthy period of time.

“They played various roles which has been reflected by the sentences they received from the judge.

Article continues below

“The sale and the use of drugs brings criminality and misery to towns and communities, and Lancashire Police will thoroughly investigate those involved in the supply of drugs in order to put them before the courts.”

Operation Warrior is Lancashire Police's response to tackling serious and organised crime in Lancashire, which is backed by Police and Crime Commissioner Clive Grunshaw.

News.title: Moment triple killer boasted 'Ian Huntley is dead' minutes after brutal murder
News.content:
Moment triple killer boasted 'Ian Huntley is dead' minutes after brutal murder

Anthony Russell received a second whole life term today for his pre-planned execution of the man he described as an 'arrogant narcissist'. Russell, 44, dramatically changed his not guilty plea on the second day of his trial at Newcastle Crown Court

Russell shouts 'Ian Huntley's dead' in prison yard after attack

A smirking triple killer proudly shouted "Ian Huntley is dead" after murdering him in a 'cold-blooded' attack in a prison workshop.

‌



‌



Anthony Russell received a second whole life term today for his pre-planned execution of the man he described as an 'arrogant narcissist'

‌



Russell, 44, dramatically changed his not guilty plea on the second day of his trial at Newcastle Crown Court.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 4 Images Ian Huntley’s killer Anthony Russell being interviewed at HMP Frankland after his lethal attack on his fellow inmate (Image: Crown Prosecution Service Media)

He had initially claimed manslaughter on the grounds of diminished responsibility. Flanked by four security guards, the tattooed, shaven-headed killer entered a guilty plea after hearing the overwhelming evidence against him on the opening day of his trial.

‌



Prosecutors released footage of Russell shouting “Ian Huntley’s dead” and boasting he was “proud of it” as he was marched through a prison yard moments after the fatal attack at HMP Frankland on Feb 26 this year. In a second clip, he told prison governor Craig Phipps that he had decided "to do him in" about a week-and-a-half earlier. In the video captured on bodyworn camera, Russell was asked what he meant by “do him in”.

He replied: “Kill him… that’s why I caved his head in about six, seven times with a metal steel bar.”

‌



View 4 Images Ian Huntley’s killer Anthony Russell being interviewed at HMP Frankland after his lethal attack on his fellow inmate (Image: Crown Prosecution Service Media)

Describing a previous incident with Huntley in March 2025, when the Soham killer threatened him in front of prison officers, Russell said: "I thought 'f*** you, you ain’t getting away with it, I’ve got nothing to lose, I’m never getting out.'"

‌



Russell felt Huntley was protected by prison guards because of "how high profile" he was, the court heard. The child-killer had also been even more "arrogant" and "cocky" since Russell walked away from an earlier argument. He told guards he wanted to do the job of murdering Huntley "properly."

Tyrone Smith KC, defending, admitted Russell was not remorseful about the murder.

‌



But he said that he did apologise “for the distress caused to those who may have had to witness what he did and the aftermath”.

‌



View 4 Images Ian Huntley pictured in Soham at the time of the murders of Holly Wells and Jessica Chapman (Image: Handout/Press Association)

Mr Smith said: "It was Huntley who started and perpetuated the dispute between the two of them. He said Ian Huntley was a very arrogant and narcissistic person.

‌



"He said that he walked around the wing like he was some kind of big man and something special.

"He said Ian Huntley felt like he was protected - if anything happened, he knew the other person would be moved from the wing." The judge Mr Justice Hilliard said he had no option but to pass a whole life sentence due to the premeditated nature of the attack.

‌



He told Russell: "You describe caving his head in about six or seven times with a metal bar. When staff got over to where you were, you stopped what you were doing.

"Though you were delivering what you intended to be a fatal attack, you were in control of yourself and able to stop when you wanted to." Huntley did nothing to annoy Russell; Huntley had not shoulder-barged him or grinned at him, the jury heard.

‌



View 4 Images Ian Huntley during a 2006 hospital visit (Image: Andy Stenning/Daily Mirror)

Russell shouted from the dock as prosecutor Matthew Bean KC outlined to Newcastle Crown Court the details of his murder and rape convictions from 2020.

‌



Russell's previous murders of David Williams and Julie Williams at separate flats in Coventry took place on October 21 and October 25, 2020, respectively. As the prosecutor described how the sentencing judge had said Russell appeared to have murdered Mr Williams due to the “unfounded belief” he had slept with his girlfriend, Russell shouted out in protest. When Mr Bean took the court through the murder and rape of his third victim, Nicole McGregor, the defendant shouted “that’s not true” from the dock.

The prosecutor said Russell was jailed for life and given a whole life tariff.

‌



Huntley was serving a life sentence at the high security Frankland jail for murdering Holly Wells and Jessica Chapman in Soham, Cambridgeshire, in 2002.

He died on March 7 at Newcastle's Royal Victoria Infirmary from unsurvivable brain and skull injuries.

‌



Speaking after the verdict, senior Investigating Officer Detective Chief Inspector Alfie Keane, of Durham Police thanked his team, adding: “This was a premeditated attack inside a prison workshop by Russell, which resulted in Ian Huntley sustaining fatal injuries. “Russell acted alone and the evidence suggests he decided before entering the workshop that morning that he was going to kill Huntley."

Judge Hilliard told Russell: "You will never be released and never be eligible to apply to the parole board for release."

Article continues below

The quadruple killer showed no emotion - and waved at the press box as he left the dock.

News.title: Disability benefit review calls for closer link with claimant costs
News.content:
The main disability benefit in England and Wales should be more closely linked to the additional costs claimants face, a government-commissioned review has recommended.

The review on personal independence payment (Pip) led by Disability Minister Sir Stephen Timms said the current system was "not appropriate" for claimants who do not have any extra costs arising from their condition.

The government has committed to some of its recommendations, including fast-track payments for people with severe conditions, but will not respond fully to the plans until early next year.

The Conservatives said the year-long review was a "compete farce" and showed a "complete absence of substance".

Shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately added: "All we have is a report that tinkers around the edges of a failed system".

Pip is available to people with long-term physical or mental health conditions who have difficulty doing every day tasks, regardless of whether they work, and it is not linked to income or savings.

The number of people claiming Pip in England and Wales has roughly doubled since 2019 to around four million.

The Timms review was set up last year by Sir Keir Starmer's government after his aborted attempt to cut welfare spending, which was derailed by the threat of a rebellion by Labour MPs.

It was co-produced with groups representing disabled people, who had a role in drafting the report.

News.title: Two arrested on suspicion of burglary at Prince and Princess of Wales's Norfolk home
News.content:
Two men have been arrested on suspicion of burglary and trespass at the Prince and Princess of Wales's country home on the Sandringham estate, police say.

Norfolk Police said it received a call just before 18:00 GMT on Monday following a report of suspicious activity at Anmer Hall.

Police deployed dogs, drones and a helicopter to search the area and arrested two men on the estate, who remain in custody.

The property was unoccupied at the time, police added. Kensington Palace said it did not comment on security matters.

William and Catherine do not live at Anmer Hall full-time, but use the estate as a country retreat during the holidays.

Val Blackmur, an 83-year-old resident who lives on the road leading up to the house, told the BBC it was "amazing" if anybody had been "stupid" enough to try breaking in.

News.title: Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away
News.content:
As the market bell rang out at the Nasdaq today, the Nvidia super-bounce faded.

Its shares slid and are down almost 30% over the past six months, well before the scandal involving Jensen Huang emerged earlier this month.

The legitimate fears about the staying power of the tech boom pre-dated Huang's exit. They have not gone away with his return.

Investors are jittery. Already Anthropic is now trading notably lower than last week's stock market flotation. The firm is the first purely AI company to be publicly listed, and is being seen as a big test for continued investor appetite for the technology.

President Trump's extraordinary phone call to CNBC taking credit for telling the board to reinstate Huang showed the extent of the operation - of some in Silicon Valley and within the US administration - to get him back at the helm.

Among the truly astonishing reflections from President Trump was a suggestion that a two-day investigation of allegations was done and had cleared Huang of national security concerns.

The President said his remarkable move to intervene was because Huang is a "national treasure" who has the next generation of AI chips "in his head". Trump says this is why he needed to act.

In markets, those sceptical about the AI boom say they have never seen an operation to prop up a stock market boom like this. The bond vigilantes and short sellers are now up against Silicon Valley and the White House.

Investors are trading not revenue numbers but levels of political support at a time when US voters have just delivered a backlash against AI data centres.

Against this backdrop, the recovery of the central cash-generating foundation of the tech boom - Nvidia and its $400bn (Â£304bn) annual sales of advanced chips - looks politically fragile.

This worsens other uncertainties and risks, such as Nvidia's central role in the web of financing, borrowing and cross-ownership to support every corner of the build out of data centres.

The brief interim Nvidia chief executive Colette Kress had already signalled a rowing back from elements of this strategy last week. Where is that now?

The fall back in Anthropic's share price also raises questions about OpenAI's planned listing on the stock exchange. Ultimately these two companies might be the most critical part of all this.

They remain valuable companies with phenomenal technology relied on by the world's biggest companies. The real question is whether that reliance eases, as corporations eschew expensive frontier models for cheaper generic models offered by China.

In turn, all this could be affected by the political backlash, to which the Nvidia psychodrama now contributes.

It is simply not normal to have trillion dollar swings in the value of individual companies.

The extraordinary volatility shows the fragile mood of investors.

News.title: 'I'm proud of it': Killer confesses after murdering Ian Huntley
News.content:
A triple murderer who beat the notorious child-killer Ian Huntley to death in prison has been given a second whole life jail term.

Anthony Russell, 44, repeatedly bludgeoned Huntley, 52, with a metal bar at the high security Frankland Prison near Durham in February, Newcastle Crown Court heard.

In footage released by the Crown Prosecution Service, Russell confesses to planning to kill Huntley and says: "I'm proud of it."

Russell, who was jailed for life with no chance of parole in March 2022 for raping and murdering a pregnant woman and killing a mother and son in the West Midlands, admitted Huntley's murder on the second day of his trial.

Sentencing him for what prosecutors called a "cold-blooded" and planned attack, Mr Justice Hilliard KC said Russell would never be freed from prison or eligible for parole.

Huntley was serving a life sentence at the high security Frankland jail for murdering Holly Wells and Jessica Chapman in Soham, Cambridgeshire, in 2002.

Read more on this story.

News.title: Businesses supporting Ukraine told to 'act now' to protect against Russian sabotage
News.content:
The UK government has warned that any businesses providing support for Ukraine's armed forces could become a target for Russia, and should "act now" to protect themselves.

An alert issued on Tuesday warned of an increased risk of Russian sabotage attacks such as arson and threats to staff, premises and operations.

Any businesses that are providing support to Ukraine's armed forces, including organisations in the supply chain, have been urged to take extra precautions, both physically and online.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and there has been a recent increase in Russian sabotage attempts against defence related facilities in Europe.

In September, a man appeared in court accused of planning to "torch" UK drone factories on behalf of Russia's intelligence services in an alleged sabotage plot.

Estonia has also accused Moscow of being behind an attempted arson attack at a drone factory last week, and Germany blamed it for a drone attack at Leipzig's airport in August.

The joint alert, external between MI5's National Protective Security Agency (NPSA) and the Ministry of Defence, has advised businesses to remove unnecessary detail that can be found online, emphasising that hostile reconnaissance usually begins with internet research.

It also suggested that companies install visible protective security measures "such as CCTV, secure entrances and robust access controls" to "deter hostile activity". These security measures should be "actively promoted... without giving away information that could be used to plan an attack".

When it comes to personal security, any staff members - not just those at the top - should "remain alert to their surroundings, avoid predictable routines where practicable, and consider how personal information, movements and behaviours could be used to build a picture of them, their role and their organisation".

Leaders should ensure their staff know how to manage their personal security, and know what to do if they notice anything suspicious or concerning.

The government said it will give closed-door threat briefings to critical national infrastructure and defence sector CEOs in Whitehall on Tuesday and Wednesday.

Gen Sir Richard Barrons, who co-authored last year's Strategic Defence Review, said the latest warning was "significant but not new" and the relevant companies will be "quite savvy" about the risks of cyber attacks.

He told BBC Radio 4's World at One that while there had been a recent "uptick" of these kinds of attacks across Europe, "we are not expecting an epidemic".

"These actions so far are significant but not strategic. They cause disruption, dismay and some damage but they have not reached the level of them being a strategic threat to the security of Europe," Gen Barrons added.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has warned that threats from Russia are aimed at deterring the UK's support for Ukraine, which "must not" happen.

Speaking to the Commons Foreign Affairs Committee earlier on Tuesday, Miliband said the threat from Moscow will endure beyond the Ukraine war and reiterated that any peace settlement must not reward Russia.

Security Minister Dan Jarvis said recent sabotage attempts across Europe "demonstrate the seriousness of the threats we face".

Minister for the Armed Forces, Louise Sandher-Jones, added that Russia and other hostile actors "pose a growing threat", while companies have a responsibility to strengthen their security "and help protect Britain".

News.title: Former police chief inspector jailed for rape
News.content:
A former police chief inspector who once worked with convicted murderer Wayne Couzens has been sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison for two counts of rape and one of sexual assault.

Glen Mahony, 54, who was convicted at Maidstone Crown Court in September following a 10-day trial, carried out two attacks while his victim was asleep.

Mahony worked in the Civil Nuclear Constabulary (CNC) and previously worked with Couzens, who is serving a whole life tariff for the rape and murder of Sarah Everard in 2021.

In his sentencing remarks on Tuesday, Judge Gareth Branston dismissed Mahony's claims that he was targeted because he had once managed Couzens.

"You were not targeted. You were arrested because of what you did," he said.

He described Mahony's behaviour as "appalling", saying it had left his victim, who was known to him, suffering panic attacks and unable to work.

The judge said that when arrested in March 2022, Mahony told Kent Police officers that he had been Wayne Couzens's overall manager, though not his line manager.

The CNC, which guards the UK's nuclear facilities, is the force where Couzens served for six years before joining the Metropolitan Police.

Mahony, who was an inspector in charge of day-to-day police operations at the Dungeness power station before being promoted, was his commanding officer for some of that time.

Mahony was suspended on full pay by the CNC in March 2022 and resigned the day before a disciplinary hearing in January of this year.

The CNC said he would have been dismissed for gross misconduct if the disciplinary process had been carried out.

In an impact statement read to the court, his victim said she was made to feel worthless, and that "it was all about control for him".

"His actions didn't just hurt me at the time but have continued to do so each day. He has stolen my confidence," she said, having described ongoing nightmares and mental health struggles.

Det Ch Insp Tracy Evans, of Kent Police, said: "To take advantage of a woman while she is asleep and at her most vulnerable is utterly disgraceful and to then deny it happened and force the victim to relive her ordeal during a trial makes things even worse."

She also praised the "tremendous courage" of the victim in coming forward to report Mahony.

CNC Chief Constable Simon Chesterman said his immediate thoughts were with Mahony's victim, who he also commended for her bravery.

"Former officer Glen Mahony's crimes were despicable, committing the most serious sexual violence to a vulnerable female victim, who was not able to consent," he said.

"Mahony's behaviours are entirely contrary to the high standards required of a police officer with the CNC. And his actions go on to undermine the trust and confidence that the public, and particularly women, have in the police service."

Two WhatsApp groups to which Mahony belonged were also investigated by CNC professional standards.

"In these groups, Mahony sent sexist and misogynistic messages, and he did not challenge or leave the group when others sent similarly offensive messages," Chief Constable Chesterman said.

"This further underlines his disgusting opinion of women."

Mahony was promoted to chief inspector for the south division in 2020. It meant he was number three in the division's chain of command for the four nuclear sites in the south - Dungeness, Sizewell and Hinkley Point power stations, and the nuclear research centre at Harwell, Oxfordshire.

He spent most of his working life as an armed officer based at the Dungeness nuclear plant in Kent.

He joined the force in 2006, becoming a sergeant in 2011 before being promoted to inspector in 2016. This put him in operational charge of security at the site. He would have worked with Couzens, who was a constable at Dungeness between 2012 and 2018.

Couzens was also in a separate WhatsApp group with six other officers who transferred to the Met from the CNC. The messages they shared were found to be sexist, misogynistic, racist and violent, raising questions about the culture among officers at both the CNC and the Met.

News.title: Sacked London Pride boss given suspended prison sentence
News.content:
The sacked boss of London Pride has been handed a suspended prison sentence after "harvesting" confidential documents to disrupt an investigation into his alleged misconduct and set up his own rival company.

London's High Court heard how Christopher Joell-Deshields had downloaded more than 50 private documents just days after agreeing to a court order to hand over all company property.

Mr Justice Cotter said the 55-year-old had downloaded documents on a "large and significant scale" with the intention of "disrupting the organisation" and "advancing his own causes".

Lawyers for Joell-Deshields said he had mental health issues and couldn't recall deliberately downloading private information.

The former Pride in London (PIL) chief executive was held in contempt on two separate counts, after admitting failing to hand back company property and failing to provide a witness statement confirming he had done so.

He was sentenced to six months imprisonment for the first count, and four months for the second.

Both sentences were suspended for 18 months, with Cotter warning the defendant the court would "not be in any way likely to be as lenient if there were to be any further breaches".

The sentencing brings to a close a long-running legal battle between the organisers of the UK's largest pride event and its former boss.

Joell-Deshields was suspended in August 2025 after being accused of bullying and misappropriating vouchers donated by a sponsor in order to purchase luxury perfumes and Apple products. He denies those claims.

News.title: Tories accuse Burnham of turning No 10 into 'joke' after influencer video row
News.content:
Andy Burnham has been accused of turning the UK into "a joke" on the world stage by Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, amid a row about social media videos posted from an event in Downing Street.

Social media influencer Max Balegde has deleted a video filmed outside the door of Number 10, which was posted on TikTok, in which he mimed along to explicit lyrics.

Badenoch said it was a "disgrace" that the prime minister allowed 10 Downing Street to be "degraded".

The prime minister's spokesperson said the content was clearly not acceptable and it was "right" that Balegde had taken down the social media posts.

Balegde's video appears to have been filmed earlier this month at an event for around 60 social media influencers hosted by Burnham, who is eager to use social media to reach younger voters. Balegde also gave a speech to those present at the event.

In the video, the influencer, whose real name is Max Trobe, mouths the words "bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets", using audio from a meme that is trending online.

Bomboclaat is a Jamaican profanity referring to a menstrual cloth, while pussy is a slang term for female genitals.

It is unclear when Balegde's video was deleted but it no longer appears on his TikTok or Instagram accounts.

The creator has 3.6 million followers on TikTok and 640,000 on Instagram.

Videos which were filmed inside the Downing Street premises were recorded on government phones, the BBC can reveal.

Attendees at the event have confirmed they had to hand personal devices in and were given a phone and a camera to film with, with the footage they recorded sent to them after the event.

One of the distinctive features of Burnham's time in office has been his enthusiasm for engaging with social media influencers as a means to communicate with different groups of voters, especially younger voters.

It was an approach begun by Sir Keir Starmer, under whom a "new media unit" was formed, but has significantly intensified since July.

The engagement with influencers has elicited criticism of Burnham from those who fear it means reduced scrutiny and diminished opportunities to hold the prime minister to account.

News.title: Huntley murderer handed new whole life jail term
News.content:
A triple murderer who beat the notorious child-killer Ian Huntley to death in prison has been given a second whole life jail term.

Anthony Russell, 44, repeatedly bludgeoned Huntley, 52, with a metal bar at the high security Frankland Prison near Durham in February, Newcastle Crown Court heard.

Russell, who was jailed for life with no chance of parole in March 2022 for raping and murdering a pregnant woman and killing a mother and son in the West Midlands, admitted Huntley's murder on the second day of his trial.

Sentencing him for what prosecutors called a "cold-blooded" and planned attack, Mr Justice Hilliard KC said Russell would never be freed from prison or eligible for parole.

Huntley was serving a life sentence at the high security Frankland jail for murdering Holly Wells and Jessica Chapman, both 10, in Soham, Cambridgeshire, in 2002.

He and Russell, from Coventry, were both on A-wing and there was "tension" between the killers, the trial had heard.

At about 09:00 GMT on 26 February, Russell attacked Huntley in the prison's recycling workshop, repeatedly beating him about the head with a metal bar.

News.title: Record 5,200 heat-linked deaths estimated in England this year
News.content:
More than 5,000 people suffered heat-associated deaths in England this summer, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has estimated - the highest number since records began in 2016.

The UK experienced its hottest summer on record in 2026, and the estimated 5,258 heat-linked deaths were twice the previous high of 2,985 in 2022.

The most deadly period of the year for heat-related deaths was between 21 and 28 June, when there were an estimated 2,401 heat-associated deaths. Temperatures peaked at 38C in that period.

Climate change is expected to increase the length, frequency and intensity of extreme heat, the UKHSA has warned.

News.title: Government probe into housing scheme 'exploitation'
News.content:
SEA is designed for people in the UK with additional needs, including people recovering from addiction and women fleeing domestic abuse.

In many cases it works well for people, but BBC investigations over the past five years have uncovered stories of vulnerable people, including care leavers and people with mental health problems, being let down by the system designed to support them.

Some residents said they had been left living alongside drug dealers and criminals, and fearing for their lives, despite some providers reportedly claiming more than Â£200 a week at the time for every person they house.

Supported housing expenditure had risen faster in Birmingham than the national average in recent years, a government spokesperson said.

Pat McFadden, Work and Pensions Secretary, said there were "real concerns" about how the system was operating.

"Sir David's investigation will get to the bottom of what's going on, and where we find wrongdoing, we will act to make sure money is spent on supporting people who need it," he said.

The council paid out Â£404.4m for SEA in the 2024-25 financial year, with a further Â£211.8m paid between April and July 2026.

More than 34,000 people in the city currently live in SEA, compared to about 22,000 living in London, despite its population being more than seven times larger.

The BBC has previously heard evidence of claims that some housing providers were willing to make benefit claims for people who did not live in their properties.

The council introduced controls, requiring SEA providers to submit evidence they were delivering more than minimal care to their tenants.

But a recent internal audit showed the authority could not show the review had been completed for 72% of the claims tested.

At the time the results were published, 12,700 live cases were waiting review, of which around 7,100 had exceeded the six-month limit.

Bosses said a plan was in place to reduce the backlog to zero by the end of the year.

Preet Gill, the Labour MP for Birmingham Edgbaston, said she welcomed the independent review.

"I have campaigned on exempt accommodation for nearly a decade and worked with residents, the council and police to shut down Saif Lodge, the first exempt accommodation property in the country to be closed in 2021," she said.

"Neighbours have had enough of the antisocial behaviour, and vulnerable people are being let down while some providers profit."

It is not the first time politicians have investigated the issue.

An inquiry by the Levelling Up, Housing and Communities Committee in 2022 reported that some vulnerable people had faced rape and exploitation by landlord "gangsters" in England's "complete mess" of an exempt housing system.

That was two years after Birmingham was named as one of five pilot projects, external designed to improve quality, enforcement, oversight and value for money in the sector.

News.title: Man charged with murder of missing 20-year-old woman
News.content:
A man has appeared in court charged with the murder of a missing 20-year-old woman in Dumfries and Galloway.

Kelsey Hunter was last seen in Castle Douglas at 17:00 on Saturday. A major search is under way in the nearby village of Springholm where she lives.

Daniel McKnight, 21, has appeared on petition in Dumfries Sheriff Court charged with murder and two other charges, including defeating the ends of justice.

He made no plea and was remanded in custody.

News.title: Girl, 14, repeatedly stabbed by boy told friends he 'begged' to see her, murder trial hears
News.content:
Warning: This article contains details some readers may find distressing

A teenage girl who was stabbed to death by a 14-year-old boy told friends he had been "begging" to see her on the day she was last seen alive, a murder trial has heard.

Lilly Jones, from Blaina, in Blaenau Gwent, left home at about 18:30 on 20 June, telling her father she was "popping out for a bit".

The boy, who cannot be named because of his age, was seen on CCTV meeting Lilly near the town's Red Lion pub that evening. He denies her murder.

Her body was discovered face down in woodland close to Duffryn Park two days later. She had been stabbed about 55 times, including knife wounds to her heart and lungs.

Newport Crown Court heard on Tuesday that Lilly sent messages to a friend saying, "he's begging me to go out" shortly before she went to meet him.

The friend asked: "Are you going to?"

Lilly replied: "Idk" (I don't know).

In a message to another friend, she wrote: "I just don't wanna get back with my ex."

That friend replied: "Then don't."

In a group chat on Whatsapp, Lilly also wrote: "Guess who is asking to meet up?"

One person answered: "I know" and Lilly replied: "Uhm. What should I say?"

The jury was shown a compilation of CCTV images of Lilly walking through Blaina to the park.

The boy was dressed in black and walking approximately three to four metres behind her all the way. He could be seen using his phone continuously. None of the CCTV images showed them walking closely together.

Lilly was also dressed in black. She was wearing a dark skirt and hoodie with a corset top she had bought at a shop in Cwmbran the previous day, her 14th birthday.

The last time Lilly was seen on CCTV was at 18:50, as she walked across a grass bank towards a footbridge across the A467 towards Duffryn Park, with the boy following behind her.

An hour and 38 minutes after Lilly and the boy were last seen together on the cameras, the boy could be seen leaving the park alone.

At 20:23 that night, a friend sent a message to Lilly asking: "Are you ok? Your dad just knocked on our door asking where you were."

The court was told the messages were not delivered to Lilly's phone. She did not respond.

At 22:19, her family called police to report her missing.

News.title: Southport survivors' parents 'disgusted' by school recovery funding
News.content:
Parents of children injured in the Southport knife attack have criticised "huge discrepancies" in support money given to schools in the area after the stabbing.

Schools attended by 10 of the survivors received more than a million pounds in recovery funding between them, while schools attended by 13 other survivors received no direct funding, the families' lawyers have said.

Council documents, external published this afternoon reveal that Â£1,013,920 has been allocated to seven schools in the Sefton local authority area following the attack in July 2024.

The council says it was up to schools to tell it of the help and funding they needed, as seven local schools have done.

ââThe largest recipient was Churchtown Primary School, which was given Â£546,815. It was attended by two of the girls who were killed, as well as children who survived.

The council also allocated Â£52,360 to Presfield High School and Specialist College, which was attended by the attacker, Axel Rudakubana.

Three girls - Bebe King, Elsie Dot Stancombe and Alice da Silva Aguiar - were murdered in what was described as the worst mass stabbing in modern British history.

Twenty-three girls survived the attack, which happened at a Taylor Swift-themed dance and yoga workshop for children.

News.title: Nephew demands reforms after uncles killed by schizophrenic man released from custody
News.content:
Lewis-Ranwell, who had a history of paranoid schizophrenia and had been sectioned under the Mental Health Act twice before, was arrested again on 11 February following an incident at an Exeter hotel, the inquests heard.

This time, an MHA assessment was completed and he was found to be acutely psychotic.

Lewis-Ranwell was charged with murdering Payne and the Carters, but found not guilty by reason of insanity. He was given a direct hospital order.

Coroner Philip Spinney said he would be considering writing Prevention of Future Deaths reports.

Such reports are sent when a coroner thinks action is needed to protect lives.

Devon and Cornwall Police said its Professional Standards Department liaised with the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) on 13 February 2019 and requested that the matter be considered as a voluntary referral.

The force also said: "Areas of learning and change identified during the inquest and prior reviews are being, and have been, addressed."

An IOPC spokesperson said: "We received a complaint referral from Devon and Cornwall Police in March 2020, in relation to the contact the force had with Alexander Lewis-Ranwell prior to the deaths of three men, in Exeter, in February 2019.

"After assessing all the available information provided by the force, we decided that an investigation was required and it was appropriate for the investigation to be carried out by Devon and Cornwall's Professional Standards Department.

"The complainant would have had the right of review to the IOPC should they have been dissatisfied with the investigation outcome.

"To date, we have not received a request to carry out a review."

G4S Health Services no longer operates. A G4S spokesperson said: "We offer our condolences to the families affected by these tragic events."

The Devon Partnership NHS Trust said: "We would like to extend our sympathies to the families of Richard and Roger Carter and Anthony Payne.

"Our organisation will reflect on the jury's conclusions and we remain committed to continuous learning and ensuring that improvements are embedded in our systems and practice."

You can hear more about this story in File on 4: Why Was He Released? on BBC Sounds.

Follow BBC Devon on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to spotlight@bbc.co.uk, external.

News.title: Baby P's mother given open prison recommendation
News.content:
The mother of the toddler known as Baby P - who died after months of abuse - has been told she will not be freed from jail, although the Parole Board has recommended she should be moved to an open prison.

Tracey Connelly, now 45, was jailed in 2009 for causing or allowing the death of her 17-month-old son Peter at their home in Tottenham, north London, in August 2007.

Connelly has been freed twice, in October 2013 and July 2022, and recalled to prison both times, in February 2015 and August 2024.

Public parole hearings took place last October, but the case was adjourned after the panel decided there needed to be a further psychological assessment.

News.title: Influencer Christie Miller, 60, announces own death in heartbreaking pre-recorded video
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Influencer Christie Miller has died at the age of 60, four years after being diagnosed with breast cancer.

Miller announced her own death in a pre-recorded video shared to her Instagram page late Monday night.

“Hey, hey hey, it’s Christie Miller. And if you are seeing this video, it means that I am dead. Which also means that I have been reunited,” the influencer began before the video cut to a montage of photos of her and her husband, who died of cancer in 2025.

“That’s right, I have crossed the veil,” Miller continued after the montage. “I am sitting with my sweetie,” she said of her husband of 36 years.

Miller went on to declare that she is “feeling absolute bliss, with no regret and how I played the game of life and how I won.”

Miller was diagnosed with stage 4 HER2-positive breast cancer in June 2022. She shared frequent updates with her 51,000 Instagram followers as she navigated the diagnosis.

“Now Dr. Seuss has a saying that I think is actually wrong. It goes like this, ‘Don’t be sad because it’s over, be happy because it happened,’” she continued in her video.

“So, if you’re missing me, please be sad. It’s normal to be sad. But also be happy that we got to spend time together. Whether it was in-person friends or a chance meeting, or we’ve known each other forever.”

Miller ended her video with a piece of advice for her followers: “Go out there and live your life, feel the fear, and do it anyway. Stop frickin caring about what anyone thinks. They’re too self-involved in their own life. They’re not worried about you. Go out there and find joy every single day and buy yourself a joy bell, just like this.”

open image in gallery Christie Miller, left, has announced her own death in a pre-recorded Instagram video ( Christie Miller / Instagram )

Devastated followers have turned the comments section of the Instagram video into a tribute to Miller.

“I can’t even wrap my head around how she was walking the beach and how quick this happened , although she said it was coming,” one person wrote.

“Thanks for showing us all what it means to prioritize LIVING. I hope you’re having the amazing reunion you deserve,” another wrote, as someone else said, “We love you sweet force of nature. I can only imagine the bliss and expansion you are feeling with Mark. You will be missed. Thank you for being you.”

Someone else chimed in: “What a shining light and I know her light will continue to shine from the other side.”

News.title: Cornish Christmas market cancels bookings after ‘AI slop’ backlash
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A Christmas market will cancel and refund all bookings after facing backlash for not living up to its AI-generated promotional material.

Kernow Christmas Market in Redruth, Cornwall, was advertised on Facebook with posters created by AI, showing a wonderful winter scene complete with festive stalls, bright lights and decorations.

The market was set to be an addition to Cornwall’s Winter Wonderland, based in Pool market hall.

However, many were left underwhelmed when - in reality - they arrived to what appeared to be markets around the sparse warehouse space.

One commenter on Facebook said: “It's like the wonka event all over again”, referring to a failed Willy Wonka experience that took place in Glasgow in 2024 but closed just hours after opening.

open image in gallery ( Social media )

Another said: “Nothing like promised severely disappointed and no communication to vendors.

In a Facebook post on Sunday, the organisers addressed the criticisms.

It said: “Our original idea was to work alongside Pool Market, helping to increase footfall into their market while using their wonderful location as our winter trading home.

“We have worked as closely and cooperatively as possible within the space, facilities and rules that have been made available to us.

“As this is the first time we have undertaken something like this, we appreciate that there have been a few misunderstandings and perhaps different expectations of what the indoor setup would look and feel like.

“Unfortunately, some aspects of the venue and its layout are outside of our control, but that doesn’t mean we aren’t listening or that we don’t want to make things better.”

One user commented: “Maybe stop using unrealistic AI images to promote standards you cannot uphold!”

Another said: “As soon as I saw the AI adverts, I knew a car crash was coming.”

open image in gallery Kernow Christmas Market was advertised with AI images ( Facebook )

“Maybe avoid the AI slop of your promotional adverts, it created an unrealistic image of what people where (sic) expecting”, a fellow commenter said.

On Tuesday, the organisers issued another statement, again addressing the criticism. They said that attempts to bring a “little festive magic into Pool Market” had not worked as planned and current bookings will be refunded.

The statement said: “We are gutted, just as much as you all that things didn’t go as planned. The criticism we have faced and the words that have been seen on social media and across the news make us look at the world slightly differently.

“Kindness and compassion goes out of the window so easily to knock something that people don’t care to understand the full story of.

“As a result of this, we are going to cancel and refund all current and future bookings and Kernow Christmas Market will take no further bookings for 2026. Any current bookings will be fully refunded.”

News.title: Daughter on trial for attempted murder of mother, 100, ‘told her to hurry up and die’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

For free real time breaking news alerts sent straight to your inbox sign up to our breaking news emails Sign up to our free breaking news emails Sign up to our free breaking news emails Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

A daughter accused of attempting to murder her 100-year-old mother by giving her morphine told her to “hurry up and die”, a court has heard.

Sarah Pickering, 72, and her brother, Browns Brasseries founder Jeremy Mogford, 79, are charged with the attempted murder of Pamela Mogford, who died on February 15 2022 after she was given a dose of oral morphine solution by her children.

Giving evidence at Oxford Crown Court on Tuesday, Pickering said she believed her mother had suffered a stroke the day before she died and was in a “terrible state”, drifting in and out of consciousness.

The defendants travelled to be with their mother at her house in Bledlow Ridge, Buckinghamshire, on 14 February 2022.

Recalling how Mrs Mogford seemed when she arrived, Pickering told the court: “She was not like my mother – she wasn’t sparky, she was lying on her back, moaning and groaning a bit, and she was very grey.”

open image in gallery Pamela Mogford died on 15 February 2022 after she was given a dose of oral morphine solution by her children ( Crown Prosecution Service )

Mrs Mogford was attended to by paramedics, who classed her as “end of life”, as well as her GP, Dr Thomas Neale, who gave her two doses of Oramorph – a liquid form of morphine designed to be swallowed.

The drug had been prescribed to Mrs Mogford to ease back pain, and was kept in a kitchen cupboard, the court was told.

Jurors previously heard that when Dr Neale left the house that evening, he advised the defendants not to give their mother any more of the medication.

But Pickering said no such instruction had been made, rather she and her brother had been “left to our own devices”.

She said her mother, who was “clearly in pain”, had been agitated and restless when Dr Neale visited and was much the same after he had left, so the siblings decided to give her another dose of Oramorph.

Mrs Mogford was then visited by a family friend, Stephen Cox.

Pickering’s defence barrister, Benjamin Newton KC, put to her that she had “surprised” Mr Cox during his visit, by saying: “For f***’s sake mother, hurry up and die.”

Newton asked: “Is it the kind of thing you would say?”

“Absolutely,” Pickering replied, prompting laughter from the public gallery packed with the siblings’ supporters.

open image in gallery Sarah Pickering, 72, and her brother, Browns Brasseries founder Jeremy Mogford, 79, are charged with the attempted murder of Pamela Mogford ( PA )

Asked what she had meant by the comment, Pickering said: “More really for her, so she’s not suffering anymore.

“It’s not that I wanted her to die but I knew that she wanted to die.”

Pickering added that she thinks her mother, with whom she shared a “very similar” sense of humour, would have found the remark amusing.

She said Mrs Mogford again became “very agitated” after Mr Cox left, so she and her brother gave her another dose of Oramorph, which she said calmed her mother down.

Jurors heard Pickering had texted Mogford after he had returned home, to get his agreement to give their mother a third dose of Oramorph.

She had told him their mother’s breathing had become a “death rattle”, which was “awful” to listen to.

Mogford replied: “Yes, go ahead.”

In her response, Pickering told Mogford she would “wait a little while she’s fast asleep”, jurors heard.

In messages sent to various friends and family members, Pickering described the situation as a “waiting game”.

open image in gallery Pamela Mogford was attended to by paramedics, who classed her as “end of life”, as well as her GP, Dr Thomas Neale, who gave her two doses of Oramorph – a liquid form of morphine designed to be swallowed. ( Crown Prosecution Service )

She told the court: “We knew mother was dying. It was just a matter of time. Neale had told us, the paramedics had told us.”

Asked whether she had intended to do anything to “make that waiting game shorter” by hastening her mother’s death, Pickering replied: “Absolutely not.”

Asked about a message she had sent to her husband, in which she told him, “I am actually killing her”, Pickering told the court she knew morphine could be a dangerous drug when used inappropriately but said they had been using it “to manage her pain”.

“I think after two glasses of wine I was probably out of my brain a bit,” she added.

Asked what she had meant by the message, Pickering replied: “I can’t answer that question.”

In another message shown to the jury, Pickering told her husband: “I shall wait until Foyle is over then I can go to my grave knowing I have topped someone.”

Asked what the intention behind the message had been, Pickering said there was no intention, adding: “I had had too much to drink.”

She told the court she did not end up giving her mother any more Oramorph because Mrs Mogford fell asleep, adding she would have done, had she shown signs of being in pain.

Mrs Mogford died shortly after midnight.

Asked how she felt after her mother had died, Pickering said she was “very sad”, but relieved that her mother was no longer suffering.

The trial continues.

News.title: Senegal re-crowned Afcon champions after appeal upheld
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Senegal have been re-crowned the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations champions after the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) unanimously upheld their appeal against the decision to strip them of their title on Tuesday.

Senegal contested Confederation of African Football's (Caf) decision to declare Morocco champions, wiping the Teranga Lions’ title from the records despite winning January’s Afcon final 1-0 after extra time in Rabat.

The final was fraught with controversy after Senegal staged a walk-off in protest to an injury-time penalty was awarded against them in the dying stages of normal time, with players ordered into the dressing room by manager Pape Thiaw, where they remained for 14 minutes.

Play was eventually resumed before Morocco’s Brahim Diaz missed the spot-kick, sailing a tame ‘Panenka’ effort into the arms of Edouard Mendy. Senegal went on to win the match in extra time through Pape Gueye.

open image in gallery Brahim Diaz missed the penalty after Senegal staged a 14-minute walk-off ( AFP/Getty )

However, they were stripped of the title two months later after Caf’s Appeal Board ruled that Senegal had forfeited ⁠the match by walking off the pitch, overturning the result and awarding a 3-0 ​victory to ⁠Morocco.

Senegal quickly followed with an appeal to sport's highest court, Cas, which was lodged on 25 March and have now successfully fought their case to be reinstated as champions, with the original 1-0 result restored.

The three-man Cas ‌panel, presided over by French sports law ​expert Gerald Simon with assistance from ‌Italian international law professor ⁠Luigi Fumagalli and Hamburg-based ⁠attorney Ulrich Haas, ‌unanimously found that referee Jean-Jacques Ndala “did not commit any error of law”, said Cas secretary general Matthieu Reeb.

Ndala’s decision to resume the match after Senegal’s walk-off fell within his sole authority and was therefore covered by the “field of play” doctrine, something Morocco’s federation argued was not the case.

The court published its reasoning in a press release issued on Tuesday afternoon, which read: “By blowing his whistle to restart play, the referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met – both teams were on the pitch again, and both expressed their willingness to resume.

“In the panel’s view, there is no doubt that the effects of the referee’s decision were limited to the pitch.”

The panel clarified that Articles 82 and 84 of Caf’s tournament regulations, cited in the Moroccan federation’s appeal, apply only to determining match results if team conduct forces a referee to permanently call off a game, and were therefore not applicable in this instance.

"In conclusion, the panel considers that in resuming the match, the referee did not err in law," a court press release added.

open image in gallery The Cas panel found referee Jean-Jacques Ndala did not commit any error when he allowed the match to continue ( AFP via Getty Images )

“The panel acknowledged that the referee had to make a decision in an atmosphere of extreme tension. However, these circumstances do not justify describing the decision as 'arbitrary'. On the contrary, the referee's judgment did not appear to have been affected by factors external to the game."

Cas noted that disciplinary action has already been taken against then-Senegal boss Thiaw, the Senegalese federation and certain players following separate proceedings by Caf.

Senegal took to social media to celebrate the verdict, posting a picture of the team lifting the trophy with the caption, “Encore et toujours champions d’Afrique” - which translates to, “Champions of Africa, once again and always”.

The Moroccan federation and Caf are yet to respond to the ruling, but Caf president Patrice Motsepe has said they will respect the Cas verdict.

Cas initially promised a decision within days of the 8 October in-person hearing in Lausanne but then decided to issue a complete ruling, including legal grounds, known as a Cas Award - a process that requires several weeks.

Cas Awards hold the same value as a national court judgement, enforceable in accordance with the New York Convention on the Recognition ‌and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards.

The full Cas Award will be published in due course.

News.title: House Dems demand Donald Trump Jr.’s firm records as investment investigation expands
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

House Democrats investigating the business activities of Donald Trump Jr. have requested records from four firms linked to venture capital firm 1789 Capital, where the president's son serves as a partner.

The targeted entities include prediction market platform Polymarket, vaping brand Juul, online firearm seller GrabAGun, and manufacturing firm Hadrian Automation.

The requests were detailed in letters released on Tuesday by Rep. Jamie Raskin, a Maryland Democrat slated to take over leadership of the House Judiciary Committee next year.

Raskin requested comprehensive records of all communications exchanged between the specified companies, 1789 Capital, and its executive team.

"The probe examines whether the President’s son and his business partners helped steer federal contracts or regulatory decisions to companies in which they had a significant financial interest or used advance knowledge of those forthcoming decisions to make investments and profit," Raskin's office wrote in a press release.

Raskin initially launched the inquiry in August.

Rep. Jamie Raskin ( Reuters )

With Democrats set to assume control of Congress in January, lawmakers are preparing a broad series of probes targeting Republican President Donald Trump and his administration.

These inquiries will encompass government contracts, potential financial conflicts of interest, immigration policies, and the investigation concerning the late financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Speaking at an Axios event last week, 1789 Capital President Omeed Malik and Trump Jr. refuted any claims of wrongdoing.

"We responded to Congressman Raskin back in September pointing out in detail the many flaws in his understanding of how 1789 has operated and a number of basic factual errors,"

Bill Burck, an attorney representing 1789 Capital, said in a statement. "These are personal attacks untethered to actual evidence."

Juul stated that it plans "to cooperate with any Congressional effort to understand our company."

Meanwhile, a spokesperson for online gun retailer GrabAGun rejected the claims, asserting, "Congressman Raskin's letter is a political document, and its allegations are baseless."

Representatives for Trump Jr., Polymarket, and Hadrian Automation did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

In a move legal experts expect will face challenges, President Donald Trump issued an order on Friday attempting to restrict corporate cooperation with congressional investigators.

The directive instructs firms holding federal contracts to inform the White House prior to sharing material with lawmakers and to withhold confidential data.

Under the U.S. Constitution, Congress maintains broad oversight authority and subpoena powers to compel information, mechanisms the administration has sought to limit in scope.

Raskin’s expanded probe concentrates on whether the four businesses "benefited, or stand to benefit," from Trump administration contracts, regulatory decisions, or proposed rule adjustments, which Raskin said could indicate misconduct or conflicts of interest.

In his letter to Polymarket, Raskin pointed out that the firm was effectively barred from operating in the US and faced federal scrutiny before Trump returned to office.

In July 2025, regulators concluded that probe and approved Polymarket's acquisition of a US platform, paving the way for its market re-entry.

The following month, 1789 Capital disclosed a strategic investment that news outlets reported was worth tens of millions of dollars. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission has since reopened its inquiry into Polymarket.

Raskin also noted that in July 2025, months after 1789 Capital invested $5 million into Juul, authorities loosened sales restrictions on certain products, with further authorizations granted earlier this year.

GrabAGun went public in 2025 following a merger with a special-purpose acquisition company backed by Malik. In May 2026, the Trump administration proposed rules to simplify direct-to-consumer gun shipments.

The GrabAGun spokesperson noted these proposals were well known across the industry and that the business only provided input through public comment channels.

Raskin also contacted Hadrian Automation, noting that the manufacturing firm received nearly $1 billion in US government contracts shortly after 1789 Capital secured a stake in the business.

Raskin cited public remarks made by the president himself regarding his family’s commercial affairs, recalling his statement to CNBC in July: "I feel badly in a way for my kids ... Almost anything they do ... they have inside information."
