Sports.title: Meet the world's most famous pub team: How a Sex Pistol, Superman and Vinnie Jones took Hollywood United  beyond Sunset Boulevard via private jet - and even rubbed shoulders with David Beckham's LA Galaxy
Sports.content:
Meet the world's most famous pub team: How a Sex Pistol, Superman and Vinnie Jones took Hollywood United beyond Sunset Boulevard via private jet - and even rubbed shoulders with David Beckham's LA Galaxy

They had a World Cup winner in defence, Superman in their squad and a Sex Pistol in charge of recruitment.

There's a clue in the name, but Hollywood United must have been the wildest, most star-studded pub football team of all time.

Ray Winstone, Jason Statham, Mike Myers and Vinnie Jones all turned out for a team that grew out of a gathering of British expats at the Cat & Fiddle pub in the late Eighties.

It being Hollywood, they travelled to matches by private jet and they even took on David Beckham in a charity match.

Now, as the Sex Pistols prepare to embark on a tour marking the 50th anniversary of their debut single, guitarist Steve Jones has revealed how he assembled the extraordinary side on Hollywood's Sunset Boulevard.

Among those who pulled on the shirt were France's World Cup-winning defender Frank Leboeuf, former Scotland captain Richard Gough and Brandon Routh, the American actor who played the superhero in the 2006 film Superman Returns.

Routh was given no special treatment by his team-mates, who would mockingly shout ‘Superman!’ whenever he made a mistake.

Hollywood United is the world's most famous pub team - featuring a littany of high-profile stars

Created by British expat and Sex Pistols star Steve Jones (right), United have rubbed shoulders with the likes of David Beckham

Vinnie Jones, meanwhile, had apparently lost none of the competitive instincts that characterised his career in English football.

In 2002, it was reported that he had been sent off just 15 seconds after coming on as a substitute in a Hollywood United friendly.

Anthony LaPaglia, the Australian actor who starred in the hit television series Without a Trace, was their goalkeeper.

There were members of the Sex Pistols, The Cult and Def Leppard, as well as actors such as Ralf Little.

But there were also rather less celebrated footballers.

‘The start of it was with me and Anthony LaPaglia; he was a goalie, and from there it turned into Hollywood United,’ Jones told the Telegraph.

‘We always used to play in a league with a bunch of regular blokes, carpenters and so on, then we got a few more faces who wanted to start kicking about with us like Vinnie Jones.’

The two Joneses met in a video shop in Los Angeles and the former Wimbledon hardman, who had embarked on a film career with Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels, needed little persuasion to join.

‘He was up for a laugh, and he knows where to put a ball. Most of the team were amateurs, but we were decent and reached a certain level.’

In November 2007, Hollywood United took on Beckham's LA Galaxy in a charity match.

England manager Steve McClaren had flown to California to assess Beckham's fitness ahead of a European Championship qualifier against Croatia. It's not clear whether he attended the match, which Hollywood United lost 12-4. Beckham scored twice, as did Leboeuf and over 5,000 spectators raised more than $100,000 for victims of the California wildfires.

Steve Jones, now 71, had himself broken one of football's golden rules by changing his allegiance.

Vinnie Jones (left) and Ray Winstone (right) have turned out for the amateur football team

Actor Anthony LaPaglia lets the team travel on his private jet to matches across America

Having followed QPR as a schoolboy in west London and also been associated with Fulham, he became a Chelsea supporter after moving to California and getting sober.

Chelsea's games were available on American television and his lifelong friend and fellow Sex Pistol Paul Cook was already a diehard Blues fan.

‘Cookie had always been a Chelsea diehard fan, so I just picked Chelsea.’

Hollywood United played at Griffith Park, beneath the famous Hollywood sign, but their adventures would take them considerably further afield.

LaPaglia would arrange private jets to transport the players to matches.

Gough recalls one trip when the team flew to Vancouver for a charity match before heading straight to the Mexican resort of Puerto Vallarta to play a side of former Mexico internationals.

Vinnie Jones also told the Guardian in 2007 that Hollywood United had fielded nine former international footballers in a single match.

The club's ranks included former Liverpool and Newcastle defender Barry Venison and United States internationals Alexi Lalas and Eric Wynalda.

Winstone, a lifelong West Ham fan, found playing in the Californian heat rather more demanding than he had anticipated.

He later recalled being so exhausted by the time the ball reached him that he was barely able to kick it. And he wasn't particularly impressed by the willingness of former Chelsea defender Leboeuf to pass the ball, describing the Frenchman as a greedy player.

Among those watching from the touchline was the actor John Hurt, who was in town filming Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull with Winstone.

Some of the rock stars had impressive footballing pedigrees.

Ian Astbury, the lead singer of The Cult, had played boys' club football in Glasgow alongside future Everton and Scotland striker Graeme Sharp.

Gough, meanwhile, struck up a conversation with a team-mate from Northern Ireland without having the slightest idea he was Vivian Campbell, the guitarist of Def Leppard.

Sex Pistol Jones, who has lived in Los Angeles for more than 40 years, is returning to Britain next month for a tour marking the 50th anniversary of the release of Anarchy in the UK.

He still regularly attends football matches whenever he is back in England, although he has little time for the corporate hospitality enjoyed by many of his celebrity contemporaries.

‘I don't care where I sit, but I'm not interested in sitting in some box with a bunch of t***ers.’

Sports.title: 'Moments aren't enough': Inside Ethan Nwaneri's struggles on loan at Borussia Dortmund ahead of his return to the Emirates tonight - as Arsenal face dilemma over talented youngster suffering crisis of confidence
Sports.content:
'Moments aren't enough': Inside Ethan Nwaneri's struggles on loan at Borussia Dortmund ahead of his return to the Emirates tonight - as Arsenal face dilemma over talented youngster suffering crisis of confidence

Despite being shipped off to Germany’s finest finishing school for young English talent, Ethan Nwaneri’s time at Borussia Dortmund is already at a crossroads.

The 19-year-old joined the Bundesliga side on a season-long loan in September after enduring a frustrating five-month spell at Marseille earlier in the year.

This was supposed to be the loan move to reinvigorate one of England’s best young forwards, at a club well-versed in doing exactly that.

Nwaneri became the fifth Englishman aged 21 or under to sign for Dortmund in the past decade, following in the footsteps of Jadon Sancho, Jude and Jobe Bellingham, and Jamie Gittens. The stars seemed aligned for Nwaneri to shine.

But the opposite has happened. Having impressed and forced a Hoffenheim own goal off the bench on his Dortmund debut, Nwaneri started the team’s next four Bundesliga matches, but was hooked off around the hour mark in each one. The teenager has not made a starting XI since a goalless draw with Union Berlin on October 17.

It is understood Arsenal – who host Dortmund in the Champions League tonight – are closely monitoring the situation around Nwaneri’s lack of minutes, and there is a January recall clause in his contract. The clause was initially inserted as insurance in case an attacking injury crisis arose at Arsenal. Nwaneri's lack of minutes wasn't expected.

Ethan Nwaneri is on loan at Borussia Dortmund from Arsenal but has struggled for minutes – he last started a match on October 17

The 19-year-old is one of the most talented youngsters to emerge from Arsenal's prolific Hale End academy, but his career is in danger of stalling on loan in Germany

So why isn’t his move at Dortmund, a club that made their name by developing young players, working out?

Well, Nwaneri's short career so far has been a complicated one, featuring enormous highs and challenging hurdles. To understand his trajectory, you have to look back at his time at Hale End.

Having risen through the academy rapidly upon joining aged eight, Nwaneri burst onto the first-team scene in September 2022 against Brentford, becoming the youngest player to appear in the Premier League, aged 15 years and 181 days.

Mikel Arteta still values the player but hinted on Monday that he needs to produce more than just ‘moments’.

‘You can have patches, but to find that consistency and to play a big amount of minutes and have a huge impact in big football clubs like Arsenal or Dortmund, it's extremely difficult,’ he said.

‘That's the reality. You can just shine in moments, but moments are not enough. Now you need to show the consistency. Ethan has the capacity and the mentality to do that, and it takes some time.’

There's a feeling at Arsenal that Nwaneri has time on his side and shouldn’t be written off. He signed a five-year deal in August 2025 after all, with a plan to fully integrate the attacker into the first-team squad. His brother Emerson, 16, is thriving with the Under 18s.

However, if Nwaneri were to be sold in future, he would, as an academy graduate, generate pure profit on Arsenal's accounts.

‘His time at Borussia has been a disappointment so far because he was brought in to help immediately after Giannis Konstantelias tore his ACL,’ says Sebastian Wessling, who has covered Dortmund for 15 years at the Funke Media Group.

‘They tried to bring Nwaneri in, the summer before. So having tracked and spoken to him previously, they thought he would be ideal for short-term help. But he really hasn’t been that, it’s not worked out well so far.

‘He’s found it difficult to contribute with goals, assists, or just generally in Dortmund’s offensive game.

‘What the coach is looking for is a player to make a lot of runs in behind. Whereas Nwaneri looks to drop deep and have time on the ball, which the manager, Niko Kovac, isn’t looking for.’

'He lacks confidence and I think that shows in his play,' says Dortmund expert Sebastian Wessling of Nwaneri

There is still a serious player in Nwaneri, as seen in his two assists for England Under 21s in their 3-2 victory over France last week

Nwaneri's lack of confidence and progress feel striking. This summer, he joined England's pre-World Cup training camp in Florida, and was an unused substitute in the warm-up match against New Zealand. Nwaneri was alongside Bournemouth's Alex Scott, Fulham's Josh King and Liverpool's Rio Ngumoha – both Scott and Ngumoha have since made their senior England debuts, while King made Thomas Tuchel's squad this month. All three are flourishing as Nwaneri struggles to even feature.

To make matters worse for him, back at Arsenal 16-year-old Max Dowman is competing for a place in the starting XI. Nwaneri may have bundles of talent, but he is yet to fully kick on.

Wessling adds: ‘He lacks confidence and I think that shows in his play. Niko wants him to be brave on the pitch, but he plays it very safe.

‘When he did feature, he often played short passes and didn’t advance Dortmund’s play. He’s not a total disappointment, but he hasn’t really contributed.’

There is still a serious player in Nwaneri, as seen in his two assists for England Under 21s in their 3-2 victory over France last week. He is eligible to feature at the Emirates tonight, and will be desperate to show Arsenal what they are missing.

In any case, his next two months at Dortmund will reveal plenty about his future. It’s now about consistency – more than mere ‘moments’.

Sports.title: Parrott fires Republic of Ireland into Nations League play-offs
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott fired the Republic of Ireland into a Nations League play-off berth with two penalties in their 3-0 victory over 10-man Kosovo at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin.

The result ensured the Republic finished runners-up in group B3, and also propelled the Euro 2028 co-hosts into a coveted pot-two seeding for next month's qualifying draw for that competition.

Tuesday night's contest turned on its head in the 26th minute, when Kreshnik Hajrizi was sent off for handling the ball off the line, and Parrott took advantage with a top-corner finish.

The Real Betis striker doubled the Republic's lead from the spot five minutes after the restart, and Jack Moylan added a 75th-minute cushion to keep alive the hosts' hopes of booking a place in League A for the first time through the March play-off.

Image: Parrot struck twice from the penalty spot

Heimir Hallgrimsson's lone change from Saturday's defeat to group winners Austria was the insertion of John Egan into the line-up, replacing injured captain Nathan Collins.

How Ireland finished as group runners-up...

It was a contest that lacked fluidity in the opening 10 minutes, before the Republic found a foothold and Finn Azaz looked to pick out Parrott, but was blocked.

Kosovo then twice missed chances to take the lead. Lindon Emerllahu fired just wide in the 17th minute, and Caoimhin Kelleher was called into action for the first time a minute later to deny Vedat Muriqi.

What had been a largely uneventful encounter suddenly took a dramatic twist in the 26th minute, a red-card incident sparked by Moylan's cross, glanced on by Liam Scales to Parrott.

His effort - clearly goalbound - was cleared off the line by Hajrizi, who extended his arm like a goalkeeper, and was immediately shown a red card by Latvian referee Edgars Malcevs.

Parrott stepped up and gave Arijanet Muric no chance when he rifled into the top right corner to set the Republic on their way.

It remained just a one-goal advantage at the break despite a handful of chances falling the Republic's way, while the visitors created one when Kelleher denied Ilir Krasniqi with 10 minutes remaining to ensure there would be no first-half equaliser.

There was a flurry of Republic chances immediately after the second half kicked off before Parrott added his second penalty.

Muric had just denied Jayson Molumby's effort from range and Parrott was rushing forward to meet the loose ball when he was taken down by the Kosovo keeper.

This time he dove in the right direction, but failed to stop Parrott from doubling the hosts' lead.

The Republic were less successful from open play, unable to put the game away from a string of subsequent chances despite finding themselves in plenty of space, and should have added a third before the hour.

Moylan's persistence finally paid off with 15 minutes remaining, nodding home substitute Liam Kitching's cross in off the post.

The Republic nearly added a late fourth when Adam Idah stung the palms of Muric with two minutes left.

Parrott dreaming of home Euros

Republic of Ireland striker Troy Parrott speaking to RTÉ about the 2028 Euros:

"I've been thinking about it since I was a kid, I think everyone has.

"Look, it's not a guarantee that we are going to qualify for that tournament, so I think tonight was very important to get into pot two so that we have a better draw.

"We'll be going into the qualifiers now, trying to make sure that we qualify for the tournament.

"A tournament that's one of the host nations being Ireland, without Ireland it would be heartbreaking for all of us, so I think it's a mission now to make sure that we're there.

"It was disappointing that we didn't win the group because that's what we all wanted to do at the start.

"There's been so many nearly matches where we've nearly won, we've played really well and haven't won, and I think tonight we went out there with the mindset that no matter what we have to win.

"Obviously the red card helped us, but I have no doubt in my mind that group of players who were out on that pitch would have won that game."

'We want to play the top teams'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson speaking at his post-match press conference:

"Everybody, and especially us, likes to play the top teams. To compare yourself with the best teams, that's one thing.

"Second is those teams will expose your weaknesses, and that helps you in your growth to play these teams, so we can continue our growth.

"We're already looking forward to March. Tough teams in the pot. Whoever we draw is going to be a tough two games, and it's good for this team at this time to play these matches instead of friendlies.

"We're really excited for March, and looking forward to meeting the players again."

Sports.title: Kalajdzic scores late as Republic of Ireland taste defeat in Austria
Sports.content:
Sasa Kalajdzic dealt the Republic of Ireland a late blow in Linz with the only goal in Austria's 1-0 Nations League victory at the Raiffeisen Arena.

The result ensured that, no matter how the closing contests in Group B play out, Austria sealed promotion to League A.

Ireland enter Tuesday's critical home clash at the Aviva Stadium in third place, with one point fewer than their final opponents, Kosovo.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's men were not without chances, but only Kalajdzic made one count when he broke the deadlock in the 79th minute.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson urges UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in a behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; there were allegations of spitting by an Israeli player at half-time, while the Israeli government criticised the Irish players for bowing their heads during the national anthem

Republic of Ireland: Heimir Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future after tense draw

Ireland's head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson has called for UEFA to keep his team and Israel separate in future

Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

The Ireland boss was speaking following his side's 1-1 UEFA Nations League draw with Israel behind closed doors in Serbia.

The games between the two nations this international break were overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

This continued in Serbia, as Ireland fitness coach Damien Doyle was allegedly spat on by an Israeli player at half-time, according to reports in the stadium.

Irish media reported that the incident took place as the teams went down the tunnel. Ireland boss Hallgrimsson confirmed there was an allegation, but he admitted he didn't see it and declined to comment further on it.

However, when asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Israeli Government accuses ROI of 'moral blindness'

The Israeli Government have accused the Ireland football team of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during their national anthem.

For the second time in a week, the Irish players, coaching team and FAI all bowed their heads while the Israeli national anthem was played pre-match.

Image: Republic of Ireland players bowed their heads during the national anthem

The official Israeli Government X account posted: "While some use the football field as their political theatre, for us this is personal.

"1939: Irish players raised their arms in salute to Nazi Germany.

"2026: Irish players bowed their heads during Israel's anthem.

"Different generations. The same moral blindness.

"Today, Israel's players wear black armbands to remember those brutally massacred by Hamas on October 7 - including former professional footballer Lior Asulin.

"Some of us have skin in the game. Others just make a show of it."

Sky Sports News has contacted the FAI for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged that a derogatory term had been used, which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. The term is not associated with antisemitic or anti-Israeli abuse.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying: "That's completely untrue," before bringing the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called following an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist, who said a microphone had been taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands that no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland draw with Israel in second Nations League meeting
Sports.content:
Match report and reaction as Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out after the break; sides clashed at half-time

Republic of Ireland 1-1 Israel: Troy Parrott scores again as sides draw second controversial Nations League meeting

The Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in the second controversial Nations League fixture between the sides.

Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out by Dor Peretz after the break in the behind-closed-doors game in Serbia.

The Republic's 'home' fixture was held on neutral territory at the 4,500-seat TSC arena in Backa Topola, due to "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil" according to a June Football Association of Ireland (FAI) statement.

Both sides wore black armbands. The Republic's, the same as in Hungary to acknowledge - as the Football Association of Ireland chief David Courrell explained before that contest - "all lives lost" in the ongoing Israel-Hamas conflict.

Israel's armbands - which read "7.10" - were to commemorate the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on southern Israel, their official X account confirmed.

The pitch featured no sponsored content or branding, just UEFA graphics with slogans like "football for all", a decision taken by the FAI.

Image: The referee pleads with the benches in Serbia

Tensions rose at half-time after a fracas broke out in front of the tunnel and players from both sides engaged in a heated argument, with the Israeli Government later accusing Irish players of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during Israel's national anthem, as they did in Monday's first match.

Officials broke up a second altercation in three minutes of added time, and there were more heated words exchanged after the final whistle.

On the pitch Parrott, who has now scored 10 times in his last seven competitive internationals, fired the Republic in front from the spot in the 39th minute before Dor Peretz drew the sides level two minutes after the restart.

The result puts Ireland third in Nations League Group B3, level on points with second-placed Kosovo.

Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future

Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

Speaking after the 1-1 draw, Hallgrimsson also declined to comment on the half-time fracas between the two sides.

When asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

On the half-time incident, he said in his post-match press conference: "I was there. I'm not going to comment on it. It's something that a disciplinary committee is probably going to look at."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called due to an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist who had the microphone taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there was no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Ireland news conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland vs Israel is being played in Serbia as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott; protests briefly halted Ireland's draw with Austria on Thursday over opposition to Sunday's Israel fixture

Republic of Ireland vs Israel: Heimir Hallgrimsson's press conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media

Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson's pre-match press conference ahead of Sunday's match against Israel in Serbia ended abruptly after a tense exchange with Israeli media.

The media access was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed they were racially abused by Irish players during their match in Hungary last Sunday.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close as one of his colleagues remonstrated with the reporter.

Image: Ireland's players bowed their heads before facing Israel in the reverse fixture last week

Hallgrimsson later labelled the accusation a "verbal attack" during a separate briefing for members of the Irish press.

The exchange in the main press conference took place after Hallgrimsson was also asked a question about a co-pilot who attacked a pilot and tried to hijack a flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv earlier this week.

The reporter's question was shut down by the FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there are no open UEFA investigations at this stage from the previous meeting between Israel and Ireland last weekend.

The FAI are conducting their own investigation into whether striker Adam Idah was racially abused by Israeli supporters during their 3-0 UEFA Nations League win but have yet to make an official complaint to UEFA.

Image: Protesters interrupted Ireland's draw with Austria by throwing tennis balls onto the pitch with Palestine flags on them

Despite the high-profile nature of the fixture, members of the Irish media later reported that there was no UEFA delegate present at the news conference.

Sky Sports News was told a UEFA match delegate does not have to attend press conferences. The duty is left to the venue media manager, whose job it is to report anything if there is an incident.

Sunday's match is being played in Backa Topola, Serbia, as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott.

Sky Sports News has approached the FAI for comment.

Sports.title: Ireland held by Austria despite Parrott double as protests interrupt game
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott scored twice but the Republic of Ireland were forced to settle for a 2-2 draw after Austria came back in the second half of their Nations League encounter at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin.

The contest was twice interrupted in the opening 45 minutes, first due to what campaign group Stop the Game later referred to in a statement as a "limited tennis ball protest", when - around the 20th minute - tennis balls wrapped in stickers featuring the Palestinian flag and the text '#StopTheGame' were launched onto the pitch.

The match paused a second time when an invader carrying what appeared to be a Palestine flag entered the pitch and was promptly tackled and carried off by security.

The protests came after Ireland's decision not to boycott their game against Israel last week - although goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu did make himself unavailable.

Ireland are due to face Israel again on Sunday.

Image: Tennis balls with Palestine flags were throw onto the pitch

Before the protests, Parrott scored a sensational 12th-minute opener, and then added a penalty on the stroke of half-time.

A pair of substitutes proved Ireland's undoing after Alexander Prass halved the deficit in the 71st minute and Michael Gregoritsch drew the sides level six minutes later.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had a chance to top Group B3 with a victory, but they sit third behind Austria and Kosovo at the halfway point of the group stage.

Hallgrimsson made three changes, including the reintroduction of Finn Azaz, who was greeted warmly when his name was announced over the PA system before the match.

Bazunu was back in the squad, while Liam Scales and John Egan were awarded starts.

There was a significant security and police presence outside the stadium, where a small group of protesters also gathered before kick-off.

There was an audacious early effort from Sasa Kalajdzic, who tried to catch Caoimhin Kelleher off his line with a lob from midfield, before Ireland enjoyed a couple of attacking spells deep in the visitors' half.

Image: Parrott is congratulated after scoring his second goal against Austria

It was a brilliant opener from Parrott, who realised he was on his own after bringing down Adam Idah's glanced-on header from a goal kick.

The Real Betis striker was sandwiched in a triangle of white shirts, before nutmegging Philipp Lienhardt and evading every other challenger with a mazy run before planting the ball past Florian Wiegele and into the bottom corner.

Image: A protestor was carried off the pitch during the game

Kelleher denied Patrick Wimmer and there were a few more promising spells for Austria before Parrott doubled their lead.

Ryan Manning won the penalty after he was clipped in the box by Nicolas Seiwald. Parrott stepped up after a VAR check and blasted it past the Austria 'keeper.

Austria cut the deficit after Liam Kitching was caught out and Austria worked the ball to the unmarked Prass, who blasted the ball beyond Kelleher. The offside flag was initially raised, but the decision was reversed after a VAR check.

The Brentford goalkeeper then failed to stop Gregoritsch's free-kick as Ralf Rangnick's side fought back for a point.

Ireland captain Dara O'Shea was denied by an excellent leaping Wiegele save, Gregoritsch directed a shot over the crossbar and both sides fended off attempts at a late winner.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson admits 'toughest days' of career after Ireland beat Israel
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in their controversial Nations League fixture at a neutral venue in Hungary.

Players did not shake hands with each other before their meeting at the Nagyerdei Stadion in Debrecen and there was no exchange between Ireland captain Dara O'Shea and Israel's Manor Solomon.

Ireland players also appeared to bow their heads while Israel's national anthem was played out before kick-off.

Black armbands were worn by Ireland players, which Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell said was a gesture to recognise "all lives lost" in the Israel-Gaza conflict.

Goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu was the only player who chose not to play after the squad voted to proceed with the match on Saturday amid calls for the game not to go ahead.

Goals from Troy Parrott, Adam Idah and Jack Moylan sealed the victory for Heimir Hallgrimsson's side.

Moylan celebrated his goal by kissing and raising his black armband before kissing his badge.

Hallgrimsson: I couldn't be more proud of the players

Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"It has been some of the toughest days of my coaching career, but its not about me.

"The game, the desire the players showed to make a statement on the pitch - they are football players, they wanted to show on the pitch, make that talking with their feet.

"What they did was impressive. In tough times that's when you find your leaders, there were so many players that stepped up in these tough times. The energy levels they showed was impressive.

"The performance was good given all the preparation, the lack of training, all of our meetings were about something other than football.

"I couldn't be more proud of the players.

"By playing I know we are making some people unhappy. By playing we are making others happy. Winning probably pleases everyone, but there will still be people angry that we played the game.

"I hope we can settle that slowly down and stay together as a team. I wish people in Ireland continue supporting these boys, because they certainly deserve it."

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland slip to deserved defeat in Kosovo
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland slipped to a 1-0 defeat away to Kosovo in their Nations League opener in Pristina.

The build-up to the League B3 encounter had been overshadowed by the controversy around upcoming fixtures against Israel, which Republic boss Heimir Hallgrimsson had admitted many of his squad members were uncomfortable about playing.

Chiedozie Ogbene had fired an early chance over before Kosovo responded to finish the first half strongly at the Fadil Vokrri Stadium.

The home side saw two shots cleared off the line and Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher then clawed away a header from Vedat Muriqi as Hallgrimsson's side got to the break on level terms.

Ireland - who are scheduled to play Israel in Hungary on Sunday and then again in a 'home' tie at another neutral venue in Serbia seven days later - dug in for the second half but were eventually undone with seven minutes left when Kosovo captain Muriqi bundled the ball in from close range.

Udinese defender James Abankwah was handed a first competitive start as part of a back five, with in-form Real Betis striker Troy Parrott the lone forward and Dara O'Shea taking the captain's armband.

Image: The Republic of Ireland have won two of their six games in 2026 so far

Ireland created what ended up being their only real clear chance in the 22nd minute. Abankwah got away down the right and ran into the Kosovo penalty area before cutting the ball back to Ogbene, who sent a curling effort over the crossbar.

Kosovo, who are in League B for the first time, went close on the half-hour mark when a cross from the left found its way through to Muriqi, whose angled shot was cleared off the line by Jayson Molumby.

Veldin Hodza then saw his 10-yard strike blocked in front of goal by O'Shea before Kelleher got up to claw away a looping header from Muriqi, which was set for the top corner.

Ireland made a positive start to the second half, with a deep cross from the right by Abankwah finding Parrott at the far post and his header was gathered by Kosovo goalkeeper Arijanet Muric.

Image: Vedat Muriqi scored the winner for Kosovo

Kosovo, though, continued to carry a threat themselves. Baton Zabergja sent a 20-yard effort just wide of the top corner, which again got the home supporters into full voice.

Muriqi forced Kelleher into another smart reaction save from an angled shot at the near post before Kosovo eventually made the breakthrough in the 83rd minute.

Ermal Krasniqi's shot was deflected onto the crossbar and Muriqi reacted quickest in a crowded six-yard box to nod the ball over the line.

Kosovo should have got a second late on when substitute Krasniqi dragged his shot wide after being set up by Muriqi following a break onto a long ball.

Ireland pay price for 'off day'

Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson told RTE:

"[Kosovo are] a good team, momentum with them, crowd with them, and to be honest they deserve the win.

"There was nothing that we didn't know about how they would play, where their threats would be, but [it was] an off day for a lot of our players and [it is] a tough place to come to if you have an off day, so a deserved win for Kosovo."

Hallgrimsson added: "We were the team that needed to defend today and didn't connect in possession or passes, not as sharp as we have done.

"We have to quickly find out the reason that we had an off day. We can all do better than we did today.

"It is a two-day turnaround for the next one, so we better be quick…and do better than this versus Israel. They are probably in the same position as us [having lost to Austria]."

Asked if the controversy from playing the fixtures against Israel had impacted on his team's performance against Kosovo, Hallgrimsson said: "I couldn't say now. It is difficult to measure that one."

He added: "This is the situation, we have to cope with it. And like I said before the game, this camp is a test of character.

"We need to do better in that area than we did here today. We knew that we needed to win the duels, win the one-vs-ones, but sadly they had the upper hand on all the basics."

What it means and next fixtures

Sports.title: Huge crowd gathers for funeral of Irish boxer Lee Reeves after he passed away following knockout in the ring and three-month coma
Sports.content:
Huge crowd gathers for funeral of Irish boxer Lee Reeves after he passed away following knockout in the ring and three-month coma

Huge crowds have gathered today for the funeral of Irish boxer Lee Reeves who died this week.

The 31-year-old died in hospital on Monday after being placed in a medically induced coma following a fight in August.

After being knocked down twice in the 10th round, the Irish southpaw was carried from the ring on a stretcher following his defeat to fellow countryman Gary Cully and taken to hospital.

His promoters, Queensberry, later revealed he was in a 'critical but stable' condition before undergoing surgery.

Reeves was then placed in an induced coma, where he remained until his death three months later, surrounded by his family.

Along with being a professional boxer, Reeves was a serving member of the 12th Infantry Battalion out of Sarsfield Barracks, an ambassador for Limerick Treaty Suicide Prevention and a model.

A large crowd gathered at the Church of Our Lady, Queen of Peace for the funeral mass in Roxboro, Limerick, on Friday, with thousands also tuning in to a livestream of the service.

Dreams by The Cranberries played in the church as the coffin carrying Reeves' body, draped in the Irish tricolour, was carried inside.

Irish boxer Lee Reeves died on Monday after spending three months in a medically-induced coma

Family members accompanied the hearse carrying the coffin of boxer Lee Reeves arriving at Our Lady Queen Of Peace Church, Limerick, for his funeral with full military honours on Friday

Members of the Irish Defence Forces carry the coffin of boxer Reeves out of Our Lady Queen Of Peace Church, Limerick, on Friday

It had been brought to the church on an adapted gun carriage, as part of the military honours for the service.

His Defence Forces cap was also placed on the coffin.

Reeves' boxing gloves and belt, his Bible, and a pizza box were among items placed at the altar to represent his interests including his love of his religion – along with photographs of the Limerick-born boxer.

The mass heard tributes from some of his four sisters: Louise, Shannon, Jodie and Jessie, who described him as 'one of the greatest men on this earth' and 'an inspiration to everyone he met'.

Jodie told the funeral mass that Reeves was a family man who 'did everything' for his sisters.

'He was my mother's whole life, and she was his. He dedicated every fight to her, and no doubt made her proud.

'She was his number one supporter from day one.

'You were a father to us all, and that even includes Dad.'

She added: 'Nothing is going to be the same without you around, but I promise you'll never be forgotten.'

Jodie, also reading a tribute from Reeves' father, said: 'You had a heart and a presence that touched so many lives.'

Continuing that tribute, she added: 'God knows how much we will miss you, and how much of a piece of our hearts will go with you. Rest easy, son.'

Reeves had been carried out of the ring on a stretcher after his defeat to his countryman Gary Cully and taken to hospital (Source: Instagram/Lee Reeves)

A car is pictured following the funeral cortege of Reeves as it leaves Our Lady Queen Of Peace Church, Limerick, after his funeral mass on Friday

Wreaths and tributes are seen on display before the funeral of boxer Lee Reeves at Our Lady Queen Of Peace Church, Limerick,on Friday

Shannon said: 'I will miss you every day that I'm on this earth.'

She added: 'You never deserved this, brother, but it's not the end.

'Your story will live on, and your legacy will live on.'

Outside, a large screen and several framed photographs depicted images of Reeves and his loved ones as well as his boxing gloves.

The images carried captions such as 'brother', 'son', 'nephew', 'uncle' and 'pride of Limerick'.

Attendees included Mayor of Limerick John Horan as well as Defence Forces colleagues including the General Officer Commanding 1 Brigade, Brigadier General Caimin Keogh and Officer Commanding 12th Infantry Battalion, Lieutenant Colonel Ian Harrington.

Reeves was placed in a medically-induced coma and had emergency surgery after a junior welterweight fight in Dublin on August 1.

He had won 16 of his 18 bouts after turning professional in 2018, with several of his fights in Canada and Colombia.

The hearse is pictured carrying the coffin of boxer Lee Reeves arriving at Our Lady Queen Of Peace Church, Limerick, for his funeral with full military honours, on Friday

Family members stand behind as soldiers from the Irish Defence Forces place the coffin of boxer and serving soldier Reeves on an adapted gun carriage at Our Lady Queen Of Peace Church, Limerick, on Friday

Reeves' August clash with final opponent Gary Cully saw the 31-year-old knocked down twice in the 10th round

He was also a contestant on BBC reality show, Survivor, in 2023.

Defence Forces head chaplain Fr Paschal Hanrahan said Reeves showed physical courage in the boxing ring but also moral, courage and integrity in his mental health advocacy.

'We hold in our prayers today his colleagues serving overseas at this time with the 128th Infantry Battalion in Unifil, along with their chaplain Fr Piotr, who I know are gathered at this very moment in prayer for Lee.

'With all the agility and dexterity of a professional boxer, Lee moves seamlessly from being a model to being a role model in the Defence Forces.

'And those who served with him in Sarsfield Barracks saw our Defence Forces values in the way that he lived.'

He added: 'They saw his respect in the way he treated people, his loyalty in the way he stood by his comrades, and his selflessness in the time he gave to those who needed encouragement.'

Reeves, who was nicknamed 'El Champo', had won 16 of his 18 professional bouts since turning professional in 2018, and had been challenging Cully for the vacant BUI Celtic light-welterweight title.

He had been knocked down twice in the 10th round against Cully before being taken out of the ring, and in his tribute message for his opponent, Cully admitted that he was still in shock at how their match had ended.

Members of the Irish Defence Forces walked in procession alongside the coffin of boxer and soldier Reeves on an adapted gun carriage at Our Lady Queen Of Peace Church, Limerick, on Friday

'I still remember the stadium days when I used to watch Lee in the nationals, the weight above me, and (I would) always be impressed by his fights and his flashy gear,' Cully wrote.

'What a character and a gent. It's never been nothing but love between us champ, can't really believe I'm writing this but RIP brother.'

Sports.title: 'It's amazing that Scotland now has TWO world champions'... Meet the Kilmarnock kid who idolises Prince Naseem Hamed and is part of the Scottish boxing boom with Willy Hutchinson
Sports.content:
Only last month, the mutterings were about where Scottish boxing goes from here, three years after Tartan Tornado Josh Taylor was toppled and with doubts mounting about the health of the sport’s grass roots.

Three weeks on, seemingly from nowhere, the nation has not one but two new world champions.

Willy Hutchinson claimed the WBC light heavyweight belt in a tussle with Joshua Buatsi earlier this month in the full glare of the television cameras. But slipping beneath the radar were the achievements of Aaron Sarwar, who was anointed the under-19 world flyweight champion in Montenegro on October 27.

Both men sobbed in the ring and fell to their knees as the simple raising of a referee’s hand detonated identical emotional explosions in them – sudden vindication of years of grinding roadwork, gruelling gymwork and grafting ringwork.

With beautiful symmetry, the only other Scot to have won a world amateur title was Hutchinson himself, in Russia in 2016. Now his ascent to the top of the pro game has lit the path for Sarwar to follow. And if there are still mutterings, they are that this kid from Kilmarnock could be the real deal.

Compared with big-ticket bouts, youth boxing’s short contests can appear cagey and sterile – but it’s hard to peel your eyes off Sarwar’s compelling repertoire of shots, defence, switches and occasional showboating.

Kilmarnock fighter Aaron Sarwar with his trophy for winning the Under-19 world championship

Those who know him best say his most remarkable asset is an iron psyche that, even at such a tender age, has created a machine-like drive to reach whatever peak is placed in front of him.

Having become a world junior karate champion and double black belt by the age of 11, the ring became his home during the Covid-19 pandemic as he looked for a fresh challenge.

Speaking to Daily Mail Sport, Sarwar insists he has already set off on a mission for another Montenegro moment.

He said: ‘People ask me about that feeling. It’s indescribable. I wish I could go back and relive that ten, 15 seconds of getting my hand raised because I don’t think anything will come close to it again.

‘But I’ll be chasing it. I want to make my mum and dad proud again. I watch [the video of] it every day. I get goosebumps every time.

‘I’d spoken to Willy before, but we met at a boxing show this week and had a good chat about what’s next for us.

Sarwar admits he still struggles to describe the euphoria he felt on being crowned the winner

‘It’s amazing that in the space of two weeks, Scotland’s got two new world champions. It’s crazy.’

Sarwar turned to boxing when lockdown meant karate was reduced to online seminars. He stumbled across a basic gym with punchbags behind the shop from where he’d buy lunch on school breaks – and from there he joined the local club.

The 18-year-old was back to his roots this week at the Northwest ABC in Onthank, the estate made infamous by the BBC Scotland fly-on-the-wall documentary The Scheme.

Hitting our screens in 2010, the series won a Bafta award but also stood accused of creating a ‘poverty safari’ for the chattering classes and creating dubious celebrities out of light-fingered drug addict Marvin Baird and his dog Bullet.

Northwest ABC was feted and funded for being a beacon among the anti-social behaviour, even receiving a personal visit from Justice Secretary Kenny MacAskill. Now Graeme Marshall’s committed coaching team has helped create a new poster boy for The Scheme.

Down at the club, they are proud of their prodigy, but the mood is more about hope than hype. They remorselessly tease Sarwar about his fussy fringe and point out, to rein in expectations, that he’s still so young he’s yet to even fight without a headguard.

Sarwar bumped into his fellow world title holder Willy Hutchinson during a boxing show

But Marshall – who Sarwar refers to as akin to a second father – is in no doubt about their boy’s freakish potential.

He said: ‘When he asked to come to the club after lockdown, it was Aaron himself who called up, which was unusual for a 12-year-old.

‘We knew straight away there was a talent there — he’s fast and strong and dedicated. After a few months, we entered him for the Scottish championships. It was his first fight, but he went and won the tournament.

‘Second season, he won the GB championships. I took him all over to fight. In Sweden, he stopped the Swedish champion, and when you see him beating Irish boys in Ireland, you know you’re dealing with something special.

‘He’ll turn professional at some point; it’s every young boy’s dream. And there’s no reason why he can’t go on and match what Willy Hutchinson’s done and become a world champion.’

The calls have started coming from managers testing the water about going pro – as Hutchinson did immediately after winning amateur gold – and McBookie are already offering odds of 8/1 that he goes right to the top.

Hutchinson brought Scottish boxing out of the doldrums with his defeat of Joshua Buatsi

But, for now at least, Sarwar – who ditched his engineering college course to concentrate on the sport – remains focused on fighting for Scotland at the 2030 Commonwealth Games in India.

He said: ‘I’ve got all the time in the world. I’ve opened myself a lot of doors now. I’ll speak to my coaches and mum and dad about what they think is best for me. But I know what I can achieve off the back of this now.

‘For karate, I was dedicated and hard-working but I didn’t have that same passion. Boxing, it’s all I do. I’ve left all my education to box full time. It’s all my eggs in one basket so there’s no choice, I have to do it. It’s boxing or nothing.’

Sarwar names his inspiration as Prince Naseem Hamed, the flamboyant featherweight world champion from the 1990s, for ‘his style, his flashiness, his power’. He added: ‘I’ve got that flashy side too, but if they get serious, I’ll stand toe to toe. I can box, I can fight, I can do it all.’

Despite training solely with Boxing Scotland now, Sarwar can’t keep away from his home club. He added: ‘I try to carry myself well all the time and inspire the young ones to come to the gym and train that bit harder, and it’s good to be around the coaches all the time.

Sarwar is in no rush to turn professional and is eyeing the 2030 Commonwealth Games in India

‘The support they’ve given me over the years has been second to none, I can’t thank them enough. There’ll be no way I can ever repay them the sacrifices they’ve made [for me].’

Meanwhile, in the ring at the Northwest, a small boy’s fists are a deadly blur, thwacking the pads held out by his coach with awesome efficiency. To misquote Muhammad Ali, he has the legs of a sparrow but the sting of a bee.

Aidan Sarwar – 12 years old – is already part of the Scotland set-up.

It was a Glasgow music hall crowd that first memorably coined the heckle, ‘Oh no, there’s two of them’ when English comedian Bernie Winters joined his brother Mike on stage. Boxers across the land may soon empathise.

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua becomes a father for the second time: Boxing star welcomes baby girl in secret with mother of his son - but won't meet her until after his fight with Tyson Fury on December 11
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua has revealed he is a father again, welcoming a new baby girl into the world with Nicole Osbourne.

Former heavyweight world champion Joshua, who is gearing up to fight long-term rival Tyson Fury at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff, already has a son with Osbourne called JJ, aged 11.

Now JJ is a big brother, with Joshua deliberately not finding out the sex of his newborn during pregnancy. His daughter is yet to be named but was born on November 14, weighing 5.5lb.

Joshua is yet to meet his daughter as he is in Marbella preparing for his long-awaited showdown with Fury in the early hours of December 12, but will meet and hold his newborn after the fight. In the meantime, there have been FaceTime calls with Osbourne to see their daughter.

'It's been amazing, a big blessing, and I can't believe I'm a girl dad. I didn't want to find the sex out during the pregnancy,' the 37-year-old told The Sun.

'I love boys but as soon as I found out we had a little girl I said, "No more Fifa, no more motorbiking, no more PlayStation!".

Anthony Joshua has announced that he is a father again, welcoming a baby girl into the world

The ex-heavyweight world champion already has a son called JJ who is now 11 (duo in 2021)

'I'm going to do it all, so you might see me with some eyeshadow on, some nail polish on, drinking some tea in a doll's playhouse and just trying to do the right thing by her, you know? I will change nappies, I've gotta go through all that stinky bum time again!

'Now I've got a daughter, I will get an insight and a bit more understanding of what it means to be a woman, and how I can be supportive.

'My daughter will give me a first-hand experience of the power of a woman - I've spoken to all the women in my family, and it's amazing the amount of support that women give each other.'

Joshua, who almost lost his life in a devastating car crash in Nigeria that killed two of his best friends last year, said the ordeal has taught him not to take life for granted.

'This past year has been incredibly tough, I realised how precious life is, and how short it can be. I’m just going to live my life by duty, and even having a baby girl was part of my duty. I wanted to bring life in, it was a conscious decision, 100 per cent. If something happened to me, I didn’t want JJ to be out here alone,' he added.

The wholesome news comes less than a year after Joshua was devastated by the loss of his best friends Sina Ghami and Latif 'Latz' Ayodele last December, after the trio were involved in a car crash near Lagos.

Joshua has been deeply affected by the death of his friends and surviving the fatal crash himself, with the accident coming just ten days after he took down YouTuber-turned-boxing star Jake Paul.

Upon his return to the ring in late July with his fight against Kristian Prenga, Joshua broke down during his post-fight interview as he credited Ayodele and Ghami for getting him through a tough first round.

The 37-year-old is preparing to fight long-term British rival Tyson Fury in Cardiff next month

'I don't want to talk about it anymore,' Joshua had said quietly as he let out his emotions.

Earlier in the evening he had stepped into the ring wearing his friends' names on pennants pinned to his chest and had admitted before the fight that he had spent months suppressing the pain of their loss.

Joshua was being driven along one of Nigeria's deadliest roads in December when his SUV crashed into a stationary truck on the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway.

He is thought to have narrowly escaped major injury or worse after having switched to sit behind the driver in the back seat on the left-hand side of the car.

Joshua was admitted to hospital with 'minor injuries' after being pulled from the wreckage of the crash.

In February, Joshua added the names of 'LATZ' and 'SINA' to the tattoo outline of Africa he sports on his bicep.

Sports.title: Tragic boxer's heartbroken final opponent pays tribute to 31-year-old rival in emotional Instagram statement after Irish fighter lost his life following three-month coma
Sports.content:
The final opponent of boxer Lee Reeves has paid an emotional tribute following the death of the man he shared a ring with in August.

Gary Cully, 30, knocked Reeves down in the bout and his fellow Irishman was in a coma for three months before tragically losing his life on Monday.

The 31-year-old Reeves, who was nicknamed 'El Champo', had been challenging Cully for the vacant BUI Celtic light-welterweight title and was sent to the canvas twice in the tenth round before being taken out of the ring on a stretcher and rushed to hospital.

Cully shared his shock and grief at Reeves's death on Instagram, writing: 'We shared the ring back in August but we been going back for years.

'I still remember the stadium days when I used to watch Lee in the nationals the weight above me and always be impressed by his fights and his flashy gear myself and Luke Thomas used to plague him to spit us out an MC when we were staying in Dublin on training camp and they’d always be fire.

'What a character and a gent. It’s never been nothing love between us champ can’t really believe I’m writing this but RIP brother.'

Lee Reeves died on Monday having been in a coma for three months after fighting Gary Cully

The 31-year-old (right) was knocked down twice in the 10th round and Cully (left) shared an emotional tribute

Cully shared a number of pictures from their fight and also screenshots of messages between them from the last few years.

In one, Reeves wrote: 'Take a bow son! Fantastic win well done champ!' Cully replied: 'Thank you bro, congrats on your two also.'

Limerick-born Reeves spent time away from the ring as a competitor on BBC reality show Survivor in 2023, and served as an ambassador for Limerick Treaty Suicide Prevention group.

The fighter, the oldest of four siblings, lost his mother Cathy to suicide in 2015.

Reeves had initially been declared as in a critical but stable condition in hospital when he was placed into a medically-induced coma.

But the grim news was announced on Monday by his friend and coach Jonathan O'Brien, who paid tribute to Reeves in a poignant statement on social media.

'Goodbye son, sleep tight, you fought so hard till the end,' O'Brien wrote. 'We love you so much, rest in peace with your mam and brother waiting at the heavenly gates.

'Look over your sisters and your father, give them the strength to get through this. We love you Lee.'

'Limerick is a very dark place tonight with the loss of Lee Reeves. Lee was not just a boxer that excelled in his career - he was a mental health advocate who highlighted mental health and how it can affect young people,' Limerick City councillor and Reeves' family friend Catherine Slattery said in her tribute.

Cully shared screenshots of messages between him and Reeves over the years

Reeves (second from right) was described as a 'character and a gent' by his last opponent Cully (centre)

'Lee was a very proud Limerick man, he loved Limerick and its people and any chance he got to promote Limerick, he took it.

'Lee loved his family. He was very proud of his dad, Tony, and he adored his sisters and his nieces and nephews and they, in return, adored him.

'Lee had great faith in God and the only (consolation) is that Lee's mam and brother are embracing him in their arms in heaven.

'The loss of Lee will be felt in Limerick for a long time to come and I am heartbroken for Lee that he lost his fight.

'Rest in peace El Champ - you will be missed by us all.'

Queensberry also shared a statement after news broke, writing: 'Everyone at Queensberry is devastated to learn of the passing of Lee Reeves.

'Lee was an immensely talented boxer, as well as a true role model and inspiration to his community.

'Our deepest condolences go to Lee's family, friends and all those who loved him. We ask that their privacy be respected at this incredibly difficult time. Rest in peace, Lee.'
