Sports.title: Chris Eubank Jr in talks to fight Kell Brook in first bout since Conor Benn loss - with 'Special K' to come out of retirement
Sports.content:
Chris Eubank Jr in talks to fight Kell Brook in first bout since Conor Benn loss - with 'Special K' to come out of retirement

Chris Eubank Jr is in talks to fight Kell Brook in his return to the ring.

Brook, 40, has not fought since beating Amir Khan in 2022, but has emerged as a potential option to fight Eubank in his first fight since losing to Conor Benn late last year.

According to Elliott Amoakoh, the executive director of Eubank Jr's management team, Nova Sport LLC, any agreement is still a way away.

He told Sky Sports: 'Talks are ongoing but the date, purse and location are yet to be confirmed.'

Ben Shalom, however, who has represented both fighters in the past, told talkSPORT: 'It's a fight that we have been trying to make for a couple of months.

'They have pretty much agreed terms on both sides, there is just some final bits to go. It is one of the biggest fights in British boxing. I think you are right on February and in Manchester.'

Chris Eubank Jr (pictured) is in talks with Kell Brook to face off in his return to the ring

Brook (pictured) hasn't fought since 2022 and retired after beating long-term rival Amir Khan

Brook retired after beating long-time rival Khan in Manchester, having been linked with a fight with Eubank in the aftermath.

Brook has seemed almost certain to return to the ring, having revealed his return fight would be 'announced soon'.

He retired with 40 wins from 43 fights, and is a former International Boxing Federation welterweight champion.

Having debuted as a professional in 2004, he didn't lose until September 2016, when he was stopped in the fifth round by Gennady Golovkin.

Eubank Jr, meanwhile, had faced questions over retirement following his defeat by Benn but has refused to call it quits on his 15-year career.

He had claimed to have major fights scheduled for 2026, but has taken a whole year out of action.

Sports.title: English boxer, 18, banned from World Championships after extraordinary sex test mix-up: 'Broken' teenager reveals how his dream was shattered after team forgot to prove he was a man
Sports.content:
English boxer, 18, banned from World Championships after extraordinary sex test mix-up: 'Broken' teenager reveals how his dream was shattered after team forgot to prove he was a man

A teenage English boxer has said they have been left 'broken' after being denied the chance to compete at the World Championships due to officials failing to organise a sex verification test to prove he is male.

George Francis, 18, had been due to represent England at the Under-19 World Championships in Budva, Montenegro last month.

Francis was withdrawn from competition on the eve of the event after an administration error by England Boxing, with the governing body having failed to arrange the necessary sex verification test.

'They got me in a room and told me that I couldn't box because they didn't know if I was a boy or a girl, basically,' Francis told the BBC.

'The explanation was that they couldn't provide a blood sample for me in time. Everyone else was able to provide a blood sample, but they just forgot me.

'Somehow I wasn't on the system.

George Francis, 18, missed out on competing at the Under-19 World Championships after England Boxing failed to arrange a necessary sex verification test. Source: Instagram/georgefrancis_07

'It was the worst news I've ever had in my life.

'I wouldn't wish it on anyone, to be honest. I was just broken. They were speaking to me and I couldn't even really hear. I was devastated.

'I couldn't really talk. I literally couldn't feel anything. There was a hole left there.'

Francis's situation, first reported by The Times, followed the mandatory introduction of sex verification tests by the sport's governing body World Boxing.

World Boxing announced the move last year, with genetic sex testing initially introduced for female competitors aged 18 and above. The governing body stated the move was due to a 'duty of care to deliver safety and competitiveness fairness'.

It followed controversy at the Paris 2024 Olympic Games, where boxers Imane Khelif and Lin Yu-ting won gold.

Khelif and Lin had been disqualified from the previous year's World Championships, with boxing's former governing body – the International Boxing Association – claiming the pair had failed sex eligibility tests.

Earlier this year, Lin was cleared to compete in women's events following a review of her sex eligibility.

World Boxing's mandatory tests were extended to include male boxers earlier this year.

Francis had been required to undergo a test due to turning 18 four days before travelling to the World Championships.

Francis, a multiple national champion, had been required to undergo a mandatory test after turning 18 days before the World Championships. Source: Instagram/georgefrancis_07

World Boxing introduced sex testing last year amid the controversy surrounding Algerian boxer Imane Khelif's participation at the Paris 2024 Olympic Games

The multiple national and GB champion has claimed he is considering turning professional following the mix-up.

England Boxing reportedly contacted Francis's father to apologise for the 'administrative oversight', with the governing body stressing it will 'strengthen processes' to avoid a repeat incident.

'We maintained open communication with George and his family throughout, despite this, a resolution was not possible,' an England Boxing statement read.

'George remained a valued member of the England team, including representing the squad as flag bearer.

'England Boxing has no greater priority than the health and wellbeing of athletes on its performance pathway and are committed to learning from this experience and strengthening our processes to prevent a recurrence.'

World Boxing's policy requires boxers to undergo a once-in-a-lifetime PCR (polymerase chain reaction) test to determine their sex and their eligibility to compete in either the male or female category.

The PCR test is a laboratory technique used to detect specific genetic material, in this case the SRY gene, which reveals the presence of the Y chromosome that is an indicator of male biological sex.

A dozen boxers, representing five nations, were last year blocked from competing at the World Championships in Liverpool because deadlines for their sex tests were missed.

Under World Boxing rules, national federations are responsible for testing and will be required to confirm the sex of their athletes when entering them into World Boxing competitions

Sports.title: Viddal Riley opens up on why he stuck with his dad instead of moving to Las Vegas to train with a Mayweather as he eyes fighting Oleksandr Usyk
Sports.content:
Viddal Riley opens up on why he stuck with his dad instead of moving to Las Vegas to train with a Mayweather as he eyes fighting Oleksandr Usyk

Derrick Riley almost never speaks publicly. Ahead of his son's European title defence against Seydi Coupe at Wembley on Saturday, father and son sat down together to talk about trust, tough love, Joe and Enzo Calzaghe, and why Oleksandr Usyk returning to cruiserweight is 'a little bit greedy'.

But to understand where Viddal is going, you first have to understand the man in his corner.

Derrick Riley has been watching his son get punched since he was a little boy. He still can't put into words what it does to him.

'It's strange,' he exclusively tells Daily Mail Sport. 'I've been doing it for a long time. But you have to try and separate it. You have to shut off the emotion and the sentiment. If you let that sentiment in, I think that's a bad thing. That's your boy in there. He's getting hit and he's getting hurt. I would say it's not easy, and some people can't separate it.'

It's rare to hear Derrick say anything at all. He stays out of the spotlight, and he leaves the talking to his son. Sitting beside Viddal days before the biggest night of his career, when the unbeaten Londoner headlines OVO Arena Wembley against Frenchman Coupe, you quickly see how their relationship works.

'Only my dad would be able to speak to me the way he does,' Viddal says. 'But it comes from a place of genuine care. It's not a job. Someone can only care so much when it's a job. It's like being an employee at a company and having your own business. It's a completely different mentality. This is my business, so he cares and I care.'

WATCH THE EXCLUSIVE INTERVIEW ON THE DAILY MAIL BOXING YOUTUBE CHANNEL

Derrick Riley (R), the father and trainer of son Viddal Riley (L), almost never speaks publicly

Viddal is set to take on Seydi Coupe at Wembley on Saturday evening, headlining the event

Derrick added: 'Part of caring too is the fact it's the same brain you've got now that you're going to need after boxing. You can't go to the shop and buy a new one, so you need to protect it. That's why it's difficult to separate the two.'

Viddal grins and says: 'It's the same brain I need for the grandkids.'

The partnership was not always a given. At 21, Viddal went looking for something of his own.

'I was at a stage where I was trying to find some independence. That's the truth,' he says. 'I was presented with the opportunity to go to Vegas, train with a Mayweather and work with Jeff Mayweather. I was thinking, "Yeah, I'm doing this my way. I'm doing things differently."

'But the truth is, I knew my ceiling was getting lower. And I knew the only person who could push that ceiling higher, and continue to do so, was my dad.

'So when I came back to the UK, I said, "Dad, can you train me?" He was like, "Nah, I'm alright. I'm not doing it." And I was like, "Nah, I need you to do it, because that's the only way this dream we've been talking about is going to be fulfilled."

Derrick's refusal was not stubbornness. It was self-preservation.

When asked why he initially said no, Derrick admitted: 'I know what the game is about. I know what boxing involves, and I thought to myself, do I want that in my life? It's a good question when you're in your 50s. I've lived life. There are no rose-coloured glasses. I know what boxing is. But I had to think about it.'

Derrick Riley has been watching his son get punched since Viddal was a little boy

The irony was that he was already qualified for the job. 'By this point I already had a British Boxing Board of Control licence, because I was in the corner with Viddal in Dubai,' he laughs. 'So, funnily enough, I already had the licence.

'He looked at me with those puppy-dog eyes, and I thought, you know what? We've got to do this. But I did say to him, "It's not going to be easy, son. We're going to have to do this properly. You're going to get no ranking belts, no intercontinental belt, nothing like that. You're going to have to do it the old-school way, with the British, Commonwealth, European, and it's going to be hard." And we've done it, man.'

The record backs him up. Viddal is 14-0 with seven knockouts. He won the European title in April with a wide points win over the vastly experienced Pole Mateusz Masternak at The O2, a fight that also served as an IBF world title eliminator. Saturday is his first defence, and it's a mandatory one against a challenger who is also unbeaten in 14.

For a template of what father and son can achieve together, Derrick points to Wales.

'I appreciate Enzo [Calzaghe] more now than I did before,' he says. 'I've always appreciated him, but I appreciate him even more now because I'm doing it myself. People have no idea what it takes, and for him to do what he did with Joe was absolutely amazing. I take my hat off to him.

'Don't get me wrong, I had a boxing background. I wasn't great, I wasn't pulling up trees, but I had a boxing background. Enzo had no boxing background whatsoever, yet he managed to do what he did with Joe. That is amazing.

'It's funny. During the fight with Bernard Hopkins, I think Enzo was saying something to Joe, and Joe gave Enzo a look. I know that look. I give Viddal that same look.'

Viddal and his father have become a force to be reckoned with but they've faced criticism

Joe Calzaghe has described his own brief split from his father, and how he came back because he realised he wanted those highs to be shared with Enzo. Viddal sees the same story in his own.

'We relate to that story because we were severely doubted,' he says. 'It wasn't celebrated. The partnership is only now starting to get some recognition, with people acknowledging that it works. It wasn't like that at the beginning.

'It's been suggested to me that my dad shouldn't train me and that there are people better suited to the job. That's what we walked into. It wasn't accepted as, "Oh yeah, this is a nice family dynamic, let's get it going." It was challenged. The aim was to separate us.

'When we're up against it, we just keep proving ourselves, time and time again. That's what I take from Enzo and Joe. It wasn't celebrated either. They had to keep doing what they were doing, and he turned his son into a 46-0 fighter and one of the best to have ever done it.'

Fathers who train their sons are often accused of living through them. John Fury, so often more visible than Tyson, is the obvious example. Derrick, a former boxer himself, rejects the comparison.

'I don't live vicariously through Viddal. I don't want that,' he says. 'I'm not hogging the camera. It's not about me. It's about Viddal. He asked me to help him, and I'll help him.'

Viddal is just as clear about who he fights for. 'I do it primarily, first and foremost, for me,' he says. 'And very quickly after that, it's for everyone around me that's put work into me achieving it, because it couldn't be done by myself.

Derrick has said he resonates with Enzo (pictured right) and Joe Calzaghe (pictured left)

'When I became British champion, it made me give my dad the belt. We sat down at home for years watching people pick up the Lonsdale belt and hold the Lonsdale belt. So I heard the announcement, "British champion", and I'm like, "Dad, hold this." That's something he's always deserved.'

By rights, Viddal should already have fought for a world title. When Jai Opetaia was stripped of the IBF belt after signing with Zuffa Boxing, the Masternak win put Viddal in line for a shot at the vacant title against New Zealand's David Nyika. Then Opetaia sued the IBF, the governing body held off sanctioning the fight, and Viddal was left waiting.

At the same time, the division has been turned upside down. Opetaia is moving up to heavyweight to face Deontay Wilder on the Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua card in Cardiff on December 11. David Benavidez holds the WBA and WBO belts and faces WBC champion Michal Cieslak next month. And now Oleksandr Usyk wants to come back down.

'As I have been saying, it's messy, but I'm trying to get in the mess,' Viddal says. 'I don't want to be on the outskirts of that mess. I'm trying to be in it.

'Right now, I'm just on the outside of the door. I can hear the music in the club, I can hear the bassline. I know there's a vibe in there. I've been seeing the people getting in the door, walking past me. I want to get in there. And Coupe this weekend is another step towards that.'

The most famous person trying to get through that door is Usyk. The Ukrainian became undisputed at cruiserweight, moved up to become undisputed twice at heavyweight, and his team says he now plans to return to 200lbs to chase Benavidez and become undisputed at cruiserweight again. He hasn't fought at the weight since knocking out Tony Bellew in November 2018, and he turns 40 in January.

Viddal admires him. But he isn't convinced.

'It's a bit greedy. It's a little bit greedy,' he says. 'He's completed the level here. He's gone up, he's completed it there, and I think he's just needing that challenge. He's a guy you can tell lives for challenge. All he does is take challenges. "If I'm fighting for a world title, I'm going to go to your country and I'll beat you there." He's that character. That's what makes him a GOAT. That's what makes him a legend.

Viddal has said Oleksandr Usyk is 'greedy' for returning to the cruiserweight division

'But it's dangerous too. Forty years old, dropping all that weight. He hasn't been a cruiserweight since 2018. If I'm in his circle, I'm saying, "Bro, you ain't got to do this. Why? There's no need to." It's not going to be financial. It's just that craving for a challenge.'

Regardless, Viddal is happy with where he is at.

'What I like is that if I'd done this interview four or five years ago, everyone would have asked me, "Do you want to fight Tommy Fury or Jake Paul?" he says. 'Now people ask me, "Would I fight Usyk?"

'Clearly, I'm doing something right.'

Sports.title: What's next for Herta after F1 2027 snub?
Sports.content:
Cadillac's decision to stick with veteran incumbent Valtteri Bottas to partner Sergio Perez is a choice for continuity and stability after a debut campaign plagued with issues for Formula 1's 11th team in 2026. It also raises key questions over what's next for Colton Herta.

With Cadillac's majority owner TWG enamoured with the prospect of having an American driver in one of its cars before too long, the team spared no expense on bringing Herta over, leaving the comfort of his IndyCar seat with sister team Andretti Global for a now-or-never shot at making it to F1.

Herta, a nine-time IndyCar race winner and the youngest to ever do so, faced a tricky challenge of adjusting to European racing in Formula 2, including mastering the peculiar Pirelli tyres that he would also find in F1.

That was dovetailed with private testing - Cadillac has no previous cars, so it rented a test from Alpine - and a number of grand prix FP1 sessions to boost his number of superlicence points to the critical number of 40.

After his sixth such test of the year in Brazil, Herta finally got to the magic number. But around that time, Cadillac CEO Dan Towriss and team principal Marcin Budkowski started aligning on the idea of retaining Bottas, deploying Herta as the official reserve driver for 2027, ready to step in if Bottas couldn't raise his performance ceiling over the first part of the season.

What Cadillac perhaps wasn't factoring in, is how Herta took the news of being snubbed. It is understood that the 26-year-old American has turned down the reserve role for now and has also decided against finishing his troubled F2 campaign with Hitech, forfeiting the final two rounds in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

Valtteri Bottas, Cadillac Racing, Sergio Perez, Cadillac Racing Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

While that decision may be clouded by his initial disappointment at missing out and Herta is desperate to keep racing competitively, rather than sit on the sidelines, it's a somewhat surprising position to hold. Being Cadillac's third driver behind 37-year-old Bottas still appears to be the position with the best odds of F1 promotion across the entire paddock, whether over the course of 2027 or in 2028.

"We've offered him a reserve position," Towriss said in Las Vegas. "The seat's open for ’28, so there are options on the table for Colton. There are options in other sports as well. I think he's decided on a direction, but we're still in conversations on that and look forward to seeing what Colton wants to do.

"It was definitely a tough decision, a tough discussion with Colton. I think he was disappointed. There was a lot of work, a lot of a build-up [that went] into this. I know Colton was very brave in even taking on this risk, going into F2 and trying to cram all this learning in."

The role, which is understood to be rather lucrative for a reserve driver, could also be paired with a one-off Indy 500 outing when the grid expands to 33 entries.

Why 2028 is a make-or-break year

Herta is now facing a career defining decision because of what's at stake in 2028. That is now the earliest he can get onto the F1 grid full-time if he makes a good enough impression to replace Bottas. It is likely also the last opportunity to do so, given how quickly reserve drivers tend to lose career momentum.

At the same time, his old home is also due a major renovation. For the first time in over 16 years, IndyCar will introduce an all-new car in 2028, the Dallara IR-28 which debuted to rave reviews in testing and is armed with a beefier 2.4l twin-turbo V6 engine.

Dallara IR-28 Photo by: Joey Barnes

With no full-time opportunities in IndyCar left for 2027 at this stage of the silly season, if Herta is deciding to call time on his F1 dream, then he needs to reposition himself as soon as possible to land a competitive seat for IndyCar 2028's season, whether that be with TWG or elsewhere. Returning in 2028, when the new chassis offers a blank slate, would be the most desirable timing from a competitive standpoint.

In any case, Herta has a decision to make as 2028 will be his make-or-break year. Either he swallows his pride and gives his F1 dream one last shot with Cadillac, or he abandons that dream prematurely and starts working on returning to a competitive IndyCar seat.

That process starts with his next move - right here, right now.

Sports.title: Max Verstappen considering 2027 Daytona 24 Hours entry
Sports.content:
Ahead of the Formula 1 Las Vegas Grand Prix, Max Verstappen first paid a visit to Daytona.

The Dutchman said he was primarily there to film content with Red Bull, but the visit also raises the question of whether he is seriously considering taking part in the Rolex 24, the endurance race held on the road course of Daytona International Speedway.

When Autosport put that question to him during the Dutch media session in Las Vegas, Verstappen revealed that an appearance on the grid next winter has not been ruled out.

"We're looking into it, whether that's possible, but for now the visit was more about filming things with Red Bull."

Daytona is one of the endurance races high on the four-time F1 world champion's wish list. "That's definitely one that I want to do, yes," Verstappen confirmed.

It is also one of the races Verstappen could already contest during his F1 career, as the event takes place during the winter break. The 65th edition of the Daytona 24 Hours is scheduled for the weekend of 28-31 January 2027.

"Yes, that race is definitely possible already during my F1 career, so I hope so. But we'll have to wait a little longer [for news]. We still have some time for that as well."

Race start Photo by: Art Fleischmann

Verstappen made it clear that he would contest that race in a GT3 car, which at Daytona would mean competing in the GTD Pro category.

Following his adventures on the Nürburgring Nordschleife and the guest appearance for his own racing team at Portimao, it would mark Verstappen's first GT racing outing on American soil.

As for the Le Mans 24 Hours, Verstappen has already indicated that he will not compete there next year. The Dutchman only wants to race at the Circuit de la Sarthe with very thorough preparation, but he explained that Daytona is a different story.

"I really only want to do Le Mans in a hypercar. And then you have to think carefully about how you want to approach it. Do you want to do it yourself, or do you want to do it with a factory team? I still have time to figure that out as well.

"If I want to race at Daytona, or on the Nordschleife, that would be in a GT3 car. I don't want to say that's easier, but it is a little easier to organise than with a hypercar."

When it was pointed out that Verstappen would at least be giving motorsport fans something to look forward to during the F1 winter break – just as Fernando Alonso will do with the Dakar Rally – he laughed: "That's nice, isn't it? I always enjoy seeing drivers doing other things outside F1 and also getting enjoyment out of other racing series.

"The F1 season is already long enough, of course, but if I can combine it with bringing the family along, for example, then I'll still try to take part in other events."

That will most likely also apply to the Nürburgring 24 Hours in 2027, although the preparatory NLS races clash with F1 Grands Prix. Verstappen laughed, however: "Luckily, I already know that track!"

#3 Mercedes-AMG Team Verstappen Racing, Mercedes AMG GT3 EVO: Max Verstappen, Daniel Juncadella, Jules Gounon Photo by: ADAC Motorsport

He is still considering arranging a test day with his team as part of the preparations for the 24-hour race in the Eifel region.

"Yes, but of course you also have to look at that with the track, to see which days are possible. But we're going to see whether we can schedule another test day, because that's what every good team competing there does. So yes, that's definitely something we're going to look into as well."

Sports.title: F1 2027 grid: Who will be racing and where?
Sports.content:
The 2027 Formula 1 grid has very much taken shape with all but one spot now confirmed following a rather safe ‘silly season’ that didn’t present much drama.

There is only one team - Haas - that is changing its line-up for next season as many potentially enthralling storylines failed to materialise in regards to the 2027 grid.

So, here’s a look at the situation.

George Russell, Mercedes, Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes, Toto Wolff, Mercedes Photo by: Hector Vivas / Formula 1 via Getty Images

The 2026 season has witnessed a significant shift in the dynamic down at Mercedes between Kimi Antonelli and George Russell, as the latter headed into the year as the heavy title favourite - only to fall flat early on.

It came after Russell finished 169 points ahead of Antonelli last season in what was a very up-and-down rookie campaign for the Italian, while the Briton arguably delivered his best yet. So, with Mercedes expected to master the regulation switch, which it did, Russell was the natural favourite yet Antonelli learned his lessons impressively fast to vastly improve upon 2025.

This eventually led to the 20-year-old becoming F1’s youngest ever world champion by securing his maiden title at the Mexico Grand Prix, with four rounds still to play at the time. Although this came as a surprise to many, Mercedes would have argued that his performances had been as forecast when it plucked him from karting and into its junior programme.

Read Also: Formula 1 How Antonelli rose so rapidly to become F1 world champion

As for Russell, his season has been a “complete disaster” - per Max Verstappen - and with two grands prix left in 2026, he sits fourth in the standings and could easily drop to fifth as he is level on points with 2025 world champion Lando Norris.

Nevertheless, he will remain with Mercedes for 2027 with his and Antonelli’s fate known for quite some time.

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari, Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Photo by: Colin McMaster / LAT Images via Getty Images

Ferrari and Charles Leclerc agreed upon a new deal earlier in 2026 - announced in June - meaning the 29-year-old is continuing his length association with the Italian outfit. Leclerc joined its junior programme in 2016, made his F1 debut with customer squad Alfa Romeo Sauber in 2018 before moving to the works’ outfit in 2019.

The Monegasque has won nine grands prix in that time, which can be seen as a disappointment considering the promise displayed early on. But with Ferrari’s improved performance in 2026, jumping from fourth to second in the championship, Leclerc’s hope is that the team can press on and finally deliver a championship-winning car having signed a multi-year contract.

But he will have Lewis Hamilton to worry about in the neighbouring garage, as the seven-time world champion is understood to be under contract until the end of 2027 after joining in 2025. Last year was a disappointment for the Briton, finishing 86 points behind Leclerc, but he’s strengthened in 2026 with a 17-point advantage over his team-mate.

Tensions have also been high recently, with the two colliding on various occasions, most notably Monza, Mexico and Las Vegas, so that is a dynamic Ferrari must manage heading into 2027.

Oscar Piastri, McLaren, Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Clive Rose / Formula 1 via Getty Images

It was known that at one stage Verstappen held some level of talks with McLaren when his Red Bull future was up in the air. Though this simply may have been a tactic to secure a more lucrative deal with the Austrian outfit, which is something he eventually earned, so McLaren is remaining with Norris and Oscar Piastri.

The Briton seems content with being a one-team man for the time being, staying with McLaren since his debut in 2019, and why not? Norris has secured that world title he so strived for and has been impressive in 2026 with three victories, even if the car hasn’t been quite there on several occasions.

As for Piastri, what happens with him is an on-and-off talking point given the Australian would have likely been the man to move had Verstappen joined. This year has been a disappointment for him, continuing on from his late title collapse in 2025, as he is seventh in the standings and 97 points behind Norris. His most recent victory was Zandvoort in August last year.

But he is on a “multi-year contract”, signed in 2025, and looks set to stay for now.

Red Bull: Max Verstappen, Isack Hadjar

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing, Isack Hadjar, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Manuel Eletto

The 2026 season has been quite similar to 2025 for Red Bull, having started quite slowly before a late rejuvenation with Verstappen enjoying four wins and nine podiums since this year’s summer break.

That has vaulted him into second in the drivers’ standings and should he carry such momentum into 2027, then a fifth world title could easily be on the way for the Dutchman. That would put him one short of Hamilton’s record for the most championships with one team - he achieved six at Mercedes - as Verstappen signed a bumper deal until at least 2030 this year.

It will see him start a second season alongside Isack Hadjar, who has had a solid first campaign at Red Bull and gave the team no reason to replace him. Perhaps the team now has its ideal number two driver to assist Verstappen in his title charge next year.

Arvid Lindblad, Racing Bulls, Liam Lawson, Racing Bulls Photo by: Rudy Carezzevoli / Getty Images

The situation down at Red Bull’s sister outfit was one of the biggest sources of uncertainty, given it was only in November that Racing Bulls confirmed its pairing for 2027. It will be an unchanged duo, however, as Arvid Lindblad will return for his second season in F1 alongside Liam Lawson, whose seat was in doubt despite his best year yet.

Lawson is on course for a career-best ninth in the standings with 89 points, securing a top 10 finish at all but six grands prix, which in itself is enough for the Faenza outfit to secure its highest-ever constructors’ championship finish of fifth.

But Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov has impressed as an F2 rookie this year, sitting second to Rafael Camara, and historically Racing Bulls doesn’t keep drivers for long if a promotion to the main squad isn’t on the cards.

With 2027 going to be Lawson’s third proper season at Racing Bulls, historically the team may have dropped him in favour of its next protege. Tsolov, however, will have to settle for a reserve driver role in 2027 while Lindblad continues to perform, taking 38 points from his rookie year so far and 11th in the standings.

Pierre Gasly, Alpine Photo by: Lars Baron / LAT Images via Getty Images

Pierre Gasly signed a contract extension with Alpine last year, demonstrating his commitment to the cause despite the team being adrift at the back of the constructors' order across 2025. The arrival of Flavio Briatore, Steve Nielsen, and Mercedes has put the team back into the midfield battle, and the Frenchman is hoping that the Enstone squad can deliver a car worthy of his immense - and oft-underrated - talent.

Gasly is 10th in the 2026 standings with 52 points, helping Alpine sit sixth in the constructors’ championship and although he’s the French outfit’s clear number one driver, Franco Colapinto has still made a considerable step.

The Argentine has taken 35 points in 2026, compared to zero last year, and that earned him a new deal in August for 2027.

Haas: Oliver Bearman (?), Rafael Camara

Oliver Bearman, Haas F1 Team, Rafael Camara, Haas F1 Team Photo by: Bryn Lennon / Formula 1 via Getty Images

Haas is another squad to have endured serious question marks surrounding its driver pairing for next year. The first concerned Esteban Ocon, who just couldn’t make things click ever since he joined the American outfit from Alpine for 2025.

At the time he was seen as a real coup, the first grand prix winner to drive for Haas, but instead he was consistently outperformed by his much more inexperienced team-mate - Oliver Bearman - across both last year and 2026.

In the end things turned quite ugly and after it being confirmed that the 198-time grand prix starter wouldn’t continue into 2027, he was dismissed by Haas with five rounds still to play in the season.

His replacement is F2 championship leader Camara, who has signed a “multi-year” deal and given up his title ambitions in the feeder series to finish the season in F1 before his first, full campaign in 2027.

That will likely come alongside Bearman, who has mightily impressed in his time at Haas so far. But in Vegas, the 21-year-old Briton said he was “disappointed” to not yet have his contract wrapped up for 2027 with the reason believed to be a disagreement in salary. Bearman’s seat is the only one not confirmed for next year.

Gabriel Bortoleto, Audi F1 Team, Nico Hulkenberg, Audi F1 Team Photo by: Guido De Bortoli / LAT Images via Getty Images

Audi F1 boss Mattia Binotto confirmed in September that it will retain Nico Hulkenberg and Gabriel Bortoleto for the 2027 season. At the time it didn’t really cause any particular conversations because the announcement came as little surprise, considering how well both drivers have done - thus giving Audi no reason to change its line-up.

The German marque, which made his F1 debut in 2026 after taking over from Sauber, has the perfect blend of youth and experience, plus a harmonious relationship between the pair.

Bortoleto is set for his third season in the championship, compared to Hulkenberg’s 16th, and both drivers have scored 14 points this year to give Audi eighth in the standings.

Alexander Albon, Williams, Carlos Sainz, Williams Photo by: Peter Fox / Getty Images

Williams' decision to lock in Alex Albon and Carlos Sainz for at least another year demonstrates the buy-in for its long-term ambitions from both drivers, even if this season has presented a step back in fortunes. Some might uncharitably suggest that there was nowhere else for either driver to go, which is probably also true, but the retention of both drivers is a significant boost for the team.

Had Sainz decided to do something else, Williams is said to have hedged its bets and had spoken to the management of Sergio Perez and Colapinto for 2027, while Luke Browning has also impressed in his FP1 outings with the team.

Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin Racing, Lance Stroll, Aston Martin Racing Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

The situation at Aston Martin was another which promised potential drama for 2027 but failed to materialise as such. That is because for months the questions surrounding Fernando Alonso’s future were strife, considering he is 45 years old, driving for a backmarker and heavily dislikes the current regulations with his previous contract expiring at the end of 2026.

But all speculation stopped in September when the two-time champion announced his extension with Aston Martin into 2027. It is believed that him not publicly committing to F1 through the summer months was partly an effort to put pressure on the series to make changes.

As for team-mate Lance Stroll, his extension into 2027 arrived on the same day as Alonso, but was far from the same talking point considering father Lawrence owns the team. So, the 28-year-old Canadian, who next season will have had a decade in F1, effectively has a contract for as long as he likes.

Cadillac: Sergio Perez, Valtteri Bottas

Valtteri Bottas, Cadillac, Sergio Perez, Cadillac Photo by: Bryn Lennon / Formula 1 via Getty Images

F1 newcomer Cadillac was the final squad to hold intrigue surrounding its driver pairing for 2027. Said intrigue didn’t really concern Sergio Perez, who in October signed a multi-year extension, but more Valtteri Bottas.

The 10-time grand prix winner has been outperformed by Perez this year, with a losing 16-10 head-to-head record in qualifying (including sprints), causing his seat to be thrown in doubt. Team management refused to publicly commit to him for some time as it weighed up the possibility of promoting reserve driver Colton Herta, given its desire to have an American driver racing for an American team.

One sticking point for Herta was his lack of an FIA Superlicence - required to compete in F1 - despite winning nine races in IndyCar. But he eventually obtained one via six FP1 appearances this year, yet that still wasn’t enough to grab an F1 seat with his highly disappointing F2 season, sitting 19th in the standings, in mind.

So, in November Cadillac announced its decision to stick with Bottas for 2027.

Sports.title: Was the Las Vegas GP best race of the year - or too fake?
Sports.content:
The nature of the Las Vegas Grand Prix divided opinion in Formula 1's fanbase, and these opposing views were shared across the grid as the myriad overlapping passes were lauded and derided in equal measure.

Among the numerous changes for the lead, as Max Verstappen had to bat away passes from George Russell, Kimi Antonelli, and Lando Norris at various intervals throughout, the race was characterised by further chopping and changing in the overall order throughout.

Turn 14 was the most favoured overtaking zone, as the drivers used a combination of a powerful slipstream and overtake mode to make passes, but these were often temporary overtakes as the previous defending driver could often supply a riposte on the corner exit and reclaim position.

As such, although gaining position was simple enough, it required a lot more effort to retain it - even if a driver could build a gap, the slipstream-overtake combination could quickly close this down.

Across the range of opinions across the grid, Lewis Hamilton stated that it was a "great race" and found the style of racing on show exciting, and Mercedes CEO Toto Wolff agreed that it was "different" and "entertaining" - and more like a combination of oval races blended with modern-day F1.

"I thought it was a really great race. We knew that we have a pace deficit on the straights, but we weren't expecting it to be so brutal here with these long straights. It was important always to make sure you're behind the car and trying to move forwards," Hamilton said.

"You always have to make sure you're in a tow. Otherwise, you're just a sitting duck to people around. The Mercedes and the Red Bull, their power on the straight line is impressive, really impressive. My engine was on the limit. There was nothing else coming out.

Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

"I was pressing the button as hard as I could to make moves. I thought this race was one of the most interesting and most exciting. The car felt great today. Apart from the straight line, it felt great otherwise."

Wolff remarked that: "I guess you will have many people that will say, well, that's not racing.

"Personally, we need to be open-minded. Susie was in paddock club and she said that 90 minutes, people screaming with the overtakes. You were not quite sure whether you had the position or not.

"The instant feedback I got from friends watching, our sponsors, that was awesome. Stefano [Domenicali, F1 CEO] liked it very much. I think that's not going to happen everywhere.

"In a way, it's fitting that that was the Las Vegas race, like NASCAR and Indy 500 all together. To be honest, I don't know how long the race was, 90 minutes. For me, it was like 20 minutes. Because it was so different and so entertaining to watch."

Haas' Ollie Bearman took a slightly more dim view, stating that it was a fun race but rued that drivers were "penalised for passing" due to the chance for the following driver to supply an attack into the following corner.

He also disliked the "joke" slipstream tactics seen in qualifying, with cars jostling for position in the final runs to make the best use of the tow effect along the straight. He noted that the race had taken an unexpected path as the simulations conducted by the team had shown the overtake mode would only have a small effect.

Gabriel Bortoleto, Audi F1 Team, Oliver Bearman, Haas F1 Team Photo by: Guido De Bortoli / LAT Images via Getty Images

However, the power of the slipstream changed the dynamic of the race and retaining the tow was important to stay in the race. For Bearman, who had spent his afternoon battling the Audi pair, his slim chance of points had ebbed away when his pack dropped away from the top 10 and were unable to catch up having lost the slipstream to the cars ahead.

"It was definitely fun, I would say. It's a bit strange because you almost get penalised for passing, because you then lose the overtake. To be honest, I was just trying to stay in the race," Bearman said.

"I spent a lot of time sandwiched between the two Audis and I had a lot of opportunities to pass, but I opted just to stay behind, because I knew that if I go in front I would lose the overtake and lose a lot of race time.

"I was just trying to do my best race possible, knowing that the Audis were quicker than us and it was almost just a matter of time that they come past, but trying to delay it as much as possible.

"From simulations the overtake effect is very small, but then of course you have the slipstream effect as well, which is incredibly big. If I'm honest, it's a bit disappointing that we're doing these types of races, because even when you lose the slipstream, you lose so much time every lap, that you lose a lot of race time just from being alone on track.

"You saw it in quali yesterday, everyone coming out together like go-carts to take the slipstream. It's a bit of a joke, really."

Alpine's Pierre Gasly took a more cautious view, likening the Las Vegas spectacle to the Tour de France in choosing when to attack and when to be more conservative.

Arvid Lindblad, Racing Bulls, Pierre Gasly, Alpine Photo by: Guido De Bortoli / LAT Images via Getty Images

Although he also derived general enjoyment from the race, he noted that he would not want a full season of 'peloton-style' races.

"I mean, if you're leading, you can drive as fast as you can, you're not going to pull away. At some point in the race, I was like, this feels a bit like Tour de France," he said.

"You've got to be in the peloton and save your legs. Basically, that's what we did. We were saving our legs for the last sprint when we were managing the engine for the last few laps.

"It was fun but I don't want to see 24 races like that. I'm sure from the fans' point of view, it was incredible. I just don't feel it rewards all the driving in the corner because it's mainly a tow game. It was definitely very, very enjoyable."

Additional reporting by Filip Cleeren, Ronald Vording, and Cihangir Perperik

Sports.title: Why Ferrari believes written rules won't help manage Leclerc and Hamilton
Sports.content:
The post-race media session with Ferrari Formula 1 team boss Frederic Vasseur in Las Vegas was, in several respects, almost a carbon copy of the conversation in Mexico City.

On both occasions, the discussion with the written press took place in a small, almost cosy room at the back of the Ferrari hospitality area, partly because Formula 1 teams cannot rely on the hospitality units used during the European part of the season when travelling to flyaway races.

Just as in Mexico, there was considerable media interest, and just as at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez, one topic dominated the conversation: the clash between Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton.

Before Vasseur arrived, as the press officer tried to create a little more space, a colleague remarked that the room had quite a relaxing atmosphere. The press officer laughed: "Well, it's a very relaxing evening for us as well…"

It was, of course, sarcastic. This time, the collision between the two red cars had not cost Ferrari a potential 1-2 finish, unlike in Mexico, but that did nothing to ease Vasseur's frustration.

"Honestly, you can't imagine the frustration for me, but it’s even more important for all the guys at home," the Ferrari team principal said.

Apart from the word 'frustration', another word that came up during the session was 'powerless'. Following the clash in Mexico, constructive discussions were held in Sao Paulo, with all parties subsequently saying that those talks had been very productive and that the limits had been established.

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari, Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Photo by: Yuri Cortez / AFP via Getty Images

The central message was that a driver's interests must never take precedence over those of 2,000 team members back in Maranello, and that the drivers must never let those team members and sponsors down through actions that harm the team.

When Autosport asked whether, in a sense, Vasseur felt powerless, given that he had clearly communicated that message but it had still proved insufficient once the visors came down, the Ferrari team principal responded: "That is a good point… And that's why I want to once again have a discussion tomorrow, also to try to digest the situation.

"I think it's not the right place to discuss it with them two minutes after the race. I saw Charles a bit down and I told him what I have to say. I've got to discuss the rest with him tomorrow."

Vasseur immediately made it clear over the team radio that he wanted to see Leclerc before the Monegasque did anything else – such as speaking to the media – but it emerged that what happened on Saturday evening had not so much been a conversation.

"No, it was not a discussion, I spoke. I think he apologised; he understood, but the result is there. You do a mistake. You can say, my mistake, I'm sorry, but you still did a mistake," Vasseur said.

The more substantial discussions will therefore take place this week, although the question remains what will help and what is needed to prevent a repeat of the same situation – particularly if Ferrari wants to challenge for the title in 2027.

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari, Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Photo by: Guido De Bortoli / LAT Images via Getty Images

The most obvious answer would seem to be rules of engagement or strict guidelines, but Vasseur made it clear that, in his view, putting things in writing would not necessarily guarantee success either.

"Honestly, it's not a matter of rules. It's not a matter of rules. What can you do differently, except that you have to respect your team-mates?" Vasseur said.

According to Vasseur, it ultimately comes down to that last point: showing respect for your team-mate regardless of the situation.

The Frenchman made it clear that this must be a mindset that carries through into every situation, rather than simply a sheet of paper containing rules. In his view, it is impossible to devise a rule for every scenario, and rules would not have prevented what happened in Las Vegas either: "I think the race of today, nobody will write a scenario like this. Nobody can imagine a race like this. They just have to act in a professional way."

In both cases, it could be argued that the track layout played at least a minor role. Leclerc said in Mexico that the opening sequence of corners encouraged such battles, while the slipstream in Las Vegas was so powerful that drivers were almost forced to overtake one another on the straights.

Those are valid points, but Vasseur was unwilling to accept them as mitigating circumstances, particularly because other team-mates had managed to avoid problems.

Frederic Vasseur, Ferrari Photo by: Alex Pantling / LAT Images via Getty Images

"You can't freeze the position on this kind of race, because you are in the slipstream. If you slow down, the guy who is behind you is overtaking you," he said. "But all the other teams, they were able to overtake each other 20 times during the race. Antonelli and Russell, Norris and Piastri, even Isack overtook Max."

That is precisely why Vasseur was not yet convinced on Saturday evening that written rules were the solution. It remains to be seen how that position evolves over the coming days, but in Vegas the team principal continued to emphasise respect above all else.

The sense of powerlessness surrounding the whole situation, however, is that the same message was delivered in Sao Paulo, only for history to repeat itself just two weeks later.

Sports.title: Herta replaced at Hitech to end F2 season early
Sports.content:
Colton Herta will end his torrid time in Formula 2 early by not returning for the final two rounds of the 2026 season following a “mutual agreement” with Hitech.

The nine-time IndyCar race winner made the transition to European single-seaters this year as part of his bid to gain an FIA Superlicence that is required to compete in Formula 1.

But F2 has not gone as planned for Herta, who is 19th in the standings with only 26 points from 12 rounds, achieving a best result of fifth at Barcelona from third on a reversed grid.

The 26-year-old American is not returning for the final race weekends in Qatar and Abu Dhabi and will be replaced by Roman Bilinski - who was already set to take Herta’s seat in 2027.

Jan Sumann, Hitech's F2 head of race engineering said: “We're delighted to welcome Roman to Hitech for the final two rounds of the season.

“These two weekends will give us an opportunity to start building important relationships before the winter.

“I would also like to thank Colton for his commitment and determination throughout his time with Hitech, despite a challenging season. We wish him the very best for the future.”

Roman Bilinski, Monza in F3 2025 Photo by: Formula Motorsport Ltd

Herta was not quoted in the team statement and it is not yet known what his plans for next year are because, despite a poor season, he was still in the frame for an F1 promotion.

That was via his role as Cadillac’s reserve driver and thanks to six FP1 appearances in 2026, he has now obtained a superlicence but days after doing so, Valtteri Bottas was confirmed for next year alongside Sergio Perez.

As for his replacement at Hitech, Bilinski also contested his rookie F2 campaign this year but didn’t fare much better, sitting 16th in the standings with 36 points for DAMS.

“I'm really excited to be joining Hitech for the final two rounds of the season. Having the opportunity to work with the team ahead of 2027 is a real bonus,” said the 22-year-old Polish-Briton, who finished 11th in F3 in 2025.

“It means we can start working together straight away, get to know each other and build a strong foundation ahead of next year. Of course, I’ll be hoping for some strong results to close out the current season.”

Sports.title: Why Bearman’s expected 2027 Haas F1 deal remains unsigned
Sports.content:
Ferrari protege Oliver Bearman remains the only driver on the F1 grid without a contract for 2027. It is a situation that would have been hard to imagine just a few weeks ago, given that his retention at Haas had been taken for granted since last summer.

The announcement of Rafael Camara as Bearman's 2027 team-mate, which came ahead of the Brazilian Grand Prix, was expected to be swiftly followed by that of his British team-mate. Instead, the silence has dragged on to the point of becoming a talking point, even prompting rumours of Bearman driving elsewhere next year. The paradox is that Bearman and Haas have strong reasons to reach an agreement.

Bearman has ruled out racing elsewhere in 2027, while Haas has long been expected to retain him, yet the negotiations have dragged on far longer than initially anticipated.

In recent weeks, there has been speculation about the reasons for the deadlock, some linked to the contractual relationship between Bearman and Ferrari and to the future prospects of the 21-year-old Briton.

According to information obtained by Autosport, however, the issue holding up the signing does not concern the driver’s long-term future, but rather the financial terms of the deal with Haas.

Ferrari has already exercised the option allowing it to retain Bearman within its driver programme. Given that Maranello has invested financial resources in the young Briton ever since he joined the Driver Academy in 2021, allowing Bearman to leave on a free transfer would be a big waste of all those efforts.

Rafael Camara will finish the 2026 season for Haas as he prepares for his full 2027 debut alongside Oliver Bearman. Photo by: James Sutton / LAT Images via Getty Images

Bearman could be in a position to leave Ferrari at the end of 2027 if he has not received a call-up to join the works team, but this scenario does not represent an obstacle to renewing with Haas, and there is no need to finalise his relationship with Ferrari in the short term – especially given that Lewis Hamilton is in the twilight of his career. The Scuderia has not ruled out any of its longer-term options.

The immediate negotiations therefore centre on two parties: Haas and Bearman’s entourage. The sticking point is the salary offered by the American team, a figure that the driver and his staff do not consider commensurate with their expectations.

This has led to a prolonged deadlock, despite both sides being aware of the need to reach an agreement. On the eve of the Las Vegas Grand Prix, Bearman made no secret of his disappointment at a situation that has now been dragging on for months. “There’s nothing new to say. To be honest, I’m rather disappointed to find myself here, at the twentieth round of the season, without a signed contract for next year. It’s a strange situation, but we’re getting there.”

The Briton admitted that the uncertainty is becoming difficult to cope with, especially after a season in which he believes he has proved his worth as the team's lead driver.

Bearman categorically ruled out the possibility of moving to another team in 2027, though. When asked if there was even the slightest chance of racing elsewhere, with no more seats up for real discussion, his answer was unequivocal: "No, zero chance."

He added: "My goal for 2027 is very clear. I think we have unfinished business here. Then looking further into the future, it's not really in my hands, let's say it like that."

Bearman has been open about his ambition to make it to Maranello, but he is aware that decisions regarding the Scuderia’s future do not depend solely on his performance.

"Of course I'm under contract with Ferrari. Ferrari have given me this incredible opportunity to step into F1 with them for the first time," he acknowledged. "I'm still a Ferrari junior driver and my ultimate dream is to race for Ferrari. First of all, they're the most iconic team and they're the first team that believed in me as a kid.

Oliver Bearman, Haas Photo by: Lars Baron / LAT Images via Getty Images

"It's still my ultimate dream, but there's no doubt that looking into the future, there may be some challenges there. There's no denying that, it's very clear. I don't really have much say in the matter. We just need to see how things develop over time."

The immediate contract situation is more straightforward. Ferrari has already clarified its contractual position and is not the party holding up Bearman’s confirmation. The ongoing negotiations concern only the terms of the agreement between the driver and Haas. Autosport understands the matter is expected to be resolved before the final weekend in Abu Dhabi, in all likelihood through an inevitable compromise on the financial front.

That doesn't make the lack of a deal by the end of November any less frustrating for Bearman. "It's not a good feeling to be sitting here with two races to go without things sorted out," he said. "Even though I know that we're pretty much there, the fact is that we're not. There's no excuse for being here without a contract signed, quite honestly."



Those comments show just how much this whole tug-of-war has weighed on the driver. Barring an unexpected breakdown in negotiations, Bearman is expected to remain with Haas in 2027 as well, forming one of the youngest driver pairings on the grid alongside Camara.

Sports.title: F1 plans two-team engine supply limit under 2030 V8 rules
Sports.content:
Formula 1 is planning a shift to just two power unit supplies per manufacturer in 2030, Autosport has learned, raising questions over the status of Mercedes' three current customers.

Over the Las Vegas weekend the FIA announced there was unanimous support to bring the next generation of power unit regulations forward to 2030. That includes a move to 2.1-litre V8 engines, including a turbocharger, a maximum of 200 kilowatts of electric power and the use of sustainable fuels.

That move satisfies the demand for cheaper and less complex engines, which FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem and F1 chief Stefano Domenicali had been pursuing in unison. Meanwhile, adding a turbo was a key requirement for the likes of Audi and also ensures engine noise remains at a suitable level for some of F1's urban venues.

What was also part of a wide-ranging document the FIA produced on the 2030 framework, but wasn't part of the public announcement, is an agreement between the six 2030 power unit manufacturers to supply just two teams each. This also includes their works team, leaving just one single engine supply available for external customer teams.

Autosport understands that one aim of the move is to reduce the political influence of manufacturers supplying a large share of the grid, in this case Mercedes and Ferrari, while the manufacturers in question had also been willing to downsize as supplying F1 engines is a loss-making operation, with supplies capped at just $18m per season.

Ferrari is currently supplying the works team, Haas and Cadillac, but the latter will be moving to in-house engines from 2030, meaning the question of Ferrari's supply is solving itself. Red Bull Powertrains will also be taking care of two teams, Red Bull Racing and Racing Bulls, while at present Audi, Aston Martin partner Honda and Cadillac's shareholder General Motors will all have their own works teams as their one and only confirmed customer.

Photo by: Manuel Eletto

The Mercedes question

That leaves the question of what will happen to Mercedes and the customers of Mercedes High Performance Powertrains. Alongside the works team in Brackley, the Brixworth operation is currently supplying McLaren, Williams as well as Alpine, whose parent company Renault recently abandoned and sold its in-house engine operation.

Per the 2030 framework, two of those three teams would be looking for a new engine supply if the FIA World Motor Sport Council approves the proposal in Shanghai next month. That seismic shift will set up months of political intrigue in the F1 paddock as teams scramble to secure what has been F1's most reliable and performant power unit supplier ever since F1 moved to hybrid engines in 2014, or conclude deals with currently less desirable options.

Autosport understands that both McLaren and Williams are fancying their chances of remaining with Mercedes. And while McLaren at least explored the idea of becoming its own power unit manufacturer when a move to a cheaper formula would make that more feasible than it is now, CEO Zak Brown indicated that ship has sailed for 2030 as he aims to remain a Mercedes customer.

"It's something we've looked at in the past, but we're very happy with HPP," Brown said in Las Vegas on Thursday. "I think we've proven that we can win championships with them, so we don't have any intention to have anything in the back of our car other than a Mercedes."

Mercedes' intentions about what its ideal customer team would look like are less clear right now. Having been beaten by McLaren in 2024 and 2025, CEO Toto Wolff maintained that a win for a customer is still a feather in the cap for HPP and the Mercedes brand as a whole, while a strong customer team also provides a valuable chassis benchmark for the works operation.

And while Brown hailed HPP as an "awesome partner", it's no secret that the relationship between HPP and McLaren has at least come under some strain at the start of this year amid a knowledge gap between the works team and its customer over how to exploit and deploy the complex new power units.

Photo by: Alex Pantling / Getty Images

Whether Mercedes will continue to lease engines to its most formidable rival or whether a deal with a midfield team is the preferred option will likely become the subject of plenty of intrigue in the coming months.

Why FIA engine is dead

What is certain is that the FIA's proposed third-party engine plan is now dead in the water. With F1 power units becoming less complex and expensive in 2030, FIA president Ben Sulayem had floated the idea of sourcing a supply of off-the-shelf, white-label engines to further alleviate concerns over team independence.

However, that plan never seemed economically viable for any prospective engine builder, and with all six PUMs at the table now unanimously agreeing to 2030's key infrastructure, a cap of two supplies would mean there are at least 12 power unit supplies available for 11 teams.

The FIA did include a safety net in case one of the six manufacturers decides to drop out, adding a clause under which a departing manufacturer’s F1 power unit intellectual property would transfer to the FIA, which could then assign it to a new manufacturer coming in.

As is the case today, there will also be an "obligation to supply", meaning the FIA could force one of the manufacturers to supply an additional, third team with an engine if that outfit can't arrange a deal to find one, which may well end up becoming a key clause.

What has also been agreed is the basis for the power unit cost cap for the 2030-2034 period. The cap will remain at today's figure of $190m for 2030 before falling by $7.5m per year, ending at $160m for the 2034 season.

Photo by: Alex Bierens de Haan / LAT Images via Getty Images

That sliding scale helps manufacturers with the initial development cost of the new power units. A development freeze of the current engines from 2028, as well as a ban on V8 dyno testing until the summer of that year, is expected to help F1's current manufacturers manage their resources between the two projects. Existing manufacturers will also receive more cost-cap headroom than newcomer General Motors, which can now abandon its V6 plans and just focus on the V8 programme in Charlotte. GM is understood to be signing up to a budget cap of $170m for the first couple of years.

Why early deal is so crucial for F1

There are still several important topics to be fleshed out further by the manufacturers, such as the exact nature of the electric push-to-pass system as it would need to work in conjunction with the chassis design to promote close racing.

But by defining the overarching framework and key engine architecture, which will be rubber-stamped by the FIA World Motor Sport Council, both the manufacturers and the FIA can now get to work on the next rules cycle on a reasonable timeline.

That should help the governing body come up with chassis regulations which are tuned to work well with the new power units and deliver a more pure and exciting set of rules, without facing the prospect of having to adapt to late U-turns by OEMs, which led to 2026's compromised and criticised formula to begin with.

Sports.title: ‘Maybe I’m delusional but I genuinely feel like a podium was possible’ – Lindblad | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Arvid Lindblad says he and Racing Bulls are still seeking an explanation for the spin which put him out of the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

He was running sixth behind the Safety Car when he lost control and spun to a stop. He was then unable to select reverse and rejoin.

In a social media post two days after the race, Lindblad said he remained “absolutely devastated” by the result.

“For the first time in my career [I was] fighting in the top five with a genuine chance of a special result. To end it in the way it did, losing the car under SC, is just incredibly hard to take.

“No words to describe how I’m feeling right now. We work for years, our whole lives, for these moments and opportunities. In a midfield car, they come very rarely, and when they do, you need to grab them with both hands. The pain of missing out on something like this, and the endless thoughts of what could have been, will always hurt.”

Lindblad said he experienced something strange before his spin and the team still does not understand what caused it.

“Naturally, as the driver, you blame yourself in these moments,” he said. “Honestly, I still don’t really understand what happened.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“I experienced a terrible shift, something very abnormal, and the team are working hard to understand why. I don’t know whether there was anything I could have done differently or if it’s just one of those things but it’s hard not to question yourself.

“Regardless, that doesn’t change the missed opportunity or how much it hurts right now.”

He had just gained a position from Andrea Kimi Antonelli during the pit stops when he spun out. Antonelli started the penultimate lap in second place and Lindblad believes he could have been in contention at the front.

“Maybe I’m delusional, but I genuinely feel like a podium was possible,” he said. “It felt like one of those special days, a different type of race where opportunities rarely present themselves, and we were right there to take advantage.

“Luckily we’re racing again in a few days, but it’ll take much longer than that for the pain of this one to settle.”

Sports.title: ‘I’d rather blow up the f***ing engine’: Gasly’s fury over cooling problems | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Pierre Gasly’s power unit problems in the Las Vegas Grand Prix pushed the Alpine driver to breaking point.

He fumed at race engineer Josh Peckett after falling from third place to seventh in the space of just four laps.

Peckett repeatedly urged Gasly to cool his car down. “Why are they not struggling?” Gasly asked as he lost place after place. “I don’t know mate, but we are,” Peckett replied.

Gasly complained the lack of power made him a “sitting duck” while Isack Hadjar, Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Lewis Hamilton and Arvid Lindblad cruised past him.

Gasly’s patience snapped when the Racing Bulls driver overtook him, telling Peckett he’d “rather blow up the fucking engine” than continue like this. “No more talking, stop calming me down,” he added as Peckett tried to offer reassurance.

The Safety Car appeared soon afterwards which gave Gasly the chance to cool his car down more. He went on to finish fifth.

Sports.title: Featured Comment: Herta deserves credit for trying to make the switch from IndyCar | Brief
Sports.content:
Colton Herta’s bold attempt to make the leap from IndyCar to Formula 1 – via Formula 2 – appears to be over with yesterday’s news he won’t return to the feeder series this year.

It was always a risk, one I’m glad he took and sorry it didn’t work out. I’ve loved the cross overs when they’ve happened.

I loved it when Jacques Villeneuve turned up with his day-glo helmet, gangsta rap overalls and bleached hair. Juan Pablo Montoya ‘effing and jeffing’ and going out of his way to not show Michael Schumacher any respect. Nigel Mansell just being in Milwaukee, let alone winning. Alex Zanardi leaving and winning in that beautiful Target-liveried Reynard then coming back and doing nothing with Williams. Sebastian Bourdais being a winner and also very much not a winner…

It’s a risk, and one that seldom pays off on both sides of the Atlantic. Though Hill, Clark, Fittipaldi, Andretti prove it’s possible, and I guess Villeneuve also if we ignore Sauber, Renault and most of what he says.

It didn’t work for Colton, but he wanted to make the jump and I hope this doesn’t dissuade others from giving it a go in the future. You never know unless you try and most drivers end up not succeeding somewhere in their career, it may as well be because of a leap into the unknown.

@Bernasaurus

Sports.title: Was Hadjar helping himself or Verstappen when he collected a penalty in the pits? | Formula 1
Sports.content:
A front wing failure ended Isack Hadjar’s hopes of scoring points in the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

The Red Bull driver was running in second place before the Safety Car came out. Pitting for a fresh front wing after the Safety Car period meant he took the chequered flag in 14th place.

But even if he had finished the race in second place, his 10-second time penalty would likely have relegated him off the podium and down to the lower reaches of the points places.

The stewards ruled Hadjar “drove unnecessarily slowly under Safety Car conditions” and had a strong case for believing so. As they noted, as the field drove towards turn 14 Hadjar reduced his speed to around 100kph less than his team mate Max Verstappen, the only car in front of him.

Why did Hadjar back off so much? The stewards determined he did so “slowly for tactical reasons”, but did not elaborate on what these were.

The most obvious explanation is that as Hadjar was about to follow his team mate into the pits, Red Bull wanted to avoid him having to wait immediately behind Verstappen. Other drivers have done this before.

At least one other driver appeared to do the same in this race. The two Mercedes cars were running immediately behind the Red Bulls and Andrea Kimi Antonelli, the second of them, dropped back from George Russell.

But Antonelli did not receive a penalty, nor was he investigated. He also did not drop anything like as far back as Hadjar did: as the radio messages to the two drivers show, Red Bull wanted their cars five seconds apart, which was twice the gap between the two Mercedes as they entered the pits.

Clearly, Mercedes were not willing to risk holding the Safety Car queue up as much as Red Bull did. Red Bull took the practice to such an extreme it meant Hadjar received a penalty. What were they trying to achieve?

One unusual feature of last weekend’s race was how little the field spread out over the 19 laps before the Safety Car was deployed. At the moment the field was neutralised there were eight cars within five seconds of Verstappen.

As Red Bull could expect every driver in the field would want to take advantage of this perfectly-timed Safety Car period, they knew a train of cars would follow Verstappen into the pits close behind him. This presented a problem: as Red Bull had the third pit box after the start of the pit lane, many of those cars would pass Verstappen’s stationary car on their way to making their pit stops, making it harder for them to release him into the queue of cars.

Verstappen’s race engineer Tom Hart warned him: “Expect a busy pit lane, so on your delta.” But while one Red Bull driver was being told to stay on his delta time, the other was opening up a significant gap.

Getting Hadjar to slow down and back the field up by five seconds solved this problem. But the cost turned out to be a 10-second time penalty, which Red Bull may or may not have anticipated.

Red Bull is arguably the most consistently sharp team when it comes to strategy. They surely foresaw the effect the lack of field spread in Las Vegas would have on the likely scenario of a mid-race Safety Car deployment.

Clearly, the timing of the Safety Car period was incredibly important. The cards could easily have fallen differently and changed the circumstances drastically: 35 seconds before the Safety Car was deployed, Russell’s car was in between the two Red Bulls; 24 seconds before that, Russell was leading the race.

Coincidentally, this weekend F1 is heading to a venue where a similar scenario caught out McLaren last year. The team said its race-losing decision not to pit its drivers during a Safety Car period in Qatar arose from a concern they would become trapped in their pit boxes when the whole field pitted en masse.

Sports.title: Russell says he’d worked out how to beat Verstappen to the finishing line | Formula 1
Sports.content:
George Russell says he’d worked out how to beat Max Verstappen to the finishing line in Las Vegas, unlike his team mate.

The Mercedes driver took himself out of contention to win when he went off at turn five late in the race.

Russell spent the early part of the race scrapping with Verstappen, who led much of it and went on to win. The pair swapped the lead repeatedly and Russell crossed the finishing line ahead four times.

At one point Verstappen warned his team he wasn’t sure he would be able to win a sprint to the finishing line on the final lap.

However Russell fell to third place behind his team mate Andrea Kimi Antonelli with 12 laps to go. Although Antonelli managed to beat Verstappen to the finishing line once, Russell believes he was better-placed of the two Mercedes drivers to snatch victory from the Red Bull driver.

“I think I was in a very good strat mode,” he told Viaplay. “My energy deployment was very good to pass Max and then also be ahead at the finish line, whereas Kimi was passing him but then being re-passed before the finish line.

“But with my energy deployment I was very vulnerable in the middle sector. I lost three positions, at one point I was down in P5 and I had to change my energy management to then get myself back up the order again and that’s when I felt that was my chance to attack Kimi. Then I would have changed into the last lap. I was looking forward to it.”

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Russell wasn’t able to make his last-ditch attempt to pass Verstappen after he locked up and ran wide while trying to take second place off Antonelli on lap 48.

“I knew I needed to be behind Max into the last lap or two to win,” he said. “Kimi didn’t have the Overtake [Mode] and I just felt that was my chance. I had to go for it.

“[But it was] too high-risk [and I] paid the price. But equally I don’t regret it because I want to win the race.

“I could have easily been conservative and come home in P3 and I also wouldn’t have been satisfied. So obviously it’s not ideal, but no regrets.”

Sports.title: Stewards right to blame Leclerc for collision with Hamilton, says Vasseur | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Ferrari team principal Frederic Vasseur says Charles Leclerc must shoulder the blame for colliding with his team mate in the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Leclerc knocked Lewis Hamilton into a spin while the pair were running sixth and seventh. Hamilton recovered to finish seventh while the FIA stewards ruled Leclerc was to blame for the collision and handed him a 10-second time penalty which dropped him to 10th place.

The stewards ruled Leclerc was “wholly to blame” for the collision. Asked whether he held Leclerc solely responsible for the collision or divided the blame between his drivers, Vasseur said: “No, I think it was… The decision of the FIA, was quite clear.”

Leclerc backed out of an attempt to pass Hamilton in the high-speed turn 17 two laps before their collision. Vasseur indicated the team warned Leclerc to take care shortly before the collision.

“We passed a message to Charles five corners before,” he told Viaplay. “For me, it’s a professional mistake.

“I know that he apologised, I know he was sorry, but once again we destroyed the race today. We could have done much better. I don’t know what could be the outcome of the race because it was quite chaotic, but we can’t lose points like this.

“And more than points, it’s the motivation of everybody, the reward of the job done, the rewards of the effort and this is a huge frustration for me.”

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Leclerc’s radio was largely silent between the collision on lap 38 and the end of the race. After he took the chequered flag, Vasseur told him: “Charles, I want to see you just after the race, before everything.”

Leclerc said Vasseur told him “that it was not acceptable again.”

“I think it’s been too many times,” he continued. “I took the 10 seconds penalty, which I guess – I mean, not ‘I guess’ – which means that I am predominantly at fault in this clash and I will take the blame for that.”

“The result is that today, because of something I did, we don’t score the points that we should have and that is not acceptable,” Leclerc added. “I will look back at the incident and try to understand what I could have done better, differently and to make sure that I don’t ever find myself in this situation again. That’s all I can say.”

Sports.title: Peugeot WEC team axed, Citroen and Opel Formula E squads to close after 2027 | WEC
Sports.content:
The World Endurance Championship and Formula E will lose three teams between them after carmaker Stellantis announced an end to its motorsport activities.

In a statement released on Monday, Stellantis announced the change as part of a strategic plan called ‘FaSTLAne 2030′ (sic). The decision affects the company’s brands including Peugeot, Citroen and Opel.

Peugeot’s WEC team will not return to the endurance series in 2027. The team managed a best finish of fourth in the championship since returning in 2022, when only four manufacturers competed. Facing seven other competitors this year, it only finished ahead of Aston Martin.

The two Stellantis brands competing in Formula E will complete the first season using the series’ new ‘Gen4’ specification chassis next year before withdrawing. The 2027 season will be Opel’s first in the series.

Stellantis previous competed in Formula E with its Maserati and DS brands. The latter enjoyed considerable success, taking Jean-Eric Vergne to the title in the 2018-19 season and repeating the feat with Antonio Felix da Costa a year later.

In its statement, Stellantis said it will “refocus its motorsport activities and resources on customer racing and high-performance vehicle development.” The company’s motorsport division will focus on developing high-performance models for its various brands.

“Stellantis intends to retain and redeploy employees impacted by the conclusion of its official FIA world championships activities, working with them to identify internal opportunities within customer racing, high-performance vehicle development and other core activities related to the execution of FaSTLAne 2030,” it added.
