Just as the night was kicking off, with Felen and Christensen anticipating Trump's appearance — a big problem presented itself.

Christensen was kicked out.

He was approached by a couple people and told he must leave. Christensen said he was told it was because he's been sharing pictures online — and for being in touch with the media.

The organizers did not reply to an email from NPR seeking comment.

It was raining as Christensen stood all the way outside the golf course — still trying to figure out what happened.

"There's a first for everything, and I guess it was at the Trump gala," he said, sounding a little dejected.

The latest Trump meme coin dinner has come amid intense media scrutiny.

The White House has defended the events with meme coin holders as being part of Trump's private business — and not part of his public functions. Trump — who effectively has a royalty deal with the company that runs the meme coin — earned over $600 million last year from the cryptocurrency according to his disclosures.

But the latest event was held just weeks after corruption was a defining issue for voters in the midterm elections, which handed Democrats control of Congress next year.

Prominent Democrats including Sen. Adam Schiff from California and Sen. Richard Blumenthal from Connecticut have demanded more information about the latest meme coin dinner.

toggle caption i Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images North America

Trump speaks

Felen and Christensen decided she would stay behind. They figured they came to hear Trump speak and at least one of them should get to do it.

Trump finally made his appearance to big cheers from the crowd. It wasn't a focused speech, Felen said.

"He jumped from topic to topic. It was interesting but just him rambling," Felen said. "Speaking, speaking, speaking — but not making a lot of important points I guess."

Sponsor Message

For Felen though. it was still a moment to finally see the president.

The trip back to the hotel

Felen — and "soaking wet" Christensen — made their way to the hotel. Christensen tried to sound philosophical.

"It happens, you know. It was a different experience this time around. Could have been better, but I will just laugh about it," he said. "All good. It's part of the game."

Final thoughts

Heading to the airport to catch their flights out of the U.S., Felen and Christensen were still trying to process the night.

Felen still can't believe she got to go.

"My friends and people who know me from my village are like how did you end up here?," she said.

Nonetheless, both of them sounded more subdued. Felen said she wished her brother had a better night.

"I was definitely disappointed for him, especially later when I saw some people who were VIP actually get, like, a one-on-one selfie with Trump, probably also got to shake his hand," she added. "So that would have been a great opportunity for Morten."

As for Christensen, he said all he wanted was a chance to meet Trump, stressing again that he's not political.

Waiting to catch their flight, he was still unsure of how to feel about Trump's latest meme coin dinner. He does know, though, this will be his last.

"That's a wrap on me on the Trump events," he said.

World.title: Black travelers on Route 66 weren't welcome at most gas stations — except this one
World.content:
Black travelers on Route 66 weren't welcome at most gas stations — except this one

toggle caption i Nick Oxford for NPR

During the Jim Crow Era, Black families traveling Route 66, the historic highway that ran more than 2,000 miles from Chicago to Los Angeles, needed to carry food and gas with them. Most restaurants, gas stations and motels wouldn't serve them.

But there was one place they were guaranteed to find respite: a small, family-owned business just east of Oklahoma City that offered fuel, food and a place to stop for the night. The Threatt Filling Station, according to the National Trust for Historic Preservation, was the only known Black-owned and operated gas station along the famous Mother Road.

Sponsor Message

"Grandpa took care of whatever they needed to have," said Linda Fisher, the granddaughter of the station's founder, Allen Threatt Sr. Her family still owns the station and the 150 acres around it.

"If they didn't have any food, they fed them," she said. "If they needed some kind of shelter or blankets or those types of things, Grandpa and Grandma made sure they got those kinds of things."

toggle caption i Nick Oxford for NPR

Threatt moved from Alabama to the farming community of Luther, Okla., in the early 1900s as part of the Great Migration. His father had been born into slavery, and Threatt and his wife, Alberta, seeking stability and refuge, wanted their own farm.

At the time, Oklahoma was a place where Black migrants could own land and form their own towns. Between 1865 and 1920, Black Americans settled more than 50 "all-Black" municipalities in Oklahoma, the largest number of any state.

But Oklahoma also had its issues — by the time of the Great Depression, many of those all-Black towns had ceased to exist. And there was a rise in "sundown towns": all-white communities that warned non-white people to get out before dark, or they would face violence or police harassment. There was a sundown town on either side of the filling station during the Jim Crow era, Fisher said.

toggle caption i Nick Oxford for NPR

But at the Threatt Filling Station, "everyone was welcome," Fisher said.

Sponsor Message

The building, which closed to the public in the 1970s, is now on the National Register of Historic Places.

A century of welcome

Allen Threatt Sr. built the original filling station in 1915, when he started to notice people driving by a corner of his property on what was then the Ozark Trail.

In 1926, Route 66 was founded, and the trickle of cars became a steady stream. When the old wooden building burned down, Threatt replaced it with a charming sandstone one, built like a small, welcoming house.

Eventually, the station and the property surrounding it became a community hub. There were dances in the restaurant next door, social club meetings, barbecues. Occasionally, players from the Negro Leagues would have a game on the baseball diamond.

toggle caption i Nick Oxford for NPR

Allen and Alberta Threatt had 11 living children, and a couple of them took over the running of the station in the 1950s.

But the building of the Interstate Highway System, launched under the Eisenhower administration, led to dwindling traffic on Route 66, and by the mid-'70s, the station had closed.

A half-century later later, the building was derelict. In 2021, the National Trust for Historic Preservation listed the station as one of America's 11 Most Endangered Historic Places.

But hope was around the corner: A few years earlier, a trio of Allen Threatt Sr.'s grandchildren decided to restore the property. Now, thanks to nonprofit grants and a lot of cousin elbow grease, the filling station has a restored exterior.

toggle caption i Nick Oxford for NPR

Ceramic Conoco gas pumps from the 1940s stand proudly outside; new signs inside detail the history of the family, the gas station and Route 66, and visitors can talk to the Threatts themselves and buy a T-shirt.

Eventually, the family is planning to build an RV park, a restaurant and perhaps even a new baseball diamond.

"We're all standing on Grandpa's shoulders — Grandpa and Grandma's shoulders," said Edward Threatt, another grandchild of Allen Threatt Sr. who is one of the leaders of the restoration.

Sponsor Message

"We have this property today because of Grandpa, and so we represent him, we represent our mothers, our fathers. And we're just trying to do them proud, that's all."

Broadcast and digital story edited by Steven Drummond; audio mixed by Chloee Weiner. Photo editing by Emily Bogle.

World.title: For workplace culture champions, Jensen Huang's return is 'unfathomable'
World.content:
For workplace culture champions, Jensen Huang's return is 'unfathomable'

toggle caption i Chung Sung-Jun/Getty Images AsiaPac



On Monday morning, a couple hours after Nvidia's board announced it had reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO, President Trump shared an AI-generated image on social media.

It's based on that striking photo of the president from 2024, just after he survived an assasination attempt. Surrounded by Secret Service agents, his face bloodied, Trump hoists a defiant fist in the air.

In the doctored photo, instead of Trump, it's Huang. An Nvidia flag flies behind him. And in his hoisted fist, he holds a red bra.

Sponsor Message

"I was absolutely flabbergasted," says Bo Young Lee, who worked as chief diversity officer at Uber for five years starting in 2018.

To Lee, it seems Trump is suggesting that the Nvidia CEO is as important to the country as he is.

"But then also the red bra is an indication that it's open hunting season for women," she says. "It stirs up all sorts of stereotypes and misogynistic perspectives about women."

To others, the image drives home the idea that in Silicon Valley, as long as you're successful, anything goes.

The White House has not responded to NPR's questions about what Trump was trying to say with the image.

Spy intrigue overshadows workplace transgressions

Even as Huang's return to Nvidia has been cheered by investors, some employees and Trump, it has sparked shock and disbelief among others, including those who have long worked to improve workplace culture in Silicon Valley.

"It's actually unfathomable to me," says Lee, who now serves as an adviser to AI4ALL, a nonprofit dedicated to increasing diversity, inclusion, and responsible practices in artificial intelligence.

After The New York Times revealed that Huang had engaged in an extramarital affair with a woman the U.S government believes is a Chinese intelligence asset, Lee watched as the broader conversation was dominated by concerns about national security, corporate governance and Nvidia's stock price.

Sponsor Message

That scandal overshadowed allegations of other problematic behavior in the workplace, specifically Huang's alleged affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, one of Huang's many direct reports.

"Everyone is minimizing that alleged relationship there because of who she is," says Lee.

The fact that Powell is herself a senior leader who makes a lot of money shouldn't matter, Lee says. She argues that people in subordinate roles, even powerful ones, can't properly consent, "simply for the fact that there is this power differential."

Nvidia's board did find that Huang's behavior was "inconsistent" with the company's code of conduct. By Monday morning, that didn't seem to matter.

"The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang's candor and ability to lead Nvidia," the board said in a statement.

Lee says that response sends a message to Nvidia employees and all of Silicon Valley that it's OK to break the rules as long as you come clean.

"'Just be transparent with us,'" she imagines the board saying.

Nvidia did not respond to NPR's questions about Lee's concerns.

A deepening of "tech bro" culture in Trump's second term

In Silicon Valley, there have been private conversations about Huang's alleged workplace transgressions and the power dynamics at play, but women don't appear eager to speak publicly.

NPR reached out to two dozen women who work in the tech space. Freada Kapor Klein was one of the few willing to talk. The social impact investor says conversations about workplace behavior are much quieter than they have been in other eras, such as in 2017 and 2018, when a number of venture capitalists resigned amid allegations they were sexually harassing female entrepreneurs.

In 2017, Kapor Klein and her husband, Mitch Kapor, used their positions as early investors in Uber to publicly call out the company over its toxic culture, one they said tolerated bullying and harassment. The co-founder and CEO Travis Kalanick ended up resigning. Kapor Klein hoped it'd be a teachable moment.

Sponsor Message

But now, she feels Silicon Valley has gone backwards.

"Tech bro culture is stronger now than I have seen it in decades," she says, adding that Trump's attacks on DEI have amplified that culture.

Among women and people of color in Silicon Valley, she says there's now real trepidation about the anti-DEI sentiment — the axing of programs, chief diversity officers and employee resource groups.

"All of the supports or mechanisms have been pretty much stripped away," she says.

toggle caption i Angela Weiss/AFP via Getty Images

"All that matters is money"

To be clear, Huang has not been accused of predatory behavior. Still, Kapor Klein says his swift comeback is troubling.

"It is a resounding message that all that matters is money," she says. "If you are thought of as a singular talent, you can violate corporate policy, you can possibly threaten national security, you can make up your own rules as you go, you can create toxic workplace culture — as long as you bring in the money."

By the end of last week, Nvidia's stock had fallen almost 49% from its peak in October, and about 27% from before Huang's resignation. On Monday, it rebounded significantly.

Lee says Silicon Valley has always had an unhealthy relationship with its "genius founders."

"We elevate these leaders to god-like levels, and that's been done to Mark Zuckerberg, and that's being done to Sam Altman, and that's definitely [been] done to Jensen Huang," says Lee. "You become untouchable at that point."

Kapor Klein says what's unfolded at Nvidia has made abundantly clear that AI companies need guardrails for their CEOs, not just for the tools they're creating.

"We see a board that ignored that," she says. "There are no guardrails on this CEO's behavior."

NPR's Scott Horsley contributed to this story.

World.title: Democrats probe whether Trump Jr.-aligned businesses benefit from government access
World.content:
Democrats probe whether Trump Jr.-aligned businesses benefit from government access

toggle caption i Brandon Bell/Getty Images

Congressional Democrats, led by likely House Judiciary Committee Chair Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, are expanding their investigation into the investment firm 1789 Capital, which brought on Donald Trump Jr. as a partner days after his father's reelection to the White House.

Since then, investigators say the firm has grown from "a middling venture capital firm" with $150 million in managed assets to "the darling of the venture capital world" with $3 billion in managed assets.

Investigators want to determine whether the growth was boosted by the president's son leveraging political influence or government information to secure federal contracts and regulatory changes for companies with connections to the investment firm.

Sponsor Message

Trump Jr. told Axios last week that the timing of his hiring at 1789 Capital was coincidental, noting that he had already been working with founder Omeed Malik for years. He also said he draws a clear line when marketing and raising money for the firm.

"I make it very clear [to foreign investors] that I have nothing to do with government," Trump Jr. said. "[The president is] my father, but he's also busy and I probably haven't spoken to him in three weeks."

He also suggested he doesn't use or need government connections to make smart investments. "Trying to do the things that we're alleged to be doing every day, I think that would last for about two seconds before it was out there very publicly," Trump Jr. said. He added that the firm relies on teams of analysts to make investments in industries where there are obvious public and national security demands but relatively few companies who are able to meet those needs.

NPR reached out to Donald Trump Jr. for comment and did not hear back.

Regarding Raskin's request for documents from 1789 Capital, Bill Burck, an attorney representing the firm, told NPR, "We responded to Congressman Raskin back in September pointing out in detail the many flaws in his understanding of how 1789 has operated and a number of basic factual errors. He never bothered to reply. Facts are facts and Congressman Raskin has them wrong here but persists in his tall tales against 1789. These are personal attacks untethered to actual evidence."

Sponsor Message

What investigators are interested in

On Monday, congressional investigators sent letters to four companies — military contractor Hadrian, electronic cigarette company Juul, prediction market Polymarket and online weapons dealer GrabAGun — asking them to preserve their records and turn over a broad array of records to the committee.

The committee is interested in Hadrian's contracts with the armed forces, signed in March of this year, worth close to a billion dollars. Investigators allege that, in 2024, the company had a single manufacturing facility and "no history of fulfilling government contracts." They also noted that CEO Chris Power donated tens of thousands of dollars to Trump-aligned political organizations in advance of the 2024 election.

Political donations are constitutionally-protected speech and not necessarily evidence of wrongdoing. 1789 Capital first invested in Hadrian in July 2025. The company is also backed by a number of bluechip investors, including Morgan Stanley, T. Rowe Price, Andreessen Horowitz and JPMorganChase. Hadrian did not reply to a request for comment from NPR.

Investigators also allege that Trump Jr.'s firm took a stake in e-cigarette company Juul in March 2025, as the company teetered near insolvency following rulings during the first Trump administration limiting the sale of various flavor cartridges. Four months after that investment, though before it was publicly disclosed, investigators say the company's fortunes rebounded after the Trump administration authorized five new Juul e-cigarette products. The company has announced plans for more flavor authorization applications moving forward.

In a statement to NPR, a Juul spokesperson said the company had received Rep. Raskin's letter and are "reviewing it closely. As always, we intend to cooperate with any Congressional effort to understand our company, our commitment to combating underage vaping, and our mission to help adult smokers of combustible cigarettes transition completely away from smoking."

Investigators are also interested in betting site Polymarket. They say that following a meeting between Polymarket leadership and Trump Jr. at the 2024 Republican National Convention, 1789 Capital invested in the company — which at the time was banned in the United States. In July 2025, after President Trump took office, the Justice Department and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission notified the company that they had closed investigations launched during the Biden administration, according to reporting from Bloomberg News. The CFTC later authorized a U.S. version of the platform to launch. Investigators allege 1789's investment resulted in a 70-fold return.

Sponsor Message

GrabAGun, a company that "believe[s] people should be able to use their computers, phones, and tablets to shop for firearms the same way they purchase everything else," became, according to investigators, a publicly-traded company with the help of 1789 Capital leadership, including Trump Jr., who serves of its board.

In May 2026, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) proposed a draft rule that would make it easier to ship guns directly to people's homes. At the time, GrabAGun claimed that the company is "uniquely positioned to capitalize on this potential opportunity." Investigators are seeking to understand what knowledge and involvement Trump Jr. had of the proposed rule change.

In a statement to NPR, GrabAGun said the investigators' letter is "a political document, and its allegations are baseless." It added that the ATF's review of its regulations was well known across the firearms industry, and the agency published numerous proposed rules for public comment.

"GrabAGun's only input came through public comments on several of those proposals," the company said.

World.title: Bank of Canada expects 2nd round of oil-linked inflation in 2027, Macklem says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem sees high energy prices continuing to sting consumers at the fuel pump and beyond in 2027, even as oil prices fall from recent peaks.

In a speech on Tuesday, he warned a second round of the recent oil shock linked to war in the Middle East will stoke inflation next year. His remarks dampen expectations that a recent decline in benchmark oil prices would yield meaningful relief for consumers and businesses.

"This second-round effect of the oil shock will add to inflation persistence," he said at an event hosted by the Economic Club of Canada, in Toronto on Tuesday.

"Historical lags and our own business surveys suggest more pass-through to the consumer in the year ahead."

Macklem added that so far, businesses have largely absorbed higher production and transportation costs linked to high energy prices.

The October inflation data from Statistics Canada gave little evidence of high oil prices spilling into other segments of the economy. The consumer price index rose 3.1 per cent on a year-over-year basis last month, matching a 3.1 per cent increase in September.

Last month, the Bank of Canada hiked its policy interest rate by 25 basis points to 2.5 per cent, ending a year-long pause at 2.25 per cent with its first increase since 2023.

WATCH | Will the Bank of Canada hike in December?: Tiff Macklem on what might prompt another rate hike | Duration 2:24 Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem, who held rates in October, says the bank needs to see 'clear evidence' that core inflation is moving down.

In their summary of deliberations published on Nov. 10, policymakers said further hikes may be needed as high oil prices and rising business costs collide with a resilient economy, risking broad-based inflation through 2027.

In its October Monetary Policy Report, the Bank of Canada called for inflation to remain near three per cent through much of 2027. At the time, policymakers said they expect prices to ease toward two per cent, the mid-point of the central bank's target range, in 2028.

Since then, global oil benchmarks have fallen to roughly three-month lows, due in part to potential military de-escalation between the United States and Iran. The situation has been helped by rising exports of Middle Eastern oil to global markets through the Strait of Hormuz, the vital shipping route that’s been heavily disrupted by the conflict.

Looking ahead, Mackelm said the Bank of Canada is preparing to respond to "larger and more frequent supply shocks."

"Inflation is likely to be pushed off course more frequently and for longer," he said on Tuesday.

"Monetary policy can’t lower global energy prices. But it can limit how much they spill over. Our goal is to avoid a situation where Canadians face rising prices for a wide range of goods and services."

The Bank of Canada is scheduled to make its final rate decision of 2026 on Dec. 9.

Its governing council will have two fresh economic data points to consider ahead of that meeting. Statistics Canada is scheduled to release its gross domestic product reading for the third quarter on Nov. 30, followed by the November Labour Force Survey on Dec. 4.

World.title: Alberta premier, justice minister to introduce Sovereignty Act motion
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Alberta government says it plans to introduce a new motion under its Sovereignty Act on Tuesday.

A news release says Premier Danielle Smith and Justice Minister Mickey Amery will introduce a motion "to defend Albertans’ fundamental rights and freedoms."

The news conference starts at noon in Edmonton. You can watch it here.

The UCP government passed the Alberta Sovereignty within a United Canada Act in 2022. It allows the province to push back on federal laws or policies that the legislature deems unconstitutional, violate Albertans' rights or negatively impact the province.

Last year, the province introduced a Sovereignty Act motion against federal firearms legislation.

World.title: A teenage runaway turned to a Mountie for sanctuary. He had other plans
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

On a bone-chilling night in January 1983, Kim Budd, just 15, sits in handcuffs at the Riverview RCMP detachment in a suburb of Moncton, N.B.

She’s run away from home — again.

"I spent the whole night with them," recalled Budd, now 59 and living in western Quebec. "They locked me to a chair."

There's no mug shot and no charges because the teen has committed no crime. But the officer who picked her up off the frigid street isn't sure what to do with this runaway, and worries she'll bolt if she isn't restrained.

Tired and uncomfortable, the girl sits there until the morning shift arrives. One of the Mounties who has just come in pays her special attention.

"The first time I ever laid eyes on him I had a cold pit in the centre of my stomach," Budd recalled decades later. "He was sitting on the desk and he kept looking at me and watching me."

Budd, with her dark eyes and hair cut in an '80s shag, glares back with a scowl perfected by teenagers.

Then the Mountie approaches with an unexpected offer. He tells her he and his wife run an emergency foster home for kids like her. Would she like to stay with them?

The teen, who has already bounced from abusive home to group residence to reform school and then back to the same abusive home, agrees.

"He just wanted to help me. That's what I thought," she said.

In fact, the Mountie would demand much more from the troubled runaway, and the shelter and security he offered her would soon turn into a new form of confinement. She would learn that none of the adults who were supposed to protect her — not the police, not the doctors, not the child welfare officials — could be trusted when she needed them most, and the more she cried out for help, the less anyone would listen to the terrible truth she struggled to tell.

Kim Budd, now 59, at an Ottawa-area horse farm where she says she finds a sense of peace and security after everything she's been through. (Turgot Yeter/CBC)

Kim Budd was a runner. She ran away from adults, and often into trouble.

Born in a small town along New Brunswick’s Miramichi River, Budd was the youngest of six children and the only girl. Her father took off for good a few weeks later, leaving the family struggling financially.

Budd describes a difficult childhood, including being molested by a neighbour when she was four.

"I had some issues with that growing up," she said.

Her mother later remarried a man Budd remembers as volatile, strict and abusive.

"The physical abuse was as long back as I can remember," she said. "I was about nine or so, he would start putting his hands on my breasts or between my legs and he almost made it into a game."

Budd’s step-father denies the abuse, and it’s unclear what her mother, a woman Budd describes as passive and unaffectionate, actually knew over the years. She did not want to talk to CBC.

Budd first ran away from home at 13. 'The physical abuse was as long back as I can remember,' she told CBC. (Submitted)

By 13, Budd was starting to act out. She shoplifted, drank alcohol, experimented with drugs and hitchhiked, earning the label "juvenile delinquent."

Budd says in reality, she was shy, vulnerable and often frightened.

"I had some anger issues, but I wasn't tough," she said. "I didn't care whether I lived or died. I knew it was risky."

By the time she turned 14, her mother and step-father had had enough. They called New Brunswick’s social services and the girl was placed in a group home, then reform school.

After 11 months at the Nova Scotia School for Girls in Truro, Budd was sent back to live with her mother and step-father. But that didn't last long.

"I needed to make some changes," Budd recalled. "My parents needed to make some changes…. They never recognized what they were doing that contributed to my running away."

So she ran again, and that's when the RCMP picked her up.

Gilles Plouffe had been with the RCMP for about five years when he first encountered Kim Budd. Due to his standing in the community, he and his wife were quickly approved to be foster parents. (Submitted by Gilles Plouffe)

In 1983, Const. Gilles Plouffe had been with the RCMP for four years and was already on his third posting.

Plouffe was fluently bilingual and stood over six feet tall with broad shoulders and a wispy mustache. As a kid he’d been an altar boy, a boy scout, an air cadet and a school crossing guard.

He married his high school sweetheart when they were still in their teens, and by 25 they were helping raise other people's children in addition to two young kids of their own.

In a system desperate for foster parents, the young couple was welcomed with open arms. He was an officer of the law, after all.

"I think they saw us as a blessing," he recalled in a recent interview with CBC. "They cut corners like you wouldn't believe. We didn't have any formal background check."

Soon, the Plouffe foster home became a handy option whenever the RCMP picked up a young person like Budd. They'd simply notify social services, and that was that.

Michel Cormier, a retired social worker in Moncton, N.B., stands near the Petitcodiac River in the early fall of 2026. Despite dealing with hundreds of cases over his career, he says he still remembers Kim Budd from the 1980s. (Michael Heenan/CBC)

Michel Cormier, a New Brunswick social worker tasked with overseeing the care of teens in the early 1980s, got that call the day Budd arrived at the Plouffe foster home.

Budd had been under Cormier's supervision during her months in group homes and reform school, and he can still remember her all these years later.

"She was a nice kid," Cormier told CBC. "I tried to respect her, not treat her like a juvenile delinquent — basically as a child that was in a difficult situation."

Placing Budd with the Plouffes seemed like an ideal solution.

"These were the perfect foster parents," Cormier recalled everyone thinking at the time. "This Disney kind of family, that everything was beautiful."

A recent photo of the house in Riverview, N.B., where Gilles Plouffe and his wife fostered children in the 1980s. (Michael Heenan/CBC)

Budd, a kid who had long dreamed of belonging to a "normal" family, settled in with the Plouffes and started Grade 9 at Riverview Junior High.

While her basement bedroom was being prepared, the teen slept on a pull-out couch.

One night when her foster mother was away, Gilles Plouffe came in wearing only a bathrobe and slipped under the covers with her.

"I kept falling asleep off and on, and he kept getting closer. And he had intercourse with me that night," Budd recalled. She remembers being afraid.

Plouffe apologized to the teen shortly after, telling her what happened had been an "accident." But the abuse continued, becoming more frequent and opportunistic.

"There was never a choice for me," Budd said. "He was my foster father and what he did to me that night, and the many times afterwards, was illegal."

While Plouffe disputes certain details, he now acknowledges he had sex on multiple occasions with the teenager in his care.

"It wasn't set out to be a predator looking for a prey," he told CBC. "I didn't mean to do anything bad, I just wanted to have a girlfriend."

Gilles Plouffe talked openly with CBC's Julie Ireton about his history with Kim Budd. He wore his RCMP-issue leather boots to the interview. (Francis Ferland/CBC)

Now 69, Plouffe needed no convincing to talk openly with CBC about his history with Kim Budd. Plouffe's then wife, Budd’s former foster mother, died in 2007.

During a lengthy interview, Plouffe showed no anger, hostility or concern. Rather, he appeared to welcome the opportunity to provide his own version of what happened in the foster home.

"It was a love connection," he insists. "And it's hard to say, 'Hey, you're a Mountie and you're supposed to enforce law and you're supposed to know better,’ and all this kind of stuff. I know all that."

Plouffe acknowledged he was aware of the sexual abuse Budd had endured as a child and as a runaway.

"It's not like she hadn't done it before. OK, I said it. It's not nice to say that, but she did do it before," said Plouffe. "I was showing her that people could be gentle, that it wasn't like the truckers she had met while running, that she could be passed on as a slave from one truck to the next."

The way he tells it, he provided the teen with food, shelter, clothing and "good values."

And yet he was keenly aware that what he was doing to his foster daughter was illegal.

Every male person who has illicit sexual intercourse with his step-daughter, foster daughter or female ward ... is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for two years. Section 153, Criminal Code of Canada c. 1983

Back then, Section 153 of the Criminal Code clearly stated that a man who has "illicit sexual intercourse with his foster daughter … is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for two years." (Today the crime falls under sexual exploitation. )

"I had the Criminal Code in the house, and I showed her," said Plouffe. "I told her, as a Mountie, I had no intention of going into jail. That's the last place any police officer wants to end up."

"He showed me in the book that he could go to prison," Budd recalled. "He just thought he was above the law."

The abuse continued. But almost two years into her stay with the Plouffes, it's Budd who would find herself in handcuffs once again, being taken away in a police car.

Two days after Christmas 1984, Budd, by then 17, got into a heated argument with her foster mother.

"She started going on and on about responsibility," Budd recalled. "She had been irresponsible in my view. She wasn’t being a responsible wife and I had to have sex with her husband."

The argument escalated and the woman threw a slice of pizza in Budd's face, then ran to her bedroom.

Budd followed. She had had enough of the lying and sneaking around, and of her foster father's late night visits. She was going to reveal the secret.

"I was running to tell her that Gilles had been sleeping with me," Budd said.

But Gilles Plouffe was right behind her.

"He grabbed me and put the chokehold on me and he made me unconscious," Budd said.

When she came to she was handcuffed, put in the back of Plouffe's RCMP cruiser and driven to the Moncton Hospital.

Moncton Hospital documents from December 1984 and early 1985 detailed Budd's admission, diagnosis and discharge. CBC has redacted some private information. (Submitted)

Hospital documents from December 1984 confirm that Budd arrived in restraints and that Plouffe told hospital staff the teen had "threatened to kill his family."

"Foster father is an RCMP officer. He used force to subdue her," the emergency admission form notes. "He feels the death threats are real."

Budd insists the only threat she'd made was to tell her foster mother that her husband had been having sex with her.

The 17-year-old was admitted to the adult psychiatric ward where she was medicated, underwent tests and attended group therapy. The hospital psychologist noted that Budd was insecure, impulsive, angry and suicidal, and that she felt "unloved" and had a "strong need for affection."

A couple weeks into her hospital stay, Budd disclosed to the staff psychologist what was really happening in the foster home. Documents from the time refer to Budd’s "alleged accusations" but provide no details.

"I just needed to get it out. I needed the sex to stop," Budd recalled telling the psychologist.

Then she told Plouffe what she had done. That forced him to admit the truth to his wife.

Budd spent three weeks in the psychiatric ward of the Moncton Hospital when she was still 17. She told a hospital psychologist here that her foster father had been abusing her. (Marc Grandmaison/The Canadian Press)

The psychologist summoned the Plouffes to the hospital for a meeting. Eventually, Budd was brought into the room.

"They told me never to talk to anyone about the abuse that had happened in their home," she said. "They made me promise."

Looking back, Budd says staff at the hospital never regarded her as a child, but as a mistress.

"I had a nurse reprimand me: ‘How dare you sleep with a married man?’ So she blamed me for the abuse, and that’s pretty much how I got blamed for what happened, instead of Gilles."

The teenager had endured two years of abuse in her foster home. She’d finally worked up the courage to tell someone in a position of authority. And then the adults colluded against her.

Plouffe said he informed child welfare authorities that he and his wife would no longer be fostering children, but no one reported the abuse to the RCMP.

"I didn't ask anybody to cover anything," Plouffe insists. "I don’t know. They see me as a Mountie. What are you going to do?"

Budd models a borrowed outfit for an upcoming job interview. (Submitted)

In fact, in yet another incredible twist, Budd — not Plouffe — would find herself in trouble with the law once again, this time as part of a spurious murder claim made by her abuser in January 1984, shortly after she was hospitalized.

"She had told [us] that she had killed somebody," Plouffe told CBC.

While the details remain vague, Plouffe said Budd had admitted to him that she’d killed a trucker in the U.S. after he had "taken advantage of her." He told his superiors at the RCMP and an investigator was assigned to the case.

Today, Budd calls it all a fiction concocted by Plouffe to distract his superiors from what was really happening to her in the foster home.

"I’ve never killed anybody — never," Budd said. "Gilles made me go through and told me to tell them."

But at the time, Budd, still just 17, went along with the ruse.

"I was just trying to protect Gilles," she said. "It’s hard to explain it now, but I was a shell."

RCMP files confirm an investigation in 1984, but no charges were laid and the case was quickly closed when no evidence was found to corroborate Budd's confession.

Still, the teen was now firmly under Plouffe's control, as though handcuffed once again.

Budd and Plouffe married in 1988 and moved from New Brunswick back to Plouffe's hometown of Gatineau, Que. (Submitted)

Budd was released from hospital in the winter of 1984 and went back to live with her mother and step-father. She dropped out of school and worked nights cleaning offices.

Before long, Plouffe, now separated from his wife, reappeared. He would turn up suddenly in his police vehicle, letting Budd know he was never far away.

"He was supposed to stay away from me, but he never did," she said. "I couldn't go to the RCMP because he was the RCMP."

Budd knew she couldn't run again.

"I believed he could have found me anywhere," she recalled. "I was afraid he was going to make me disappear…. He had weapons at the house, in his police car."

Eventually, she relented to his frequent calls. The sex continued.

"I can’t explain the hold Gilles had over me," Budd said. "He didn’t court me. We didn’t go to movies or restaurants, he didn’t buy me gifts. I was his toy."

Shortly after turning 18, Budd moved in with Plouffe and his two young children. When her former foster mother found out she became furious, and this time went to the police.

WATCH | Gilles Plouffe tells his side of the story: Gilles Plouffe tells his side of the story | Duration closed caption 0:55 Former RCMP constable Gilles Plouffe sat down with CBC’s Julie Ireton for a lengthy interview to explain his history with Kim Budd.

The RCMP began an investigation in 1986, according to documents obtained by CBC. Plouffe’s police colleagues set out to determine if the sexual relationship had started while Budd was still in foster care.

They never talked to the alleged perpetrator, however.

"They did not interview me. They interviewed Kim," Plouffe confirmed. "But they never asked me if I did anything wrong."

It’s unclear whether the RCMP questioned anyone at New Brunswick’s child protection services, which oversees foster care in the province. And yet both Plouffe and former social worker Michel Cormier confirmed that employees within the department knew about what had gone on in the Plouffe home.

"The people that knew, I imagine probably had the idea that it was not any of their business. So they didn’t go forward with a complaint to the police like it should have been done," Cormier said. (He left the agency shortly after Budd's placement with the Plouffes, but later returned to work there part-time.)

New Brunswick's Social Development office is responsible for child protective services including foster care. Budd was a ward of the province when she was in foster care in the early 1980s. (Michael Heenan/CBC)

According to Budd, Plouffe coached her to tell anyone who asked that the sex had started after she turned 18.

"He kept telling me that if I told his lie often enough, it would become my truth," she said.

Once again, the teen lied for Plouffe and the RCMP wrapped up the investigation.

"The allegation that Cst. Plouffe had sexual intercourse with Kimberly Ann Budd while she was a ward of Cst. Plouffe is unsubstantiated. There is no evidence to support this fact and no way we will ever be able to prove this fact," states an RCMP memo from August 1986.

But Plouffe’s association with this teen runaway and one-time murder suspect created a new problem for him: He was deemed a security risk – not because of anything he'd done, but because of her.

"His security clearance has been downgraded," states the memo. "We do not feel there is any further action to be taken at this point with the exception of verifying periodically if Budd becomes involved in her former activities."

Budd became pregnant with her first child at 19. She and Plouffe would have three sons together. (Francis Ferland/CBC)

Budd was 19 when she became pregnant with her first child, giving birth to a baby boy in May 1987. She would go on to have two more sons with her former foster father.

"I was very trapped," she said.

With no proposal or engagement ring, Budd and Plouffe married in a civil ceremony in January 1988 at the Moncton courthouse. No friends or family attended, and Plouffe did not wear his red serge.

"They harassed him about it until he quit the RCMP," Budd said, suggesting that despite dropping their investigation, Plouffe's superiors may have had their suspicions.

Later that same year the newlyweds left New Brunswick and moved to Plouffe's hometown of Gatineau, Que., initially moving in with his mother.

There, years later during a therapy session for one of their children, Budd told the therapist about the origins of her relationship with Plouffe.

"She kept giving me cards to go see a women's shelter," said Budd. "I started looking at my marriage … how dysfunctional it was."

At 27 — 12 years after first meeting him — Budd finally left Plouffe for good. She took computer courses and eventually secured a job with the federal government where she remained for more than 20 years.

RCMP officer Sandra Lavallee interviews Budd at the national police force's Ottawa office in 2017. During the interview, Budd reported the sexual abuse she suffered as a teen in the Plouffe foster home. CBC obtained a video of the interview through an access to information request. (RCMP)

In April 2017, Budd sat in an RCMP interview room in Ottawa to detail her complaint against Gilles Plouffe for historical sexual abuse.

In a video of that interview, Budd’s pain is raw. Through tears, she recounts what she went through between the ages of 15 and 17 in the Plouffe foster home.

"He told me that I couldn’t tell anyone. Nobody would understand ... it was our secret," Budd told the interviewer.

Shortly after, RCMP Const. Simon Boucher of New Brunswick’s Codiac detachment launched an investigation.

Kim Budd speaks with reporter Julie Ireton outside the RCMP offices in Ottawa where in 2017 Budd reported the abuse she suffered in the 1980s. (Turgut Yeter/CBC)

CBC obtained through access to information the interview video and close to 400 pages of documents related to the 2017 investigation. While much has been redacted, the police files note that Boucher searched "different databases" for witnesses including Budd’s former social worker, Michel "Mike" Cormier.

"The attempt to contact Mike Cormier … were negative," the records state. "Cst. Boucher followed up with social services in Moncton, no one from their office are aware of a Mike Cormier that worked there between 1980 and 1990."

Yet CBC easily found Cormier through social media. He still lives in the Moncton area, and during several conversations shared what he knows about Budd’s childhood.

Cormier said he would have given the RCMP the same information — including the open secret about what went on at the Plouffe home — had an investigator ever called to ask.

Despite the RCMP's claim that it couldn't find him in 2017, Michel Cormier was still living in New Brunswick and employed as a social worker at a Moncton hospital. (Michael Heenan/CBC)

The RCMP closed the investigation into Budd’s complaint in August 2018.

"There is not enough likelihood of conviction," Boucher concluded. "The main issue in the matter is the reliability and credibility of KB because there is no eye witness to the alleged sexual acts."

But there was another eye witness: Gilles Plouffe. Yet the RCMP never contacted him, reducing what Boucher called a case of "he said, she said" to a simple matter of "she said."

Plouffe spent hours talking openly with CBC about his past, demonstrating that he’s not shy to discuss what happened in his foster home in the early 1980s. But he said he was never aware of the RCMP investigation until told about it by CBC.

Once again, Budd had tried to tell the truth, only to be dismissed.

"There was evidence there that he had abused me. They just ignored it," said Budd.

Daphne Gilbert, a law professor at the University of Ottawa, reviewed Kim Budd's legal files. 'We don't believe women when they come forward and talk about sexual assault. We start from the position that they are lying,' she told CBC. (Mathieu Deroy/CBC)

"There's no other victim where we assume that they are lying about what happened to them. That is unique to sexual assault, still today," said Daphne Gilbert, a law professor at the University of Ottawa who reviewed the legal documents in Budd’s case.

"We don't believe women when they come forward and talk about sexual assault. We start from the position that they are lying."

Gilbert thinks Michel Cormier’s evidence could have made a difference.

"I am embarrassed for the RCMP that they couldn't find him," she said. "Even without him testifying, the RCMP speaking to him and hearing that she had disclosed her sexual abuse, I would have thought would have been a persuasive reason to lay a charge."

RCMP Const. Simon Boucher was "not able to do an interview" with CBC, according to the force’s media relations officer in New Brunswick.

According to Sunny Marriner, national lead for the Improving Institutional Accountability Project, investigators displayed "textbook behaviour" when they claimed Budd was an unreliable witness because as a teen she'd lied, done drugs and run away.

"Children who are experiencing sexual abuse may withdraw. They begin to have difficulty attending school or engaging in activities. They frequently run away," she said. "It doesn't undermine credibility, it supports that something was happening to the child at that time."

'It wasn't abuse, it was love,' Plouffe said of his relationship with Budd when she was still in her teens and he was her foster father. (Francis Ferland/CBC)

Decades later, Gilles Plouffe still frames what happened in his foster home not as abuse, but as a love story.

"It's wrong, but that doesn't mean we have to go and and really shove it down my throat and say that was really wrong, beat me on the head," Plouffe said. "It wasn't abuse, it was love.”

That’s a story Marriner says she’s heard before in her work with survivors.

"It is not love, it is exploitation," she said. "Many people will be familiar with the term grooming.… It means very slowly creating a bond with the person that you intend to exploit that makes them believe that the two of you are on the same team together against the entire world."

Looking back, Budd realizes the odds were stacked against her.

"He got away with it because he was in the RCMP, so it got covered up for him and he got protected and he'll never be charged," she said.

Budd, right, shows Ireton the statement of claim in her case against her former foster father. (Francis Ferland/CBC)

In the spring of 2019, Budd filed a lawsuit against the province of New Brunswick, the Moncton Hospital, the regional health authority and Gilles Plouffe.

"Plouffe was given the power and duty to discipline and punish the plaintiff, which he used to perpetrate the physical, emotional and sexual abuse," noted the statement of claim.

The lawsuit alleged the institutions were negligent and the hospital psychologist breached his fiduciary duty by failing to report the sexual abuse to the RCMP.

Those institutions denied all allegations, and in formal statements of defence noted that any injury, loss or damages suffered by the plaintiff were no fault of theirs. They also declined to talk to CBC about the case.

In July 2026 a judge at the Moncton Court of King's Bench heard a trial for damages against Gilles Plouffe. A decision is pending. (Michael Heenan/CBC)

There was no trial, and in 2024 the suit was resolved out of court. Details are not public.

Plouffe didn’t defend himself against the claim and in November 2019 was found in default — the civil court’s way of saying he didn't bring forward any evidence to deny the allegation that he repeatedly sexually abused, assaulted and molested Budd for two years, starting when she was 15.

This July, the Court of King’s Bench in Moncton heard a trial for damages in the case of Kimberly Anne Budd vs. Joseph Yves Gilles Plouffe.

"I want his acknowledgement. I want some accountability for it," said Budd, who has been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety disorder and a persistent depressive disorder — conditions that will require treatment for the rest of her life.

Budd and her lawyer are still waiting for the judge’s decision in the case.

WATCH | Kim Budd says she hopes her family will now understand her past: Kim Budd says she hopes her family will now understand her past | Duration closed caption 0:37 On a visit to an Ottawa-area horse farm, Kim Budd says being around the animals relaxes her and helps in her recovery.

Plouffe has never acknowledged that what he did changed the course of a teen girl’s life, and no one has ever asked him to. Marrying Budd and having children with her didn’t change anything.

For two years, between the ages of 15 and 17, she was a child and her foster parents were in charge. Institutions failed her, and worse, sought to discredit her when she tried to tell them the truth.

Gilles Plouffe’s position with the police gave him privilege and standing in the community. The reaction of the systems intended to protect children exemplifies the entitlement he enjoyed as an officer.

It's why Budd feels she has to keep telling her side of the story, over and over again.

"Some people might call it revenge, but it's not — it’s justice," said Budd. "I want the record set straight."

Budd’s story is tragic, and repeating it is embarrassing and painful, but she realized long ago that she needed to stop running from it.

"I want my kids to hear it. They're old enough now they can process it … and they can make their decisions."

Kim Budd was a troubled teenager, a vulnerable kid whose imperfections placed her in a perfect position to be victimized over and over again.

Today, she’s a survivor.

WATCH | How her search for safety turned into a twisted nightmare of control: How her search for safety turned into a twisted nightmare of control | Duration closed caption 8:52 In 2017, Kim Budd finally reported to police that she was groomed and abused by her foster father — an RCMP officer she would eventually marry. CBC’s Julie Ireton unpacks a haunting true story of institutional failure and a survivor's fight to be heard.

World.title: Anthem singer apologizes for botched O Canada lyrics at Leafs game against Islanders
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The anthem singer at the Toronto Maple Leafs game against New York Monday night apologized on social media after singing the wrong lyrics to O Canada.

Sarrah Strimel Bentley, a former Broadway actress, bungled the words to the Canadian national anthem multiple times during her performance at UBS Arena in New York on Monday.

“We lend our hearts to thee,” the singer sang repeatedly, missing the mark on the correct lyrics, “we stand on guard for thee.”

She also messed up the words in other places, singing, “True patriot love, with all of us command,” rather than, “in all of us command.”

Auston Matthews’ reaction to the Canadian national anthem being sung wrong is incredible 😭 “We lend our hearts to thee” 🤨 #leafs https://t.co/Ar59glBfGS —Leafslatest

Videos of the anthem circulated online immediately afterwards and social media was flooded with reactions from fans who were unhappy with Bentley's rendition.

“This is disgraceful,” said one user on X.

“Anthem singer on Long Island is just making up her own words,” wrote another.

Many of the social media posts included clips of Leafs fans looking confused in the stands, along with clips of Leafs captain Auston Matthews who appeared perplexed as the wrong lyrics echoed through the arena.

Bentley apologized for the fumble in a tearful video she posted on Instagram during the game.

“I botched the lyrics and I’m really sorry,” she said in the video, adding that she loves Canada.

Bentley said she had repeatedly practiced O Canada, but "getting up in front of 18,000 people and singing an anthem that you haven't heard for your whole life is scary.”

Monday was the New York Islanders’ Hockey Fights Cancer Night. Bentley said breast cancer treatment caused her to enter menopause which can cause lapses in memory.

“I just wish that you’d be a little easier on someone who’s just a human being,” she said, visibly choked up in the video.

Jake McCabe, would lend my heart to thee https://t.co/Qi1U3YWoIm —MapleLeafs

The Maple Leafs beat the Islanders four to two Monday night, ending the team's nine-game losing streak. The club poked fun at the anthem debacle in social media posts.

One of the team’s posts featured a clip of Leafs defenseman Jake McCabe scoring the team’s first goal of the game. “Jake McCabe, would lend my heart to thee,” the post reads.

“Thou lend, thou win,” the team wrote on X following the win.

Toronto city councillor Mike Colle is calling on the Leafs to invite Bentley to perform O Canada at a game in Toronto. He asked fans to "knock off the hate," in a Facebook post on Tuesday.

"Let’s show our compassion and kindness as Canadians," he said in the post.

World.title: Smart watches and glasses no longer allowed in Manitoba schools
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Smart glasses, smart watches and other wearable technologies are now included in the ban on cellphones in schools that has been in place since September 2024, says the Manitoba government.

Education Minister Tracy Schmidt sent a directive to school leaders last week, telling them to include the devices in their cellphone ban.

"As technology evolves, so must our guidelines to ensure students are learning in healthy, safe environments that support their education and well-being," Schmidt said in a statement sent to the CBC.

The intent of the original cellphone ban was "to reduce distractions in classrooms and minimize the harmful impacts associated with social media and online platforms," said the Nov. 17 letter, which was sent to all school division superintendents as well as principals of independent schools that receive public funding.

"As technology continues to evolve, students increasingly have access to a wide range of personal devices … that allow access to messaging, social media, internet browsing, photography, audio or video recording, artificial intelligence tools, or other cellphone-like functions can create many of the same distractions and harms that cellphones cause."

Meta smart glasses have built-in artificial intelligence, cameras, speakerphones, microphones and touch controls. (Shane Fowler/CBC)

The directive was issued one week after Hanover School Division became the first in the province to ban smart glasses in its schools.

A letter sent to parents by the division in southeast Manitoba cited privacy implications because "they can record audio and video without others readily knowing."

A Canadian media literacy expert said Manitoba is on the right track, but she would like to see rules established on a federal level.

"What we don't want to end up with is a sort of patchwork of 13 different provinces and territories trying to regulate this in a sort of different shade of grey, if you will, around the same kind of technological challenge," said Kara Brisson-Boivin, director of research at Mediasmarts, a digital media literacy advocacy group based in Ottawa.

As technology evolves, students increasingly have access to a range of personal devices that offer the same functions as cellphones, and can cause the same distractions and harms as cellphones, Brisson-Boivin said.

Meta, one of several makers of AI glasses, says on its website that its product includes an LED light that blinks to alert others the wearer is taking a picture or recording video, and the glasses will automatically disable the camera if they detect the capture light was covered or tampered with.

"That's difficult to recognize, especially when we're talking about children and youth. We have to teach a lot of privacy-forward practices that are increasingly difficult to do, with especially younger children," Brisson-Boivin said.

Wearable devices that 'allow access to messaging, social media, internet browsing, photography, audio or video recording, artificial intelligence tools, or other cellphone-like functions' can create the same distractions as cellphones, Manitoba Education Minister Tracy Schmidt says. (Steffi Loos/The Associated Press)

The subject of the recording also has to notice the light, and online criticism says the LEDs are small and easy to miss in direct sunlight and even bright indoor lighting, from the side or in crowded spaces.

While Brisson-Boivin appreciates Manitoba's efforts around wearable tech, she doesn't believe policing it should fall on the shoulders of teachers and other school staff.

"Educators are already so overwrought and overrun with all of their day-to-day challenges that placing an additional challenge of managing new tech … is really difficult to do," she said.

She's also not convinced a blanket long-term ban is the right way to go.

The drawbacks to the tech are clear but consideration needs to be given to those who rely on it, Brisson-Boivin said.

Students with visual impairments and hearing impairments could be aided by it, "but we don't know enough yet about the potential benefits," she said.

"It makes good sense to want to slow down the integration of new forms of technology, to be able to do it in a way that feels controlled, that we sort of study the benefits as well as the harms.”

Taking advantage of any potential benefits must be done with the proper protections in place, she said.

There must be regulations that hold developers accountable for privacy considerations and a support around education on "how, when and where to use the technology" and when not to, Brisson-Boivin said.

"Manitoba is taking important steps, but I think that we need to have a broader conversation across the country about the role and the place of wearable technology," she said.

"AI, like any other technology, is a tool, and tools can be used to hone our skills, but we don't want those tools to be used to replace our skills."

World.title: 11-year-old Carly Rae Jepsen song surges up the charts thanks to GTA VI needle drop
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Carly Rae Jepsen's saxophone-backed track Run Away With Me is getting a boost more than a decade after its release, thanks to its inclusion in the blockbuster video game Grand Theft Auto VI.

The song, originally released in 2015, is taking on a new life with a surprise remix in the game: between Nov. 16-22, there was a week over week increase of 157 per cent for listens to Run Away With Me on Spotify.

"Secret's finally out! GTA 6 let's run away together," Jepsen wrote on Instagram.

In a special mission sequence in the game, the song plays while the characters Jason and Lucia ride Sea-Doos.

Jepsen's fans have reacted across social media, with several commenting on YouTube under the music video for the song. " This scene in that mission had me floating bro," wrote @VincentNNS, while @voxious07 wrote, "I love how everyone felt the same feeling at that mission, it was surreal. What a game. What a song. What an experience."

WATCH | The official music video for Run Away With Me:

The Weeknd's music also appeared in Vice City, courtesy of French electronic duo Justice.

The Toronto superstar is credited on My Only Vice, an unreleased track featured in the score for the long-awaited video game.

The song is among several original compositions credited to Justice, who created the game's main score. Rockstar Games lists the Weeknd, born Abel Tesfaye, as a co-writer alongside Justice members Gaspard Augé and Xavier de Rosnay.

The collaboration follows their work together on Wake Me Up, a track from the Weeknd’s 2025 album Hurry Up Tomorrow.

The Weeknd’s 2013 track Wanderlust is also featured on Flash FM, one of the game's fictional radio stations, alongside fellow Canadian Tate McRae's Sports car and Justin Bieber's 2017 collaboration with BloodPop, Friends.

WATCH | The official music video for Sports car:

Toronto rap star Drake also has several tracks in the game, including Nonstop, Nokia and Love Me, his collaboration with Lil Wayne and Future.

His 2013 hit Hold On, We're Going Home, featuring Toronto R&B duo Majid Jordan, is also included.

The official score for GTA VI is set to be released Dec. 11.

Toronto instrumental jazz group BadBadNotGood is featured on Leonida Jazz Radio with Blowin’ Smoke, an apparently unreleased collaboration with American trumpeter Randy Brecker.

Electronic artists also received a boost

Over on Stockyard FM, Vancouver-bred electronic duo Bob Moses appear with their Elderbrook collaboration Inner Light, which gained renewed attention after being featured in a GTA VI trailer earlier this year.

The Grammy-nominated pair, Tom Howie and Jimmy Vallance, told the Canadian Press that the song had racked up more than 50 million new streams since the trailer's release in August.

The duo’s track Nothing But You, remixed by DJ Tennis, is also included in the game, along with Never Come Back by Dundas, Ont.-born electronic artist Caribou.

WATCH | The official music video for Never Come Back:

Montreal metal vets Voivod also get some shine in the game, with their track Panorama featuring on The Chamber 106.6, a heavy music station.

Flip the dial to V-Rock, and you’ll hear Roller by Halifax rock greats April Wine, as well as Loverboy’s ubiquitous ’80s anthem Working for the Weekend.

Montreal-based producer Martyn Bootyspoon is among the musicians credited with contributing to the game's supplemental score.

Music has long been integral to the GTA experience, with the franchise’s fictional radio stations exposing generations of players to an eclectic mix of sounds as they cruise city streets and flee the cops.

Bob Moses said they were paid a relatively modest licensing fee, but the payoff was in the exposure to their music.

“I forget how much money it was, but it’s not enough to remember,” said Howie.

“The opportunity is definitely in the potential for the reach, not in the paycheque.”

World.title: Canada's air force charts a potential future without the Gripen in 'Project Arrow'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada's air force has developed a vision of a future fighter jet fleet — one that is built around the F-35 and includes autonomous drones as well as another kind of manned aircraft, but makes no mention of the Swedish-made Gripen.

The proposal is called "Project Arrow," according to a discussion paper obtained by CBC News that is circulating within the Department of National Defence and Canada's defence industry.

The department confirmed the document's authenticity and said it was developed within a branch of the Royal Canadian Air Force (RCAF), while emphasizing it is primarily intended to stimulate discussion and does not constitute a formal military policy or procurement project.

Despite that caveat, Project Arrow confirms a desire to place American F-35 fighters at the centre of Canada's air capability planning.

Defence analyst Justin Massie believes Project Arrow is further proof that the RCAF doesn't want the Gripen, as the federal government is still considering whether to proceed with its full purchase of F-35s.

The Royal Canadian Air Force has already officially taken delivery of and affixed its insignia to two F-35 aircraft manufactured by Lockheed Martin. (Cpl. Nicholas Brunshaw/Canadian Armed Forces)

"Canada makes its defence policies with little public debate," he said. "What are the needs of the Canadian Armed Forces? How do we defend Canada?"

The government of Prime Minister Mark Carney has had discussions with Saab about possibly buying the latest version of the Gripen fighter and assembling them in Canada.

For now, Canada is maintaining its plan to acquire at least 16 F-35s and has begun paying for 14 more of the American aircraft — while studying the potential acquisition of Gripens to create a mixed fleet.

Mapping out role of autonomous drones

Project Arrow also emphasizes the eventual development in Canada of collaborative drones, a new type of aircraft described as an essential component of future fleets.

Eventually, these autonomous aircraft could carry out missions alongside modern human-piloted fighter jets such as the F-35. The goal is to increase the combat power of fighter fleets at lower cost while protecting human crews.

According to a Defence Department spokesperson, Project Arrow was developed by the autonomous collaborative platform program within the air force and does not take sides in the debate surrounding the Gripen.

An example of a collaborative combat drone: the MQ-28 Ghost Bat, manufactured by Boeing in collaboration with the Australian Armed Forces. (Boeing)

"It is a capability development concept that does not advocate for any particular fighter fleet composition or procurement outcome," said departmental spokesperson Andrée-Anne Poulin.

However, the discussion paper notes that Project Arrow "empowers more than just final assembly in Canada," which appears to be a barely veiled criticism of Saab's intentions for the Gripen.

Project Arrow identifies the need to focus on three areas:

Continuing the integration of F-35s into the Royal Canadian Air Force, a process already underway with the delivery of two aircraft this fall.

Developing, in Canada and by Canadian companies, a fleet of collaborative drones that would fly in formation with F-35s and whose intellectual property would belong to Canada.

Increasing Canada's participation in the Global Combat Air Program (GCAP), led by the United Kingdom, Italy and Japan, to develop what is known as the "sixth-generation" of fighter aircraft.

Canada joined GCAP as an observer last summer. For now, that status establishes partnerships with the other countries and allows Canada to obtain intellectual property benefits.

Canadian interest in the program, however, has already shown some benefit with a memorandum signed between the U.K.-based BAE Systems Inc. and Montreal-based Bombardier at the end of October. The two companies intend to explore mission-system design and digital engineering for the future sixth-generation fighter.

The Project Arrow proposal suggests Canada could simultaneously learn from the F-35, an aircraft at the cutting edge of current technology, while participating in the development of collaborative drones and sixth-generation fighters under GCAP.

The project would draw in particular on expertise already established in Canada in software, sensors, communications tools, electronic warfare and weapons, while continuing co-operation with allies in the United States, Europe and Asia.

According to experts, the development of Canadian capabilities in collaborative drones could take place under the leadership of Bombardier or Dominion Dynamics, a newcomer based in Ottawa.

WATCH | More about collaborative drones: AI drone warfare is here. Should Canada buy in? | Duration closed caption 6:05 Governments are spending billions on the autonomous arms race — should Canada join in? For The National, CBC’s Jennifer Yoon examines the future of AI-powered military weapons, what it means for international humanitarian law and where Canada fits in.

Dominion Dynamics is moving full-speed ahead on a roughly $500-million project to develop a Canadian collaborative drone nicknamed the Dominion Scout, which would be particularly well suited to missions in the Arctic.

The company recently announced an agreement with engine manufacturer Pratt & Whitney Canada, guaranteeing access to an advanced propulsion system.

Although the federal government has not yet committed to the project, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly has praised the effort for "positioning Canada to lead in the next generation of aerospace manufacturing."

Eliot Pence is founder and CEO of Dominion Dynamics. Behind him to the left is a model of the Dominion Scout, an uncrewed aircraft the company is developing. (Matthew Kupfer/CBC)

The founder of the Ottawa startup, Eliot Pence, says the future Dominion Scout will operate alongside F-35s and other fighters, ships, ground-based sensors and the GlobalEye radar aircraft that Canada is in the process of purchasing.

According to Pence, the Scout will distinguish itself from its competitors by being able to receive orders from airborne, shipborne or ground-based command systems.

"Canada needs to focus on sixth-generation capabilities, that is where air dominance is going," Pence said in a recent interview.

'Economic return' part of Carney's decision

In an interview with the New York Times earlier this year, Carney said his government was still studying the option of purchasing the Swedish fighter jets.

"It is a real decision because of differing capabilities, because of strategic dependencies and because of the economic return," he said.

Retired lieutenant-general Yvan Blondin believes the air force is trying to move past the Gripen issue.

"What's happening with Project Arrow is that the Royal Canadian Air Force is planning only [to continue using] the F-35," said Blondin.

The former air force commander says this illustrates the extent to which some military officials are prepared to ignore the risks of placing the F-35 at the heart of their long-term strategy.

Those risks include a future U.S. president being able to "control not only the use of our F-35s, but also the use of our combat drones," he said.

Massie said Project Arrow could fuel an important discussion about the future of Canada's aerospace defence program.

For now, he said he fears the debate surrounding the Gripen is focused on economic issues rather than Canada's long-term strategy for defending the Arctic against Chinese or Russian threats.

"We don't make defence policy to create jobs. Otherwise we'd have an economic policy," Massie said.

World.title: Gisèle Pelicot 'deeply shocked' after nude images from her rape case used in book promotion
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Gisèle Pelicot says she is deeply shocked that a Paris publishing house used nude images taken of her by her rapist ex-husband as promotional materials for a book that examines her watershed fight for justice.

The 73-year-old Pelicot became an icon of courage and feminist causes during the drugging-and-rape trial in 2024 that convicted all 51 of the accused men, including her ex-husband, Dominique Pelicot.

In a statement to the French news channel BFMTV, she denounced the book, Emprises, and the publisher's use of intimate photos in promoting it. The broadcaster published extracts of the statement on Monday.

"I am deeply shocked that images of the most private aspects of my life could be exhibited and exploited for commercial gain," the statement said, according to BFMTV.

"I refuse to let my private life be used as a selling point."

The nude images of Pelicot were apparently taken by Dominique Pelicot and were part of the court case that saw him sentenced to 20 years in prison, said Christophe Bigot, a lawyer for Gisèle Pelicot, speaking Tuesday to The Associated Press.

Bigot said he has seen the images and that they show Gisèle Pelicot alone — without the men convicted for rapes and sexual assaults while she was unconscious, knocked out with drugs that Dominique Pelicot slipped into her food and drink.

Gisèle Pelicot's statement also criticized the book itself, saying it "describes scenes of me being raped and gives an interpretation of my life that is unbearable."

"Above all, I refuse to let my story be re-written to suggest that I was complicit with what I was subjected to," she said, according to the statement extracts.

"Today, I find myself humiliated, exposed and hurt once again. As if the ordeal of the trial hadn't been enough!"

'Unfortunate and ill-suited'

The publisher, Éditions Tinbad, didn't respond Tuesday to emailed questions. On its website, it acknowledged that promotional efforts had been "unfortunate and ill-suited."

It offered "sincerest apologies" to Pelicot and to author Sabine Prokhoris.

The company said that it won't print any additional runs of the book beyond the 280 copies now in the hands of its distributor, and that it will stop promoting it.

WATCH | Pelicot talks to CBC News: Gisèle Pelicot talks about first seeing images of her assaults | Duration 1:37 In a Canadian broadcast exclusive interview, Gisèle Pelicot told Piya Chattopadhyay, host of CBC Radio’s The Sunday Magazine, about the moment police first showed her photos of her being sexually assaulted by men she didn’t recognize inside her own home.

But it also said that "absolutely no images of her being raped or video of a pornographic nature were sent to the press."

The weekly newspaper Le Canard Enchainé first reported last week that the publisher sent photos and videos of Gisèle Pelicot to several media outlets. The newspaper described the images as pornographic and said they were taken by Dominique Pelicot.

It quoted the publisher as saying: "Of course we don't have Mrs. Pelicot's permission to distribute these photos. That is why we sent them to you solely for private, informational purposes."

The police evidence against Dominique Pelicot included his library of images documenting years of abuse — more than 20,000 photos and videos in all, stored on computer drives and catalogued in folders marked "abuse," "her rapists," "night alone" and other titles.

He and all but one of his co-defendants were convicted of sexually assaulting Gisèle Pelicot over a period of nearly a decade. The other co-defendant was convicted of drugging and raping his own wife with Dominique Pelicot's help.

Gisèle Pelicot became a hero to many in France and beyond for demanding that all the evidence be heard in open court, waiving her right to anonymity as a survivor of sexual abuse and insisting that shame should fall on her abusers, not her.

World.title: 22 injured after car bomb strikes central Colombia governor’s office
World.content:
Twenty-two people were reportedly injured and more than 80 buildings were damaged in a car bomb attack on the Governor’s Office of Meta in Villavicencio, central Colombia.

According to Meta’s Security Secretary, Franklin Olivos, the car that exploded carried approximately 100 kilograms of explosives and caused damage to buildings that were located more than 100 meters away from the blast.

Among the injured are five private security guards. One of them needed surgery, according to his employer.

Olivos blamed the attack on the 39th Front, a unit of the FARC dissident group EMC, which has opposed the peace process that started 10 years ago on Tuesday and controls large swathes of jungle territory in the south of Colombia.

In an initial response, President Abelardo de la Espriella said that “narcoterrorism is desperate because we are confronting it head-on. It seeks to intimidate us and force us to back down so we seek another sham peace process.”

De la Espriella, an opponent of the peace process, has been advertising an “iron fist” policy against organized crime and illegal armed groups.

The president’s alleged offensive has failed to produce any results and guerrilla groups have continued to attack State security forces and infrastructure.

World.title: Colombia strips key critics of security details
World.content:
Colombia’s National Protection Unit (UNP) has withdrawn the security details of journalist Daniel Coronell, a major critic of President Abelardo de la Espriella, after vowing to protect the freedom of the press.

Coronell’s local security detail was removed because he lives in the United States, which would make it impossible for the UNP to reassess his protection plan.

The Miami-based journalist frequently travels to Colombia for his work and was in Bogota to receive a lifetime achievement award from the national journalism prize.
