While receiving the prize, Coronell sharply criticized De la Espriella for promoting self-promotion over governance. using state resources to censor critics, restricting public information to “friendly media,” and leveraging a history of aggressive lawsuits against reporters.

The journalist’s criticism triggered a clash with Interior Minister Alejandro Ordoñez, who accused Coronell of being angry for having State subsidies pulled.

After press freedom foundation FLIP responded to defend Coronell, Ordoñez claimed that “the freedom of the press enjoys full protection and guarantees from the government.”

We value and defend freedom of the press as a cornerstone of democracy. The press is free, but it is also responsible. It is not a license to abuse, slander, defame, fabricate stories, spread misinformation, or engage in politics. Nor is it a license to destroy democracy or its institutions with lies. Interior Minister Alejandro Ordoñez

Coronell played a key role in Colombian journalism since the late 1980’s and was forced to flee Colombia in 2005 after reports on the ties of former President Alvaro Uribe and paramilitary groups escalated death threats.

The journalist currently works with Noticias Uno and Caracol Radio, and has more than 700,000 subscribers on YouTube.

The UNP previously stripped former President Gustavo Petro and former presidential candidate Claudia Lopez of their security details.

World.title: Illegal armed group carries out first urban drone attack: three injured in northeast Colombia
World.content:
A couple and their 18-month-old baby were injured in a drone attack on a police station in Cucuta, the first major city to be struck from the sky by guerrilla explosives.

The attack damaged more than 60 homes near the Norte de Santander Police Department in the Tasajero neighborhood in the north of the regional capital, the province’s security secretary, George Quintero, told press.

As of now, the situation is as follows: more than 60 damaged homes located just 20 meters from the police headquarters, and three people injured. Security secretary George Quintero

The homes were hit because the police department’s signal-jamming systems reportedly caused the drones to miss their target.

An unknown number of drones were able to reach the interior of the Police Department’s compound, leaving only minor damage.

Guerrilla group ELN has been carrying out multiple drone attacks in Catatumbo, a nearby region with major coca cultivations, and exercises control in the peripheral slums of Cucuta.

The group was accused of attacking the same police department with home-made mortars in August. This attack injured seven policemen.

In a response to the guerrilla attack, President Abelardo de la Espriella in October ordered the militarization of the border city, which has been struggling with security issues for years.

De la Espriella vowed that he “will not allow narco-terrorism to continue sowing fear and threatening families” in Cucuta and the surrounding Norte de Santander province.

According to the authorities, the militarization of the city sought to “strengthen territorial control, protect citizens, and confront” the illegal armed groups that operate in and around Cucuta.

The president’s offensive against illegal armed groups and organized crime has been hampered by an increase in the use of drones that are equipped with explosives.

All kinds of illegal armed groups use the relatively new technology to push back the authorities from areas under their control.

World.title: Colombia asks X to suspend Petro’s social media account
World.content:
Colombia’s communications ministry said Sunday that it had requested social media platform X to suspend former President Gustavo Petro for “possible incitement to violence.”

In a statement that was published of X, the ministry said it reported Petro’s account to X’s Public Affairs, Safety, and Rules Enforcement Team.

According to the statement, the request to suspend the leftist former president, who has more than 9 million followers, was due to a November 21 post in which Petro asked “the people of Colombia to demand Abelardo’s resignation now.”

Petro has been trying to promote popular opposition against De la Espriella, who he has called an illegitimate president.

According to the ministry, Petro’s call to “take action in the streets” could constitute a call for violence against the government.

In a response, the former president said the De la Espriella administration sought to impose censorship on him, which is “expressly prohibited by the Constitution.”

The ministry’s request “demonstrates the extent of the current government’s illegitimacy,” added Petro.

The former president is now the leader of the Historic Pact (PH) opposition party and has actively been promoting a general strike in response to his successor’s controversial policy decisions.

Petro is a member of the PH’s more radical wing and can still count on a significant following among Colombia’s population.

World.title: The deteriorating press freedom in Colombia and the Americas
World.content:
I sat down with Joshua Collins of Pirate Wire Services to discuss the deteriorating press freedom situation in Colombia and the rest of Latin America.

World.title: De la Espriella calls on US to prosecute Petro in response to call to “resign now”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the US Justice Department to “investigate, prosecute and hopefully jail former President Gustavo Petro after the latter called on the people to “rise up” and “restore real democracy.”

De la Espriella addressed the nation at the end of a day of anti-government marches that mobilized tens of thousands of people throughout Colombia.

Petro led the march in Cali and called on his supporters to “rise up,” call a general strike and force the president to “leave now,” less than four months after De la Espriella took office.

Reiterating fraud accusations and the president’s business ties to paramilitary warlords and drug traffickers, the former president told the crowd that “it is not about waiting until 2030; an illegitimate government must leave now.”

A government whose policy goes against the people must leave now. A government whose policy builds hunger and death for the people of Colombia must leave now. Life must be restored, democracy must be restored, and the slogan “Abelardo, resign now!” must become the slogan of the majority of the Colombian people. An agreement will eventually be made to transition back so that the Constitution of Colombia and the laws in favor of the Colombian people prevail. But from here on out—and that is why we must move to a national strike, that is why we must move to a general strike—within the people’s right of expression and decision, an illegitimate government that goes against the interests of the Colombian population must leave now. Gustavo Petro

De la Espriella told Petro that he would never accept they “attack democracy, promote a coup d’état or attempt to destroy Colombia, just as he did when he was a guerrilla fighter.”

The president claimed that the former President and congressional opposition leader Ivan Cepeda “have no moral authority whatsoever. However, as I tell you, I will not accept them attacking democracy, attacking institutionality, or promoting a coup d’état in an attempt to destroy Colombia.”

De la Espriella repeated his threat to extradite his predecessor if requested to do so by the administration of his ally, US President Donald Trump.

I make a direct call to the judicial authorities of the United States so that investigations related to acts of corruption, drug trafficking, or any other criminal conduct move forward with full rigor and the independence of the judicial system in the United States. Petro’s government was a criminal enterprise, and international laws and provisions were violated. The United States has jurisdiction to investigate him, prosecute him, and hopefully imprison him. Let the North American justice system act, let the whole truth be known, let the evidence be examined, and let those found responsible answer before the law without regard for anything other than the application of the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president has tried to criminalize the opposition and the former government ever since taking office in August without much success.

World.title: Colombia rejects US proposal to conduct joint strikes against drug trafficking: NYT
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella rejected a US plan to conduct joint military operations, anonymous US officials told the New York Times (NYT).

According to the NYT, De la Espriella told the US government he supported working with the US military, but lacked congressional support invite US soldiers on Colombian soil.

The conversation would have taken place in the week ahead of US defense secretary Pete Hegseth’s visit to Colombia on Wednesday.

In a response, the president and the defense secretary said that the alleged US plan was “fake news.”

“I have not rejected any proposal of the Government of President Donald Trump,” De la Espriella said on social media platform X.

Colombia and the United States maintain strong and increasingly close cooperation in the areas of security, intelligence, and the fight against drug cartels and narco-terrorist organizations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president confirmed that congressional approval would be required for him to invite foreign troops into Colombia.

Between visits to Venezuela and Ecuador, Hegseth briefly stopped in Colombia, and met with Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora and Foreign Minister Omar Bulla.

The defense secretary expressed his support for the government’s plans to combat drug trafficking.

“You, sir, are never going to have a stronger partner than President Trump, Secretary Hegseth an the War Department,” Hegseth told Bula.

Both the US and the Colombian governments have assumed a militaristic approach to drug trafficking, contrary to their predecessors.

World.title: “Basic food stuffs exempt from sales tax:” De la Espriella on tax reform bill
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella rolled back his government’s plan to impose sales tax on basic food stuffs in an attempt to seek approval for his tax reform in Congress.

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella said that “basic household goods will be exempt from VAT. I made that clear from the very beginning.”

Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo and Finance Minister Miguel Gomez last month announced the introduction of a 19% sales tax on basic food stuffs and the creation of a mechanism that would allow the poor to recover this money.

The radical proposal was necessary to prevent Colombia from defaulting on debt, said Gomez.

However, “after several analyses, they adjusted the proposal to protect the basic food basket, which required a greater effort on the part of the government,” the president said Sunday.

De la Espriella’s tax reform, which will have to pass before December 16, got stuck in Congress after the coalition Liberal Party said they wouldn’t support taxing the basic food basket.

Also the far-right Democratic Center party opposed the measure, which almost immediately triggered calls for a national strike.

The president suggested that he would cut expenses he blamed on the leftist “criminal organizations” that won the 2022 elections with former President Gustavo Petro.

My true tax reform is the fight against corruption, against the criminal organizations that squandered the state’s resources for so many years. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“There is still a lot to do, but you can’t fix that disaster in three months,” said De la Espriella.

Contrary to campaign promises to reduce the State apparatus, De la Espriella proposed a 2027 budget that increased state spending.

On top of that, the government has been talking to the International Monetary Fund about a credit line that would support his increased spending.

World.title: AI Data Centers: Local Damage, World Threat
World.content:
Demonstrators protest against a planned data center in Decatur, Georgia. ‘Concerns over AI, rising energy costs and the environment are intermeshing.’ Photo: Erik S Lesser/EPA

By Jomo Kwame Sundaram and Rachel Gong (IPS)

HAVANA TIMES – Mass local opposition to AI data centers influenced the US mid-term elections. Perverse incentives have driven speculative investments to build more despite poor returns so far. Worse, financing investments using loans risks causing a major financial crisis.



The massive computing demands of AI (artificial intelligence) requiring hyperscale data centers have grown rapidly over the last decade, greatly exceeding traditional storage cloud providers for general web hosting or standard information technology.



The number of such data centers worldwide has nearly tripled, with most in the US, but local opposition has slowed plans to build more. It is unclear how many data centers are being built, as details are often withheld, even from governments.



AI data centers in the US have been very unpopular with local communities. They are noisy and ugly, draining energy and water resources, with most profits going to the mainly US companies building them.



They use much electricity, straining electricity grids and driving up electricity prices. Data centers largely run on fossil fuels, exacerbating greenhouse gas emissions and planetary heating.



Data centers need a huge amount of freshwater to prevent overheating. Yet, more are being built despite spreading droughts and water stress.



There are also other significant health and environmental concerns that promoters hide, claiming modern data centers use ‘closed-loop systems’ reducing their adverse impacts.

Rachel Gong

Governments claim they create employment, although only a small fraction of promised jobs have materialised. Unsurprisingly, there is growing local opposition to AI data centers worldwide.



After meeting with China’s leader Xi Jinping following the midterms, Trump threatened tough measures against building data centers abroad, deeming their US presence necessary to maintain US dominance.



AI expects AI bubble to collapse



Dean Baker asked various AI chatbots whether pension and hedge fund investment managers face perverse incentives when investing in AI-related companies.



If they did not invest in companies which have far outperformed others in recent times, their performance would fall behind their peers, costing them bonuses and even their jobs.



And if all AI stocks fell, they would not be penalised as other fund managers had done likewise. AI agreed that asset managers would keep investing in AI even though their market performance did not make sense.



They would continue such investments as keeping their jobs required following the herd and ‘riding the wave’.



Such perverse incentives may also induce similar behavior among top executives at Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle.



All of them have “committed hundreds of billions of their companies’ capital to building data centres to support the AI producers, primarily OpenAI and Anthropic”.



And what if AI companies have ‘over-invested’ trillions in data centers with limited prospects of profitability? If this view of AI’s future is widely shared, it would make sense to stop building and cut losses.



But what if AI top executives still believe it is better to continue investing? Perhaps AI will eventually pay off. And if they stopped investing to cut their losses, they could also lose trillions, probably ending their careers.



Hence, they keep building data centers even if they suspect they are pouring in good money after bad. AI generally agrees that top executives are likely to continue investing.

Jomo Kwame Sundaram

After the AI bubble bursts, it is likely there will be some obligatory investigations into how and why the AI boom became a dangerously unsustainable bubble until ‘business as usual’ resumes.



When the bubble bursts



William H. Janeway notes the notion of an ‘AI speculative investment bubble’ has recently been widely accepted. Since bubbles inevitably burst, fears are now rising that time is running out.



Janeway warns that the AI industry’s heavy and still growing reliance on borrowed money risks triggering a major financial crisis. AI hyperscalers have to keep increasing profits to justify the still rising investments and borrowings.



If generative AI delivers productivity gains across a wide range of applications, the current frenzy may be remembered as a productive bubble.



But it is unlikely these gains will be large and soon enough to justify the huge investments in AI infrastructure to date.



Growing reliance on private credit to fund current data center building, with lenders themselves borrowing from banks, implies the AI bubble is enmeshed with the financial system.



The AI bubble can still deflate gradually rather than burst abruptly. Hence, slowing AI growth and data center construction delays may actually be better for the economy.



However, the risk of sudden collapse remains. The second Trump administration’s record so far generates broader concerns about how it is likely to handle an AI bust.



Thankfully, however, history reminds us that speculative bubbles may leave behind some valuable infrastructure in their wake despite bankrupting those financing them.



Rachel Gong is Associate Director of Research at the Khazanah Research Institute studying the intersections of digital technologies, society and policy.

World.title: Those Who Really Mistreat You and Don’t Care About You
World.content:
Eggs for 130 pesos each or 3,600 for a carton of 30.

By Lien Estrada

HAVANA TIMES – In his song “La sal no sala” (Salt Doesn’t Make Things Salty), Argentine singer Charly García has a line that goes: “The girl on the corner is treating me badly, she sells me a drug I can’t afford.” When I first heard it, I found it quite amusing. I’ve enjoyed his entire discography thanks to a friend abroad who was kind enough to get it for me.

Back then, we didn’t have Internet access, and Charly García’s music wasn’t heard in Cuba because, as I understand it, like John Lennon, he had made statements unfavorable to the dictator, Fidel Castro. And, of course, he was never forgiven for that.

However, I had seen a television interview with Colombian singer Carlos Vives, who said that Charly Garcia’s music was exceptional, and that was when I asked my friend to do me the favor of getting it for me. And he did. Like Fito Paez’s music, I find it revealing. But the line that has stayed with me the most is this cheeky one about the girl who sells a product at such a high price that it cannot be purchased, and the singer interprets that as mistreatment.

Perhaps this line has resonated so deeply with me because I live in a context where buying anything is a real challenge. When you find that a package of seasoned sausages costs far more than most people’s retirement pensions. A 10-pound package of chicken costs 9,500 pesos when the minimum wage is 3,210 pesos. A piece of candy costs 40 pesos. And to think that I had naively believed that everything would improve once the currencies were unified, supposedly in 2021.

That experience with stores where prices were in US dollars, but salaries and pensions were paid in Cuban pesos was never a good one, not even for those who belonged to the country’s sole political party, which runs everything and controls everything. Therein lies the difference between Cuban reality and the line from Charly’s song “La sal no sala.”

We know that those who mistreat us with these economic measures to “save the Homeland” are certainly not the girl on the corner. Nor is it the young man with the pushcart trying to sell lemons that will eventually rot because most people cannot afford them. Those mistreating us are not the women who resell goods, because there are few other business opportunities in this land. Cuba stopped producing things quite some time ago.

Those who mistreat us are those elderly gentlemen dressed in olive green, whom there seems to be no way of convincing that building an economy is essential to saving that very Homeland they are forever mentioning in their speeches, and that our daily bread cannot be obtained by talking about ideological work among the people.

But we don’t know how to get the message across by force (through sabotage, gunfire, and bombs), and these army officers won’t listen to reason. They see no mistreatment whatsoever in their political and economic management of a country that is increasingly falling apart, but rather “decisions that are not fair, but necessary,” as the tyrant Commander-in-Chief Fidel Castro once put it.

People decide to leave. Even sensing the truth of what the French say: “To leave is to die a little.” It doesn’t matter. More than a million Cubans have decided they will no longer endure mistreatment at the hands of a government that refuses to budge and is utterly convinced that it is right. More and more people are leaving. Every day.

One thing, however, is clearer than ever: it is not the girl on the corner who is mistreating us. And that is an important fact.

Read more from the diary of Lien Estrada here on Havana Times.

World.title: International News Briefs for Tuesday, November 24, 2026
World.content:
HAVANA TIMES – We bring you some of the top international news stories compiled by Democracy Now on Tuesday, November 24, 2026.

Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO After Trump Intervenes

Nov 24, 2026

Image Credit: X/@aburducky

Jensen Huang is back as CEO of the chip giant Nvidia, after President Trump personally called into a meeting of the company’s board on Sunday to push for his reinstatement. Huang had resigned less than two weeks ago, after news reports revealed he had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman who was allegedly in communication with China’s top spy agency. The woman worked with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company suspected of buying advanced Nvidia chips and then diverting them to China in violation of U.S. export rules. On Monday, the Commerce Department added Megaspeed to its trade blacklist. During an interview on CNBC, President Trump was questioned about his role in reinstating Huang.

Eamon Javers: “Mr. President, did you give the board of directors an assurance that Jensen Huang would not be prosecuted at all for any of these” —

President Donald Trump: “I didn’t use the word ‘prosecuted.’”

Eamon Javers: — “questions around export controls?”

President Donald Trump: “But I said — I said that we believe — and I put out a statement. I think you probably saw that.”

Eamon Javers: “We did, yes.”

President Donald Trump: “That we believe he’s fine, he’s absolutely fine. I gave them enough” —

Carl Quintanilla: “There was a” —

President Donald Trump: — “assurance.”

Meanwhile, President Trump used his Truth Social platform to share a bizarre AI-generated meme that altered a photo taken moments after Trump was shot in Butler, Pennsylvania, in 2024. The doctored photo depicts a bloodied Huang holding a red bra in the air, with an Nvidia flag replacing the U.S. flag behind him.

Trump’s Stake in Nvidia Grows by Up to $15 Million as Stock Price Soars on Jensen Huang’s Return

Nov 24, 2026

Image Credit: Joyce N. Boghosian

News of Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia sent share prices soaring by over 30%, recovering much of the value lost since Huang resigned two weeks ago. Among beneficiaries of the stock surge is President Trump, whose stake in Nvidia grew to as much as $62 million before the scandal broke. Trump’s net worth grew by up to $15 million on Monday. Also benefiting is Cantor Fitzgerald, the investment firm that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick ran for decades before joining the Trump administration. It’s now controlled by Lutnick’s sons, Brandon and Kyle. Cantor Fitzgerald held shares in Nvidia worth hundreds of millions of dollars, even as Lutnick made key decisions affecting Nvidia’s operations.

Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as CEO comes after Reuters reported Nvidia’s accounting practices have prompted an investigation by the Securities and Exchange Commission. Nvidia and Huang also face a class-action shareholder lawsuit in California alleging securities fraud and misleading investors. And Huang is scheduled to testify on Capitol Hill next week, both in private testimony to lawmakers and in a public session of the Senate Banking Committee. We’ll have more on this story after headlines.

Analysis Estimates More Than 700,000 Russian Soldiers Have Died Fighting in Ukraine

Nov 24, 2026

A new report estimates more than 700,000 Russian soldiers have died in combat since President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine nearly five years ago. The finding is based on an analysis of leaked data from Russia’s state statistics agency, published by a pair of Russian-language news outlets operating outside of Russia.

On Monday, the Kremlin warned that Ukraine will face “painful consequences” for drone attacks on Russian ships in Libya and the Baltic Sea. Overnight, Russian drone and missile attacks on Zaporizhzhia left two people dead and more than 40 others injured, after a guided aerial bomb hit an apartment building near a bridge crossing the Dnipro River.

UNICEF Says Russian Attacks Are Killing Three Children, on Average, Each Day in Ukraine

Nov 24, 2026

Russia’s latest deadly strikes came as the U.N. Children’s Fund said the number of children killed or injured in Ukraine is approaching levels not seen since 2022, during the first year of Russia’s full-scale invasion. This is UNICEF’s Louise Wateridge.

Louise Wateridge: “According to the Human Rights Monitoring Mission for Ukraine, at least 1,144 children have been killed or injured in Ukraine in the first 10 months of 2026. This is a higher number of verified child casualties than in any other of the previous three years here in Ukraine, and that is more than three children who have been killed or injured every single day.”

Russia Threatens “Open War” with Estonia, a Former Soviet Republic Turned NATO Member

Nov 24, 2026

Russia has threatened to attack Estonia, after the Kremlin accused the country of allowing Ukraine to launch attacks from Estonian territory. On Monday, Russia’s Foreign Ministry declared Estonia was “on the verge of triggering open war.” The threat came after Estonia announced the closure of its land border with Russia. Estonia is a former Soviet republic, and has been a NATO member since 2004.

Rapid Support Forces Launch Drone Attack on Sudan’s Capital as Electrical Grid Nears Collapse

Nov 24, 2026

Sudan’s military says it intercepted drones launched by the Rapid Support Forces over the capital Khartoum, following a series of attacks that struck the city’s main airport and several buildings, including a U.N. facility. At least four people were reportedly killed in those attacks. They came as Sudan’s power grid is on the brink of collapse following attacks on electricity stations

Yemen’s Houthis Say 41 Civilians Are Killed in Saudi Attacks Using U.S. Arms

Nov 24, 2026

In Yemen, officials with the Ansar Allah movement, also known as the Houthis, say Saudi warplanes killed 41 civilians in a single day, in a series of strikes carried out with U.S.-made ordnance. One Saudi airstrike targeted a telecommunications hub, leaving 17 civilians dead, according to a Houthi spokesperson. Other attacks targeted buses and public transport vehicles in Hodeidah and Lahij, reportedly with GBU-49 and GBU-12 bombs. The U.N. warns over 1,600 people have been killed and 300,000 displaced since the ceasefire in Yemen between the Saudi-backed government and the Houthis collapsed in July.

Oxfam Report Finds Israel’s Military Assault “Has Turned Gaza into a Toxic Wasteland”

Nov 24, 2026

In Gaza, an Israeli airstrike on a security post killed two police officers and another Palestinian in al-Mawasi, a narrow strip of land that Israel has designated as a so-called safe zone. Another strike killed three brothers traveling by donkey cart — one of them, a child. In Gaza City, Palestinians held a funeral for Adel al-Helo, an employee of the U.N. agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA, killed in an attack a day earlier. This is his brother, Nizar al-Helo.

Nizar al-Helo: “He was working at the water dam in Jabaliya camp, supplying the water for the people of Jabaliya camp, and have been killed by an airstrike in Jabaliya camp by the Israeli army. They doesn’t make any difference between the civilian people and other people, even the people of the United Nations.”

Meanwhile, Oxfam has published a new report titled “Environmental War Crimes: How Israel’s military assault has turned Gaza into a toxic wasteland, threatening human survival.” It finds contamination from heavy metals, explosive residue, asbestos fibers, dioxins, crystalline silica, persistent organic pollutants and biological contaminants across 99% of Gaza’s territory.

Lebanese Immigrants Are Set to Lose Protected Status in U.S., Despite Ongoing Israeli Assault

Nov 24, 2026

In southern Lebanon, Israeli forces launched a series of airstrikes, artillery and machine-gun attacks earlier today — the latest in a series of violations of a U.S.-mediated ceasefire Israel agreed to earlier this year. The violence has uprooted 1.2 million people from their homes — about one-fifth of Lebanon’s population.

Here in the U.S., a program granting temporary protected status to Lebanese immigrants and refugees is due to expire on Friday. A bill introduced by lawmakers in Michigan, a state home to a large Lebanese diaspora community, would extend TPS. It’s co-sponsored by Congresswoman Rashida Tlaib.

Rep. Rashida Tlaib: “Without temporary protected status, our neighbors are at risk of being deported to Lebanon, where the ongoing Israeli invasion — illegal Israeli invasion — and ethnic cleansing campaign has already killed 4,000 people this year. I introduced the Lebanon TPS Act because the safety of our neighbors cannot be left up to the whims of Trump and Stephen Miller.”

Mexico to Try Alleged Drug Kingpin “El Chapo Isidro” After Denying U.S. Extradition Request

Nov 24, 2026

Mexico’s military says it captured one of the leaders of the Beltrán Leyva cartel and two of his lieutenants during an operation in Sinaloa state on Friday night. The arrest of Fausto Isidro Meza Flores sparked a wave of armed ​clashes between Mexican security forces and cartel members, who set up flaming roadblocks in some areas. Meza Flores is known as “El Chapo Isidro” and is one ​of the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives. His arrest reportedly came in coordination with U.S. intelligence agencies. Mexico denied a U.S. request to extradite him, saying he will be tried in a Mexican court. The Trump administration has threatened to take unilateral ⁠military action inside Mexico after accusing the government of failing to halt narcotrafficking.

Alarm Grows over U.S. Army Plan to Explode Lead-Containing Munitions on Wednesday

Nov 24, 2026

The U.S. Army is proceeding with plans to blow up a stockpile of toxic explosives at a munitions plant in southeastern Iowa. The acting Army secretary said late Monday the “extensively mitigated, carefully controlled detonation” would occur on Wednesday morning, based on forecast wind conditions. The statement came hours after a federal court denied a request for an emergency stay from environmental groups who warn the plan could send a plume of toxic lead up to 100 miles away. In response, Senator Tammy Duckworth, an Army veteran whose home state of Illinois is potentially downwind of a lead-release disaster, wrote, “The Army still has failed to explain to the public why this detonation needs to happen this way — and too many people fear for their family’s health and safety. This is an extreme failure of communication, planning and leadership. And they must be held accountable for the harm done.”

Pete Hegseth Faces Call to Resign from His Former Chief of Staff

Nov 24, 2026

A former top aide to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is calling on him to resign, saying he has badly mismanaged both the Pentagon and the ongoing war in Iran and let showmanship get in the way of doing his job well. Joe Kasper, Hegseth’s chief of staff during the first three months of the second Trump administration, told Politico, “Pete’s been belligerent in his stewardship of an office that will outlive him or any memory of his service.”

Jimmy Gomez Quits Congress as Ethics Committee Finds Evidence of “Unwelcome Sexual Conduct”

Nov 24, 2026

In more news from Capitol Hill, outgoing California Democratic Representative Jimmy Gomez announced he’ll resign from Congress next week, after a House Ethics Committee report found substantial evidence that he had engaged in “unwelcome sexual conduct” with a female aide. The report determined Gomez’s behavior might have constituted a “criminal misdemeanor sexual abuse.” Gomez is the third congressman to resign over sexual misconduct allegations this year, following Democrat Eric Swalwell of California and Republican Tony Gonzales of Texas.

JD Vance Faces Senate Scrutiny for Allegedly Helping Campaign Donor Secure Venezuelan Oil Licenses

Nov 24, 2026

Image Credit: Reuters/Juan Carlos Hernandez

A Senate committee is investigating whether JD Vance used his position as vice president to help a major political donor secure lucrative business opportunities involving Venezuelan oil. That’s according to Reuters, which reports Vice President Vance met in December 2025 with John Addison, a trader with the commodities giant Vitol whose company went on to land ⁠special licenses to sell hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth of Venezuelan oil following the January U.S. military operation that abducted President Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores. Reuters reports Vance and Addison met at Montana’s Yellowstone Club, an ultra-exclusive ski and golf resort. Both Vance and Addison have denied having the meeting, but in a letter to Vance, New Hampshire Democratic Senator Maggie Hassan writes, “Despite denials from your office and Mr. Addison, flight records place his private jet and ⁠your government plane at the same Montana airport on the day of the reported meeting.” John Addison had been an early backer of Vance, contributing $300,000 to Vance’s successful 2022 campaign for an Ohio Senate seat.

Read more news here on Havana Times.

World.title: A Christmas of Fake Snow and Empty Pockets is Coming to Havana
World.content:
“Un turrón, 9.000 pesos. Yo no gano eso de salario al mes”, se queja una joven vestida de enfermera ante un anaquel con vinos, dulces y un reno de peluche / 14ymedio

Dressed as the Virgin of Charity of El Cobre, a woman begs for food at a traffic light: Cuba’s patron saint transformed into a beggar reflects the country’s sad reality.

By Yoani Sanchez (14ymedio)

HAVANA TIMES – The early morning brought rain to Havana, and Monday dawned in a mess of blackouts and mud, paralysis and hustle. Before I got out of bed I could already smell the odor of the coffee factory near my house. For days now a burnt small has invaded the neighborhood, accompanies by smoke that seeps in through the windows. A good part of that coffee will end up being sold for dollars, a currency that this Monday reached 965 pesos in the informal market.

I go out seeking provisions. The forecast predicts strong storms for the coming days, but another whirlwind has already hit the markets. What cost 2,000 pesos Sunday, yesterday, today costs 2,100 or more. In the window of a private bakery, a sign tries to justify the 690 pesos price for a bag of bread. “The cost of raw materials has gone up,” it explains. In front of the counter, where before you had to push your way through the customers, I find no one. Inflation has managed to eliminate the lines.

In my building’s WhatsApp group, at last, some good news appears: Today there is bread. However, the lack of electricty converts this small victory into a, obstacle course for the elderly residence on the upper floors. Going down more than a dozen floors and climbing back up is not a small thing, especially when the reward is that ever small and tasteless ration and sold in the ration market.

Christmas is beginning to timidly appear in some private businesses and dollar stores. The red hats worn by the clerks seem to have come from a distant planet, in stark contrast to the dull reality. “A nougat bar, 9,000 pesos. I don’t earn that much a month,” complains a young woman dressed as a nurse in front of a shelf laden with wines, sweets, and a stuffed reindeer.

In Carlos III Plaza, the stores that sell in hard currency remain empty of customers, but the employees are putting up little trees, garlands and fake snow made of cotton. The winter decorations contrast with the market’s sticky heat, where the air conditioning barely works.

At the corner of Ayestarán and 20 de Mayo, a woman dressed as the Virgen de la Caridad del Cobre approaches the cars stopped at the traffic light. She carries a basket with a doll also adorned in gold and asks for something to eat. The Patron Saint of Cuba, transformed into a beggar, encapsulates the country we live in better than any speech.

In a city where almost nothing gets repaired, the gas station business seems to be the only one with any vitality. / 14ymedio

Further along, I come across the only construction site I’ve seen on my entire journey: a gas station. Several construction workers are working inside a enormous hole where fuel will be stored. They’re building walls and sealing cracks while, all around, the sidewalks remain in ruins. In a city where almost nothing gets repaired, the gas station business seems to be the only one with any semblance of life.

In a private market, I stumble across a ten-pound bag of chicken quarters for 9,550 pesos. The price takes me back to my childhood and that television program, 9,550, whose title alluded to the kilometers between Havana and Moscow, while the pipeline of subsidies fueled the political deliriums of Castroism. Today, the Russian bear offers only declarations of friendship and economic agreements that rarely materialize, even though they fill the headlines of the official press.

Before leaving the store, I see a little girl who insists on buying a jar of American peanut butter. It costs 4,500 pesos. Her mother promises to buy it for her for Christmas. “I won’t forget,” she assures her. The clerk is wearing a red hat. I look at the little girl and wonder how many promises that woman will have to make before December, and how many she’ll be able to keep. Outside, the sky is clouding over again.

The storm hasn’t arrived yet, but in Havana we’re already living under a downpour.

Translated by Translating Cuba.

Read more from Cuba here on Havana Times.

World.title: The Daily Struggle to Find Food
World.content:
Photo: Nike

By Nike

HAVANA TIMES – No matter how hard I try to make each day different, it always turns into the same routine when it comes to finding food.

I get up early and go to the kitchen to make coffee over charcoal. That means spending half an hour getting the precious fuel lit. Even though they tell you it’s made from marabu wood and is the best charcoal in the world, lighting it takes blood, sweat, and tears. And I mean that literally, because on more than one occasion I’ve burst into tears. It’s expensive on the market, and the price keeps rising every day. A sack now costs around 3,000 Cuban pesos. Three thousand pesos is the basic monthly salary of a Cuban worker, while a retiree’s pension ranges between 1,200 and 1,500 pesos. In other words, an entire month’s work for a sack of charcoal that, even when used sparingly, won’t last the whole month.

The coffee I have right now was a gift from a friend. His grandmother has several coffee plants at her home in Camagüey, and she roasts and grinds the beans herself. It’s good Cuban coffee. Imported coffee costs between 3,500 and 4,000 pesos, while locally grown coffee—like the kind my friend’s grandmother produces—costs 1,500 pesos for 250 grams. Despite the high prices, Cubans make sacrifices to buy it.

After coffee, I head out into the streets in search of the day’s food, like any ordinary Cuban. I bring my own shopping bags because otherwise I have to pay 15 or 20 pesos for each plastic bag. The days when merchants gave you bags or paper sacks at no additional cost are long gone.

The first thing I buy is rice. It isn’t particularly nutritious, but it fills your stomach. It costs 450 pesos a pound. I prefer root vegetables and other starchy staples, which are more nutritious, but buying them is like opening a box of surprises. They may look perfectly good on the outside, but when you peel them, they can be black or green, like sweet potatoes affected by the sweet potato weevil. It’s a pest with a French-sounding name that givers sweet potatoes a bitter taste that not even animals can eat them. That’s like throwing your money away, so I stick with rice. I call this survival.

They also sell plantains, the kind known as plátano macho, but they’re not the same ones I remember from childhood. They’re a hybrid developed to make the plants produce more frequently. Their flesh is firmer, and they’re smaller than the original plantains. I’ll take the plátano macho of the 1980s any day. Today’s plantains cost between 150 and 200 pesos apiece.

There are also plátanos burros, another variety of banana. A bunch of eight small bananas sells for 300 or 400 pesos. They go further because what matters to us is quantity—having enough to fill a stomach that roars like a lion in heat and needs to be silenced.

There’s no fruit. The onions aren’t good, and at 600 pesos a pound they’re unaffordable anyway. I can’t buy them with the money I have. At home, I season our meals with Cuban oregano, basil, ají cachucha peppers, and some green onions I’ve planted myself.

As I continue my search, I settle on rice and, like “Martina the Little Cockroach” from the children’s story, I count my money and figure out that I have enough for some black beans, whose price has risen to 700 pesos. They’ll last for two meals, provide nourishment, and fill our stomachs.

I look for some protein, but chicken costs 850 pesos a pound, and eggs are 130 pesos each. I pass a house and notice a sign advertising “dehydrated eggs.” The man there very kindly explains how to prepare them. I buy a pound for 600 pesos.

I’ve almost completed the food shopping for my family, but I still need some vegetables. At the produce market, the only thing for sale is some very ugly cucumbers, and I can’t afford them on my budget either. So I head to the coast and gather salicornia—a type of sea vegetable—and purslane, which contains omega-3 fatty acids. They’re free and nutritious.

I’m worried because my children get hungry at night. So I stop by a recently opened bakery called Riki Pan. The owner is a doctor who gave up his medical career to make bread. He bought a house, installed an electric generator, set up ovens, and has been baking bread nonstop ever since, with help from relatives abroad.

People welcomed the bakery enthusiastically, and it has become a favorite here in my town. Lately, however, customers have been upset because he raised bread prices, and he has even faced criticism on Facebook.

I stop at the bakery and buy a bag of the least expensive bread rolls for 400 pesos. It’s for snacks between meals, which are yet another food-related problem in this country.

Add up my expenses yourselves and tell me whether, with today’s salaries, a Cuban can afford breakfast, lunch, and dinner every single day.

This is how families in my country live, day after day.

Read more from Nike’s diary here on Havana Times.

World.title: Princess Anne visits South Georgia and sees British Antarctic Survey science at first hand
World.content:
Princess Anne visits South Georgia and sees British Antarctic Survey science at first hand

24th Tuesday, November 2026 - 13:31 UTC Full article

Photo: Government of South Georgia & the South Sandwich Islands

Princess Anne, the sister of King Charles III, visited South Georgia as part of her South Atlantic tour, meeting British Antarctic Survey scientists and staff stationed on the island, the Government of South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands said on Monday. The visit to the islands, which began in the Falklands, was rejected by Argentina as a “provocation”.

The Princess, accompanied by her husband, Vice Admiral Sir Tim Laurence, experienced “firsthand the work of those who live and work on this remarkable Island”, the local government said in a series of posts on X, accompanied by photographs. At King Edward Point she met the British Antarctic Survey team, the UK's national operator in Antarctica, which explained the scientific research taking place on the island. At that station, the groundfish survey marks 40 years this season.

1/5 Her Royal Highness The Princess Royal and Vice Admiral Sir Tim Laurence visited South Georgia, experiencing firsthand the work of those who live and work on this remarkable Island. #SGSSI #RoyalVisit https://t.co/twCuKDGk92 — Government SGSSI (@GovSGSSI) November 23, 2026

The Princess also met Government staff stationed on the island, “whose work is instrumental to South Georgia's operations, heritage and environment”, and visited its post office, which connects this remote territory with the rest of the world. The local government also highlighted the icebergs, landscapes and wildlife that accompanied the journey. The posts do not give the date of the visit or mention the planned programme, which included unveiling a memorial at a former whaling station, opening the restored Stromness Managers' Villa and commemorating the explorer Sir Ernest Shackleton.

The Princess, Patron of the South Georgia Heritage Trust, an organisation dedicated to protecting the island's heritage and environment, arrived in the islands on November 9. The following day she opened Stanley's new National Sports Complex, an investment of about £5 million.

On November 17, the Argentine government rejected the visit, calling it a “provocation” at a time when, according to Buenos Aires, the United Kingdom is advancing hydrocarbon exploitation in waters whose sovereignty Argentina claims. Argentina had also protested against the Princess's previous visit in 2022. The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea will announce on Saturday, November 28, its decision on Argentina's request to halt the Sea Lion oil project.

World.title: Argentina receives two bids for the Ushuaia naval base pier amid Sea Lion tensions
World.content:
Argentina receives two bids for the Ushuaia naval base pier amid Sea Lion tensions

24th Tuesday, November 2026 - 12:39 UTC Full article

The Ushuaia naval base, where the new military pier will be built.

The Argentine government has received two bids to build the military pier at the Ushuaia integrated naval base, a project President Javier Milei relaunched in September, four days before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea rules on Argentina's request to halt the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands.

The Argentine government has received two bids to build the military pier at the Ushuaia integrated naval base, a project President Javier Milei relaunched in September to turn the country into a “central logistics hub of the South Atlantic”, four days before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea rules on Argentina's request to halt the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands.

Of the 15 companies that had expressed interest, only two submitted proposals, both above the official budget of about 189.3 billion pesos set by the Navy, according to Infobae. Concret Nor bid about 192 billion pesos, 1.4% more, and Lemiro Pablo Pietroboni about 210.3 billion, 11.1% above. Both companies have already won sections of the privatisation of the national road network. The process now moves to technical and economic evaluation.

The first phase envisages building, over 18 months from early 2027, the first 240 metres of the pier, to be used by boats of the Navy's Southern Patrol Division. The full project, with a 585-metre main pier and the involvement of the state shipyard Tandanor, is due to be completed in 2029 at an estimated cost of US$450 million to US$500 million, and aims to turn Ushuaia into a logistics hub for operations in Antarctica. Its second stage depends on funds included in the 2027 budget, still under debate in Congress.

The base is not a new initiative. It stems from a 1990 plan that formally began in 2022 under Alberto Fernández's government and was virtually halted in December 2023 at 9% completion. Milei relaunched it on September 4 through a decree reallocating Defence Ministry funds, on the same day he announced sanctions against companies linked to Sea Lion.

Those sanctions have already had an effect. Britain's Rockhopper Exploration reported on November 20 that its partner and the project's operator, Israel's Navitas Petroleum, is at an advanced stage of replacing two contractors that declined to fulfil their contracts for fear of Argentine sanctions, although it said it does not expect a significant adverse impact on the timetable. According to Argentina's Foreign Ministry, the Singapore shipyard Seatrium is also considering cancelling the upgrade of the project's production vessel.

The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea will announce on Saturday, November 28, its decision on the provisional measures requested by Argentina, while the arbitral tribunal that will rule on the merits of the dispute is constituted.

World.title: Colombia's peace deal turns ten with 36% of its commitments fulfilled
World.content:
Colombia's peace deal turns ten with 36% of its commitments fulfilled

24th Tuesday, November 2026 - 12:35 UTC Full article

Juan Manuel Santos (L) and FARC leader Rodrigo Londoño, known as Timochenko, shake hands next to Cuban leader Raúl Castro, after the peace agreement.

The peace agreement between the Colombian state and the former FARC guerrillas turns ten on Tuesday with only 36% of its commitments fulfilled, according to the Kroc Institute, more than 500 former fighters killed and a government that considers it a mistake.

The peace agreement between the Colombian state and the former FARC guerrillas turns ten on Tuesday with only 36% of its commitments fulfilled, according to the Kroc Institute, more than 500 former fighters killed and a government, that of President Abelardo de la Espriella, which has cut back the institutions created by the deal and considers it a mistake.

The agreement was signed on November 24, 2016, at the Teatro Colón in Bogotá, after Colombians narrowly rejected a first text in a referendum and Juan Manuel Santos's government renegotiated it. More than 13,600 fighters handed over their weapons, and in 2017 the country recorded its lowest homicide rate in more than three decades.

Implementation, however, has been slow and uneven under three governments. Rural reform, the first point of the agreement, promised to hand three million hectares to landless farmers within 12 years; at the current pace, the Comptroller's Office estimates it would take about 400 years. According to the Ombudsman's Office, 521 signatories of the agreement have been killed over the past decade. The UN Verification Mission confirmed 13 killings of former fighters in 2026 up to September, and attempted murders rose from five in 2025 to 15.

In his three months in office, De la Espriella has cut the budget of the Special Jurisdiction for Peace, the court that tries former guerrillas and soldiers, broken off talks with armed groups, which he declared terrorists, and stepped up military offensives. “The false peace has cost Colombia dearly!” he said on the eve of the anniversary, calling the agreement a “mess”. At his government's request, the UN mission, renewed for a year, will no longer monitor rural reform, a decision backed by the United States.

Santos, who received the Nobel Peace Prize for the agreement, argues that the problem is not the deal but the failure to implement it. “The lack of implementation is what has caused many of the problems,” he said.

The state never filled the territories left by the FARC. The National Liberation Army, dissidents who rejected the agreement and the Clan del Golfo now fight over cocaine routes, gold mines and border crossings. According to the armed forces, these groups have some 29,000 members in 165 structures, compared with about 13,000 in 2022.

“We did not sign a peace agreement to die for it,” Osvaldo Mendoza, a former fighter who organised disarmament in a village in Cauca department, told El País.

World.title: Pneumonia complicates Jair Bolsonaro's hospital stay in Brasília
World.content:
Pneumonia complicates Jair Bolsonaro's hospital stay in Brasília

23rd Monday, November 2026 - 22:09 UTC Full article

Jair Bolsonaro, 71, remains in intensive care at the DF Star hospital.

Former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro has been diagnosed with pneumonia at the Brasília hospital where he has been admitted since Friday with an intestinal obstruction, his doctors said on Monday, although they ruled out surgery after his intestinal condition improved.

Former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro has been diagnosed with pneumonia at the Brasília hospital where he has been admitted since Friday with an intestinal obstruction, his doctors said on Monday, although they ruled out surgery after his intestinal condition improved.

Cardiologist Brasil Caiado told a press conference that Bolsonaro's health had improved since his admission, but that on Sunday afternoon he suffered chills, pain and vomiting. Tests detected bilateral aspiration pneumonia, although less serious than the one diagnosed during another hospital stay in March, according to the doctors.

Surgeon Cláudio Birolini said the intestinal obstruction, the reason for his admission, had improved, so doctors opted to continue clinical treatment rather than operate. The 71-year-old former president will remain in the intensive care unit of the DF Star hospital, and there is no forecast for his discharge.

Bolsonaro, who governed from 2019 to 2022, has had numerous hospital stays and operations since he was stabbed in the abdomen at a campaign event in September 2018. His fragile health was one of the arguments the Supreme Federal Court considered in allowing him to serve under house arrest the 27-year sentence imposed on him for plotting a coup. The court will vote between December 4 and 15 on the constitutionality of a law that reduces the sentences of those convicted in the coup plot.

World.title: UK expresses support for Pedro Alliana's government in Paraguay
World.content:
UK expresses support for Pedro Alliana's government in Paraguay

23rd Monday, November 2026 - 22:05 UTC Full article

Pedro Alliana is sworn in as president of Paraguay, next to his wife.

The United Kingdom has expressed its support for the government of Paraguayan President Pedro Alliana, who took office just over two weeks ago after the removal of Santiago Peña over the collapse of Ueno Bank, Paraguay's Foreign Ministry said on Monday.

The United Kingdom has expressed its support for the government of Paraguayan President Pedro Alliana, who took office just over two weeks ago after the removal of Santiago Peña over the collapse of Ueno Bank, Paraguay's Foreign Ministry said on Monday.

Paraguayan Foreign Minister Rubén Ramírez received a call from Chris Elmore, Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State at the UK Foreign Office, “who conveyed his country's support” for Alliana's administration, the ministry said in a statement. The two reviewed the main issues on the bilateral agenda and agreed on a round of political consultations for early 2027.

Since taking office, Alliana has received calls from Argentine President Javier Milei, Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Alliana, previously vice-president, was sworn in on November 6 amid the crisis over the takeover of Ueno Bank, a bank linked to Peña that received large deposits from public bodies during his term, including five pension funds. Peña remains in pre-trial detention at a military facility, charged with breach of trust, self-serving administration and criminal association. Former Central Bank president Carlos Carvallo, also in pre-trial detention, is charged in the same case.

World.title: Brazil's Supreme Court summons Flávio Bolsonaro by public notice over alleged slander of Lula
World.content:
Brazil's Supreme Court summons Flávio Bolsonaro by public notice over alleged slander of Lula

23rd Monday, November 2026 - 21:44 UTC Full article

Senator Flávio Bolsonaro at a public event.

Brazilian Supreme Federal Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes on Monday ordered that Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who is in the United States, be summoned by public notice to submit within 15 days his defence against a charge of slandering President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the state news agency Agência Brasil reported.

Brazilian Supreme Federal Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes on Monday ordered that Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who is in the United States, be summoned by public notice to submit within 15 days his defence against a charge of slandering President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the state news agency Agência Brasil reported.

The Prosecutor General's Office charged the senator, eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, last week over a post on X on January 3, the day of the US military operation in Venezuela that removed Nicolás Maduro from power. “Lula will be informed on. It is the end of the São Paulo Forum: international drug and arms trafficking, money laundering, support for terrorists and dictatorships, rigged elections,” Flávio Bolsonaro wrote at the time. According to the charge, he linked the president to those crimes.

In his decision, Moraes recalled that the senator had been required to surrender his passports and that he left for the United States after the presidential election, so he must be summoned through a notice published online. “Supreme Federal Court case law holds that summons by public notice is valid when the defendant remains at an uncertain and unknown location, including abroad, with the evident purpose of frustrating the application of criminal law,” he said. If by the end of the period the senator has not appointed a lawyer, the judge may assign his defence to the Public Defender's Office.

Flávio Bolsonaro lost the October 25 presidential run-off to Lula, did not concede defeat and left Brazil via the border with Argentina — with valid documents, according to Argentine authorities — bound for the United States. He is also under investigation for money laundering. The senator denies the allegations and says he is the victim of political persecution.

His father, sentenced to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup, remains in intensive care in Brasília with an intestinal obstruction.

World.title: Brazil cuts its 2027 growth forecast to 1.8% and raises inflation to the top of its target
World.content:
Brazil cuts its 2027 growth forecast to 1.8% and raises inflation to the top of its target

23rd Monday, November 2026 - 21:40 UTC Full article

The Banco Central do Brasil headquarters in Brasília.

Brazil's Finance Ministry has cut its economic growth forecast for 2027 from 2.3% to 1.8% and raised its inflation forecast from 3.8% to 4.5%, the upper limit of the official target, according to its November Macrofiscal Bulletin. The government attributes the slowdown to high interest rates and more expensive credit.

Brazil's Finance Ministry has cut its economic growth forecast for 2027 from 2.3% to 1.8% and raised its inflation forecast from 3.8% to 4.5%, the upper limit of the official target, according to its November Macrofiscal Bulletin, published on Monday. The government attributes the slowdown to high interest rates and more expensive credit.

For this year, the growth forecast was lowered from 2% to 1.9%, and the inflation forecast raised from 4.9% to 5.3%, above the ceiling of the target, which is 3% with a tolerance band of 1.5 percentage points. These are government figures; the Central Bank's latest survey of analysts, published on November 16, is more pessimistic, forecasting growth of 1.7% this year and 1% in 2027.

Economic Policy Secretary Débora Freire said the slowdown is consistent with the Central Bank's tight monetary policy and that third-quarter data confirm it. The ministry expects gross domestic product to have held steady on the second quarter, although it does not rule out a slight decline. By sector, industry will grow 1.4% this year and services 1.7%, while agriculture, the only sector revised upwards, will grow 3.1% thanks to better soybean, maize and coffee harvests.

The report expects the benchmark Selic interest rate, now at 13.75%, to remain high for longer and fall gradually, which will continue to weigh on consumption and investment. Among factors that could push prices up, it cites a stronger dollar, higher state taxes on fuel and gas, tensions in the Middle East, the El Niño phenomenon and the effects of tax reform. The ministry raised its forecast for the price of Brent crude in 2027 from US$79.50 to US$95.20 a barrel.

Some factors could support activity, such as the income tax exemption for lower earners, debt renegotiation programmes and a resilient labour market.

The revision comes days after the Central Bank sold US$1 billion from its reserves to curb the rise of the dollar, amid market distrust of the fiscal adjustment by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's government, which the Chamber of Deputies will vote on this week.

World.title: Uruguay will not announce its CPTPP accession this year and will consult business and unions
World.content:
Uruguay will not announce its CPTPP accession this year and will consult business and unions

23rd Monday, November 2026 - 21:36 UTC Full article

Foreign Minister Mario Lubetkin at a press conference in Montevideo.

Uruguay's Foreign Minister Mario Lubetkin has ruled out the government announcing before the end of the year the country's accession to the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), and said it will not move forward without consulting business and trade unions.

Uruguay's Foreign Minister Mario Lubetkin has ruled out the government announcing before the end of the year the country's accession to the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), which brings together 12 countries, and said it will not move forward without consulting business and trade unions, amid opposition from industrial unions to the terms under negotiation.

“We are in the phase of exchange and negotiation, of understanding the parameters, comparing them with our parameters and our laws,” Lubetkin said, according to Ámbito. “We will not do anything without permanent consultation with the different actors,” he added, referring to business and union organisations. The government aims to conclude the technical negotiations before the end of the year, but the political decision to join will not be announced in the coming weeks.

Deputy Foreign Minister Valeria Csukasi, who is leading the process, said meetings of the bloc's chief negotiators and trade ministers will be held in Vietnam next week and will be decisive in setting the timetable. The CPTPP brings together 12 countries, including Japan, Australia, Canada, Mexico, Chile, Peru, the United Kingdom and Vietnam.

The Confederation of Industrial Unions rejects accession under the current terms. It warns that opening up without tariffs would hurt sectors such as clothing, footwear, metalworking, plastics and auto parts, and questions possible restrictions on public procurement and the operation of state-owned companies UTE, Ancap, Antel and OSE, as well as the state's exposure to claims by foreign investors. It is calling for a sector-by-sector impact study and tariff phase-out periods of at least 15 years. The main business chambers, meanwhile, are awaiting information from the government on the terms being negotiated.

Uruguay is also focusing its December agenda on Mercosur. On December 2, Punta del Este will host the first Mercosur-European Union business forum; on December 3 the Trade Council of the interim agreement with the EU will meet for the first time, and on December 4 Montevideo will host the bloc's 69th summit of heads of state, at which Uruguay will hand over the pro tempore presidency.

The distribution among members of preferential-tariff export quotas to the EU remains unresolved. Paraguay favours an equal split; Uruguay and Argentina propose taking into account each country's trade with the EU, and Brazil, each partner's global trade. Lubetkin acknowledged that the political crisis in Paraguay and the expected cabinet change in Brazil are slowing the talks, so no decisions are expected at the summit.

World.title: Inflation rises to nearly 4% in first half of November
World.content:
Annual headline inflation in Mexico ticked up to 3.96% in the first half of November, the highest rate since early May, fueled in part by a 20% year-over-year surge in fruit and vegetable prices.

Reported by the national statistics agency INEGI on Tuesday, the headline rate came in slightly above the 3.92% median forecast of economists surveyed by Reuters.

It is 0.21 percentage points higher than the 3.75% reading for October. The last time Mexico’s annual headline rate was higher was in the first half of May, at 4.11%.

The annual headline rate has now risen in five consecutive quincenas (15-day-periods) between the first half of September and the first half of November. It appears likely that headline inflation will rise for a fourth consecutive month in November after declining every month between April and July.

INEGI also reported on Tuesday that Mexico’s annual core inflation rate — which excludes volatile food and energy prices — was 3.68% in the first half of November, down from 3.80% across October. That was lower than the 3.88% forecast of economists surveyed by Reuters. The annual core rate — which is watched closely by economists and policymakers — was the lowest since the first quincena of March.

INEGI also reported that consumer prices increased 0.54% in the first half of November compared to the second half of October.

The publication of the latest inflation data comes almost three weeks after the Bank of Mexico board voted in favor of lowering the central bank’s benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 6.25%. Three of five board members voted in favor of the cut, despite recent increases in Mexico’s headline inflation rate. The board is expected to vote in favor of maintaining the central bank’s key rate at 6.25% at its final monetary policy meeting for 2026 on Dec. 17.

The Bank of Mexico targets an annual headline rate of 3%, with a tolerance range of 2%-4%.

Inflation data in detail

INEGI’s data shows that fruit and vegetable prices were 20.05% higher in the first half of November than a year earlier. Those prices are sensitive to adverse weather conditions, which can disrupt production and reduce supply.

Compared to the second half of October, prices for green tomatoes surged 39.31% in the first half of November, while regular tomatoes were 28.95% more expensive and poblano chiles were 26.97% dearer.

Annual inflation rates in the first half of November for other categories monitored by INEGI were as follows.

4.66% for processed food, beverages and tobacco

1.86% for non-food goods.

4.17% for services.

3.53% for energy, including electricity and gasoline.

Meat prices fell 2.15% on a year-over-year basis. Annual inflation for agricultural products (fruit, vegetables and meat) was 6.65% in the first half of November.

With reports from La Jornada and Reuters

World.title: Aeroméxico now offers 7-day Mexico City stopovers as tourism to the capital surges
World.content:
Mexico City’s government wants travelers who change planes in the capital to stay a while.

The city’s Tourism Ministry and the airline Aeroméxico announced on Nov. 18 a “stopover” program that lets connecting passengers stay more than 24 hours and up to seven days before continuing to their final destination. Travelers can take advantage of the offer from both the Mexico City International Airport (AICM) and the Felipe Ángeles International Airport (AIFA), and can use it on the outbound trip, the return or both.

The goal, according to a press release, is to lengthen visits and increase tourist spending. The program is meant to showcase the capital’s culture, food, entertainment, hotels, attractions and shopping.

“In Mexico City, there are 3,000 activities per day, so a stopover is a wonderful way for visitors and tourists to easily extend their stay,” said Tourism Minister Alejandra Frausto Guerrero during the program’s announcement.

For Aeroméxico, it’s a chance to make use of its main hub and strengthen the capital’s role as a gateway for domestic and international travelers.

Jennie Shrem Serur, director general of the city’s Tourism Promotion Institute, said the agency is working with the airline on a broader strategy that includes developing experiences, routes and tours to be offered through Aeroméxico’s platform. The aim, she said, is for travelers to see the capital as a reason to pause, not merely a stop on the way elsewhere.

The program applies in every market where Aeroméxico operates, as long as the itinerary connects in Mexico City. It is offered in all cabins and fare classes, with costs, conditions and baggage allowances varying by fare. When scheduling a flight online, select the option for “stopover”; round-trip flights will permit travelers to make two stopovers in Mexico City: one on their way out and one on the way back.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Mexico to establish smart hospital with China’s help: Tuesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🏥 Healthcare the focus at Tuesday’s mañanera: Sheinbaum outlined part of her vision for the future of healthcare in Mexico. Her remarks came as the government works on a universal healthcare scheme and an AI-assisted program to improve the control, storage and distribution of medications.

Sheinbaum outlined part of her vision for the future of healthcare in Mexico. Her remarks came as the government works on a universal healthcare scheme and an AI-assisted program to improve the control, storage and distribution of medications. 🇨🇳 Mexico and China to collaborate on a smart hospital: Sheinbaum said the two governments “agreed on at least two actions” after her visit last week to a 1,500-bed smart hospital in Shenzhen. The first is to establish a smart hospital in Mexico, although she didn’t say which existing hospital would be converted or give a timeframe. The second is greater cooperation on scientific training and research, including sending Mexican doctors to China for training.

Sheinbaum said the two governments “agreed on at least two actions” after her visit last week to a 1,500-bed smart hospital in Shenzhen. The first is to establish a smart hospital in Mexico, although she didn’t say which existing hospital would be converted or give a timeframe. The second is greater cooperation on scientific training and research, including sending Mexican doctors to China for training. 🤖 Sheinbaum backs more tech in healthcare: “We have to take advantage of technology to improve healthcare,” the president said, citing China’s levels of automation and digitalization as a benchmark.

“We have to take advantage of technology to improve healthcare,” the president said, citing China’s levels of automation and digitalization as a benchmark. 📱 Universal healthcare app is Sheinbaum’s “dream”: She said she wants every Mexican to have a universal healthcare app on their cell phone for scheduling appointments. It could also include an AI chatbot to advise users on whether they need to see a doctor immediately, although she said it “doesn’t replace a doctor.” She didn’t say when the app might be available.

Why today’s mañanera matters

Healthcare was a key focus at President Claudia Sheinbaum’s Tuesday morning press conference.

The federal government is currently working on a range of healthcare initiatives, including the establishment of a universal healthcare scheme and the implementation of an artificial intelligence-assisted program aimed at improving the control, storage and distribution of medications.

Accompanied by several health officials at today’s mañanera, including Health Minister David Kershenobich, Sheinbaum outlined part of her vision for the future of healthcare in Mexico. Her vision is informed, in part, by her visit last week to China’s tech capital, Shenzhen, where she attended the APEC Leaders’ Meeting, met with several world leaders including Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump, and visited a smart hospital — that is, a hospital that uses a range of digital technologies, including AI, to improve patient care and operational efficiency.

On Tuesday morning, Sheinbaum told reporters that her government reached an agreement with its Chinese counterpart to work together on the establishment of a smart hospital in Mexico.

Mexico and China are seeking to deepen bilateral cooperation in a range of areas, including science and technology, agriculture, healthcare, clean energy and water resources.

Mexico to collaborate with China on the establishment of a smart hospital

Asked about future healthcare collaboration between Mexico and China, Sheinbaum said that her administration and the Chinese government “agreed on at least two actions” during their meeting in Shenzhen last week.

“… The first is to establish a smart hospital in Mexico, we’re going to start with that,” she said.

“From there, we’ll look at how we can make progress in other hospitals,” Sheinbaum said.

She said that her government had not yet determined which existing hospital in Mexico would be converted into a smart hospital.

“But the hospital we visited [in Shenzhen] has 1,500 beds and it has advanced technology and provides extraordinary care. So the objective is to establish one of these hospitals [in Mexico] and continue collaborating [with China],” Sheinbaum said without providing a timeframe for establishing Mexico’s first smart hospital.

She said that the second “action” Mexico and China agreed to is “greater cooperation on scientific training and research.”

“The objective is for a group of Mexican doctors to go to China to undergo training and we’ll also look at whether doctors from China can come to Mexico to receive training,” Sheinbaum said.

Sheinbaum: ‘We have to take advantage of technology to improve health care’

A week after touring a “smart hospital” in Shenzhen, China, Sheinbaum expressed her support for the greater use of technology in healthcare facilities.

“We have to take advantage of technology to improve healthcare,” she said.

“That’s what we’re doing now. If we can reach the levels of automation and digitalization China has, including the use of robots for certain things, what could be better? What we want is to care for people in the best possible way,” Sheinbaum said.

Sheinbaum’s healthcare dream? A universal healthcare app

Sheinbaum told reporters that “the dream all of us here have is for every Mexican to have a universal healthcare service application on their cell phone.”

“You tap [the] universal healthcare service [app] and say: ‘I’m going to the doctor’s office, I want to make an appointment,” she said.
