World.title: The good, the bad and the French: EU countries get fiscal report cards
World.content:
Sofia is the only capital facing a cash fine for failing to rein in its spending. But there are plenty of other countries that have broken the fiscal rules, which are designed to keep the gap between government spending and what they collect in revenue to 3% of economic output. They also aim to keep public debt-to-GDP ratios below 60%.

Brussels currently has red flags pinned in 10 countries, including France, Belgium and Italy, to signal to investors which governments have fallen foul of the EU rules. Countries shed the undesirable labels once they convince Brussels that their spending is under control. But the Commission has allowed for extra budgetary leeway for 19 countries to build up their militaries in an effort to deter further Russian aggression.

These are POLITICO’s grades, weighing countries’ fiscal outlooks alongside Brussels’ findings.

Bulgaria and Hungary: F

Budapest and Sofia have strayed so far from their spending commitments that Brussels is prepared to punish them. Both governments could lose access to some EU funds, while Bulgaria faces a fine of up to €23 million.

Even after allowing extra leeway for defense spending, Hungary’s spending overshoot is estimated at 3.1% of GDP this year, and Bulgaria’s at 2.3%. Only eurozone countries can be fined, sparing Hungary that particular punishment.

Belgium and France: E

Passing on paper is one thing. Delivering is another. France has produced a draft budget for next year, but its government is struggling to get it through the National Assembly. Belgium’s five-party coalition, meanwhile, can’t agree on its spending plans.

World.title: COP must change after Antalya failure, UK climate chief warns
World.content:
The U.K., alongside the EU, many developing countries and small island states, rejected a draft deal that omitted any reference to fossil fuels, which fuel global warming.

Kyte, the U.K.’s special representative for climate change and one of London’s key negotiators at COP, told POLITICO that, with reform, the collapse of a deal in Turkey could yet prove a “cathartic moment” for the climate talks.

Kyte said many countries “want to look at” the way COP agreements are made. Final COP texts must currently be agreed by consensus among nearly 200 countries. EU climate chief Wopke Hoekstra also told the Financial Times this week that the U.N. “needs to look into” this approach.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, addressing the House of Commons later on Tuesday, also said the U.K. would “work to reform the COP process and uphold its integrity so it can deliver the Paris Agreement.”

Kyte said it had been “a difficult political decision” to reject the deal. “But really I think it was the right year to say ‘no text.’”

Catharsis

For the COP process to get back on track, reform is needed before next year’s conference, Kyte said. COP32 is scheduled to start in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, in November 2027.

World.title: Bulgaria faces EU fine over runaway public finances
World.content:
The threats emerged during Brussels’ latest round of economic oversight, known as the European Semester, which tries to keep public finances in check amid runaway spending and rising debt across the bloc.

The looming fine against Bulgaria is particularly symbolic, as the country only joined the eurozone in January.

The fine will be the first to be imposed for breaching the EU’s fiscal rules, which aim to keep the gap between government spending and revenue below 3% of economic output. They also try to limit public debt-to-GDP ratios to below 60%.

Bulgaria’s debt pile is well below the EU’s 60% threshold. But its budget deficit is forecast to reach 5% of GDP this year, and Brussels believes Sofia hasn’t done enough to tackle it.



The closest Brussels came to administering fines under its fiscal rules was 10 years ago against Spain and Portugal. Ultimately, it reduced the fines to €0.

The EU reformed the rules after the pandemic to address the bloc's growing debt after governments spent their way out of the deepest recession since World War II. Under the new regime, the fines are smaller so that Brussels can administer them without undermining countries' finances.

“The idea was that the massive fines would make it too unattractive to violate the rules,” Dombrovskis said. But the massive fines also made it “too unattractive to implement the rules.”

“That's why we made the [fines] much, much smaller” and “implementable” without “adding to member states' fiscal problems,” he said.

World.title: Snowden on steroids: AI agents in phones trigger surveillance fears
World.content:
"The ability for billions of devices to permanently spy on their users makes the Edward Snowden revelations look like a joke," Udbhav Tiwari, head of strategy and global affairs at Signal, told POLITICO, referring to the 2013 disclosures about mass U.S. government surveillance.

Tiwari warned that governments with a penchant for surveillance could ask tech firms for access to data gathered by AI agents, skipping the need to break end-to-end encryption or install malware on someone’s device.

Apple, Google and Microsoft declined to comment on Signal’s claims.

Itxaso Domínguez de Olazábal, policy adviser at European digital rights group EDRi, called for "serious limits" on what AI agents can access. "There is something deeply worrying about a not-so-far-away future where the companies controlling our operating systems can effectively decide how much privacy we are allowed to have, even when we deliberately choose services designed to protect it," she said.

"Probably the most sensitive device in your entire life is your phone. If it gets nicked, the person stealing your phone is not going to have access to your whole life. We're undoing all those safeguards by inviting AI agents onto these devices," said Gus Hosein, executive director of privacy NGO Privacy International.

Signal is pushing for makers of operating systems to provide tools so apps can opt out of AI data access and processing.

World.title: Farage suggests he could appeal to Le Pen to block Britain rejoining the EU
World.content:
Farage suggested that Marine Le Pen, the leader of the far-right National Rally who is leading the polls ahead of next April’s presidential election, would be “pretty much as skeptical as me” about EU enlargement.

Farage told a press conference in Westminster: “Whilst it’s slightly tortuous, there is still quite a strong probability that for us to join the European Union … the French would have a referendum and a right to veto over us joining.

“I’ve been checking this out again. It would need to go through the assembly, etc. But there is a relatively strong possibility that there will be a referendum on it and so a lot would depend on who the French president and French prime minister were at that moment in time.

“If it was to be the current bookies’ favorites of Jordan Bardella and Marine Le Pen, I don’t see them overwhelmingly endorsing the enlargement of a European project over which they’re pretty much as skeptical as me.”

Asked by POLITICO if he could try to persuade a Le Pen-led France to block the U.K.’s reentry to the EU, he replied jokingly: “Are you suggesting that I’d interfere in overseas politics? Quite possibly, yes.”

‘Europe could change’

Senior figures in Burnham’s government are already aware of the French referendum rule.

World.title: Wildberger reagiert skeptisch auf Weimers TikTok-Vorstoß
World.content:
Der Digitalminister dämpft die Erwartungen an einen europäischen TikTok-Deal. Ein Verkauf allein reiche nicht – auch die Technologie dahinter müsse nach Europa kommen.

BERLIN – Digitalminister Karsten Wildberger hat Zweifel an Weimers Plänen geäußert, das Europageschäft von TikTok mehrheitlich in europäische Hände zu überführen. Die Idee sei zwar grundsätzlich „sehr interessant“, sagte Wildberger am Montagabend bei einer Veranstaltung von POLITICO. Entscheidend sei aber, was Europa bei einem solchen Deal tatsächlich übernehmen könnte.

Ein Kauf der Plattform allein würde aus Sicht des Ministers nicht ausreichen. Auch die zugrunde liegende Technologie müsste nach Europa übertragen werden, etwa die Technologie hinter Werbung, Datenanalyse und Nutzererfahrung. „Wenn das woanders läuft, was habe ich dann gekauft?“, sagte der Minister. „Es geht ja nicht nur um den Zugang, sondern eben auch um die technologische Fähigkeit, die dahintersteht.“

Der in Peking ansässige Mutterkonzern ByteDance müsse einem solchen Deal mit europäischen Investoren zunächst zustimmen, sagte Wildberger. Wenn klar sei, dass „beide miteinander tanzen wollen“, müsse geklärt werden, welche Teile der Plattform und ihrer Technologie tatsächlich übernommen werden könnten.

World.title: MI5 warns UK defense firms they are target of Russian attacks
World.content:
The move comes after an uptick in sabotage attempts against European defense-related facilities this year.

Britain already has protections in place for its critical national infrastructure and defense firms, including specialist policing at nuclear sites and its intelligence and counter-terrorism agencies. However, it is now asking companies to take action to protect themselves from harm.

U.K. Armed Forces Minister, Louise Sandher-Jones, said in a statement after the meeting that defense firms were told to take “practical action to protect their people, technology and supply chains,” following the increased Russian threat.

These steps include removing information about the company from websites and social media, including defense facilities, what weapons they make, operations and staff roles.

NPSA also recommended staff at defense firms “avoid predictable routines where practicable,” making it harder for them to be targeted by Russia through its proxies or intelligence services.

In September, a British man from Swindon was charged with national security offenses after he allegedly was involved in a plan, on behalf of Russia's ⁠GRU military intelligence agency, to sabotage factories that manufacture drones.

World.title: Merz to meet Pope Leo, Meloni in Rome
World.content:
A German government spokesperson declined to comment, saying the chancellor's trips are announced on the Friday of the preceding week.

Merz, a Catholic, attended Leo's inauguration in May 2025 but did not meet the pontiff in private. Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul met Parolin at the Vatican in early October for talks that also covered AI, the war in Ukraine and Black Sea grain exports.

The Vatican has mediated between Kyiv and Moscow on the return of Ukrainian children who were deported to Russia, and Leo has repeatedly offered to host direct peace talks, an offer Moscow has rejected. During a visit to France in September, the pope urged European leaders to be ready to make concessions to end the war.

Leo has also made addressing the challenges posed by artificial intelligence a hallmark of his papacy. Magnifica humanitas, his first encyclical, which discusses the protection of human dignity in the age of AI, was on Merz's summer reading list.

Merz's talks with Meloni are expected to cover the EU's next long-term budget and the Ukraine peace talks, two of the officials said. Meloni secured Italy a seat in future negotiations as part of the European "E5" group, alongside Germany, France, the U.K. and Poland.

CORRECTION: This article was updated on Nov. 24 to clarify the timings of Merz’s visit.

World.title: At least 24 injured after car bomb detonates in central Colombia
World.content:
At least 24 people were injured after a car bomb exploded in Villavicencio in central Colombia on Monday, authorities said.

 

The blast damaged a regional government headquarters as well as neighbouring buildings.

Video footage circulating on social media shows piles of rubble alongside wrecked vehicles and a large crater in the road.

The attack, which has so far not been claimed by any group, comes amid a wave of violence in the South American nation.

Alexander Baquero, the mayor of Villavicencio, has since imposed a temporary ban on motorcycle traffic along several key roads in the city, which is the capital of the Meta Department.

The Colombian army's Seventh Brigade has also been deployed to the area.

Both the mayor's office and the regional government are offering up to 150 million Colombian pesos (around €38,000) for information leading to those responsible.

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella arrived in Villavicencio at around 9 am local time on Tuesday as he prepared to hold a security meeting and visit the scene of the blast.

"Narcoterrorism is desperate because we are confronting it resolutely," de la Espriella wrote in a post on social media. "It seeks to intimidate us and force us to back down in order to pursue another false peace process."

In a later update, he added that he would "not back down or negotiate with criminals."

"I will confront them with absolute determination and use every tool granted to me by the Constitution and the law to restore security," he wrote on X.

World.title: Matryoshka: What is the Russian disinformation campaign targeting Spain's election?
World.content:
Pro-Russian actors are spreading fake news reports and misleading videos ahead of Spain's 29 November snap election, impersonating media outlets to undermine support for Ukraine and European sanctions against Russia.

 

What is the Matryoshka campaign?

Today's episode of Euronews Verify takes a look at the disinformation campaign known as Matryoshka, which takes its name from the traditional hollow, wooden Russian dolls that decrease in size and are stacked one inside the other.

It's been in action since at least 2023, according to France's foreign digital interference watchdog, VIGINUM, and primarily focuses on spreading anti-Ukraine narratives to try and weaken support for it in the West, although it pushes out fake claims about other European countries too.

One of its main strategies is to mimic legitimate sources, such as news outlets and research organisations, by stealing their visual identity to spread disinformation through a veneer of credibility.

It's also sometimes known as Operation Overload, a name used to refer to the campaign's other tactic of bombarding journalists, fact-checkers and researchers with fake claims to literally overload their resources.

Why is Matryoshka going after Spain?

Spain's government has recently been hit by railway disasters, corruption scandals, and a migrant crisis, meaning the conservative People's Party is now topping most polls.

The anti-immigration and Eurosceptic Vox party could also pose a threat, as it is consistently polling in third place and pinching votes from the Socialists.

Amid all this political instability, Matryoshka and other similar disinformation campaigns aim to capitalise on the uncertainty, interfering in the democratic process to try and destabilise Spain further, weaken Europe, and shake support for Ukraine and sanctions on Russia.

In a similar vein, they also try to spread narratives that benefit politicians more sympathetic to Moscow, or those who outwardly state they will reduce aid for Kyiv.

What's Matryoshka's prime target?

The economy appears to be the weak point that Matryoshka is trying to score hits on, in order to damage citizens' trust in democracy.

"It's one of the topics that are behind the defeat of [US President] Donald Trump in the mid-term elections," Andreu Casero-Ripollés, professor of journalism and political communication at Universitat Jaume I, told Euronews Verify.

"And this type of disinformation tries to generate the sensation that the economy is going very badly and has a lot of problems that can only be solved with radical measures," he added.

Is Europe prepared for a wave of political deepfakes?

Also in today's episode, from a fake video targeting the Spanish prime minister's wife to an AI-generated campaign video featuring Greece's prime minister, AI seems to be increasingly targeting political communication, with growing concern about deepfakes.

One reason for the rising use of AI is that it is cost- and time-effective, Kuhu Badgi, from the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told Euronews Verify.

"In the past, to create a political ad, whether it be an  on TV or even a social media campaign, it would require resources like time. It would require many millions of dollars in terms of funding these initiatives."

What are the risks and how can voters spot deepfakes?

Experts claim that the use of AI-generated content is being spread and created across political lines.

In Europe, some parties using this tool are labelling their content as such, even if the font and colour are arguably too small, while others are not.

Under the EU's AI Act, manipulated video content that resembles existing persons, places or entities needs to be clearly disclosed.

These videos are also subject to national laws. For example, a former Socialist Party member in Spain has reportedly accused the People's Party of defamation and digital identity theft.

This is after a video used her likeness to hint at accusations that she worked to undermine the judiciary and law enforcement to help the Socialists.

While politicians discuss how ethically and politically correct this new wave of videos is, almost nine in 10 EU citizens agree that online manipulation, including AI-generated content and deepfakes, poses a threat to democratic processes.

Watch Euronews Verify

Join Euronews Verify live on TV, Euronews' website, and on digital platforms (YouTube, Facebook, X, and Instagram) every weekday at 6:40 pm Brussels time. In just under 11 minutes, our new format goes beyond the headlines to make sense of what's happening, fact-checking and untangling the day's most pressing issues to explain why they matter to you.

World.title: Pope Francis' private notes reveal visions of the devil and a plan to allow married men to be priests
World.content:
Pope Francis had three visions of the devil in his life. He described them in notes discovered by Argentine cardinal Víctor Manuel Fernández and published this Tuesday in a book entitled Il diario personale di Papa Francesco (Libreria vaticana edizioni).

 

"I recalled three definite episodes in which I do not doubt that he appeared physically", read the writings of Pope Francis, previewed by several Italian newspapers. "He stared at me with eyes of fire."

The book, which is being published in five languages in 94 countries, brings together diaries, notes and documents dated between 1992 and 2024, which were in a box found by the current Prefect of the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith, who is also Argentine, like Pope Francis.

The cover of Il diario personale di Papa Francesco by Cardinal Víctor Manuel Fernández Libreria editrice vaticana

What the devil looked like as seen by Pope Francis

Pope Francis, born José Mario Bergoglio, had his first vision of the devil as a bishop in Buenos Aires claiming "I saw him from the car window. I do not forget his eyes, threatening and at the same time seductive".

A "look" Bergoglio said he would never forget. The second encounter, when he was still in Argentina, was "stronger than the previous one".

"He looked at me with eyes of fire. I do not forget that look", the description states. "They were like rays of fire. Then he tried to come closer and I ran away, clutching the Rosary and pleading with the Virgin [Mary, mother of Jesus]... Curiosity struggled against the Rosary. And the Virgin saved me."

The third encounter took place in January 2021, when he was already leading the Church.

"During a meeting, I saw him and heard his voice, triumphant, master of everything: "Now I have obtained everything I wanted", the pontiff noted.

"I cannot forget the powerful rasp of his voice. The Lord gave me the opportunity to leave that meeting and so I was freed."

The Pope's notes reveal he immediately fled from these apparitions so as not to enter into dialogue with absolute evil, which is why his descriptions are brief.

Pope Francis was tormented in recent years

These were times of spiritual crisis for the Argentine pontiff, between 2021 and 2022, observes Cardinal Fernández who, although he has been one of the religious figures closest to the Pope for almost twenty years, never received confidences from him on the subject.

"The Pope perceives what he calls pagan seduction. The difficulty of managing power. The power a pope has is not only internal to the curia [administrative body of the Catholic Church]; it concerns international relations. And for him it represented a strong temptation", said the cardinal in an interview on Monday with the newspaper Corriere della Sera.

"There are no gestures of his that show a man obsessed with power, who mistreats people. It was something interior. The fear of reaching a demonic point. The need to remember that he was a simple man, a creature of God, someone in need", Fernández added, admitting that he had doubts about publishing these writings so as not to "upset anyone".

José Mario Bergoglio greets the faithful after his election to the throne of Peter as Pope Francis on 13 March 2013 AP Photo

Among the visions experienced and described by Begoglio in fact, there is also one of hell. "I saw the gates of hell. Pagan seduction with all its force", he wrote in Spanish in the original collected by the prefect.

"I leaned forward to look a little and it terrified me. It was before sleeping", Francis recounted. "Into hell one slips as the most natural thing. It is not the first time in my life that I have had this experience, but this time it was of a devouring intensity. It is dangerous to approach the gates of hell because the flames can come out and burn you."

Fernández has tried to explain what the Pope's temptations might have been, whom he describes as a "mystic".

"In no way is it a hedonistic seduction. Bergoglio was completely uninterested in hedonism, eros, sensory pleasure. He was a very moderate man. Of absolute austerity. He never took a holiday in his life, he did not even have an ice cream", he told the newspaper.

"Pagan temptation is to reject the true God in order to worship idols, or worse still to worship oneself. The strongest temptation is power badly managed", the cardinal added, citing the pontiff.

Pope Francis ordained Cardinal Víctor Manuel Fernández on 30 September 2023 AP Photo

Bergoglio would have liked to ordain married men as priests

"The temptation of power that places you above others, that induces you to subject others to your projects and to treat them like puppets, for him became terrible", Fernández explained.

Bergoglio was tormented by accusations he had received in Argentina of having been excessively harsh with subordinates and of having somehow abused his power during the ecclesiastical rise that led him to become provincial superior of the Jesuits (from 1973 to 1979) and Archbishop of Buenos Aires (from 1998 to 2013, when he was elected Pope).

A political power from which he also had to defend himself physically, according to the Argentine cardinal, who said that Francis never visited Argentina also because of intelligence information indicating that "the far right" would "organise something against him", since he was considered an "enemy".

Yet, tensions also existed within the Vatican and the Curia, against which he took several decisions while avoiding others. Among the innovations, partly moderated by his successor, Robert Prevost, the current Leo XIV, who said he was a "great shepherd and an irreproachable man", there was also the possibility of ordaining married men as priests.

"He wanted to take this decision. But he wanted to avoid internal battles, verbal violence. When we prepared the document to allow blessings for same-sex couples there was a very harsh reaction...", Fernández revealed.

The Pope wrote that he controlled temptations and doubts by entrusting himself to the the Virgin Mary, particularly during his trip to Fatima - a pilgrimage site in Portugal - in October 2023.

"I looked and I asked", he noted, "and she spoke to me".

World.title: Europe Tonight: EU budget battle, €45B Ukraine aid, and Serbia-Kosovo tensions
World.content:
Brussels clashes over seven-year spending and agriculture

A major showdown is underway over the European Union’s next seven-year budget, pitting the European Parliament against EU member states while deeply dividing national capitals over proposed spending cuts, digital levies, and agricultural subsidies. As negotiations intensify, governments remain locked in a tug-of-war over how to balance traditional farm aid with new strategic priorities.

 

The €45 billion fault line: Financing Ukraine’s future

Perhaps the most contentious sticking point in the EU’s financial planning is securing long-term support for Kyiv. The European Commission has proposed an additional €45 billion package to help cover Ukraine’s military and civilian needs, but growing frustration and resistance from several member states threaten to derail consensus; prompting sharp warnings from Berlin over potential budget vetoes.

Tonight, our Ukraine Correspondent Sasha Vakulina speaks with Ukraine’s former Minister of Economic Development to assess what is at stake for Kyiv’s economy and defense.

Diplomatic friction ahead of the Western Balkans Summit

Ahead of the upcoming EU-Western Balkans summit, European officials are voicing growing concern over ongoing diplomatic controversies between Serbia and Kosovo, following recent disputes over regional representation and Brussels' enlargement strategy.

We will speak live with former President of Kosovo Vjosa Osmani about the state of the Belgrade-Pristina dialogue and Kosovo's path toward European integration.

Exclusive: Marina Litvinenko reflects 20 years after London poisoning

Twenty years after her husband Alexander Litvinenko was fatally poisoned with radioactive polonium in London (in what became one of the most notorious Russian intelligence operations on foreign soil) Marina Litvinenko has spoken exclusively to Euronews.

Coinciding with the release of her new memoir, she reflects on her two-decade fight for accountability and what her husband's murder warned the West about the Kremlin.

You can join Euronews’ Mared Gwyn live on TV and Euronews' website as well as digital platforms (YouTube, Facebook, X, Tiktok, and Instagram), every weekday at 6 pm, 7 pm and 8 pm Brussels time.

World.title: UK warns defence suppliers to Ukraine over Russian sabotage
World.content:
Britain has warned UK defence firms supplying Ukraine's armed forces over increasing Russian sabotage attempts.

 

The National Protective Security Authority and the Ministry of Defence issued a joint alert on Tuesday offering "protective security guidance" for organisations involved "in the supply chain providing direct material support" to Ukraine.

"In recent months Russia has increased in attempts to conduct sabotage against European defence related facilities," the statement said.

"This activity is typically characterised by the use of proxy actors employing low-sophistication sabotage methodologies, such as arson," it continued, adding that such activity was intended to "undermine support" for Kyiv.

The alert warned that any organisations involved in military procurement or supplying equipment to Ukraine could be a target.

It also offered a number of steps on how companies could reduce their exposure to "hostile reconnaissance," detect and report suspicious activity and minimise the impact of any attacks.

In a separate statement, Westminster announced that closed-door security briefings were also to be given to defence sector and critical national infrastructure CEOs on Tuesday and Wednesday.

"Both the briefings and the alert will set out actions organisations can take to protect their sites, people and operations amidst the changing threat landscape," it said.

The warnings follow a fresh wave of security incidents across Europe in recent weeks, including airspace violations and reported cyber and sabotage attacks.

An Estonian naval ship sails in the Baltic Sea on Thursday, Jan. 9, 2025, as part of stepped-up NATO patrols in the region following suspected sabotage of undersea cables. AP Photo

UK Security Minister Dan Jarvis said that recent sabotage attempts across the continent demonstrated the "seriousness of the threats we face."

"It’s truly shameful that actors are seeking to disrupt our way of life and that of our allies, especially targeting organisations doing vital work in support of Ukraine," he added.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has repeatedly signalled his support for Ukraine as it continues to fight against Russia's ongoing invasion.

World.title: New terms and conditions: Tidal bans AI music in a bid to promote fairness in industry
World.content:
Tidal, the music streaming giant partially owned by Jay-Z, has announced that it's banning all music it deems to be AI-generated.

 

In a statement, Tidal says the move, that will come into effect on 9 December, is aimed at promoting fairness and economic empowerment in the industry as the technology evolves.

The decision has been sparked, according to the firm, by the rapid proliferation of text-prompted AI music generation and tools that are changing how music is created and distributed.

In a post on X, Robert Anderson, the Tidal Lead at parent company Block, wrote: "A few months ago,@Tidal tagged and demonetized all wholly AI-generated tracks to protect the authenticity of real artists. But that’s enough, as 43% of tracks distributed to us in the last 90 days have been detected as AI-generated. Something more drastic needs to be done…"

“We’ll begin removing all wholly AI-generated tracks from our catalog, and you’ll see them completely gone by the beginning of the year.”

He also added that "96% of all AI-generated songs receive zero plays and said the move will allow the firm to remove some 29 million tracks" from its platform, which reportedly already rejects between 80,000 to 85,000 songs a day.

It now remains to be seen how Apple Music, Amazon and Spotify will react.

World.title: Italy watches worryingly as Ukraine strikes Russian boats in Libya
World.content:
Kyiv has stepped up long-range drone attacks on Russian ships in the Mediterranean Sea, but Italy fears the strikes could escalate into renewed fighting in Libya, destabilising its southern neighbour in one of Rome's worst nightmares.

 

Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani voiced his concern over Ukraine's operations in Libya to his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Sybiha on Tuesday, according to a readout of the phone call.

On Sunday, Ukrainian naval drones hit two Russian vessels, one docked at the Benghazi naval base and the other just off the Libyan city. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it an "exemplary Ukrainian operation."

The attacks appear to be part of a broader maritime campaign against Russian vessels beyond the Black Sea. On Saturday, a Ukrainian drone hit another Russian ship near Finland's territorial waters.

But the strikes in Libya have rung alarm bells in Rome, where even the prospect of civil war reopening across the Mediterranean is enough to send a shiver down officials' spines.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has so far refrained from commenting on the episode publicly to avoid escalating the situation, but according to the Italian daily la Repubblica, she privately slammed the attacks as "unacceptable".

"We were not informed of absolutely anything; we did not provide any kind of support to the Ukrainians, they did everything without informing us," Tajani told reporters on the sidelines of a visit to Baku.

Tajani pledged to work to stop the conflict with Russia spreading across the Mediterranean basin, while respecting Libya's sovereignty and avoiding its destabilisation.

Libya has been split since the civil war that followed the fall of Muammar Gaddafi in 2011. A UN-recognised government in Tripoli controls much of the west, while the east is dominated by military strongman Khalifa Haftar and his Libyan National Army, which is backed by the rival administration in Benghazi.

Russia backs Haftar, while Italy supports the Tripoli government. Turkey has also been increasing its military presence in the region since it intervened in 2019 to stop Haftar capturing Tripoli.

For Rome, a renewed explosion of fighting in Libya, sparked by possible Russian retaliation in the country, is a nightmare scenario that evokes the chaos following Gaddafi's death.

Italy can do little but hope the strikes do not trigger renewed fighting between Libya's rival factions. Domestically, the Italian government also sees the risk that the attacks might undermine political support for the aid to Ukraine.

"We all know that Libya and the Mediterranean Sea have been a zone of Russian intervention for a long time. Italian politics prefers to ignore international developments rather than taking responsibility to try to prevent an escalation," MEP Lucia Annunziata (Italy/S&D) told Euronews.

Annunziata argued that Kyiv should have notified Rome of the attacks, but stressed that the Italian government cannot simultaneously recognise Ukraine's right to self-defence while imposing geographical limits on how it exercises that right.

Italy is not alone in its concern over the new flurry of Ukrainian attacks on Russian vessels. On Tuesday, a German government spokesperson warned against escalation in the Baltic Sea region.

In May, Greek fishermen found an unexploded Ukrainian naval drone in the Ionian Sea, prompting a strong reaction from Athens, which wants to keep the Mediterranean from becoming a theatre of military operations.

"Ukraine's right to self-defence cannot justify such actions," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lana Zochiou said when Athens lodged a formal protest in June.

According to an EU official who spoke with Euronews on condition of anonymity, Ukraine intended to send a clear signal that Russian vessels in the Mediterranean are within arm's reach, forcing them to reroute and raising the costs for Moscow.

"No member state wants to see the war in its backyard," the official said. "But the spillover didn't start two days ago. Russia is violating EU territory every day of the week. Russian vessels are a legitimate military target."

World.title: From the track to the gallery: Dakar's autumn in the spotlight
World.content:
This November, Dakar hosted two exceptional events: the Youth Olympic Games, which ran until 13 November, and Dak'Art, the Dakar Biennale of contemporary African art, which runs from 19 November to 19 December. The Games were the first Olympic event ever held on the African continent, and the Biennale now brings together artists from across Africa and its diaspora. In this episode, we hear from participants in both events.

Advertising

Dakar, Senegal, hosted the Youth Olympic Games from 31 October to 13 November, a landmark event widely celebrated across the country..

It was the fourth edition of the Games for young athletes, but the first Olympic event ever held on the African continent.

Dancers form the word "Dakar" during the opening ceremony of the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games at the Abdoulaye Wade Stadium in Diamniadio on 31 October, 2026. © AFP - SEYLLOU

In this episode, you'll hear from Kirsty Coventry, President of the International Olympic Committee (IOC), and from RFI English's sports journalist, Paul Myers. Both agree that it was a unique event, and they look ahead to the future of the Games in Africa.

As Senegal sets Youth Games medal record, Olympic hero calls for more investment

After sport, there's art

Then, just a few days after the Games closed, Dakar launched Dak'Art on 19 November. The Biennale runs until Saturday 19 December 2026 and features artists from across the continent and its diaspora.

The theme of this edition is "(Anti)fragility", which, according to the curator and organisers, refers to "the capacity to turn fragile situations into a space for invention and expressive power".

The main venue is the former Law Courts building, now the National Art Gallery.

Cultural exchanges beyond borders as African art gains global interest

"The project emphasises social and community bonds, co-creation, acts of care, and responses that allow the experience of shocks to be transformed into new possibilities," the curator said.

This year's artists include Nu Barreto from Guinea-Bissau, who won one of the main prizes; Ibrahima Cissé and Eva Diallo, both from Senegal; Chemu Ng'ok from Kenya; and Souad Abdelrasoul from Cairo, among many others.

Billboards advertising the Dakar Biennale 2026, the 16th Dakar Biennale of Contemporary African Art, the most important event of its kind on the continent, which showcases the best of African art and its diasporas through hundreds of cultural events combining painting, sculpture, and performance. © Patrick Meinhardt / AFP

Alpha Thiam, Senegal's Minister of Culture, Crafts and Tourism, said these events were "drawing on the philosophy of Senghor" and embracing "modernity without ever forsaking our authenticity".

In his view, the participants show that "contemporary African creation is not merely a superficial construct, but a genuine assertion of sovereignty", allowing Africans to build their future on their own terms.

In this episode, Souad Abdelrasoul, who had just arrived in Dakar for the opening, and her gallery manager, Menna Genedy, of the Misr Gallery in Cairo talked to RFI.

You'll also hear from the Senegalese storyteller, or griot, Bocar Niang, and his associate, the artist and philanthropist Amélie Mourgue d'Algue, of the French charity the Bureau of Invisible Hours (Bureau des heures invisibles).

Dak'Art is also an opportunity for other artists from the region to share their work. Among them is Bocar Niang, a griot, poet and performer, who has set up his own museum in his hometown of Tambacounda. The museum is dedicated to the culture of griots, the travelling musicians and storytellers who keep the tradition of oral history alive in parts of West Africa.

Beyond Senegal

Dakar is also a meeting point for artists from all over Africa, especially in the 'off 'programme.

The book, Made in Sierra Leone — Edition 02, will be unveiled during the fair for instance; it is the expanded second edition of the limited edition book by multidisciplinary artist Sahr Martin Kabba known as Sabanoh, from Freetown, Sierra Leone.

Made in Sierra Leone, Edition 02: by artist Sabanoh © Unx-art

The publication extends his exploration of Sierra Leone’s contemporary visual language through image, design, and cultural memory, as the artist and the curator, Sarah Hachi-Duchene of Unx-art, tell us.

This episode was mixed by Nicolas Doreau.
