World.title: European court: States can turn back migrants in some cases
World.content:
Europe's top human rights court ruled that member states can turn back migrants even under "hostile" conditions, unless they've been identified as people who may be subject to ill-treatment.

The European Court of Human Rights on Tuesday ruled that states belonging to the Council of Europe group have a right to control foreign arrivals.

But the court ruling said all 46 member states of the group — that includes all EU and some non-EU countries and promotes democracy and human rights on the continent — must ensure and uphold human rights of people even in hostile environments.

The European court ruling is a complicated one since it deals with a case concerning the entry of nationals of Afghanistan, Iraq and Cuba into EU member countries Poland, Latvia and Lithuania between 2021 and 2022.

That was a time when a border standoff was playing out between Belarus and the EU's eastern member states, with Belarus having been accused of entirely manufacturing a migration crisis to put pressure on the EU.

Belarus arranged for people from various third countries to enter their state and then pointed them to the EU's frontiers.

Europe's human rights court says countries can turn back migrants with duty of care

Europe's most important human rights court on Tuesday ruled that states have a right to control the entry of foreign nationals into their territory even when migration has been weaponized.

The court calls Belarus' hostile actions of 2021 as having been an instance of "instrumentalization of migration."

But the court said that states must still ensure that migrants are protected against inhumane or degrading treatment.

In the context of a surge in migration, for example, national authorities were still to identify people who were particularly at risk of suffering or enduring ill treatment.

The migrants in the case brought before the European court said that they had been violently prevented from crossing into the EU without their asylum applications having been examined and that their human rights had been violated.

"In a context of instrumentalization of migration, the removal of a foreign national to the instrumentalizing state would not, as such, constitute a violation of Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman and degrading treatment)," the court press release said.

The court ordered Poland, Latvia and Lithuania to pay compensation for their treatment of migrants at the EU's external borders with Belarus.

Five EU countries announce plan with Rwanda to establish 'return hub'

Five EU countries also last week announced a plan with Rwanda to establish a so-called return hub in the African nation.

The hub will host rejected asylum seekers waiting to return to their countries of origin.

But there are many concerns about the project since Rwanda ranks low on human rights measures and there are questions about whether people's rights will be sufficiently protected.

World.title: Ukraine: Zelenskyy and Hungary's Magyar meet amid thaw in ties
World.content:
Hungary's Prime Minister Peter Magyar has arrived in Ukraine for meetings with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and ethnic Hungarians. Both leaders say they want better relations after a change of leadership in Budapest.

Hungary's new Prime Minister Peter Magyar arrived in Ukraine on Tuesday afternoon for meetings with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as well as with ethnic Hungarians living in the west of the country.

The meeting comes as both say they want better relations after a change of leadership in Budapest — no doubt a welcome change for Kyiv after years of Viktor Orban obstructing funding for its self-defense against full-scaler Russian invasion.

Ukraine's Zelenskyy posted his thanks for the meeting with a photo on X, writing: "A visit that is sure to bring positive results. We already have agreements in the areas of politics, energy, and infrastructure. Thank you!"

Despite his softer approach, Magyar has said Hungary will not be sending arms to Kyiv while at the same time vowing, "we stand with Ukraine against the Russian aggressor."

Rights of ethnic Hungarians tied to war support and EU accession talks

Magyar has insisted that the rights of tens of thousands of ethnic Hungarians in the Transcarpathia — a region that was part of Austria-Hungary until the end of World War I and situated at the borders of Ukraine, Hungary, Poland, Romania and Slovakia — be resolved before Budapest can wholeheartedly back Ukraine and its possible accession to the European Union.

Relations deteriorated significantly over the issue in 2017, when Kyiv passed a law making Ukrainian the official language of all secondary education in Ukraine, something Budapest viewed as discriminatory toward ethnic Hungarians.

Last month, Ukrainian lawmakers passed legislation allowing ethnic minorities in the country expanded rights regarding the teaching and use of their native languages. The move was welcomed by Budapest and Hungary dropped its opposition to Brussels opening accession talks with Ukraine.

Magyar pitched this week's trip — the first to Transcarpathia by a Hungarian prime minister since 2015 — in April, after defeating Orban.

Before departing for Ukraine, the Hungarian leader said: "I hope these talks will be successful. I think this is a historic day and a good opportunity to put Ukrainian-Hungarian relations on a new footing and to rebuild trust as we did with our other neighbors."

World.title: Ukraine's bid for NATO membership and more air defense remains controversial
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is calling for the rapid acceptance of his country into NATO. However, the necessary unanimity for this is lacking, as shown during the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin.

It took a while for the video call to connect. When Volodymyr Zelenskyy finally greeted the delegates in Berlin, applause broke out. The Ukrainian president appealed to the gathered parliamentarians from 32 NATO member states to keep supporting his country, especially against the massive aerial bombardment from Russia.

"Dear friends, winter is now ahead of us. And of course, our number one priority is air defense," Zelenskyy told the delegates. His country urgently needs more Patriot and other comprehensive anti-air attack systems. "And your countries have them. Missiles that can stop Russian ballistic missiles should not be sitting in warehouses collecting dust. And we say this openly. Please help us with this."

Western allies boost Ukraine's defenses but clash over deep strikes To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ukraine seeks to join NATO

Zelenskyy renewed his call for his country to join the NATO military alliance. That issue is not for the NATO Parliamentary Assembly, which was gathered for its 72nd annual meeting in Berlin, to decide. But it was important to the Ukrainian president to reiterate his request.

After the war ends, Ukraine needs strong security guarantees and NATO could ensure those. "Wouldn't it be more effective to simply bring Ukraine into NATO?" Zelenskyy asked, arguing: "Wouldn't that be better for all of us, for everyone? Cheaper to put in place? And more reliable when it comes to actually protecting security?"

There is conflict among NATO members about the possibility of admitting Ukraine. The alliance has affirmed multiple times that the path to membership stands open to Ukraine — however, in the long term rather than the near future. This is primarily because of the ongoing war and the possible assistance obligations of other NATO countries for Ukraine, which was attacked by Russia.

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte rejected the Ukrainian demands at the summit, which for the first time in 26 years was held in Berlin. Ukraine had entry prospects; however, NATO members currently lack unanimity on this issue. NATO alone decides who becomes a member. "There is total clarity on that within the alliance," Rutte said.

If Russia attacked NATO, would Germany be prepared? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Merz: Denying Ukraine NATO membership in 2008 'was a mistake'

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz advocated for Ukraine to receive security guarantees similar to what NATO members have, in the instance of a possible ceasefire. In retrospect, it was clear "what a mistake it was not to follow the American suggestion back in 2008 at the NATO summit in Bucharest to admit Ukraine as a member," Merz said at a joint press conference following a meeting with Rutte.

Whether or not a NATO entry for Ukraine could be part of negotiations with Russia is another question, according to Rutte. He approved of current US efforts to bring about peace talks, and how Europe was closely consulting with Ukraine and the US for a unified position. "But it is also to test now whether Putin is willing to play ball, and then these issues might come up again."

The Russian invasion of Ukraine has led to NATO arming itself on a massive scale. Members have committed to raising their countries' defense spending to 5% of their gross domestic product (GDP) by 2035.

Rutte warned that all the allies needed a credible path to get there, "and ideally, they get there sooner than 2035." In addition, he said weapons production among member states needed to further increase because "right now, demand still far exceeds the supply."

Why Germany's military ambitions face a battle at home To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany's military budget has had a massive increase

The contribution by Germany's Bundeswehr armed forces to NATO was explained by Carsten Breuer, Germany's highest-ranking soldier. For example, the massive increase in military spending: "Our defense budget has tripled since 2021. The goal is to achieve the 5% target, which was set at the summit in The Hague, well before 2035." In the coming year, Germany's defense budget has risen to more than €139 billion ($151 billion).

The Bundeswehr was further developing into a "constantly modernized, effective and innovative army, Breuer said. Also, a much larger one than before. "To reach our current capability goals we are expanding the Bundeswehr to a total of 460,000 soldiers by the mid-2030s," the German chief of defense said. Of those, 200,000 are to be reservists. "This is like walking a tightrope because we must find the right balance between growth and operational readiness."

Following his speech, Breuer answered questions from the delegates who showed keen interest in the developments. The discussion was a preview of Breuer's new post: He has been voted in as the new chair of the NATO Military Committee and will move to the alliance's headquarters in Brussels mid-next year. Then he will become the principal military advisor to NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte. "I take this election as a sign of recognition that Germany has now accepted its responsibility as well as its role in security policy," Breuer said.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: HIV infections could rise amid aid cuts, UN warns
World.content:
The impact of United States government funding cuts has been dramatic for many HIV programs, UNAIDS warned. The agency expects that 2027 data to show an increase in new infections after being on the cusp of ending AIDS.

New HIV infections could rise next year for the first time in years, reversing a historic decline amid funding cuts and anti-rights campaigns, the United Nations (UN) warned on Tuesday.

"The world has moved closer towards controlling the HIV pandemic, but changes in funding and resulting service disruptions jeopardize this progress," the UNAIDS agency said in its annual global update.

AIDS-related death numbers has fallen to its lowest in more than two decades. According to the organization, this was made possible by broader access to treatment and improvements in the quality of care programs.

The virus claimed roughly 570,000 lives globally in 2025. This means almost 1,600 people died everyday. In comparison, this figure was 600,000 in 2024 and 1.3 million in 2010.

Based on data from 172 countries, the agency estimated that 41 million people worldwide were living with HIV in 2025, of whom 32.1 million were receiving antiretroviral treatment.

The wider use of antiretroviral medication also reduces the risk of HIV transmission, the organization said. It estimates that 1.2 million people contracted HIV in 2025, down from 1.3 million the year before. The peak in 1994 saw 3.5 million.

UNAIDS said Lenacapavir, an injection administered just twice a year, has marked another turning point in HIV prevention [FILE: July 2024] Image: Nardus Engelbrecht/AP/picture alliance

"HIV, which was once a death sentence, has become a manageable health condition for millions of people thanks to life-saving HIV medicines," said UNAIDS.

'Dramatic impacts' of US aid cuts

Despite the encouraging data so far, cuts to international funding have hampered efforts to fight HIV, the agency warned.

HIV programs faced an 18-percent decrease in international financing over the past year, said UNAIDS.

"Funding losses have destabilized HIV programs worldwide, coinciding with a wider contraction in official development assistance over the years," it said.

Although the United States remains the largest international donor for HIV programs, its contributions dropped by 26% between 2024 and 2025.

How USAID cuts could result in higher HIV transmission To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

After dismantling USAID, the world's largest foreign aid agency, last year, the Donald Trump administration has sought to replace decades of aid with new bilateral deals.

"The impact of the United States government funding cuts has been especially dramatic given the reliance of many countries on its support for core HIV programs," said UNAIDS.

Meanwhile disbursements from the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria dropped by 13% in 2025.

Next year's data may show rising infections

"We are on the cusp of ending AIDS – this has been the greatest story of global ​health – and just when we should finish it, cuts and the rolling back of human rights is ​threatening to take away our gains," Winnie Byanyima, executive director of UNAIDS, told ​Reuters.

"We haven't ‌got the data yet, but we see the signs. We see all the signs of reversals," she added.

Byanyima predicted that data released in 2027 would begin to reflect a rise in new HIV infections.

In 2015, the UN set a goal to end AIDS by 2030.

World.title: Pope Francis diaries recount spiritual crisis, him seeing the 'Devil'
World.content:
Extracts of the late Pope Francis' diaries have been published, the first release of its kind since the 1960s. They discuss his struggles with his role in the Vatican and visions of the devil and the gates of hell.

The late Pope Francis suffered a spiritual crisis during his papacy when he struggled with how to lead the Catholic Church and believed he saw and heard the devil on several occasions, according to an annotated collection of his private diaries published on Tuesday.

Francis was pope for 12 years until his death last April.

Cardinal Victor Fernandez, a compatriot and close collaborator of Francis', collated the diary entries and provides accompanying commentary, in the first set of papal diaries to be published posthumously since those of John XXIII, who died in 1963.

The 160-page sample of Francis' diaries is the first release of its kind in more than 50 years Image: Gregorio Borgia/AP Photo/picture alliance

What does the book say about Francis' difficulties as pope?

The diary entries speak of the Argentine-born pontiff not wanting to be someone "who uses others like puppets," according to the accompanying commentary.

"It was all mixed with governance issues, pressure regarding decisions to make, and aridity and desolation," a December 2022 entry from Francis said.

Although the book does not make clear exactly who Francis worried he was using like puppets or the nature of the internal pressures, Francis encountered stern resistance from more conservative forces within the Church as he urged the staid institution to modernize.

Cardinal Fernandez wrote that Francis "ultimately recognized it was the worst trial that had toremented him ... and that he felt that he was in a continual battle not to fall into this demonic seduction."

Various world leaders attended Francis' funeral last April [FILE: April 2025] Image: IPA/ABACAPRESS/IMAGO

What does the book say about Francis' religious visions and dreams?

The 160-page selection of excerpts — starting in 1992 when he was still known as Jorge Mario Bergoglio and running until a few months before his death — are arranged by theme and pay closer attention to Francis' internal spiritual experiences than Vatican politics.

But one of the three occasions listed where the late pope believed he had seen the Devil was during a meeting with Vatican officials in January 2021 early in what he termed a spiritual crisis. In that instance he even believed to have heard the figure speak.

"I can't forget the powerful raspiness of his voice," Francis wrote in an entry. "The Lord granted me an opportunity to leave that meeting, and thus he freed me."

Other entries detail how Francis believed that God spoke to him in his dreams, and one from 2018 stated: "Last night I saw the entrance to Hell. I peeked in to look a little, and it terrified me."

Pope Francis' life and legacy To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What else features in the diary excerpts?

The papers show Francis to be self-critical at times, chastizing himself for "feelings of disdain, envy, pride" or for ignoring a drunken man who approached him "because I wanted to have a serene walk."

At one point in a 2022 entry he refers to himself as the "proud, self-sufficient, cynical, self-deceptive Jorge."

They also show how in later years he felt anxious to make the most of his remaining years, and regretful about some of his deicsions earlier in his life.

"I want to do good during the little time I have left, desiring to be good," he wrote in 1996 on turning 60. "How much time I've used badly! How much badly done!"

The accounts also list his regret after a visit to Chile in 2018 when he faced stern criticism for initially dismissing allegations of sexual abuse and cover-up against a bishop there before later apologizing.

"It was hard for me to admit what happened in Chile; I didn't think it was so serious," a "devastated" pontiff wrote three years later.

Fernandez also recounts comments from Francis on some senior officials in the Vatican including his successor, US Cardinal Robert Prevost, now Pope Leo XIV. According to Fernandez, Francis called him "a great pastor, a generous missionary, and an irreproachable man."

World.title: EU enlargement: Why do some EU member states use their vetoes to block the accession of certain candidate countries?
World.content:
Individual EU member states use their veto powers to block candidate countries in the accession process — often for reasons of domestic politics. DW takes a look at some cases and examines what's behind them.

It's been quite a while since the European Union's last enlargement, when Croatia joined the bloc back in 2013.

If everything goes according to plan, another might soon be on the cards: Montenegro, with a population of just 620,000, could complete accession negotiations in the coming months and join the EU in early 2028.

But no sooner had EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos made this announcement in October than news emerged that Croatia might veto Montenegro's accession unless the country meets a series of Croatian demands. EU politicians and MEPs were dismayed.

This is not the first time something like this has happened: The veto rights that member states have on many EU matters have increasingly been used by individual countries in recent years as a means of leverage or obstruction, paralyzing the EU in the process.

EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said in October that Montenegro could become a member of the European Union in 2028 Image: Dursun Aydemir/Anadolu/IMAGO

DW takes a look at some of the most significant cases, the background to them and what are — in some instances — the serious political consequences of them.

Montenegro: Croatia's eight demands

Montenegro is the most advanced EU candidate country, with a potential accession date of 2028. It has already provisionally closed several of the EU's 33 negotiating chapters.

As of November 23, however, Croatia is blocking the closure of three chapters that have already been negotiated.

Zagreb is demanding, among other things, compensation for former prisoners held in Montenegrin camps during the Yugoslav wars of the 1990s, clarification of the fate of Croatians who have been missing since that time, and more rigorous prosecution of war crimes.

There are also disputes over the precise maritime boundary between the two countries. In addition, Croatia is demanding payment of about €2.4 billion (about $2.6 billion) for assets that belonged to the Yugoslav People's Army, the army of the former Yugoslavia to which both countries belonged before its breakup in the early 1990s.

Croatia is calling, among other things, for the return of the training ship Jadran, which used to belong to the Yugoslav Royal Navy and was based in Split (now Croatia) before the Yugoslav wars Image: Martin Vas/Depositphotos/IMAGO

Montenegro has already responded to some of Croatia's demands, including those concerning compensation for former prisoners. Others, such as the one relating to the assets of the Yugoslav People's Army, are disputed.

It is clear that Croatia's list of demands is also driven by domestic politics. No government in Zagreb can afford to appear compliant on issues relating to the Croatian War of Independence (1991–95).

Moreover, moderate conservative Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic, who is regularly accused in Croatia of being too pro-EU, can use the dispute to portray himself as a staunch defender of national interests.

Ukraine: Hungarian domestic politics in the name of a minority

After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the EU in June 2022 granted Ukraine and the Republic of Moldova EU candidate status through an accelerated procedure as a gesture of solidarity.

Many EU member states have reservations about Ukraine joining the bloc quickly. Nevertheless, only Hungary, under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, adopted an obstructive stance.

Ostensibly, Hungary's obstruction was about getting Ukraine to improve the rights of the Hungarian minority in Transcarpathia in western Ukraine. But Orban used the matter for domestic political purposes and as an election campaign issue, portraying Ukraine as a "mafia state."

A poster for a petition organized by the previous Hungarian government against EU financial aid for Ukraine in March. The slogan reads 'Let's not let Zelenskyy have the last laugh' Image: Denes Erdos/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

In an effort to appeal to widespread anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Hungary, the country's new prime minister, Peter Magyar, has also adopted a tough stance on Ukraine.

Nevertheless, Magyar's government lifted several temporary blocks on the opening of new negotiating chapters after the Ukrainian parliament passed a law in early October strengthening the educational rights of national minorities.

North Macedonia: The never-ending blockade

No EU candidate country has suffered as much or as long from veto politics as North Macedonia: It was granted EU candidate status in 2005 but only began accession negotiations in July 2022.

Greece blocked the start of negotiations for 13 years because it objected to the name "Republic of Macedonia," as the country was previously known, and accused its neighbor of laying territorial claims to the region of Macedonia in northern Greece.

The dispute was settled in 2018 through a compromise that saw the country change its name to the Republic of North Macedonia the following year.

But just as the path to accession negotiations seemed clear, Bulgaria blocked the opening of talks in November 2020.

Bulgaria regards the Macedonian language as a dialect of Bulgarian and disputes the existence of a distinct Macedonian nation.

A protest in Skopje, the capital of North Macedonia, against making any concessions to Bulgaria in 2022 Image: Petr Stojanovski/DW

Here, too, domestic Bulgarian politics is ultimately a factor.

Former Bulgarian President and current Prime Minister Rumen Radev, for example, fueled the escalation with North Macedonia to enhance his political profile.

Serbia: Croatia is not the only country obstructing progress

Although Serbia has been negotiating EU accession since 2014, little progress has been made.

In July, when the country was still led by President Aleksandar Vucic, no less than eight EU member states — including Croatia — opposed opening further negotiating chapters with Serbia.

While the main reservations relate to democratic shortcomings, deficiencies in the rule of law and corruption in Serbia, Croatia also has its own disputes with its eastern neighbor.

These concern the 1991–95 war, including missing persons, war crimes, minority rights and differing interpretations of history. Relations are also strained by nationalist rhetoric on both sides.

EU enlargement: Montenegro on track to join bloc by 2028 To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Whether the election victory of the Student List in Belgrade in late October , after almost two years of anti-government and anti-corruption protests, will change this situation is impossible to say.

Albania: Greece threatens to use minority rights as leverage

The EU opened accession negotiations with Albania, which has been an EU candidate since 2014, in July 2022.

Albania could become the bloc's next new member after Montenegro. However, Greece has repeatedly threatened (most recently in June) to block the accession process unless the rights of its Greek minority, particularly their property rights, are adequately protected.

An end to the veto system?

In light of all this, Brussels has long been debating a reform of the accession process and the EU veto system.

In early October, the European Commission proposed that decisions to open negotiations with candidate countries be made by qualified majority rather than unanimously. It also proposed that new EU members would be required to give up the right to veto decisions in certain policy areas altogether for a specified period.

The problem with these proposed reforms is that they would themselves have to be adopted unanimously. In other words, any member state could veto the reform.

World.title: CAS reinstates Senegal as 2025 AFCON champions
World.content:
The Court of Arbitration for Sport has reinstated Senegal as 2025 AFCON champions, overturning a CAF decision that stripped them of the title. Morocco, previously declared winners, are confirmed runners-up.

Just over eight months after Senegal were stripped of their 2025 African Cup of Nations (AFCON) title, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has announced that Senegal's appeal has been upheld, reinstating them as 2025 AFCON winners. Morocco, who had been declared champions after a Confederation of African Football (CAF) review, has now been confirmed as runners-up.

"The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has upheld the appeal by the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) against the Confederation of African Football (CAF) and the the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF, in French)," the CAS statement read.

"The decision rendered by the CAF Appeal Board is set aside and the decision by the CAF Disciplinary Board is reinstated. Consequently, the result obtained at the end of the AFCON 2025 final is confirmed."

The statement continued that it felt "the Referee's decision to resume the match or to stop it fell definitively within his sole authority" and that his "decision was covered by the ‘field of play’ doctrine."

The decision comes after a closed-doors hearing at CAS' headquarters in Lausanne in early October.

Before the verdict was delivered, Morocco captain Achraf Hakimi posted a message on Instagram saying he would disagree with Senegal being stripped of the title because "its players fought so hard to win."

"I respect the authorities responsible for football, but I firmly believe that what happens on the pitch should be the most important thing of all. Senegal won that Africa Cup of Nations final through their performance, their determination, and the effort of every player, just as every player represents his country. They fought for that title, and no one can erase what those players achieved on the pitch," Hakimi wrote.

"African football needs unity, fairness, and credibility. We cannot keep building our game if decisions like these leave players and fans questioning everything."

An infamous AFCON final

The final was played on January 18, with Senegal winning 1-0 after extra-time. However, the game was thrown into confusion when many Senegal players walked off the pitch following the referee's decision to award Morocco a penalty in the final minutes. Around 15 minutes later, and after furious Senegalese fans had attempted a pitch invasion, the players did return. Morocco's Brahim Diaz inexplicably missed the penalty, sending the game into extra time, which is when Senegal scored the eventual winner.

Just 10 days afterwards, the CAF issued fines worth more than $1 million (€835,000) and banned players from both teams.

Two months later, and after the Senegal team had paraded the trophy to their fans, CAF declared that Senegal had "forfeited" the final by leaving the pitch. CAF then overturned the result, awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory and the title. The Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) denounced the CAF decision and took the case to CAS.

The aftermath had rumbled on for months, with many believing it damaging for African football as a whole.

"If you look at it critically, the value of African football will definitely go down with this," Collins Okinyo, a former CAF media consultant, told DW after the result had been overturned in March.

Why African football is changing the World Cup forever To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Impact on future World Cup host

The ruling brings an end to a saga that had cast a cloud over a well-organized tournament in Morocco.

The country is emerging as a major football hub in Africa. Already confirmed as a co-host for the World Cup in 2030, Morocco also hosted the 2026 Women's AFCON and has been hosting the U17 Women's World Cup annually since 2025 and is set to do so until 2029. It is further rumored that the Morocco, along with fellow 2030 World Cup hosts Spain and Portugal, is keen to host the next Club World Cup in 2029 as a form of preparation ahead of the big event in 2030.

Although it has made significant advances in sports infrastructure, not everyone is happy about Morocco's push into the football world. In 2025, there were major protests by Gen Z questioning the country's priorities in light of struggling health and education systems.

World.title: Why Iran's medicine supply chain is failing
World.content:
Pharmacies in Iran are closing, hospital deliveries have stalled and patients are rationing doses or turning to black markets.

Ahmad,* 67, visited nearly 20 Tehran pharmacies for the antipsychotic drug chlorpromazine, but left empty-handed.

"When a patient has to go to this many pharmacies just to find an essential drug, you really have to ask who is responsible for supplying medicine," he told DW.

Mitra,* a 37-year-old Tehran resident with diabetes , spent days hunting for insulin. "These are not drugs I can postpone taking or simply give up," she said. "My life depends on regular access to this insulin."

Their ordeal reflects a wider crisis across Iran's health care system.

Along with Tehran residents, DW spoke with an official at Iran's Food and Drug Administration (IFDA) and pharmacy workers in Tehran, Rasht and Mahabad. The interviews were conducted anonymously or using pseudonyms as speaking with foreign media remains dangerous in Iran.

Iran's broken drug supply chain

The official said that Iran's falling currency, along with price controls, has drained domestic drugmaker profits, while unpaid hospital debts have delayed deliveries.

"Add our own hospitals' heavy unpaid debts to distributors, and you can see why distribution has ground to a halt and companies are no longer supplying hospitals," the official said.

"Unless the Plan and Budget Organization makes our currency allocation realistic, banks step in with loans for drugmakers and insurers settle their debts, the Health Ministry's hands will remain tied and this disaster cannot be stopped," the official warned.

Some patients are being forced to ration supplies [FILE 2024] Image: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/picture alliance

IFDA spokesman Mohammad Hashemi told Iran's semi-official ILNA news agency on November 9 that fewer than 40 of roughly 700 essential drugs faced supply difficulties. However, pharmacists told DW about how difficult it can be to get drugs on shelves.

A pharmacy manager in Tehran said insurance payments are often delayed by months, while drug prices continue to climb. Another pharmacist in the northwestern Mahabad region said distributors demand cash upfront for scarce items.

The insurance delays and shifting rules have pushed some pharmacies to drop contracts or refuse costly insured drugs.

The pharmacist in Mahabad, who prefers to be called Leili,* said that general pharmacies can lack about 40 items, and larger specialty pharmacies stocking chemotherapy and complex treatments can lack over 100, including psychiatric and Parkinson's drugs, and insulin vials.

"Many drugs can no longer be found in the official supply chain at all, such as nimodipine tablets [used to treat certain strokes] or hospital injectable antibiotics that have no substitutes," she said.

Turning to low-quality, black market medicine

As common items like cold medication become scarcer or more expensive, some people are turning to home remedies, she said. She added that for essential medicines like insulin, chronic patients are using smaller doses to preserve supply.

Many of those unable to pay are middle-class customers whom pharmacists cannot easily refer to charities, she said, with elderly and psychiatric patients among the hardest hit.

Leili warned that lower quality seen in some reverse-engineered domestic drugs presents a high risk for cancer, transplant and autoimmune patients.

She added that some families are forced to turn to street markets usually located outside of clinics, which lack cold-chain controls and sell counterfeit medicines or drugs with altered expiration dates.

Another pharmacy manager who asked to be called Khadiv* said scarce medicines can fetch up to 10 times their official price.

Sanctions and blockades

Amid the current conflict with the US, Khadiv said US sanctions, along with border disruptions and the US maritime blockade in the Strait of Hormuz inflate import costs.

In a statement, the US State Department told DW its sanctions follow international law to deny Tehran funds for "destabilizing behavior," stressing the measures allow "broad authorizations and exceptions" for food, medicine and medical devices. It pointed to what it called Iran's "corrupt ruling elite" for not properly allocating resources.

Iranian officials, however, reject that claim. In late summer, Health Minister Mohammad Reza Zafarghandi called US exemption claims "a big lie," saying banking, insurance, flight and shipping sanctions block imports.

Earlier this fall, the IFDA's raw materials chief cited currency, banking, customs and shipping hurdles as the main bottleneck.

DW emailed the Iranian Embassy's media office in Berlin for comment but received no reply.

"Seeing so many people unable to afford their medicine or reach medical centers leaves me with a sense of guilt and helplessness," Khadiv said, adding that lack of access can even lead to patient deaths.

For patients like Ahmad and Mitra, the standoff offers no relief, and every day, the gap between official assurances and what is actually on pharmacy shelves grows harder to ignore.

*Names changed for safety reasons.

World.title: El debate dentro de la Junta Electoral para abrir expediente sancionador a Silvia Intxaurrondo: una votación que terminó siete a cinco
World.content:
La Junta Electoral Central (JEC) se dividió casi a la mitad en su reunión de este lunes a la hora de abrir un expediente sancionador a la periodista de RTVE Silvia Intxaurrondo por una serie de reflexiones en forma de preguntas que formuló en su programa sobre el posible veto a la formación ultra Vox en la televisión pública. La votación registró siete votos a favor del procedimiento, que todavía no está resuelto, y cinco en contra.

En la reunión de la JEC, la discusión que más se extendió fue sobre la decisión de abrir un expediente informativo sancionador contra la periodista Intxaurrondo,que ahora tendrá dos meses para recurrir. No solo hubo diferentes planteamientos, también una votación dividida, que prosperó por los siete votos a favor, en este caso, con el apoyo del presidente de la Junta, Eduardo Calvo, y los cinco en contra, aunque faltó a la sesión la vicepresidenta Pilar Teso, magistrada del sector progresista y vinculada a la sala contencioso-administrativo del Tribunal Supremo.

Vox había denunciado a Intxaurrondo porque, tras la entrevista en La Revuelta a su líder, Santiago Abascal, la periodista formuló en su programa de La Hora de la 1 una serie de preguntas y reflexiones sobre el papel y la cabida en una televisión pública de una formación de extrema derecha y si RTVE podía ser neutral ante la defensa de los derechos fundamentales y la igualdad. La JEC comunicó este lunes a la periodista que la sanción que le podría corresponder oscilaría entre 100 y 1.000 euros, dependiendo de su pago pronto y voluntario.

Silvia Intxaurrondo respondió este martes en su programa muy en línea con la controversia que se desarrolló el lunes en la reunión de los expertos y magistrados presentes en la Junta Electoral. La mayoría de los vocales tumbaron, para empezar, la propuesta de resolución que habían propuesto los letrados del Congreso adscritos a ese órgano y que se habían limitado a sugerir que se podría enviar a la periodista y a TVE un simple apercibimiento en favor de la neutralidad informativa y la transparencia, y más ante periodos electorales, pero sin sanción alguna, como se ha hecho en otras ocasiones. No ocurrió así y la sesión acabó con una conclusión algo contradictoria: en la resolución emitida al final por la JEC se acepta que la periodista se limitó a formular una serie de reflexiones en un espacio del programa que no era informativo, sino de opinión y tertulia, pero los vocales propuestos por el PP, los catedráticos de Derecho Constitucional Carlos Vidal y Javier Tajadura Tejada, sostuvieron que “las preguntas no eran neutrales y conducían a una respuesta”.

El vocal Carlos Vidal defendió que él había visto el programa y esa parte íntegra y propuso que se visionara en la sala, cosa que sucedió. La mayoría de los vocales, tras la emisión, convinieron en que la periodista debía ser sancionada, algo bastante inédito, y pese a que se planteó también que podría optarse por castigar genéricamente a RTVE. Ese punto ni se votó. El vocal y catedrático en Derecho Constitucional Francisco Javier García Roca, a propuesta del PSOE, argumentó en defensa de la libertad de expresión de los periodistas que la cuestión formulada por Intxaurrondo sobre el cordón sanitario contra la ultraderecha era una fórmula en discusión en toda Europa. Su tesis no tuvo éxito.

La Junta Electoral Central que vigila el buen funcionamiento y transparencia de los procesos electorales la componen ocho magistrados de entre los más experimentados del Supremo, elegidos por insaculación por parte del Consejo General del Poder Judicial, y cinco catedráticos de Derecho o de Ciencias Políticas y Sociología en activo, a propuesta conjunta de los partidos con representación en el Congreso.

World.title: “Los alumnos de FP vienen con la derrota en la cara”
World.content:
Ángel Luis González, profesor de Informática y nominado al Global Teacher Prize en 2025, charla con su exalumno Borja Delgado sobre por qué la Formación Profesional es una opción de futuro sólida para los alumnos que no se sienten motivados en Secundaria y del poder transformador de la creatividad en la educación, y que él aplica en su método de enseñanza

Se sienten peores estudiantes que otros; creen que su lugar no está en las aulas; algunos, incluso, se perciben a sí mismos como balas perdidas. Puede que a muchos alumnos de Formación Profesional (FP) les suenen estos pensamientos. Se equivocan. Lo afirma Ángel Luis González, profesor de Informática en el CIFP Virgen de Gracia (Puertollano, Ciudad Real). “El alumnado de FP viene con la derrota en la cara. Pero es que, a lo mejor, el modelo que se viene trabajando en Secundaria no está pensado para ellos, y solo es una parte de lo que van a necesitar para la vida”, asegura. Palabra de un nominado al Global Teacher Prize, premio conocido como el Nobel de la Educación, que protagoniza junto a su exalumno Borja Delgado un nuevo capítulo de Pensemos el mañana, un proyecto de Fundación Unicaja y EL PAÍS para responder a los desafíos que presenta la educación del futuro.

“Trato de ser el profesor que me hubiera gustado tener”

Ambos se conocieron hace cinco años en el IES Siberia Extremeña (Talarrubias, Badajoz). Delgado recuerda con admiración el papel que jugó este profesor en su vida. “Lo que soy hoy en día te lo debo prácticamente a ti. Es indescriptible el sentimiento que tengo hacia la motivación que transmitías”, afirma sin rodeos. González cuenta el secreto: “Ese es un aspecto fundamental. Yo trato de ser el profesor que me hubiera gustado tener, y a mí me gustaría alguien que me motivara”. Autor de La Educación creativa, un manual en el que desarrolla su método pedagógico, al que bautizó como The sonic onion, en el que la motivación a los alumnos es uno de los ejes centrales, este profesor reivindica de la misma forma su ámbito de enseñanza: “Creo que la FP es genial para hacer de trampolín y que muchos alumnos cojan esa confianza que les falta”.

“Lo que soy hoy en día te lo debo prácticamente a ti como profesor”

Durante la charla, ambos protagonistas repasan cómo fueron aquellos días en los que fueron maestro y alumno. “Recuerdo que os llevé a un lugar bastante curioso, al que llamábamos el cementerio porque tiraban todos los dispositivos rotos, y empezamos a construir con nuestra propia creatividad”, rememora González. Ahí se dio cuenta de algo: “Veía ese poder transformador de la educación y ese empoderamiento que os estaba dando el conocimiento. Es algo maravilloso”.

Pensemos la educación del futuro ‘Pensemos el mañana’, un proyecto de Fundación Unicaja, busca fomentar el conocimiento, los valores de la educación, un aprendizaje sostenible y responsable y dar respuestas a los grandes desafíos de la educación del futuro. El proyecto pivota sobre seis ejes: 1 Aprendizaje y sentido vital 2 Bienestar y salud mental 3 Futuro y empleabilidad 4 Sostenibilidad y sentido colectivo 5 Tecnología y ética 6 Carácter y ciudadanía ¿Qué está ocurriendo en estos tiempos de cambios profundos y transversales? ¿Cuáles son los grandes retos para afrontar la transformación que viene? ¿Qué educación necesitamos? Diferentes personalidades de todos los ámbitos nos ayudarán a responder a estas y otras preguntas destinadas a impulsar cambios, dinamizar ideas y apoyar propuestas con impacto pedagógico y social. ‘Pensemos el mañana’ es un proyecto inspirador para las futuras generaciones llamadas a conquistar nuevas cotas del saber en un mundo complejo y cambiante.

Ángel Luis González Profesor de Informática en el CIFP Virgen de Gracia (Puertollano, Ciudad Real) Sus alumnos destacan su gran poder motivacional dentro y fuera de las aulas. Fue uno de los 50 candidatos a mejor profesor del mundo gracias al desarrollo de un innovador método pedagógico basado en el aprendizaje por capas y la motivación. También es escritor, 'podcaster' y conferenciante. Su lema: la educación empodera Borja Delgado Alumno de grado superior del IES Siberia Extremeña (Talarrubias, Badajoz) Su gran virtud, según su maestro, es el liderazgo. El primer día de clase quiso ser delegado, aunque no conocía el temario ni apenas a sus compañeros. Completó el grado medio en Informática y ahora se encuentra acabando el grado superior. Su próximo objetivo: llegar a la Universidad para ampliar su formación como ingeniero

World.title: La neutralidad ideológica de la Comunidad de Madrid
World.content:
Las instrucciones remitidas por la Consejería de Educación a los centros públicos ―y no a los concertados, que también están sostenidos con fondos públicos― causan escalofríos

Mostrar apoyo al pueblo de Ucrania tras la invasión rusa es un deber moral. Manifestar apoyo al pueblo palestino sometido a un genocidio por parte de Israel es ideologizar. Asistir al progresivo aumento de las temperaturas del planeta sin hablar en las aulas del calentamiento global consecuencia de la acción humana es neutralidad. Abordar la emergencia climática, sus causas y sus efectos, es adoctrinar. Educar en los principios y valores de determinada confesión religiosa es neutralidad. Educar en derechos humanos es adoctrinar.

Apostar por centros educativos con precisos filtros de acceso (económicos, sociales, religiosos) es promover la neutralidad. Apostar por una escuela pública de tod@s para tod@s, en que convivan niñas y niños de diferentes procedencias socioeconómicas, geográficas, culturales y religiosas, sin más suelo ideológico que los derechos humanos, es adoctrinar.

Educar literariamente con títulos (casi) exclusivamente escritos por hombres es neutralidad. Manifestar voluntad de incorporar obras escritas por mujeres es adoctrinar. Proponer títulos de ficción en que los referentes amorosos sean exclusivamente heterosexuales es neutralidad. Proponer títulos de ficción en que sus protagonistas sean gays o lesbianas es adoctrinar.

Podríamos seguir. De cada una de estas afirmaciones, que reflejan el emplazamiento ideológico del gobierno de la Comunidad de Madrid, hay pruebas en las hemerotecas. Hay pruebas también en el eco que los medios de comunicación hicieron de las modificaciones introducidas por la Comunidad de Madrid en el currículo estatal. «El currículo [madrileño] elimina una treintena de conceptos con “carga ideológica muy importante”» (La Razón, 4 de mayo de 2022). ¿Los conceptos eliminados? Emergencia climática, ciudadanía ética digital, memoria democrática, objetivos de desarrollo sostenible, etc. Y esto se consintió.

Porque sí, la Agenda 2030 de Naciones Unidas ―¡de Naciones Unidas!― se ha convertido en uno de los elementos de mayor carga ideológica para la derecha y la extrema derecha en España. Y una se pregunta si quienes se suben a ese barco han leído siquiera cuáles son los objetivos de desarrollo sostenible. Recordemos los primeros: fin de la pobreza, hambre cero, salud y bienestar, educación de calidad, igualdad de género, agua limpia y saneamiento. Estos “retos y desafíos del siglo XXI” constituyen, junto a las competencias clave emanadas del Consejo de la Unión Europea, el pilar de los currículos de la LOMLOE, el horizonte ético hacia el que orientar los aprendizajes. Pero educar para contribuir a un mundo en que se consiga erradicar la pobreza extrema, la inseguridad alimentaria, la mortalidad infantil evitable con la cobertura sanitaria universal, la violencia y la explotación sexuales; educar para un mundo que haga posible el acceso al agua potable, el saneamiento y la higiene de toda la población o la escolarización de los 84 millones de niñas, niños y jóvenes hasta hoy privados de ella es, al parecer, para la derecha y la extrema derecha, puro adoctrinamiento partidista.

Por eso causan escalofríos las Instrucciones remitidas la pasada semana por la Consejería de Educación de la Comunidad de Madrid a los equipos directivos de los centros públicos ―ojo: solo los centros de titularidad pública, que no a los sostenidos con fondos públicos, en un ejercicio insoportable de doble moral― instando a la delación de cuantas acciones se sitúen más allá de su pretendida neutralidad.

Para una Consejería que tachó en el currículo de Literatura Universal cuantas menciones explícitas a “autoras” aparecían, quién nos dice que la afirmación en clase de que el canon literario debe permitir también el acceso a la experiencia de la mitad de la Humanidad ―las mujeres―, a la experiencia también de los pueblos colonizados y esclavizados a través de su literatura, no sería objeto de delación y persecución. Qué decir de la denuncia del genocidio en curso del pueblo palestino.

El respeto escrupuloso a la libertad de conciencia de niñas y niños es incuestionable. La renuncia a prevalerse en clase de una posición de poder para promover mediante la coacción la adhesión a los propios postulados está fuera de toda duda. Pero creo firmemente, después de más de tres décadas en las aulas de Secundaria, que eso quienes mejor lo sabemos y ejercemos somos, precisamente, los maestros y maestras de la Escuela Pública.

World.title: Appeal court rejects state bid to pause Bonaire climate ruling
World.content:
The Netherlands has to draft binding national targets, the Court of Appeal in The Hague has ruled, after the state requested a suspension of its obligation.

The ruling is another step in the Bonaire climate case, which was taken to court by Greenpeace on behalf of the residents of the Dutch island in the Caribbean, where climate change is destroying the coral reef.

That case was won in January, and the court found that the government in The Hague had acted in a discriminatory manner to its people there.

Part of the ruling was that the Netherlands must set binding emissions targets for the whole economy in law by July 28, 2027, as well as draw up an adaptation plan for Bonaire that can be implemented by 2030. The ruling must be carried out even while an appeal is under way.

The government appealed the ruling in April, requesting a suspension. The Court of Appeal has largely rejected that request, but said international air and maritime transport can be left out of the targets but the government must move otherwise forward.

Marieke Vellekoop, director of Greenpeace Netherlands, said in a reaction: “The state has once again been reminded of its responsibility. Executing the judgment is not a non-binding ambition, but an obligation.”

Vellekoop said it was “incomprehensible that the state is doing everything it can to delay climate action,” while the consequences of the climate crisis are becoming increasingly severe. “On Bonaire, but also here in Europe. The cabinet must stop delaying and get to work now.”

World.title: Erasmus MC head of intensive care steps down over safety report
World.content:
The head of intensive care at Rotterdam’s Erasmus Medical Centre, Diederik Gommers, has stepped down in the wake of a damning report into a “culture of fear” that potentially compromised the safety of staff and patients.

The healthcare inspectorate IGJ said the situation in the department, the largest in the Netherlands, amounted to “a serious threat to the safety of patients or care”.

Gommers, who became one of the public faces of the Netherlands’ coronavirus response in 2020 when he was a member of the government’s Outbreak Management Team, quit his post with immediate effect when the findings became known this week.

The department’s board of directors has been placed under heightened supervision after the report said the psychological safety of staff was compromised by a management that did not accept being challenged or criticised.

The Erasmus MC hospital said in a statement on its website that it accepted it should have recognised the warning signs and taken action sooner.

“We are sorry that some colleagues did not feel safe enough to voice their concerns. Everyone should feel free to express their views, challenge each other and share signs.”

The hospital added that there was no suggestion patients had received substandard care as a result of the problems in the department.

18-month investigation

Inspectors began investigating the ICU 18 months ago after a whistleblower raised concerns about the workplace culture.

NOS late-night news show Nieuwsuur and regional news channel Rijnmond said they had seen hundreds of internal emails and documents going back five years and spoken to 26 current and former staff about the situation.

Doctors said “tensions” between medical specialists deterred staff from speaking out if they were critical of or worried about their colleagues’ decisions.

Jan Maarten van den Berg, a former healthcare inspector who specialised in intensive care, told Nieuwsuur: “These conclusions are very severe. There needs to be a breakthrough in the situation at Erasmus for the sake of the patients.”

Nieuwsuur earlier reported that Gommers did not have the legally required qualifications to carry out medical research on patients. The hospital said Gommers had not done any clinical research since 2023 and had started studying to obtain his certificates.

World.title: Juice and milk bottles to join deposit scheme in 2027
World.content:
Dutch packaging trade association Verpact has announced it will begin a deposit return system for plastic juice and dairy bottles on its own initiative, according to broadcaster NOS.

Plastic juice and dairy bottles of up to three litres will carry a deposit (statiegeld) from next year. Verpact said it is preparing a phased rollout in 2027. Labels, return machines, IT systems and logistics will all have to be adjusted.

The move follows pressure from climate and green growth minister Stientje van Veldhoven, who wants 90% of plastic bottles sold in the Netherlands to be collected by January 1, 2028. According to NOS, that target cannot be met without juice and dairy bottles.

In September, Van Veldhoven proposed making deposits compulsory on all plastic bottles up to three litres and banning the sale of bottles and cans without a deposit.

Dairy bottles have so far been exempt because producers say they are hard to clean, and the minister has made hygiene measures a condition. Many juice producers already charge a deposit voluntarily.

World.title: Cold comfort: Dutch skater smashes one-hour natural ice record
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Marathon skater Judith Krabbenborg has taken advantage of the early cold snap to smash the world one-hour record for skating on natural ice.

The 29-year-old took to the ice in Winterswijk, Gelderland, at 8.30am on Tuesday and covered a distance of 34 kilometres 878 metres, beating the previous women’s record by 2.6 kilometres.

“I could feel my legs and my back hurting at the end, but there were so many people standing on the sidelines that it gave me energy,” she told NOS.

The previous record, set four years ago by Femke Mossinkoff, also in Winterswijk, was the first official time for the hour by a woman on natural ice. On the same day Bart Vreugdenhil set the current men’s record of 36 kilometers 717 metres.

Most skating records are set on artificial ice, but Winterswijk is one of three arenas where the local club has been able to create a natural arena for early-morning skaters during the recent cold weather.

The all-time women’s record is 40 kilometres 569 metres, set by another Dutch skater, Carien Kleibeuker, in Inzell, Austria, in 2015.

The rink at Winterswijk closed a few hours after Krabbenborg’s record-breaking skate as the ice started to melt, but it is expected to be available again on Wednesday morning.

World.title: Dutch police seek witnesses to Suriname massacre, 40 years on
World.content:
The Dutch police unit for war crimes, TIM, is helping prosecutors in Suriname search for witnesses of the notorious 1986 Moiwana massacre in which at least 39 civilians were murdered by the Surinamese army.

It is believed likely that people with evidence or testimony are living in the Netherlands. The TIM put out a call for witnesses on Opsporing Verzocht, a police appeals programme, on Monday night.

The massacre occurred during Suriname’s so-called Interior War (1986-1992), a conflict between the military regime of Desi Bouterse, who seized power in a 1980 coup, and rebels led by his former bodyguard Ronnie Brunswijk. Around a third of the country’s entire population moved to the Netherlands in the years around independence in 1975.

With the massacre’s 40-year commemoration coming up, Surinamese prosecutors have asked the TIM to help revive a hunt for evidence and hold those responsible to account.

Soldiers of the army led by Desi Bouterse attacked Moiwana, which is a Maroon village close to the border with French Guiana. They were supposedly hunting Ronnie Brunswijk, a militant regime opponent who was said to be hiding in the village, though survivors say he was not there and the soldiers opened fire anyway.

The case has been stalled for decades. The police inspector leading the investigation into the incident was assassinated in 1990, and though the Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruled in favour of the survivors in 2005 and ordered reparations and apologies, no one has been prosecuted.

Bouterse himself became president of Suriname from 2010 to 2020. He died in 2024. Brunswijk became vice-president from 2020 to 2025. The Surinamese prosecution service reopened an inquiry in 2023 and preliminary judicial investigation began in 2025.

The 40-year commemoration will be held this coming weekend on November 29. TIM is urging anyone with information to come forward.

World.title: New HPV vaccine could save nearly 13,000 cancer diagnoses a year
World.content:
Nearly 13,000 people could avoid a cancer diagnosis later in life if the Netherlands raises its HPV vaccination rate, new medical research has found.

Children aged 10 are given two doses of the vaccine, which protects against a virus that causes cervical cancer in women.

A new version introduced in September covers a wider range of cancers that affect both sexes, such as vaginal and penile cancers.

Around 80% of people in the Netherlands contract the human papillomavirus, mainly though sexual activity.

Most people who are infected have no symptoms, but persistent infection is responsible for around 99.7% of all cases of cervical cancer, one of the most common types in women. Every year 1,100 women and 400 men are diagnosed with a form cancer linked to HPV, most of whom are under the age of 45.

Researchers at Erasmus Medical Centre in Rotterdam and the Dutch cancer centre IKNL said 12,800 diagnoses could be saved if the new vaccine is given to all children who reach the age of 10 in future.

The Netherlands currently has a vaccination rate of 61% for the HPV vaccine, well below the World Health Organisation’s advisory rate of 90% for girls. Around 60% of boys have had the jab as well since the public health agency RIVM added it to their vaccine schedule in 2022.

Gynaecologist and oncologist Luc van Lonkhuijsen, of Amsterdam’s university medical centre, said many parents were anxious about side effects or dismissed it as unimportant.

“We have been vaccinating for 15 years and the number of side-effects we see is really very limited,” he told NOS.

World.title: No evidence of mental illness in suspect of Lisa’s murderer
World.content:
Experts have found no evidence of mental disorder in the man accused of murdering Lisa from Abcoude, the 17-year-old girl whose killing last year sparked a nationwide uprising against femicide and public safety.

The public prosecution service (OM) had ordered an investigation into the mental state of the man, who calls himself Chris Jude, after he claimed he had heard voices telling him to commit rape and murder.

The findings were released in the fifth preliminary hearing of the case at Amsterdam district court on Tuesday.

He’d previously denied remembering anything about the incident, but then admitted to the crimes and said he’d been hearing voices.

On August 20 last year, Lisa phoned the police while cycling back to her parents house after a night out. She was feeling threatened by a man following her on a path through Duivendrecht.

By the time the police arrived, it was too late and her body was found. A manhunt led to Jude’s capture several days later. He was also charged with the rape and attempted rape of two other woman in Amsterdam days before murdering Lisa.

World.title: Erkens claims wolves can be culled despite EU protected status
World.content:
Junior agriculture minister Silvio Erkens has moved a step closer to allowing provinces to shoot wolves for population control.

Erkens said in a letter to parliament that the Netherlands could comply with EU conservation rules with 11 wolf packs, three fewer than the current number, after studying a report commissioned by his predecessor, Jean Rummenie of the farmers’ party BBB.

Experts have warned that the report by Italian independent researcher Marco Appollonio was flawed and likely to face legal challenges if he went ahead with measures based on its findings.

Rummenie ordered Appollonio to study the Dutch wolf population after rejecting an earlier analysis by Wageningen University & Research, the Netherlands’ leading agricultural college, which concluded that the Netherlands could sustainably support between 23 and 56 wolf packs.

Appolonio concluded that the wolf population in the Netherlands is “genetically healthy” and the country met the European Union’s criteria for maintaining a standing population of wolves, Erkens said.

“This confirmation that conditions in the Netherlands are favourable for a maintained population make it possible to manage wolves in the Netherlands, and that is the decision I am taking in principle,” the junior minister wrote.

Wolf-free zones

EU rules require member states to identify how many wolves they can support and recognise their place in the ecosystem as apex predators. Wolves contribute to biodiversity by controlling populations of species such as wild boar and deer and forcing them to disperse, which protects the plants they feed on.

Erkens said he wants to create wolf-free zones by asking provinces to identify areas that are suitable for wolves to roam, where they should be confined.

This would help reduce the number of confrontations with people and their pets and mean less damage caused by wolves feeding on livestock, he argued.

But ecologists say the study is likely to fall foul of EU rules because Rummenie asked Appolonio to take into account the economic impact of wolves, something the EU explicitly forbids.

The European Court of Justice said in a recent ruling against Austria that preventing loss of livestock was not a valid reason on its own for culling wolves, after a farmer was allowed to kill a wolf that had killed 20 of his sheep.

Problem wolf

Arie Trouwborst, professor of nature conservation law at Tilburg University, told NOS: “That binding report by the court has been completely ignored in the Italian report. The report from Wageningen showed that a minimum of 23 packs are needed to fulfil the [EU] criteria.”

In the Netherlands a so-called “problem wolf” was shot dead under licence last year after it attacked walkers in the near Utrecht, but only after a protracted court battle between the provincial government and conservation group Faunabescherming.

Erkens has called a national wolf summit in February where provincial and local government, vets and representatives of the tourism and recreation industry will discuss the government’s strategy.

He also plans to work more closely with Germany, Belgium and Luxembourg to draw up a common policy on wolf populations and press the EU to recognise the interests of “very small densely populated countries such as the Benelux countries.”

World.title: Poland, Lithuania and Latvia violated rights of migrants sent back to Belarus, finds European court

Poland, Lithuania and Latvia violated the human rights of migrants from Afghanistan, Iraq and Cuba who entered their countries illegally from Belarus in 2021 and 2022, the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) has ruled. However, the ECHR did also recognise that states have the right to prevent the entry of migrants who have been “instrumentalised” by Belarus in order to create a crisis on the European Union’s eastern borders. That latter finding prompted Poland’s deputy interior minister with oversight of migration policy to hail today’s rulings as a victory and endorsement of the government’s tough border policies. It was also described as a groundbreaking moment by a leading human rights organisation. 📽️ Watch a video explainer on the Grand Chamber cases concerning instrumentalisation of migration. 📽️ Regardez la vidéo explicative sur les affaires de Grande Chambre sur l'instrumentalisation de la migration. pic.twitter.com/ZhXqZ6lIur — ECHR CEDH (@ECHR_CEDH) November 24, 2026 In 2021, Belarus began encouraging, assisting and, in some cases, forcing tens of thousands of migrants – mainly from Asia and Africa – to irregularly cross into the neighbouring EU states of Poland, Lithuania and Latvia. Belarus engineered the migration crisis as part of the various “hybrid actions” undertaken alongside its ally Russia with the intention of destabilising countries they regard as hostile. In response, Poland, Lithuania and Latvia took a variety of measures intended to prevent the entry of irregular migrants from Belarus. In many cases, they carried out so-called “pushbacks”, sending migrants who had crossed the border back into Belarus. On Tuesday, the ECHR announced three sets of rulings on cases brought against Poland, Lithuania and Latvia in relation to actions they had taken against specific migrants who had entered from Belarus. The European court noted that the migrants had “entered unlawfully” as part of Belarus’s “instrumentalisation of migration”, which it described as a “hostile action” that had “the intention of destabilising the respondent states or the wider region”. This “represented a deliberate threat to the state” and “was liable to put at risk its essential functions, including the maintenance of law and order and the safeguarding of its national security”. Poland wants the European Union to deny the right to asylum for migrants who cross EU borders in organised, aggressive groups, just as Poland has itself done on its border with Belarus https://t.co/7Gbsvs6I1e — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 7, 2026 The court found that states do have the right to control entry, and even fully close their borders, as well as to “remove a foreign national to the instrumentalising state”, without it automatically being a violation of the human rights convention. However, the ECHR also deemed that, “before removing an individual in such circumstances, national authorities had an obligation to detect those individuals who would be particularly at risk of suffering or enduring ill-treatment”. That included those who had personal vulnerabilities (such as old age, ill health or a disability) or who would face a threat to their life or serious risk of mistreatment by being returned to Belarus. In the cases of Poland and Latvia, the ECHR found that they had breached the obligation to undertake such an assessment before returning certain migrants. A court has found that Poland's border guard violated the law when sending two Afghan and Ethiopian men back to Belarus after they injured themselves crossing the anti-migrant border fence. One of them had made clear his wish to claim asylum in Poland https://t.co/42yOuGEgns — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2024 For Poland, the case concerned an unnamed Afghan national who had been part of a group that had crossed back and forth over the Polish-Belarusian border multiple times, as often happened in the early stages of the crisis. The ECHR noted that it had, at the time, issued an interim measure requiring that the Afghan man not be returned to Belarus. However, the Polish authorities did not take this into account, and sent him back to Belarus on 20 October 2021, thereby demonstrating they had not complied with their obligation to properly assess his need for protection, found the ECHR. The court also ruled that, in the case of that applicant as well as a fellow Afghan national, Poland had violated their rights by preventing lawyers from having access to them. It ordered Poland to pay the two men €20,000 (89,000 zloty) and €5,000 respectively as compensation. Two Afghan asylum seekers who crossed from Belarus into Poland have been awarded compensation for their mistreatment by Polish border guards. They were detained and driven back towards the border by officers, who did not accept their asylum applications https://t.co/M9bSHakS5j — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2025 In Latvia’s case, the ECHR ruled that the country had violated its obligations by sending Iraqi Kurdish children, some of whom were infants, back into Belarus, “disregarding the[ir] evident vulnerability”. At the same time, the European court dismissed further complaints by adult migrants against Latvia and Lithuania, finding that they had not demonstrated any vulnerability or risk. However, it did find that Lithuania had violated some Cuban migrants’ rights by failing to properly inform them of the reasons they were being held in a detention camp and thereby also of their right to legally challenge their detention. It also ruled that Latvia had violated the rights of migrants on its territory due to the poor conditions they found themselves in when camped out on Latvian territory, with no access to sanitary facilities and insufficient protection from rain and cold nighttime temperatures. ⚖️ Grand Chamber cases ➡️ Responding to realities of instrumentalisation of migration at Belarus border, European Court safeguards essential rights and reiterates limits of Convention protections. 🔗 Press release: https://t.co/nflEyCWKb1 — ECHR CEDH (@ECHR_CEDH) November 24, 2026 In response to today’s ruling on Poland, the deputy interior minister with oversight of migration policy, Maciej Duszczyk, hailed it as “very important and favourable for us”. He said that the ECHR’s findings regarding states’ rights to defend their borders from instrumentalised migration effectively endorsed Poland’s policies. The Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights (HFPC), a Warsaw-based NGO, also noted that the ECHR’s Grand Chamber had, for the first time, defined the scope of states’ obligations when another state has instrumentalised migration “In the ECHR’s view, when migration is instrumentalised, states are not obliged to assess whether people being returned to the state instrumentalising migration will have access to an adequate asylum procedure there,” noted HFPC. Bardzo ważny i dobry dla nas wyrok Europejskiego Trybunału Praw Człowieka. Niezakwestionowano naszego modelu walki z nielegalną migracją. Trybunał odniósł się do instrumentalizacji jako sprzecznej z Konwencją i podkreślił prawo państ do obrony i ochrony swoich granic. — Maciek Duszczyk (@MaciekDuszczyk) November 24, 2026 A number of Polish courts have also found that the authorities violated the rights of migrants on the Belarus border. Last year, two Afghan asylum seekers were awarded 5,000 zloty compensation for their mistreatment by Polish border guards. In 2024, another court found that the border guard violated the law when sending Afghan and Ethiopian migrants back to Belarus after they had injured themselves while crossing the border. Last year, Poland’s government effectively formalised pushbacks by introducing a ban on asylum claims by people crossing the border irregularly from Belarus, who are now sent back without their applications being accepted. The measure has been criticised by human rights groups – including the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and Poland’s own human rights commissioner – as a violation of international law and Poland’s constitution. The number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants from Belarus to Poland fell from 15,500 in the first half of 2025 to 235 this year – a drop of over 98% Poland also now claims a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally https://t.co/RFZkd7CeIk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 20, 2026 Poland has also implemented a number of other tough policies, including easing rules for the use of firearms by uniformed officers protecting the border from illegal migration. This year has seen the migration crisis abate significantly, with Poland reporting a 98% decline in attempted illegal crossings from Belarus, as well as a 100% success rate in apprehending those who do cross. NATO has approved the deployment of an Airborne Warning and Control System (AWACS) to Poland in response to last week’s incident in which three Russian missiles struck Polish territory. Shortly after the decision was announced, Poland’s airspace was again violated by a Russian drone that entered from Ukraine. However, although the military was given authorisation to shoot the object down, they did not do so after the drone began to move back into Ukraine. Today, NATO Ambassadors met in the North Atlantic Council to discuss last week’s violations of Polish airspace. This was a dangerous incident and Russia bears full responsibility. NATO and Allied assets reacted quickly to the airspace violations, and the Supreme Allied Commander… — NATO Spokesperson (@NATOpress) November 23, 2026 On Friday morning last week, three objects struck at different locations in southeast Poland, not far from the Ukrainian border. The incidents took place amid large-scale Russian attacks on Ukraine, and on Sunday Poland confirmed that all three were Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles. The missiles were in Polish airspace for around three minutes before striking the ground. Two Swedish Gripen fighter jets, which were patrolling Polish skies as part of a NATO air policing mission, received authorisation from NATO’s Combined Air Operations Centre to fire upon the objects if certain conditions were met. However, the pilots were unable to confirm their identity in time due to poor weather conditions. On Monday, an extraordinary meeting of the North Atlantic Council, NATO’s main decision-making body, took place to discuss the incident. Afterwards, deputy defence minister Paweł Zalewski, who represented Poland at the meeting, announced that NATO had agreed to place an AWACS “at Poland’s disposal”. Later, NATO’s spokeswoman, Allison Hart, confirmed that “the Supreme Allied Commander Europe has authorised the forward deployment of a NATO AWACS aircraft” and is also “examining the deployment of additional assets as he continues to assess our deterrence and defence posture in Poland and elsewhere”.
