The Netherlands will become the latest country to purchase Poland’s Piorun man-portable air-defence systems, which have been increasingly in demand following their successful use during Ukraine’s defence against Russia. On Monday, their Polish manufacturer, Mesko, which is part of state-owned defence group PGZ, signed an agreement adding the Netherlands to a list of countries that will buy Pioruns with funds from the European Union’s SAFE mechanism for financing defence spending. 🇵🇱🇳🇱⚡ HOLANDIA DOŁĄCZA DO DRUŻYNY PIORUNA! W @PGZ_MESKO_SA w Skarżysku-Kamiennej podpisano aneks do umowy ramowej, umożliwiający Holandii dołączenie do wspólnych zamówień zestawów PIORUN. ✍️ Dokument podpisali gen. dyw. Artur Kuptel, Szef @AgencjaUzbr, oraz Krzysztof Marwicki… pic.twitter.com/lVH0QgdD0t — Polska Grupa Zbrojeniowa🇵🇱 (@PGZ_pl) November 23, 2026 Piorun (meaning “thunderbolt” in Polish) is a shoulder-mounted system that fires air-defence missiles capable of destroying aerial vehicles, such as helicopters, drones and low-flying planes, at short range. In 2022, Pioruns were among the large quantities of military equipment that Poland provided to Ukraine to help its eastern neighbour defend itself from Russia’s full-scale invasion. The systems have been successfully used to take down Russian aircraft. Since then, they have been in high demand, with Mesko receiving orders from the United States, Norway, Belgium and Sweden, as well as Ukraine itself. In August this year, Mesko signed an 8 billion zloty (€1.8 billion) agreement to supply further Piorun systems to Poland, Norway, Lithuania and Latvia, with the deal financed through SAFE funds. Precise details were not revealed. However, the agreement was said to involve the supply of “several hundred” launchers and “several thousand” missiles, with over 80% of the equipment going to Poland’s own armed forces. Now Mesko has signed an addendum to that deal, adding the Netherlands to the list of countries that are jointly ordering Pioruns. Deputy defence minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, who has overseen Poland’s participation in the SAFE programme, said after attending Monday’s signing ceremony that the Netherlands would not be the last country to join the procurement of Pioruns. “We promised that the list of Mesko’s buyers from all over Europe would grow, and today we have living proof of that,” said Sobkowiak-Czarnecka. “And I can reveal a secret: it’s not over yet.” She noted that Mesko has stepped up its production volumes in response to demand. Last year, it could produce “several hundred” systems annually; that has now risen to 1,500, and is set to grow even further. Last week, PGZ and the state assets ministry signed an agreement to support Mesko’s expansion with around 370 million zloty from the state Capital Investment Fund (FIK). It will help bring production capacity to around 2,500 per year. 🗣️ "Obiecywaliśmy, że lista kupujących z całej Europy będzie się powiększać i mamy tego żywy dowód. A mogę zdradzić sekret, że to jeszcze nie koniec. Dzisiejsza umowa to umowa w ramach zakupów w mechanizmie SAFE"@magdasobkowiak o zestawach Piorun dla Holandii ⤵️ pic.twitter.com/sTxG5SwnbZ — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) November 23, 2026 Growing demand for Pioruns resulted in Mesko last year posting the best financial results in its 100-year history. The firm’s revenues of 2.3 billion zloty in 2025 were up 33% year-on-year. The EU’s SAFE programme is providing a total of €150 billion in loans at preferential rates for member states to use on defence-related spending. Poland, with around €44 billion, is the largest single recipient. While most SAFE purchases are conducted individually by member states, some are also carried out jointly. Such joint procurement can also involve certain non-EU countries, such as Norway. World.title: Public astronomical observatory opens in Warsaw
World.content: Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Warsaw’s first astronomical observatory open to the public and run by a local municipal institution launched on Sunday. Its organisers say the facility, with two telescopes allowing safe observation of the Sun and photography of the cosmos, is aimed at astronomy enthusiasts as well as children and young people, who will be able to watch the night sky and participate in recording data without needing their own equipment. The new observatory, which is located on the roof of the Gocław Culture Terminal in the Praga-South of Poland’s capital, was created in response to growing public interest in astronomy, science and new technologies, says city hall. “Under the three-metre-high dome, specialised equipment awaits, allowing for observation of the sky, including safe viewing of the Sun,” said mayor Rafał Trzaskowski, who visited the facility last week ahead of its official opening. “Anyone who is interested can come here and learn about space through observation, photographing the sky and hands-on activities,” he added. The observatory will be free to use but only accessible during organised events, owing to limited space and the expensive equipment it contains, reports newspaper Super Express. “The dome houses very expensive equipment. For most of the year, it will function as a broadcasting station, and images from the telescopes will be projected onto screens in the main hall of the terminal,” Jacek Białek, head of Gocław Culture Terminal, told the newspaper. “We will invite people inside the dome as part of programs, the dates of which will be published on the cultural centre’s website,” he added. Participants in workshops and events will also be able to help collect and analyse data, with Białek noting that the centre will be working closely with scientists from the University of Warsaw The new facility cost around 500,000 zloty (€111,000), most of which was covered from the district budget, with contributions from private donations as well as grants from the state-owned military optoelectronic equipment company PCO and the national lottery foundation. The core of the new facility is a 14″ DO-GSO (Ritchey-Chrétien) telescope with a mirror diameter of approximately 35 cm and a focal length of approximately 2,850 mm, placed on an EQ8-RH equatorial mount with automatic sky tracking. This setup, along with a QHY268M Pro monochrome camera, a filter wheel and an electronic focuser, will be used for astrophotography and targeted photometric measurements, producing images suited to Warsaw’s atmospheric conditions. The observatory also boasts a specialist Sky-Watcher Heliostar 100 H-Alpha telescope, which is used for safe and detailed observation and astrophotography of the Sun, allowing viewers to see structures in the solar atmosphere invisible through an ordinary telescope. The telescope allows solar prominences – large, bright features extending out from the Sun’s surface – to be observed and compared with images produced on other days. The telescope is protected by a three-metre dome that automatically opens and rotates. Warsaw has been chosen as the location for a new European Space Agency security centre, as Poland takes another step in its ambitions to become a bigger player in the space sector The facility will be the @esa's first outside its 11 founding member states https://t.co/WnHIbrW3ze — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 13, 2026 The observatory also features a computer coordinating its measurements, a camera showing almost the entire sky, and a weather monitoring system. Observations will depend on atmospheric conditions and visibility. “Examples of how this telescope might be used include photographing the cosmos and conducting simple research, such as measuring changes in the brightness of stars and producing graphs illustrating these changes,” explained Ewa Konarzewska from Gocław Culture Terminal. Poland has placed great emphasis on developing its space industry in recent years, with the aim of becoming a major European player in the sector. Last year, the country launched its first national military satellite. A Polish firm, Creotech Instruments, signed Poland’s largest-ever contract with the European Space Agency, a €52 million deal to build and launch a constellation of Earth observation satellites. Meanwhile, 2025 also saw astronaut Sławosz Uznański-Wiśniewski become the second-ever Pole to travel into space, as part of an ESA mission to the International Space Station. Earlier this year, Warsaw was chosen as the location for a new ESA centre focused on civil security and resilience, with the agency’s head declaring that “Poland has rapidly become one of the driving forces in Europe’s space sector”. The objects struck at three different locations in southeastern Poland – Nowy Lipowiec, Rudnik and Mołodycz – not far from the Ukrainian border. The incidents took place amid large-scale Russian attacks on Ukraine. No injuries or damage to infrastructure was reported as a result of the strikes on Poland. World.title: FedEx-led consortium completes €7.8bn takeover of Polish delivery giant InPost

We cannot do what we do without your support. A consortium led by FedEx has completed its €7.8 billion (34.5 billion zloty) takeover of Polish delivery giant InPost. The deal will see InPost remain headquartered in Poland, with founder and CEO Rafał Brzoska staying at the helm. Friday’s announcement brings to a close a process that was first announced in February and received European Commission approval in August. InPost’s shares have now been delisted from the stock exchange. The takeover follows years of rapid growth for InPost, which pioneered the use of parcel delivery lockers in Poland before spreading rapidly in major western European markets, including France, Spain and the UK. A consortium of Advent, FedEx, A&R Investments and PPF has completed its takeover of Poland's InPost, which is now private. InPost has delisted from Euronext Amsterdam. Founder Rafał Brzoska stays on as CEO, and the company remains headquartered in Poland. pic.twitter.com/HWigKVPC3w — IPO Newsroom (@IPONewsroom_) November 20, 2026 Under the deal, FedEx and Advent, an American private equity firm, each hold 37% of InPost. A&R Investments, Brzoska’s own investment vehicle, has 16% and PPF, a Czech investment fund founded by the late billionaire Petr Kellner, 10%. PPF, A&R and Advent were previously already stakeholders. The consortium acquired InPost at a price of €15.60 per share, valuing the company at approximately €7.8 billion. In a statement published on Friday, Advent confirmed that InPost would retain its name, branding, Polish headquarters and operational independence following the takeover. Brzoska, who founded his business in 1999, will continue as CEO alongside the existing management team. “InPost’s home market of Poland will remain the blueprint for new innovations, which will then be scaled across InPost’s wider European network,” said Advent. They added that the new consortium would now “accelerate investment” in InPost’s operations, helping the firm “extend its reach further”. FedEx and InPost would also “explore opportunities” to cooperate with one another. “InPost has built a leading position in Europe’s out-of-home delivery segment,” said FedEx’s CEO and president, Raj Subramaniam. “Connecting our global network…with InPost’s last-mile capabilities gives both businesses a potential springboard for profitable growth.” Brzoska, who is one of Poland’s wealthiest individuals, said that the new partnership would “deliver the long-term capital, global reach and deep technology expertise we require to build on what we have already achieved together as a leading European e-commerce enabler”. President Macron has thanked Polish delivery giant InPost for its latest investment in France The firm, which already operates over 9,000 parcel lockers in France through its subsidiary Mondial Relay, will now spend a further €500m to expand its presence https://t.co/caOGNQemfm — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 2, 2026 InPost is the largest operator of parcel lockers in Europe, with around 70,000 across the continent. That includes roughly 30,000 in Poland and 16,000 in the UK, including in branches of the British Post Office, with over 23,000 more in the seven Eurozone countries where InPost operates. In the second quarter of 2026, InPost had revenue of 4.18 billion zloty (€970 million), up 18.2% year on year, while its number of parcels handled rose 16% to 380.9 million. The strongest revenue growth came in the eurozone, where sales increased 37.9%, followed by Poland, with 12.7% growth. Revenue in the UK and Ireland rose 9.8%. Poland recently managed to prevent a planned Russian “false-flag operation” at the border that, if it had not been stopped, could have “ended tragically”, says a retired general who acts as an advisor to the defence minister. His statement follows a report earlier this week by a leading newspaper, based on statements by unnamed senior officials, that Poland had foiled an attempt by Russia to carry out a major “provocation” on the border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. Polish government figures, including Prime Minister Donald Tusk, have confirmed that a Russian operation at the border was prevented, though they have not provided further details. Bieniek then revealed that, “based on information we received from both our allies and our own intelligence services, we managed to thwart an incident with potentially tragic consequences, because the planned false-flag operation could have ended tragically”. “For example, if a group of people crossed the border and later dressed in uniforms, whether Ukrainian or Polish, but were Russian citizens disguised as others, and carried out an attack on their target, the side whose uniforms were worn would naturally be blamed,” continued the general. “Fortunately, nothing of the sort happened,” he added. “Certainly this preventative action [by Poland] forced the other side to desist from these acts.” Bieniek’s comments followed a report published on Wednesday by the Rzeczpospolita daily, which said it had learned of a planned Russian sabotage operation on the border between Poland and the Kaliningrad exclave. The newspaper, citing unnamed high-ranking figures from the uniformed services, said that the planned incident could have involved Russia mounting an attack on one of its own facilities but blaming it on Ukraine. Such actions are known as false-flag operations. “It was supposed to be reminiscent of the Gleiwitz incident,” said one unnamed source, referring to a false-flag attack in 1939 staged by Nazi Germany, in which German operatives dressed in Polish uniforms. And they usually don’t admit to planning such actions. Even if we have such information, we don’t share it.” “If we took certain steps, it was because we recognised there was a real threat,” added Siemoniak. “Appropriate actions were taken by the border guard, the police and the military. Sikorski pointed to the Gleiwitz incident as an example of such an operation. On Friday morning, two Russian missiles and what is believed to be a drone entered Polish airspace and hit the ground in three locations. Tusk condemned the incident as a further “Russian escalation” and said that it was likely to have been “an intentional provocation”. World.title: Two Ukrainians charged with vandalising Polish monuments on behalf of Russia

Two Ukrainians have been charged in Poland with working on behalf of Russia to paint slogans praising the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a nationalist formation responsible for massacring Poles during World War Two, on three monuments in the Polish city of Poznań. Polish prosecutors say that the operation was intended to fuel hostility between Poles and Ukrainians. The incidents in Poznań were part of a seemingly coordinated wave of similar graffiti on monuments in three other Polish cities. Ukraińcy malowali na pomnikach hasła „Sława UPA”. Działali na zlecenie wywiaduhttps://t.co/knLgZzo8ct — Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) November 19, 2026 In early November, the words “Slava UPA” (“Glory to the UPA”) were painted in red on three monuments in Poznań commemorating World War Two soldiers. While the UPA is remembered by many in Ukraine for fighting for independence from Moscow-imposed Soviet rule, in Poland it is primarily associated with leading the Volhynia massacres, in which around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, were slaughtered as part of an ethnic cleansing operation. The history of those massacres, and the continued veneration of the UPA by some in Ukraine, has regularly stirred tension between Poland and Ukraine, who are otherwise close allies. On Thursday, the National Prosecutor’s Office confirmed to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that two Ukrainians, who can be named only as Nikita S. and Dmytro Y. under Polish privacy law, had been detained and charged in relation to the vandalism. According to prosecutors, Nikita S., “acting on behalf of Russian intelligence and in order to obtain financial benefit of $500”, persuaded Dmytro Y. to “commit an act of sabotage by painting the slogans” with the aim of “publicly inciting hatred based on national differences between the Polish and Ukrainian peoples”. The suspects were identified by police and the Internal Security Agency (ABW), who had analysed surveillance footage of the perpetrator, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. Both were detained in Poznań, according to PAP. In the wake of the Poznań vandalism, Poland-based Belarusian news outlet MOST reported that, a few days before the graffiti appeared, an advert offering $500 for someone to paint pro-UPA slogans on monuments in the city had appeared on messaging service Telegram. When an undercover journalist from the outlet contacted the person offering the job, they were told that similar work was available in other Polish cities. Around the same time, almost identical graffiti praising the UPA appeared on further monuments in the cities of Gdańsk, Gdynia and Warsaw, including one dedicated to the heroes of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising. Around a dozen monuments in Poland, including one dedicated to the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, have been defaced with graffiti glorifying the WWII Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA). Ukraine’s embassy in Warsaw has condemned the vandalism and blamed it on Russia https://t.co/iaZb2CyiPx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 15, 2026 Last week, local police in Gdańsk confirmed that they had detained a 17-year-old Ukrainian suspected of carrying out the graffiti there and in Gdynia. He has been charged with promoting fascist ideology, incitement to violence and hatred based on nationality, and desecration of monuments. The Ukrainian embassy in Poland has condemned the acts of vandalism, calling them a “disgraceful provocation” and “a manifestation of the hybrid war that Russia is attempting to wage by any means in European states”. Poland has been a primary target for Russia’s so-called hybrid actions in Europe, which have included acts of sabotage, espionage, disinformation and efforts to stir hostility towards Ukrainians. Such operations are rarely carried out by Russian operatives themselves. Instead, Russia often recruits people already on the ground, often members of Poland’s large Ukrainian and Belarusian migrant communities, as well as Poles themselves in some cases. In July this year, a Ukrainian teenager was indicted by Polish prosecutors on charges of painting dozens of pro-UPA slogans in public places, including on a monument to victims of the Volhynia massacres. World.title: Higher Prices, Fuller Hotels: Prague Is Becoming a Luxury City Break
World.content:
Prague is strengthening its position as a high-end tourist destination, attracting visitors willing to spend more on accommodation and services.

The Czech capital has ranked ahead of Vienna and Berlin in an international tourism index, while demand for luxury hotels continues to rise.

More than 2.3 million tourists visited Prague between July and September 2026, representing a three percent increase compared with the same period last year.



The city received a score of 92.7 out of 100 in the Global Tourist Perception Index, compiled by Data Appeal and Mabrian Intelligence. Vienna scored 85.6, while Berlin received 78.4.

The ranking assessed several aspects of the visitor experience, including satisfaction with accommodation, safety and the variety of tourist attractions.

According to František Cipro, chairman of the board of Prague City Tourism, the results reflect a shift in the city’s tourism profile.

“Prague clearly demonstrates that it is no longer a budget tourist destination, nor does it wish to be one,” he said.

The trend is also reflected in visitor spending. During the first half of 2026, Prague welcomed more than 3.8 million tourists, a one percent increase year-on-year. However, Mastercard payment data showed that spending by visitors from selected foreign markets rose by 18 percent.

Tourists from China and South Korea recorded the most significant increases in spending.

Accommodation figures point in the same direction. Almost two-thirds of guests staying in Prague hotels choose four- or five-star properties.

In 2025, the average price of a hotel room in the capital stood at around CZK 3,000 per night. In central Prague, the average rose to approximately CZK 4,100, while luxury hotels charged around CZK 5,800.

Demand for higher-end accommodation has remained strong despite rising prices. In September 2026, luxury hotels recorded an occupancy rate of 83 percent, their highest September result in seven years.

Germany Remains the Largest Source Market

Tourism continued to grow during the first nine months of 2026, with Prague recording more than 6.1 million visitors, a two percent increase compared with the same period in 2025.

Germany remained the largest source market for international visitors during the third quarter.

Some other markets also recorded notable growth. Visitor numbers from Taiwan increased by 27 percent, followed by Israel at 26 percent and Ireland at 23 percent.

World.title: How to Choose a High School in the Czech Republic: Open Days and School Fairs
World.content:
Choosing a high school is an important decision for students and their families.

School websites and brochures can provide useful information, but visiting schools in person offers a much better idea of what studying there is actually like.

Open days and high school fairs are two ways to explore the available options, meet teachers and students, and find out which school might be the right fit.



This is the first article in our series on choosing a high school in the Czech Republic.

Visit Schools During Open Days

Open days give prospective students and their parents the opportunity to look around a school before applying.

High schools open their doors to visitors, allowing them to explore classrooms, workshops and laboratories, meet teachers and current students, and ask questions about studying there.

An open day can help families find out more about:

Study programmes: What courses and specialisations does the school offer?

Admission requirements: What are the conditions for applying, and how does the entrance examination work?

Future opportunities: What options are available after graduation, including further education and employment?

School environment: What is the atmosphere like, and would the school be a good fit for the student?

Open days take place throughout the school year, with many schools organising them ahead of the application period.

Dates vary from one institution to another, so check individual school websites or use the online overview of high school open days to find upcoming events.

Compare Schools at High School Fairs

High school fairs offer another opportunity to explore different institutions without having to visit each one separately.

In Prague, one of the main events is SCHOLA PRAGENSIS, where visitors can meet representatives of secondary schools from different regions.

Students and parents can compare study programmes, ask questions about admission procedures and learn more about individual schools directly from their representatives.

These events are particularly useful for students who have not yet decided what they want to study or are still considering several different options. Meeting representatives from multiple schools in one place can help narrow down the choices.

If you live outside Prague, you can also find a high school fair in your region.

Use Worksheets to Help Make Your Decision

Comparing schools, admission requirements and study programmes can quickly become confusing, especially when several institutions are under consideration.

Free worksheets are available to help students organise information, compare their options and think about what they want from their future school.

You can download the worksheets here.

World.title: EF English Proficiency Index: Brno Speaks Better English Than Prague
World.content:
Prague has improved its English proficiency score, but it still trails Brno, according to the latest EF English Proficiency Index (EF EPI).

The Czech capital gained nine points over the past year, while Brno recorded a slight decline. Despite the contrasting trends, the South Moravian city remains ahead.



The Czech Republic ranked 24th out of 117 countries and regions in this year’s global index, published by education company EF Education First. Its score of 569 points represents a drop of 13 points and one place compared with the previous year.

The country remains in the high-proficiency category, although several neighboring states performed better. Austria ranked second worldwide with 613 points, followed by Germany in fourth place with 611. Slovakia came 11th with 594 points, while Poland ranked 15th with 587.

Slovakia’s performance is particularly notable. The country has gained 49 points since 2016, making it one of Europe’s most improved performers over the past decade. Although its score fell slightly compared with last year, it still leads the Czech Republic by 25 points.

Brno Maintains Its Lead Over Prague

Brno scored 613 points in this year’s assessment, placing it 28 points ahead of Prague, which recorded 585.

The gap between the two cities has narrowed, however. Prague improved from 576 points last year, while Brno fell from 620.

Brno’s result is particularly strong in an international comparison. Its score matches Austria’s, which ranked second among the countries included in the global index.

The regional figures also support Brno’s position. The South Moravian Region recorded 606 points, the highest score among Czech regions.

Sweden Takes First Place in Global Rankings

The Netherlands has lost its position at the top of the global English proficiency rankings, with Sweden taking first place this year with 615 points.

The Dutch finished fifth with 609 points. Austria, Denmark and Germany occupied the places between them, scoring 613, 612 and 611 points, respectively.

The survey was conducted through the Ipsos Instant Research application and focused on respondents’ self-assessments of their language abilities.

World.title: Massive Attack to Headline Colours of Ostrava in 2027
World.content:
British trip-hop pioneers Massive Attack will perform at Colours of Ostrava on July 22, 2027, organisers have confirmed.

The band will take the main stage at the four-day festival, which runs from July 21 to 24 at the former Dolní Vítkovice industrial complex in Ostrava.

The announcement marks Massive Attack’s return to the Czech Republic after a nine-year absence.

The Bristol-born group, formed in 1988, is regarded as one of the most influential acts in the development of trip-hop.

The band is best known for songs including Teardrop, Angel and Unfinished Sympathy. Its music combines electronic sounds with elements of hip-hop, soul and dub, creating a distinctive style that helped shape British music in the 1990s.

Massive Attack’s live performances also feature large-scale visual projections, often incorporating political and social commentary.

They join an already announced line-up for Colours of Ostrava 2027 that includes Robbie Williams, Ellie Goulding, Martin Garrix, 5 Seconds of Summer and David Kushner.

World.title: Leo Express Opens Prague–Munich Train Tickets From 49 CZK
World.content:
Leo Express has started selling tickets for its new Prague–Munich express service, which will replace České dráhy on the route from December 13.

The cheapest domestic fares currently available start at just 49 CZK for journeys between Prague and Plzeň.

The new service, known as Ex36, will be operated by Leo Express for five years after the company won a public tender. It will take over the route currently served by České dráhy’s Bavarian Express trains.



International tickets are not yet available. Although German stations already appear in the booking system, passengers can currently only book journeys within the Czech Republic. Leo Express says bookings for the full Prague–Munich route will open in the coming days.

The lowest advertised fare between Prague and Plzeň is 49 CZK. The same starting price applies to journeys as far as Domažlice. Business class tickets start at 199 CZK.

Prices will vary depending on demand and availability, so not all seats will be offered at the lowest fares. A second-class ticket between Prague and Plzeň will cost up to 236 CZK, equivalent to the standard OneTicket fare.

For comparison, České dráhy currently charges between 155 CZK and 235 CZK for the same journey, depending on the time of travel. Passengers can also use the cheaper Berounka express service by combining tickets from the Prague Integrated Transport (PID) and Plzeň Region Integrated Transport (IDPK) systems.

According to the booking system, most trains will have six carriages, including two business-class carriages. The operator will use former Deutsche Bahn carriages purchased by Spanish railway company Renfe and leased to Leo Express.

The trains will include both open-plan seating and traditional compartments. Eight services will run in each direction every day, matching the current timetable of České dráhy’s Bavarian Express.

World.title: Prague’s Abandoned Vyšehrad Station Begins Its Transformation Into Apartments
World.content:
Work has begun on the redevelopment of Prague’s historic Vyšehrad railway station, set to become part of a residential complex with 138 micro-apartments, shops and two new buildings.

Developer Karlin Port Real Estate, led by Milorad Mišković and his business partner Miki Goldshtein, began preparatory work at the end of October.

The company plans to start the main renovation and construction works in March 2027.



The developer acquired the station and surrounding land in early 2024 from Cyprus-based company Miquelira Limited, which has been linked to businessman František Savov. The deal followed months of negotiations and extensive checks, as the listed historic building was in a serious state of disrepair.

The plans include the restoration of the original station building and construction of two additional buildings. The development will offer 138 micro-apartments, around 50 underground parking spaces and up to 13 retail units on the ground floor.

The apartments will be sold rather than operated as rental accommodation. According to Mišković, they could appeal to students, young professionals, investors and families looking for temporary accommodation for children studying in Prague.

The developer also wants to improve the wider neighbourhood, including the streets connecting the station with Albertov and the Vltava riverfront.

More projects planned across Prague

Karlin Port Real Estate is also preparing other residential developments in the capital. In Hostivař, the company plans to start construction of the Výhledy Košík project in 2027. It will include 228 apartments and approximately 1,500 square metres of retail space.

The company is also exploring opportunities involving former railway properties and preparing to enter Prague 9, where it plans to focus on the redevelopment of former industrial sites.

Mišković said brownfield regeneration remains his main interest, although the company is now considering projects across Prague rather than concentrating exclusively on the city centre.

World.title: 9 Czech Castles and Chateaux to Visit During Advent 2026
World.content:
Christmas markets are not the only way to enjoy the festive season in Czechia.

Across the country, castles and chateaux are preparing special Advent programmes, with decorated interiors, traditional markets, candlelit tours and activities for families.

Here are nine places worth visiting in the weeks leading up to Christmas and during the holiday season.



1. Loučeň Chateau

Located in Central Bohemia, Loučeň Chateau is hosting a Christmas exhibition titled The Story of the Christmas Tree until January 17, 2027.

Visitors can also explore the illuminated Labyrinths of Light in the castle park. One of the main highlights will take place on November 28, when the country’s largest Advent wreath will be blessed in the courtyard.

Special Advent tours and children’s programmes will run throughout December.

2. Karlštejn Castle

One of Czechia’s most famous castles will also welcome visitors with Christmas decorations.

From November 27, 2026, to January 3, 2027, selected tours of the Imperial Palace will include festive decorations and an introduction to Christmas traditions associated with the court of Charles IV.

The castle will be closed from December 21 to 25.

3. Sychrov Chateau

Sychrov Chateau in the Liberec Region will host its traditional Advent Market on November 28 and 29.

The market will feature Christmas decorations, seasonal products and food stalls in the castle courtyard.

Visitors planning a trip during the Christmas holidays can also explore the decorated interiors through self-guided tours from December 27 to January 3, 2027.

4. Křivoklát Castle

Křivoklát Castle, one of the most important medieval castles in Central Bohemia, will host its traditional Royal Advent event on December 5–6 and 12–13.

The programme includes an Old Bohemian Christmas Market, with artisan stalls selling traditional products, dried fruit, Christmas biscuits, sausages and mulled wine.

Visitors will also be able to explore the castle interiors at their own pace.

5. Hrádek u Nechanic

Built in the Windsor Gothic style, Hrádek u Nechanic will open its doors for Advent visits on selected weekends between November 28 and December 13.

The decorated interiors will feature Christmas trees, traditional ornaments, nutcrackers and nativity scenes. Guided tours will also explain how Christmas was celebrated in the past.

Special candlelit evening tours are scheduled for November 28, December 4 and December 11, while Advent concerts will take place on December 5 and 12.

The castle kitchen will also serve traditional English punch.

6. Dětenice Castle

Dětenice Castle in the Jičín area will offer a festive programme throughout December.

On December 5, children can take part in a St. Nicholas celebration in the medieval tavern. Visitors can also see Krampus performances on December 4, 5 and 12.

The castle’s medieval entertainment programme runs daily from 7 p.m. to 10 p.m.

More Advent Destinations Across Czechia

Other places organising seasonal events include Třeboň Chateau, which will host Advent markets on December 5 and 6, and Jindřichův Hradec Castle, where a weekend programme of theatre, music, dance and traditional crafts is planned for the same dates.

In South Moravia, Valtice Chateau is displaying 30 Christmas trees decorated with more than 2,500 handmade glass ornaments. The exhibition runs until December 23.

Villa Stiassni in Brno is also offering special Christmas tours, featuring period decorations and an exhibition of historical toys.

World.title: Looking for a Team Challenge in Prague? This Venue Has 25 Different Tests
World.content:
Looking for something to do in Prague beyond the usual sightseeing?

TEPfactor offers an indoor adventure combining physical challenges, puzzles and teamwork, just a short walk from Wenceslas Square.

Located at Vodičkova street, the 1,500-square-metre venue takes inspiration from the TV show Fort Boyard.



Its main attraction features 25 challenges testing participants’ strength, logic, dexterity, patience and ability to work together.

Visitors compete in teams of two to six people, tackling a series of tasks that require both physical effort and problem-solving skills. The main game takes approximately three hours, making it an option for groups of friends, families and visitors looking for an alternative to traditional tourist activities.

For those seeking something more intense, TEPfactor also operates Fear House, a horror-themed attraction with several levels of difficulty. Options range from group experiences to more demanding individual challenges.

The most intense version, Hardcore + Kidnapping, includes a staged kidnapping scenario and must be arranged in advance.

The venue also caters to organised groups. Schools can book activities designed to encourage communication and cooperation, while companies can use the challenges for team-building events. Birthday celebrations, stag and hen parties and private gatherings are also among the available options.

Beyond the adventure games, TEPfactor offers event space for larger gatherings. Facilities include a theatre-style room with a stage, sound equipment and the option to arrange a DJ and catering.

Additional entertainment can include pub quizzes, stand-up comedy, mobile casino activities and theatre performances.

Reservations can also be made through its online booking system.

Gambling is entertainment you pay for, not a way to earn money. Set a budget you can afford to lose before you play, and treat that budget as money already spent.

Warning signs include chasing losses, betting money meant for bills, hiding play from family and feeling restless when you try to stop. If any sound familiar, use the tools above and talk to someone. The national helpline, 1-800-GAMBLER, is free and confidential.

Best Online Casinos: Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best online casino in the US judged on?

A valid license you can look up, fair payouts, clear bonus terms and support that answers. After that, fit matters: games you enjoy, banking you already use and a site open where you are. A site that suits a slot fan may be a poor match for a blackjack player.

Are online casinos legal where I live?

That depends on your state’s law. If your state licenses online casinos, you can play at those sites while inside its borders, from age 21. If it doesn’t, offshore sites may accept you, but no US body oversees them and your state’s rules still apply to you.

Can you really win real money?

Yes. Players win and get paid every day. Over time, though, the house edge means the casino keeps a share of everything bet, so most players lose more than they win. Treat a win as a pleasant surprise, not a plan, and withdraw part of any big win instead of betting it all again.

Can I try games for free before I deposit?

Often, yes. Many sites offer demo mode on slots and some table games, using play money. Live dealer games and poker rooms usually need a real stake. Free play shows you the rules and pace, but it doesn’t pay out.

What is the difference between a real money casino and a sweepstakes casino?

A real money casino takes deposits in dollars or crypto and pays cash winnings. A sweepstakes casino uses virtual coins, and prizes come through a redemption process with its own rules. Some states ban sweepstakes sites, so check the restricted list before you buy coins.

How much do I need for a first deposit?

Each site sets its own minimum, shown in the cashier for every method. If you want a welcome bonus, read the offer terms too. The qualifying deposit is often higher than the basic minimum, and depositing less can mean no bonus at all.

Can I play on my phone?

Yes. Most sites run in a phone browser, and many have apps for iPhone and Android with the same games, cashier and account tools. At state-licensed sites, geolocation checks your phone’s position, so keep location services on while you play. A steady signal also helps if you join live tables.

Before you sign up anywhere fresh, check the license, bonus terms, games, banking, legal status where you live and the tools that keep play in check.

Best New Online Casinos – November 2026

How We Choose the Best New Casino

The new gambling site has no track record yet. You can’t lean on years of player feedback, so the basics need a closer look before any money moves. These are the criteria used to judge new online casinos for US players, and what each one should show:

Banking and payout processing: Before you register, the cashier page should show which methods work for deposits and cashouts, plus the limits and how long withdrawals take.

Game library and release schedule: A healthy lobby draws on many studios rather than a handful and adds new titles every month.

Mobile play: Games, banking and help should all work in a phone browser or app, and pages should open quickly.

Support: You want live chat and email in plain sight, with agents who answer the actual question instead of pasting stock replies.

Player reviews and complaints: There won’t be much feedback at first. Still, the way a new site responds to its earliest complaints tells you plenty.

A site that clears most of these checks is worth a closer look. One that hides its license or terms isn’t.

New Casino Sites vs Established Casinos

Sweeps Coins usually come free with promotions or coin purchases, and winnings in Sweeps Coins can be redeemed for prizes, including cash. Before a first redemption, you’ll go through KYC, short for know your customer: an identity check with ID and proof of address.

They suit players in states without licensed casinos. The risk is that some states restrict or ban these sites, and redemption rules can be strict.

Offshore Sites That Take US Sign-Ups

An offshore new online casino holds a license from another country and accepts US players outside any state’s oversight. These sites often offer crypto banking and large bonuses. They suit experienced players who accept more risk. The main risk is limited recourse if a payout stalls, since no US regulator handles your complaint.

Bonuses You Can Claim at New Casinos

New online casino welcome bonuses come in a few common forms, and each is credited differently. What follows covers how each one lands in your account and which term decides its value.

Deposit Matches and Daily Free Spins

A deposit match adds bonus money as a share of what you deposit, up to a cap. If you deposit and the site matches 100%, your deposit is doubled in bonus funds. Check the cap, the wagering multiple and the time limit.

Free spins often arrive in daily batches rather than all at once. You might get a set each day for a week or more, usually on chosen slots. Check whether you must log in to claim each batch and whether spin winnings carry their own wagering.

Crypto Bonuses and Cashback

Crypto bonuses give a bigger match or extra spins when you deposit with digital currency. They’re common at new online casinos that accept US players from outside state markets. The term to check is whether the bonus can be cashed out in crypto only.

Cashback, sometimes called lossback, returns a share of net losses over a set period. It may be paid as cash or as bonus money with wagering. That difference matters more than the percentage.

Reloads, VIP Level-Ups and No-Wager Offers

Reload bonuses match later deposits, often weekly. VIP programs pay rewards as you climb levels, such as spins, cash or faster cashouts. Among the best new online casinos, level-up rewards can be paid as real cash, so check whether wagering applies.

No-wager offers pay winnings straight to your cash balance. They’re usually smaller. On new gambling sites, these are the simplest offers to value, so check the maximum win limit.

Wagering Requirements on New Casino Bonuses

Wagering requirements tell you how many times you must bet a bonus before it turns into withdrawable cash. The multiple is the number to compare, not the bonus size.

Example, with round numbers: a $100 bonus at 10x means $1,000 in bets. The same $100 at 40x means $4,000 in bets. The second offer looks the same on the banner but takes four times as much play, and more play means more chances to lose the balance.

Before you accept an offer at the latest online casinos, check these:

Most of what’s changing shows up in the cashier, the rewards page and the lobby. These are the shifts to expect:

More sites put digital currency at the top of the cashier, and stablecoins (crypto tied to the dollar) cut price swings during a cashout. Casino originals: In-house games give a site something players can’t find elsewhere.

In-house games give a site something players can’t find elsewhere. Gamified rewards: Missions, levels and progress bars replace plain loyalty points.

Pros Cons High-value launch bonuses No reputation or player reviews yet Latest games added fast Licenses that may still be pending Upgraded platform usability Fewer studios and games at launch Exclusive launch promotions Support that’s still unproven Modern technology, including crypto Restricted in more states

The pros mostly show up on day one. The cons show up later, when you try to withdraw or need help. That’s why the first cashout at new gambling sites tells you more than the welcome page does.

A few simple habits cut the risk:

Start with a small deposit.

Request a small withdrawal early to test the process.

Save copies of the bonus terms you accepted.

How to Sign Up at a New Online Casino Site

Joining a new casino online takes a few minutes if you follow the steps in order.

Confirm the site is available and licensed where you are. Check the footer for license details and the list of restricted states. Register with accurate details. Your name, address and date of birth must match your ID, or withdrawals will stall. Verify your email and identity early. Uploading ID before your first cashout avoids delays later. Read the welcome offer terms. Note the wagering multiple, the time limit and any game limits. Choose a deposit method. Pick one you can also use for withdrawals. Claim the bonus. Some offers need a code or an opt-in box before you deposit. Track bonus progress. Most sites show a meter of wagering completed.

Set deposit limits during signup too, and if play stops feeling fun, 1-800-GAMBLER offers free, confidential help.

Are Winnings From New Online Casinos Taxable?

Yes, in general. Gambling winnings count as taxable income in the US, and many states tax them too. Federal and state reporting rules decide when paperwork follows a win, and the rules differ from place to place.

Keep your own records of deposits, withdrawals and wins. It makes filing easier, whether you play at new casinos or long-running ones. This is general information, not tax advice, so check with a tax professional about your situation.

Wins are possible, but no game guarantees a profit. Every game carries a house edge, the built-in margin that favors the casino over time, and every result comes from a random number generator, software that produces unpredictable outcomes. Short winning runs happen. Long-run losses are the expected outcome.

FAQ

How often do new casino sites launch?

There’s no fixed schedule. Sweepstakes and offshore sites appear throughout the year, often in waves. State-licensed launches are slower because each brand needs approval from a state regulator first. If you live in a licensed state, expect only an occasional new brand. Elsewhere, fresh names show up far more often, which makes checking each one more important.

Is it safe to play at a site that just opened?

It can be, if the basics check out. Look for a named operator, a verifiable license, SSL encryption (the padlock in your browser bar that protects your data) and clear terms. Safety is strongest at state-licensed sites. With a brand-new name, start small and test a withdrawal before depositing more.

Will a new casino accept me if I live in the US?

It depends on the type of site and your state. State-licensed casinos accept only players located inside their state. Sweepstakes sites accept players in most states but list exclusions. Offshore sites may accept US sign-ups, but no state licenses them. Always check the restricted list before you register.

Do newer casinos pay out more often?

No. The payout percentage, called RTP or return to player, is set per game by its developer, not by the casino’s age. A slot with a 96% RTP returns the same over time on an old site or a new one. Some games come in several RTP versions, so check the game’s info screen.

Do new casinos get the latest game releases first?

Often, yes. New sites sign deals with studios at launch and tend to add fresh titles quickly to fill their lobby. That said, large established brands also get early releases through long-standing partnerships. The difference is that a new lobby is usually built around recent games, while older lobbies mix new and classic titles.

How fast do payouts arrive?

Speed depends on the method and on the site’s approval time. Crypto and e-wallets are usually quickest once a cashout is approved. Cards and bank transfers take longer, and wires and checks are slowest. Your first withdrawal may take extra time because of identity checks, so verify your account early.

Can I get a bonus without making a deposit?

Yes, some sites offer them. Sweepstakes casinos commonly give free Gold Coins and Sweeps Coins at signup. Real-money and offshore sites sometimes offer free spins or small credits with no deposit. These usually carry wagering and a cap on how much you can withdraw, so read the terms before you count on any winnings.

Types of Casino Bonuses in the UK

Most offers at the best online casinos fall into a few families. Each is credited differently, and each has one term that decides whether it’s worth claiming.

Free Spins and Wager-Free Cash Spins

Free spins are the most common welcome deal. They go on one or a few named slots at a fixed value per spin, often 10p. Winnings either carry wagering or are paid as cash. Check the spin value, the eligible games and the expiry, which can be as short as 48 hours.

A matched deposit adds a percentage of your deposit as bonus money, such as 100% up to a set amount. The money sits in a separate balance until you meet the wagering. Check the multiple, and whether it covers the bonus alone or the deposit plus bonus.

No deposit bonuses give you spins or a small credit just for registering. They’re rarer at licensed sites. Expect strict win caps and short expiry.

How Wagering Requirements Work at UK Casino Sites

Wagering requirements tell you how many times you must bet bonus money (or bonus winnings) before you can withdraw it. A 10x requirement on a £10 bonus means £100 in bets. From January 2026, UKGC rules cap casino bonus wagering at 10x.

Here’s an example with round numbers. You deposit £20 and get a £20 bonus with 10x wagering on the deposit plus bonus. That’s £40 x 10, so you place £400 in bets before the bonus money becomes withdrawable cash.

Both rules lower the house edge further. French tables are worth seeking out if you mostly bet on red, black, odd or even.

Other formats include Lightning Roulette, which adds random multipliers, and auto roulette, where the wheel spins mechanically without a host. Auto tables are faster, so you stake more per hour. Pace yourself.

UK Gambling Laws: What Players Need to Know

UK gambling laws are among the strictest anywhere, and they protect you as much as they control the sites. These are the rules that affect your play.

The regulator: The UK Gambling Commission licenses every legal operator. A licence requires fair games, secure handling of your money and data, and safer gambling tools.

Best Online Casinos UK FAQ

Are UK online casinos safe to play at?

Yes, if they hold a UKGC licence. Licensed UK online casinos must use tested games, protect your funds and data, and offer safer gambling tools. To check, find the operator’s name and licence number in the site footer. Then search for it on the UK Gambling Commission’s public register. Make sure the web address listed matches the one in your browser. If you can’t find a match, don’t deposit.

How are casino sites rated?

Licence status comes first, then safer gambling tools. After that, sites are compared on bonus value and fairness, games, mobile performance, banking and support. Everything is judged from what a player can see: published terms, the cashier, game information screens, help pages and the public register. A big offer with harsh terms scores lower than a modest one with fair terms.

Do I pay tax on casino winnings?

No. Gambling winnings are tax-free for players in the UK, whether you win a few pounds on a slot or a large jackpot. You don’t need to declare them as income. The operators pay the tax, not you. Keep your account history anyway, because it’s a useful record of what you’ve spent and won.

What documents do I need to verify my account?

Usually two things: photo ID and proof of address. A passport or driving licence covers ID. A recent utility bill or bank statement showing your name and address covers proof of address. Some sites may also ask for proof of your payment method, such as a photo of your debit card with the middle digits hidden. Upload clear, uncropped images so the checks pass first time.

Which payment method pays out fastest?

E-wallets such as PayPal and open banking services such as Trustly are usually quickest, often within hours. Some sites offer fast card payouts too. Standard debit card withdrawals and bank transfers can take several working days. Many welcome offers exclude e-wallet deposits, so weigh payout speed against bonus eligibility.

What should I check in a welcome bonus?

Start with the wagering multiple, which can’t be higher than 10x under the current rules. Then check whether it applies to the bonus alone or to the deposit plus bonus. Look at the expiry date, the maximum bet while wagering, any cap on winnings and which games count. Finally, check which payment methods qualify. Using the wrong one can mean missing the offer entirely.

What can I do if I have a complaint?

Raise it with the casino first through its official complaints process, usually found in the terms or help pages. Keep screenshots and dates. If the site doesn’t resolve it in its stated timeframe, you can take it to an independent dispute service such as IBAS, the Independent Betting Adjudication Service. The casino’s terms should name which service it uses. Using one is free for you.

Offshore Casinos vs Locally Licensed Casinos

Independent Game Testing at International Casinos

A licence and a testing certificate cover different things. Here’s what each one tells you and how provably fair games add a third check.

What the labs check

Independent testing labs such as eCOGRA, iTech Labs, Gaming Laboratories International (GLI) and BMM Testlabs examine the random number generator, the software that decides each spin or card. They also check the game maths, so the stated RTP matches how the game actually pays over time.

Why a certificate isn’t a licence

A lab certificate says the game behaves as described. It says nothing about how the operator handles your money, your complaints or your identity documents. Many internationally licensed casinos display both a licence badge and a testing seal, and you should click through each one. A badge that links nowhere proves nothing.

Blackjack and baccarat come in standard and side-bet forms. A blackjack that pays 6:5 instead of 3:2 on a natural adds roughly 1.4% to the house edge, so read the help screen first. Complete verification early by uploading your ID and proof of address straight away, rather than waiting until you’ve won. Set deposit limits in your account before your first payment. Some sites also offer loss and session limits. Read the payment and bonus terms, including which methods count towards a bonus and the maximum bet while one is active. You can decline a bonus if the terms don’t suit you. Make a small first deposit, then request a small test withdrawal. A smooth payout tells you more than any review.

If an international casino won’t let you finish verification or keeps moving the goalposts, it’s better to find out at this stage than with a balance on the account.

Safer Play at Offshore Casinos

Offshore gambling sites aren’t covered by national self-exclusion schemes, so your own limits carry more weight. A few habits help.

Decide how much you can afford to lose and how long you’ll play before you start, and stop when you reach either. Site limits: Use deposit and loss limits in your account settings where the site offers them.

Keep a note of deposits, withdrawals and time spent. Seeing the totals helps. No chasing: Never raise your stakes to win back losses; that’s how a bad night becomes a bad month.

FAQ

Can I sign up to offshore casinos from my country?

Yes, if your country isn’t on the site’s restricted-country list and local law allows it. You give up the protections your home regulator brings, such as national self-exclusion, capped bonus wagering and a local complaints process. You rely instead on whatever the foreign licence requires, which can be far less.

How do I know if a site is safe?

Start with the licence. Look the licence number up on the regulator’s register and check that the operator and domain match. Then look for testing certificates that link to a lab such as eCOGRA or iTech Labs, clear withdrawal terms and a sensible complaint history. Missing or broken links are a warning sign.

Which licences do these sites usually hold?

Common ones come from the Curacao Gaming Authority, the Malta Gaming Authority, Anjouan and the Kahnawake Gaming Commission. Tobique and Panama appear less often. Malta and Kahnawake publish the most about complaints, while Anjouan and Tobique offer little public information.

Will I be able to play in my own currency?

Often, yes. Many sites offer USD, EUR, GBP, CAD and AUD accounts alongside crypto. If yours isn’t offered, every deposit and withdrawal may be converted, and the rate can eat into your balance. Check the currency options before registering, because some sites won’t change them later.

How long do payouts take?

It depends on the method and the site’s own processing time. Crypto and e-wallets are usually quickest once approved, while bank transfers can take several days. Expect a delay on your first withdrawal while verification is checked, and watch for pending periods.

Do I still need to prove my identity?

Usually, yes. Some sites let you deposit and play with minimal checks, but most still ask for ID and proof of address before paying out. Uploading documents early avoids a long wait when you want to withdraw.

Does national self-exclusion stop me using these sites?

No. National schemes only cover sites licensed in that country. That’s exactly why offshore sites are no substitute if you’ve excluded yourself. Blocking software and support from Gamblers Anonymous or a national helpline are the better options in that case.

World.title: Hungary passes major new tax and welfare laws: Families, workers, pensioners and the wealthy affected
World.content:
Hungary’s parliament has approved a series of major changes to the country’s tax and welfare systems, including higher family allowances, a new tax break for low-paid workers, a wealth tax and a broader version of the popular KATA small-business tax regime. Several pension benefits will also increase from January 2027.

The measures were passed in a series of votes on Tuesday, 24 November. While many are intended to improve household finances, some changes will also limit existing tax advantages, particularly for higher-earning mothers.

Minimum-wage earners to pay less income tax

One of the most significant changes is a new personal income tax credit for employees earning below twice the minimum wage. Hungary’s standard 15% personal income tax rate will remain unchanged, but eligible workers will receive a credit that reduces their tax bill.

With the minimum wage set to rise to HUF 347,000 (approximately EUR 940) gross per month in 2027, someone earning this amount will save HUF 20,820 in income tax every month. In effect, their income tax rate will fall to 9%.

The benefit gradually decreases as salaries rise and disappears entirely at twice the minimum wage, or HUF 694,000 (EUR 1,880) gross per month. The government expects around 2–2.5 million employees to benefit.

Family allowance to double after nearly 20 years

Family allowance, which has remained unchanged since 2008, will double from 2027. The new monthly amounts will be:

One child: HUF 24,400, up from HUF 12,200.

Two children: HUF 26,600 per child.

Three or more children: HUF 32,000 per child.

Children raised by a single parent will qualify for higher amounts.

The allowance for children with long-term illnesses or severe disabilities will also double, reaching HUF 46,600 per month, or HUF 51,800 for single parents.

However, the rules for family tax allowances are changing rather than the amounts increasing further. From 2027, these benefits will be deducted directly from the tax payable on employment income, rather than reducing the taxable income base. This could disadvantage people who have little or no employment income but pay tax on other sources, such as rental income.

There is also a change for mothers benefiting from personal income tax exemptions. From 2027, the exemption will be capped at HUF 1 million in monthly income: any earnings above this threshold will be subject to the standard 15% tax. The existing exemptions for mothers with three or more children, mothers under 40 with two children, and mothers under 30 will remain, but the planned gradual extension of the two-child exemption to older age groups has been halted.

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

Hungary approves a new wealth tax

Parliament has also approved a wealth tax targeting individuals with assets worth more than HUF 1 billion (approximately EUR 2.7 million).

The tax will be 1% on the portion of wealth exceeding HUF 1 billion up to HUF 99 billion, rising to 1.5% on wealth above that level. It covers a broad range of assets, including cash, securities, company shares, property, expensive vehicles, jewellery and valuable art collections. Assets held abroad are also included under the legislation.

The measure was a key election promise of the Tisza Party. The government expects the new tax to generate HUF 200 billion in revenue in 2027. However, the law still needs to be signed by President András Baka before it can take effect, and its implementation could face further legal scrutiny.

Minimum pension to rise to HUF 120,000

A separate law will increase several social benefits from 1 January 2027. The minimum amount of the full old-age pension will rise from HUF 28,500 to HUF 120,000 per month for pensions newly established from that date.

The minimum orphan’s allowance will increase from HUF 50,000 to HUF 60,000, while the base amount used to calculate benefits for people with reduced working capacity will rise by 10% to HUF 162,000.

The eligibility and payment thresholds for the old-age allowance will also double. The government is separately planning additional, tiered increases for people already receiving pensions below HUF 146,000 per month. These changes are expected to affect around 455,000 pensioners, although they are to be regulated separately.

KATA tax regime to become available to more small businesses

Parliament has also approved a major expansion of Hungary’s popular KATA flat-rate tax regime, which was sharply restricted in 2022.

From 2027, pensioners, university students and people with secondary employment will once again be able to choose the scheme. The monthly flat-rate tax will be HUF 100,000 for full-time KATA taxpayers and HUF 50,000 for those using it alongside another job.

Businesses and other organisations will once again be able to receive invoices from KATA taxpayers. However, safeguards will apply: if more than 50% of a taxpayer’s revenue comes from a single company or company group, they will lose eligibility for the scheme.

The annual revenue threshold will also rise from HUF 18 million to HUF 22 million. The previous KATA regime will remain available during a transition period and is scheduled to end in 2029.

The changes are intended to restore access to a tax system that was once widely used by freelancers and small businesses, while preventing the disguised employment arrangements that were cited as a reason for the 2022 restrictions.

World.title: The road to prosperity: India’s success story, and why it matters to Hungary
World.content:
In October the World Bank published its India Poverty and Equity Brief. It is a short document with a dry title, the kind researchers file away and newspapers rarely notice. The numbers inside it deserve a much wider audience.

Author: Anshuman Gaur, Ambassador of India to Hungary

Between 2011 and 2023, the share of Indians living below the World Bank’s lower-middle-income poverty line of $4.20 a day fell from 57.7 per cent to 16.1 per cent. That is about 496 million people. Extreme poverty, measured at $3 a day, fell from 27.1 per cent to 2.6 per cent over the same period. The Bank calls it one of the fastest declines in poverty anywhere in the world.

Figures this large are hard to picture. On average, India lifted around 41 million people above the line every year for twelve years. That is more than four times the population of Hungary, year after year.

How did it happen? The American economist John Phelan, writing about the report this week, compared the fall in poverty across 51 countries and found India’s was the steepest of them all. His explanation is growth. Of the 29 countries in his comparison with incomes below $30,000 a head in 2011, not one cut its poverty rate by more than ten percentage points without GDP per head rising by more than 20 per cent.

For decades after independence, India’s economy was run through a dense system of licences, quotas and permits. Hungarian readers will know the type. János Kornai, Hungary’s great economist, explained in Economics of Shortage how such systems produce queues instead of goods. In the 1980s a family in Delhi could wait years for a telephone line, much like a family in Budapest. India began dismantling its “licence raj” in earnest in 1991, cutting tariffs, opening up to foreign investment and letting private firms compete. Hungary was making its own break with central planning at almost the same moment. Both countries learned the same lesson, at some cost: people become prosperous when they are free to produce, trade and invest.

The World Bank’s brief adds a new dimension to that story, and it concerns the last decade. Since 2014, under Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s leadership, India has kept up fast growth and worked to make sure its gains reach the poorest households directly. Far more people found work, especially women in rural areas. Employment rose by about 134 million between 2017 and 2023, nearly twice the increase in the working-age population. Rural households gained faster than urban ones, so the gap between village and city narrowed. And social transfers, food support among them, were expanded.

Behind those findings is a real change in how the Indian state now delivers. Hundreds of millions of people opened bank accounts for the first time. Digital identity and payment systems now send subsidies straight into those accounts, which leaves far less room for middlemen and leakage. Free food grains reach around 800 million people. Piped water now reaches about 82 per cent of rural homes, up from under 17 per cent in 2019. A woman who no longer spends hours each day carrying water has those hours back for paid work or for her children. Hungarian water technology companies know this part of India well, because they are already working there.

This is a fantastic achievement, but the next stage is harder. It needs better jobs, higher productivity and more skills. This is what Prime Minister Modi’s vision of Viksit Bharat, a developed India, sets out to achieve by 2047, the hundredth year of our independence.

So why should a reader in Budapest care?

The simplest reason is that people who leave poverty become customers. They buy better food and medicines, they build homes, they pay for education and they travel. India’s new middle class is forming right now, and the companies that arrive early tend to be the ones it trusts. Hungary is strong in many of the things this class will want: pharmaceuticals, water management, food and agricultural science, engineering and automotive components.

The second reason is that trade is already moving. Merchandise trade between India and Hungary reached about $2.4 billion in 2025, almost double the 2024 figure. Indian companies have invested around $3.3 billion in Hungary, in pharmaceuticals, information technology and manufacturing. The India-EU Free Trade Agreement, concluded in New Delhi in January, is close to signature, and it will make the road from Hungary to India a good deal easier.

The World Bank gave its report a modest title. What it describes is half a billion people changing their lives in twelve years. The next part of the story, the move from escaping poverty to a secure and comfortable life, will be built in factories, clinics, farms and classrooms, and there will be room in it for partners who come early. I invite our Hungarian friends to be among them.

World.title: Belgrade Court Convicts Bosnian Serb Woman of Wartime Killings
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp

The Higher Court in Belgrade has convicted Visnja Acimovic of participating in the killings of at least 30 Bosniak civilians at the Mracni dol site near Vlasenica in June 1992, according to a statement issued on Tuesday by the Humanitarian Law Centre NGO, which monitors war crimes trials.

The court sentenced Acimovic to 13 years in prison under the first-instance verdict, which can be appealed.

“The court did not give credence to statements from defence witnesses, the so-called ‘alibi’ witnesses, who claimed that Visnja Acimovic had been in Backa Topola [a town in Serbia] at the time of the crime, assessing that their statements were given with the aim of absolving her of guilt. The objectivity of these witnesses was also called into question due to the fact that they were members of her family,” the Humanitarian Law Centre said.

Acimovic did not attend the reading of the verdict. Her defence cited her poor health as the reason for her absence.

When deciding on the 13-year sentence, the Humanitarian Law Centre said the court took into account the fact that the defendant was a young adult at the time the crime was committed as a mitigating circumstance, while the number of civilians killed was taken into account as an aggravating circumstance.

Other members of the Bosnian Serb Army, some who have yet to be identified, also participated in the killing of the civilians at the Mracni Dol site.

The Bosnian state court has previously sentenced Predrag Bastah to 20 years in prison for his involvement in the killings.

According to the original indictment, Acimovic, together with several Bosnian Serb Army members, participated in the shooting of 37 Bosniak men committed in early June 1992 at the Mracni dol site near the Susica detention camp in the municipality of Vlasenica.

In 2020, the Bosnian state court asked the Serbian Ministry of Justice to take over the prosecution of Acimovic, for whom an Interpol warrant had been issued as she was no longer in Bosnia. Her trial began in Belgrade in November 2020.

World.title: Former Srebrenica Commander Oric Arrested in Attempted Murder Probe
World.content:
Naser Oric, a former commander of Bosniak forces in Srebrenica during the 1992-5 war in Bosnia, was arrested on Tuesday as part of an investigation into an attempted in East Sarajevo in August.

Jelena Miovcic, from the State Investigation and Protection Agency, SIPA, confirmed that Oric was arrested in the Olovo area in the country’s Federation entity.

Miovcic also confirmed that Nikolina Sljivic, a former member of the national assembly in Bosnia’s Republika Srpska entity, had also been arrested, adding that police are investigating the attempted murder of the man, named as Kosta Pandurovic, in East Sarajevo. Another man, Djordje Zdrale, currently on the run, is suspected of the attempted murder.

In another, related development, the Republika Srpska Interior Ministry, MUP RS, said it was carrying out an operation codenamed “Emisar” targeting an organised criminal group, with five people arrested so far.

“Searches are being conducted at several locations across Republika Srpska and the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, including properties owned by Djordje Zdrale, who is being actively sought by MUP RS,” the ministry said.

Bosnia’s top court, the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, previously sentenced Zdrale to 20 years in prison for the murder of Ljubisa Savic Mauzer, former head of the Republika Srpska Police Administration, in June 2000. He was released from prison in February 2022 after the Court of consolidated his sentences and determined he had served the combined sentence.

Oric earlier faced trial for war crimes but was acquitted.

In 2008, the Appeals Chamber of the UN International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, ICTY, acquitted Oric of failing to prevent the murder and cruel treatment of Serb prisoners. This ruling overturned a first-instance conviction.

In 2018, the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina acquitted him of murdering three Serb prisoners in the Bratunac and Srebrenica areas during the war in Bosnia.

World.title: Croatian Border Police ‘Doing Europe’s Dirty Work’ with Migrants: Report
World.content:
“The EU needs to act to ensure that Croatia respects EU law and protects the rights of those at its borders,” he added.

HRW interviewed more than 80 people for the report, including seven unaccompanied children, four children travelling with family members, and six parents travelling with their children. It also interviewed 15 aid workers and others who provide information and support to asylum seekers and migrants.

Those interviewed said Croatian police beat or kicked them, took their money, and confiscated or destroyed their phones. In some cases, they said, border police seized their documents, took their shoes or even forced them to strip to their underwear before pushing them back across the border.

“We told them that we are a family, but [the Croatian police] still took my husband away in one van and me and my daughters in another,” a woman from Ghana said.

“We were separated for two days from my husband. They pushed me and my daughters to Bosnia through the woods. No phone, no food, no water. We were walking all day. We were lost and scared for many hours,” she added.

“There were maybe 12 underage boys with us, about 16 or 17 years old. The [Croatian] police hit all these underage boys, same as the adult men,” Rasul, 31, from Pakistan, told HRW.

“When the police caught me, they beat me severely and we went back to the Croatian border in a police van … We had to run to the river and swim through the cold water, and the water was sometimes over our heads. I was scared,” Jamal A., a 17-year-old boy from Morocco, said in his testimony.

“There are mechanisms that the European Union should be using to try to insist on improvements, but I think above all what it shouldn’t be doing is continuing to turn a blind eye to consistent reports of abuse, very serious reports that this situation is ongoing,” Michael Garcia Bochenek told BIRN.

The Croatian government has not prosecuted any police officers for participating in pushbacks, even when people suffered serious injuries or extreme forms of humiliation. Seven officers received disciplinary sanctions for mistreating migrants between 2020 and 2025, the Croatian Interior Ministry told HRW.

BIRN sought a response from the ministry on the HRW report but had not received a response by the time of publication.

The Croatian government has, however, strengthened the mandate of a border monitoring mechanism established in 2021 with EU funding to prevent and address pushbacks and other abuses at the border. But the programme has had little impact on police pushbacks, HRW said.
