World.title: After ‘Propaganda’ Ban, Bulgarian LGBT Pupils Report Greater Insecurity
World.content:
After Bulgaria prohibited LGBTQ+ “propaganda” in schools in August 2024, teachers began approaching Vasil Lozanov with a question: can we still talk about it?

Thirty-three-year-old Lozanov teaches philosophy and civic education at Sofia’s Spanish High School. He also has a background in law.

“Experienced teachers, with years of experience both as people and as teachers, were in the dark about what they should do,” Lozanov told BIRN.

Lozanov did not change the way he taught. In lessons about tolerance, pupils write questions and comments on slips of paper anonymously; the papers are shuffled, selected and discussed. Sexual orientation is one of the subjects that usually comes up.

“I have never censored them and I have no intention of censoring them,” said Lozanov.

World.title: Czech PM’s Never-Ending Agrofert Saga Could Leave Taxpayers Paying the Price
World.content:
A familiar controversy

The issue of the billionaire’s conflicts of interest have been a recurring feature of Czech political life, dominating public debate ever since Babis entered politics and founded his populist ANO movement some 15 years ago.

The basis of one of the country’s biggest fortunes, Agrofert was founded by Babis in 1993, a sprawling conglomerate comprising about 200 companies active in agriculture, chemicals, transport, logistics, forestry and, until recently, the media sector.

With annual revenues of over 210 billion crowns (more than 8.5 billion euros) and employing nearly 30,000 people, Agrofert is the eighth most valuable Czech company, according to the latest Czech Elite ranking.

Babis’s ownership of such a ubiquitous company – and crucially, one of Czechia’s largest recipients of state subsidies – became a focus of public debate in 2014 when the Slovak-born businessman became deputy-prime minister and finance minister. Soon he was facing calls, including from his prime minister at the time, Bohuslav Sobotka, to give up his 100 per cent stake in Agrofert.

The ANO leader has consistently described accusations of a conflict of interest between his business activities and public involvement as a targeted defamation campaign designed to undermine his political ambitions – an argument he still employs to this day.

Passed in 2017, an amendment to the Conflict-of-Interest Act – dubbed “Lex Babis” – introduced guardrails against government members’ business activities, and barred them from accessing public procurement contracts or from running media companies.

Babis, who would go on to become prime minister later that year after a landslide election victory, initially transferred his shares in Agrofert and the SynBiol holding (a separate entity for Babis’s business interests in healthcare and real estate) into two trust funds.

From the start, however, this solution was deemed insufficient by legal experts like Transparency International, who pointed out that while no longer its direct owner, Babis nevertheless remained the conglomerate’s founder and ultimate beneficiary. A 2020 European Commission audit would eventually concur with this assessment.

Compared with the much broader EU rules on conflicts of interest, “the Czech regulation is much more specific, which allows some public authorities to navigate through it, saying that in some regards Mr Babis is in a conflict of interest, while in others he is not,” explains Krystof Dolezal, a lawyer for the Czech chapter of Transparency International.

“However, when it comes to the ban on public subsidies and public procurement, the Czech regulation is actually very severe,” he tells BIRN.

From European Parliament resolutions to Czech court rulings and a so-called “Lex Babis II”, rarely a month has gone by without the issue of Babis’s potential conflicts of interests making headlines.

History, it seems, was soon to repeat itself. Having resumed direct ownership of the holding after dissolving the trust funds in 2024 and 2025 when he was out of office, Babis’s ANO party once again claimed victory in last year’s parliamentary elections.

Now facing the obstacle of President Petr Pavel, who insisted he would not appoint him to form a government until an appropriate solution was found to alleviate any conflict-of-interest concerns, Babis was eventually sworn in after promising to distance himself from his businesses.

In February, he eventually transferred his Agrofert shares into a fund called RSVP Trust, which stands for Rodinna sprava a vlastnictvi (“Family Management and Ownership”).

World.title: Serbia’s New Leadership Won’t Transform Old Policy on Kosovo
World.content:
The spectacular victory of the Student List has reignited policy debates in Serbia that have grown dormant in recent years, given the grasp on power exerted by Aleksandar Vucic and the Serbian Progressive Party. Chief among them is the question of Kosovo and the process of normalisation.

Whilst the incoming government’s policy is unlikely to be fundamentally different, particularly when it comes to the question of Kosovo’s status, a change in approach will create distinct possibilities – and complications.

The Student List, as with other opposition parties in Serbia, has reiterated that it considers Kosovo to be an “inalienable and integral part of the Republic of Serbia”. This should not come as a surprise, given the centrality of the constitution to their platform.

While some voices within the Student List are more open to discussion about Kosovo, not least for the sake of Serbia’s European path, they will remain marginal for the foreseeable future. A criticism of consensus-driven approaches is that they tend to favour the lowest common denominator, with polarising issues approached with a degree of conservatism.

In the current context, this is understandable. The dilution of the EU perspective in the Serbian political space has undermined one of the key drivers of compromise over Kosovo. Should the government promote a more positive posture on EU membership – and on the reforms required to achieve it – then debates on Kosovo will be framed very differently.

In the meantime, Belgrade should keep its options open. Boxing itself into a corner, by suggesting that past agreements be reviewed and revised, risks further gridlocking the normalisation process.

World.title: Serbia’s Student Movement Criticises European Parliament’s Vukovar Resolution
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

Serbia’s student movement, which under the name Student List won the country’s recent parliamentary elections, has criticised a European Parliament’s draft resolution marking the 35th anniversary of the fall of Vukovar in eastern Croatia, calling for adequate recognition of war crimes committed against Serb civilians during the Croatian conflict.

In a statement on the Student List – Students Win website on Monday, it said the resolution does not contribute to an “objective understanding of historical events” or to reconciliation. It argued that the draft resolution overlooks some of the suffering of Serb civilians in Croatia, including killings, persecution and mass displacement, particularly during the Croatian military operations Flash and Storm in 1995.

“Responsibility for war crimes must be individual and established on the basis of evidence and final court judgments, rather than attributed to entire nations,” the students said.

“Serbia has an obligation to cooperate in clarifying the fate of missing persons and establishing responsibility for crimes committed, but the same approach must also apply to Serb victims and crimes committed against them,” the student movement said.

The eastern border town of Vukovar fell to the Yugoslav People’s Army and Serb paramilitaries on November 18, 1991, during the war in Croatia, after which the remaining population was expelled. Two days after the town fell, Croatian prisoners and civilians were taken from Vukovar Hospital to a nearby farm where at least 200 people were executed.

The student movement warned that remembrance of the past should not deepen existing divisions in the region.

“True reconciliation cannot be achieved by imposing one-sided interpretations of the past, but through an honest reckoning with all crimes, regardless of who committed them or against whom,” they added.

The European Parliament was set to debate the resolution on Monday, with a vote scheduled for Thursday. The debate in Strasbourg follows the submission of two motions for a resolution on November 20, commemorating the victims of the siege of Vukovar and the atrocities that followed.

One of the motions, submitted by members of the European People’s Party, EPP, the Socialists and Democrats, S&D, the European Conservatives and Reformists, ECR, and the Greens/EFA, notes that 1,725 cases of missing persons from the war remain unresolved, including 1,341 people whose fate remains unknown and 384 whose deaths have been confirmed but whose burial sites have yet to be located.

It also calls on Serbia to grant access to relevant wartime archives, disclose information about the locations of individual and mass graves, fight against impunity for war crimes and facilitate the identification and return of victims’ remains to their families. The proposal further urges Serbia to adopt its long-announced law on missing persons.

The motion condemns the denial and glorification of war crimes, specifically referring to the public honours paid in Serbia to the convicted war criminal and former Bosnian Serb commander Ratko Mladic at his funeral in Belgrade in September 2026.

It further calls for educational, cultural and commemorative programmes that promote a “fact-based understanding of the Croatian Homeland War and the 1990s”, while encouraging reconciliation and respect for all victims.

The proposal acknowledges the work of the International Criminal Tribunal, ITCY, for the former Yugoslavia in prosecuting crimes committed in Vukovar, but adds that not all those responsible have been brought to justice.

The motion also highlights the peaceful reintegration of Serb-held eastern Croatian into Croatia in 1998 as an example of successful post-war reintegration and the importance of rebuilding trust between communities.

World.title: Bosnia’s Dodik Gathers Votes, Seeking Veto Over State Policy
World.content:
On November 9, Milorad Dodik, leader of Republika Srpska's governing Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD), handed Nebojsa Vukanovic, leader of the opposition For Justice and Order movement, a slip of paper containing the names of people who might join the governing bloc in Bosnia's Serb-majority entity.

Vukanovic had asked whose votes Dodik was counting on for his promised two-thirds majority in the new entity National Assembly.

Vukanovic read parts of the note to reporters. Three days later, Dodik said Vukanovic had skipped the name of Djordje Vucinic, a deputy elected on Vukanovic’s list. Vucinic denied that he was joining the governing parties.

By November 16, two deputies had switched sides to join Dodik's camp in the Republika Srpska assembly. Vladimir Copic, elected on the Serbian Democratic Party, SDS, list, joined United Srpska, a partner of Dodik’s SNSD.

Meanwhile Snjezana Gvozden left the Safe Srpska Movement, PSS, for the SNSD – and was elected an Republika Srpska assembly deputy speaker.

Bosnian law allows deputies who change parties to keep their seats, and Gvozden defended her move, saying that voters had given her the mandate. Whatever the outcome of complaints, people who voted for the two opposition lists have seen a seat won with their votes go to Dodik's bloc.

The governing bloc thereby grew from 54 to 56 seats in the 83-member Republika Srpska assembly. Dodik’s candidate for speaker, Nenad Stevandic, received only 52 votes, however. While his coalition in theory controlled two-thirds of the seats, it still had to show that it could deliver all 56 votes on the same decision.

World.title: Bulgaria issues warning of dangerous weather for November 23 over forecast strong winds
World.content:
Bulgaria’s national meteorological bureau has issued the Code Orange warning of dangerous weather for numerous districts for November 23 because of forecast strong winds.

The districts subject to the Code Orange warning are Vidin, Montana, Vratsa, Pleven, Veliko Turnovo, Sliven, Yambol, Haskovo, Plovdiv, Pazardzhik, Kurdzhali, Sofia city, Sofia district, Pernik and Lovech.

All other districts are subject to the lesser Code Yellow warning of potentially dangerous weather, also because of strong winds.

The meteorological bureau said that on the morning of November 23, a moderate and strong southerly wind will blow. It will be cloudy with rain in many places.

It will be relatively warm for the season, with minimum temperatures between 5° and 10° Celsius and maximums between 14° and 19°.

In the afternoon, cold air will flow in a temperatures will drop quickly and significantly.

In a separate announcement, the Road Infrastructure Agency said that from November 23, a serious cold snap with rain is expected, and in the morning hours, negative temperatures and icing conditions are expected.

“The Road Infrastructure Agency appeals to drivers to prepare their vehicles for winter conditions, to set off on the road only with suitable tyres, to drive at a reasonable speed and to keep a distance so as not to block traffic and the work of snow removal equipment,” the agency said.

The national road network has been in winter maintenance mode since November 16. The regional road departments and the involved companies are monitoring weather forecasts for timely treatment of the pavements, especially in the passes and high-mountainous regions, it said.

World.title: Gavriil, Bulgarian Orthodox Church Metropolitan of Lovech, dies at 76
World.content:
Bulgarian Orthodox Church Metropolitan of Lovech Gavriil died on November 22 after a short illness, the church’s governing body the Holy Synod said in a statement.

Gavriil, who had been Metropolitan of Lovech since January 28 2001, was 76.

“His Eminence will remain in the history of the Bulgarian Orthodox Church – Bulgarian Patriarchate as a proper hierarch, a zealous monk, a fervent prayer leader, a clergyman with deep and sincere faith, and a true follower of Christ, who not only with his words, but also with his entire life and deeds proclaimed the gospel truth,” the Holy Synod said.

The statement said that the Holy Synod would meet in special session to decide on the date and time of the funeral of Gavriil, and to appoint a temporary head of the diocese.

Gavriil was born on July 16 1950 in Sofia with the secular name Tsvetan Metodiev Dinev. He took monastic vows in 1979 at the Klisura Monastery St. Petka near Bankya.

He held various clerical posts, including as head of the Bulgarian Orthodox Church in Moscow, before being elected Metropolitan of Lovech.

In 2012, a check into the Holy Synod of the time by the Dossier Commission found that Gavriil was one of only four members of the church’s 15-member governing body for which there was no evidence that he had worked for communist-era secret service State Security.

More recently, Gavriil opposed the decision of the Ecumenical Patriarchate to grant autocephaly (church independence) to the Orthodox Church of Ukraine. Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew signed the decree in January 2019.

Metropolitan Gavriil was among the three candidates for Bulgarian Patriarch both in 2013, when Neofit was elected, and in 2024, when Daniil was elected.

Gavriil’s death creates a vacancy in the church’s governing body, for which an election will be held in the coming months.

In Bulgaria’s 2021 national census, close to 63 per cent of Bulgarians said that they identified as Eastern Orthodox Christians.

(Photo via the website of the Bulgarian Patriarchate)

World.title: EC approves Bulgaria’s final payment request under NextGenerationEU
World.content:
The European Commission said on November 20 that it has partially greenlighted Bulgaria’s fifth and final payment request for 1.82 billion euro under the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) of the bloc’s NextGenerationEU post-pandemic economic recovery plan.

Bulgaria submitted the payment request on September 30, the deadline set by the European Commission, which aims to wind down the NextGenerationEU programme at the end of this year.

The Commission said that its assessment found that Bulgaria “has satisfactorily completed 53 out of 59 milestones and targets set out in the Council Implementing Decision.”

As such, the EC said that it would withhold part of the funds requested, but did not give an exact figure, noting only that it would be “proportional.”

Speaking to reporters in Sofia after the announcement, Deputy PM Atanas Pekanov, the Cabinet’s senior official tasked with securing RRF funds, said that Bulgaria was slated to receive more than 1.7 billion euro under the fifth payment request.

The policy areas in which Bulgaria pursued reforms and investments tied to this payment request include decarbonising the energy sector, strengthening the anti-corruption framework, enhancing the sustainability of transport and improving social inclusion and healthcare, the EC said.

The disbursement of the payment can be made after the Economic and Financial Committee, a body composed of senior officials from national administrations and central banks, the ECB and the EC, has issued an opinion on the Commission’s preliminary approval. It has four weeks to do so.

This is the second large RRF payment request received by Bulgaria this year, following 1.1 billion euro granted by the EC in June.

Due to years of political instability and short-lived governments, the country has lagged behind other EU member states in making the requests, raising the prospect that it could miss out on a significant amount of the 6.17 billion euro allocated to it under the RRF.

Pekanov said that this year’s two payment requests would take the amount received by Bulgaria under the RRF to between 98.7 per cent and 99 per cent of the allocated funding.

World.title: Bulgarian Parliament elects 11 members of Supreme Judicial Council
World.content:
Bulgaria’s National Assembly voted on November 20 to appoint 11 members of the country’s Supreme Judicial Council (SJC), the body tasked with the appointment of senior magistrates in Bulgaria’s judiciary.

Parliament held individual appointment votes for all 21 nominees. Vote tallies showed that the candidates that secured appointment were uniformly backed by the governing Progressive Bulgaria, alongside the opposition We Continue the Change (WCC) and Democratic Bulgaria.

The three parliamentary groups have a combined 168 MPs, enough to meet the qualified two-thirds majority of 160 MPs in the 240-seat National Assembly, required for the appointment of SJC members.

Most successful candidates, save three, were also backed by the opposition GERB and Movement for Rights and Freedoms (MRF) parties. Only pro-Kremlin party Vuzrazhdane, whose sole nominated candidate was not elected, voted against all successful appointments.

Of the 11 members of the SJC appointed by MPs on November 20, seven were nominated by Progressive Bulgaria and two apiece by WCC and Democratic Bulgaria.

The council has 25 members and is presided over by the Justice Minister, who is not, however, a member of the SJC. Of the 25 members, 11 are elected by Parliament, 11 by magistrates and three are members ex officio – the country’s prosecutor-general and the heads of the two high courts, the Supreme Court of Cassation and the Supreme Administrative Court.

The 11 members elected by magistrates are voted by their respective branches – six by judges, four by prosecutors and one by investigators. This last one is part of the prosecutors college of the SJC, as the National Investigative Service is subordinated to the prosecutor’s office in Bulgaria’s judiciary.

MPs similarly elect six members of the SJC to the judges college and five to the prosecutors college.

The current SJC line-up, often criticised as being unduly under the influence of MRF leader Delyan Peevski – who is subject to US sanctions under the Magnitsky Act – has been in office nearly five years past the expiration of its five-year term.

That is because Bulgaria’s pollical instability since 2021, which saw eight parliamentary elections in five years, resulted in fragmented parliaments, some of them very short-lived, that had little appetite for tackling the issue of electing SJC members.

World.title: EU, UK in ‘landmark deal’ on food exports, youth mobility and carbon emissions
World.content:
The European Union – United Kingdom summit on November 20 produced a “landmark deal” on food exports, youth mobility and carbon emissions, but negotiations on university student fees – with the EU wanting its students to pay the same as British students in the UK – are to continue.

The joint statement, announced at a joint news conference by European Commission President António Costa, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, is part of efforts to “reset” the relationship between the bloc and Britain, 10 years after Brexit.

Costa said: “A strong partnership between the European Union and the United Kingdom is a strategic investment in Europe’s security. But it is also an investment in our shared prosperity, in innovation, competitiveness and resilience. Because there can be no strong defence without a stronger economy”.

“There is much more we can achieve together. We are not competing against each other, we are building win-win solutions together,” Costa said.

The European Union is a union of sovereign nations which respects sovereign natures, he said: “We respected the sovereign decision taken by the British people in 2016”.

“And I recall the words of the European Council after the referendum. We regret but we respect. And we will equally respect whatever decision the United Kingdom takes about the future of its long-term relationship with the European Union,” he said.

“Of course, we follow with great interest the debate you have relaunched about our common future. And as you know, we remain open to have the closest possible relationship between the European Union and the United Kingdom.”

Von der Leyen said: “We know the world around us is changing fast, making a closer and stronger partnership between the European Union and the UK the more important. And indeed, the spirit of our cooperation is win-win. Our economies are deeply connected.”

“Last year, we agreed on an ambitious agenda, and today we are delivering. First, we are bringing our people closer together. From next year on, the United Kingdom will once again take part in Erasmus+,” Von der Leyen said.

She said that negotiations had been concluded on a youth experience scheme. “It will allow 100 000 young people from each side to spend up to three years in each other’s countries. To work, to study, to volunteer, to simply travel.”

Von der Leyen said that negotiations had been concluded on an agreement on food and other agricultural products: “This is a big success. It is a two-way street”.

“For our businesses on both sides of the channel, it means easier trade and lower costs. And for our consumers, it means more choice and more affordable food, so lowering the living costs. We have also concluded negotiations to link our carbon markets.”

“The agreement will cut emissions, and it will generate investments in cleaner industries. It will help us advance our shared climate goals. Work also continues towards the United Kingdom’s participation in our electricity market,” Von der Leyen said.

Burnham said: “We’re 10 years on from Brexit, but I think we can all confidently say this is a good day for Britain, and this is a good day for Europe”.

“The agreement that we’ve reached together is a win-win. And it is in tune with public opinion in the UK. People can see the status quo isn’t working,” Burnham said.

“It’s not good enough for Britain. Three quarters of people say that they favour closer ties with Europe, according to the most recent polls. And that is because we’ve had a decade of drift, too much division, low growth in the economy, and higher prices in the shops,” he said.

“They want a better deal than the hard Brexit we ended up with. And today, together, we have delivered that better deal. As I say, it will be good for people in Britain, and good for people in Europe,” Burnham said.

“It directly addresses the biggest challenges of our times, and the biggest worries that people have. The cost of food. The cost of energy. The lack of growth in the economy, and the cost of doing business. The levels of illegal immigration. And the challenges facing our young people.”

Ffor people who are worried about the cost of the weekly shop, this deal will help, he said.

“By cutting the costs of exporting, it will help relieve pressure. At the moment, it can cost up to £1400 to export a single shipment of salmon. And obviously, that’s too high, and it will bring costs for business down.”

The deal would bring the cost of food down “and nd it opens up the possibility of lower electricity costs”.

There are so many businesses out there who are worried about the cost of doing business, Burnham said.

Burnham said that Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey had “confirmed today that the UK Treasury has said that the deal struck here will add up to 0.5 per cent to UK GDP”.

“That is a £17 billion boost to the British economy. It is the single biggest growth measure that we could take in this Parliament,” Burnham said.

Brexit did take away opportunity from our young people, he said.

“And I can say to the young people of Britain, you will have, as a result of this deal, a new freedom. For anyone under 31, you will have much greater ease and ability to travel to any of the wonderful 27 member states of the European Union to live, to work, to study,” Burnham said.

“And that is such a positive note that we’ve been able to strike between ourselves so that the next generation can feel finally that people in our positions are directly doing something to recognise that they need more help and that they need more opportunity in their lives.”

Burnham said that a bill would be introduced in the British Parliament next week to implement this aspect of the deal.

(Photo: Council of the EU)

World.title: Two Russian missiles, Russian drone crash in Poland
World.content:
Two Russian missiles and a Russian drone have fallen in Poland, Minister of National Defence Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz told a news conference on November 20, as quoted by his ministry.

One missile exploded in Nowy Lipowiec, the other in Rudnik nad Sanem, and the drone in Mołodycz.

“This attack by the Russian Federation on Ukrainian territory, with its impact on the Republic of Poland, was one of the largest since the beginning of the full-scale war in Ukraine,” Kosiniak-Kamysz said.

He said that the missile that fell in Nowy Lipowiec, Biłgoraj County, was a Kh-101 missile.

“Throughout the night, our and allied pairs of on-duty jets operated – Polish F-16s and Swedish Gripens. Our pilots had a Dutch Air Force refueling aircraft at their disposal in the air. Our reconnaissance system, a Saab early reconnaissance aircraft, was also activated and operating in the Podkarpackie and Lublin Voivodeship,” he said.

Patriot systems located around Jasionka Airport in Rzeszów and near Świdnik in the Lublin region have been activated, as had the Poprad and Pilica+ ground systems.

Helicopters are also participating in the operation, as they continue to operate in the air, as are three brigades of the Territorial Defence Forces.

“We are dealing with another provocation by the Russian Federation,” Kosiniak-Kamysz said.

“In my opinion, the date is not accidental. Today, the Coalition of the Willing exercises are taking place, involving several countries on Nowa Dęba near these locations,” he said.

“The Coalition of the Willing exercises, the presence of the Defence Ministers of France, Great Britain, and the Baltic states, eight chiefs of staff led by our most important allies. It seems the coincidence of these events is no coincidence,” Kosiniak-Kamysz said.

“I will go to our allies, also with a request that they see what we have been facing here every day, every week, every month for four years. The threat to Nato and provocations from Russia are very serious. I will also request that the Alliance, the Secretary General, allocate additional forces and resources to support Operation Eastern Sentry. There are soldiers here from allied countries, for example, the Czech Republic, but more support is needed.”

We will not be intimidated, he said: “We will continue our actions, protecting above all our citizens, the Republic of Poland, and the strength of our Alliance”.

World.title: European prosecutors charge individual in 213.7M euro fraud probe into rail modernisation in Bulgaria
World.content:
The European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) in Bulgaria has filed an indictment in the Sofia City Court against one suspect, following an investigation into a project for the modernisation of the Bulgarian railway infrastructure, EPPO said on November 19.

The project, which concerns parts of the railway section between Sofia and Plovdiv, is worth more than 213.7 million euro in EU financing.

The contract for the execution of the project was awarded to a consortium formed by three companies.

The accused is the legal representative of a company participating in the consortium.

According to the investigation, through the manager of the consortium, he submitted false information to the National Company Railway Infrastructure (NRIC) regarding the company he represented to illegally obtain EU funds.

His conduct enabled the consortium to be eligible to and to be awarded in 2019 the EU-funded grant agreement amounting to 213 714 235.14 euro.

Between 2019 and 2024, a total of 68 213 186.03 euro was paid out by the NRIC to the consortium, co-financed by the Connecting Europe Facility (CEF) and the national budget.

In particular, the accused used the manager of the consortium, who had no knowledge of the relevant criminal circumstances, to declare that the company was not subject to insolvency proceedings. In reality, based on the evidence, it was declared insolvent already in 2012.

The investigation was supported by Bulgaria’s Interior Ministry National Police General Directorate and the State Agency for National Security.

Numerous searches and seizures were carried out throughout the investigation across various locations in Bulgaria, including company headquarters and private residences. Documents concerning the tender procedure and its implementation were also seized.

The initial crime report was submitted by OLAF, which also conducted a complementary investigation, EPPO said.

(Archive photo: NRIC)

World.title: Arrests in Bulgaria, the Netherlands and Poland in probe into multimillion euro VAT fraud
World.content:
At the request of the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) in Munich, three suspects were arrested this week in an investigation into a multimillion VAT fraud, EPPO said on November 19.

The arrests took place in Bulgaria, the Netherlands, and Poland. Searches and seizures were also carried out in those countries.

The criminal organisation under investigation is suspected of operating a cross-border VAT carousel fraud – a complex criminal scheme that takes advantage of EU rules on cross-border transactions between its member states, as these are exempt from value-added tax.

It is understood that they sold AirPods via companies and missing traders based in Germany and Bulgaria.

The activities of these suspects alone may have caused an estimated tax loss of 23 million euro in Germany.

With the support of national authorities from Bulgaria, Germany, the Netherlands and Poland, searches were carried out at the premises of the suspects and companies under investigation.

These investigative measures are part of investigation Midas , targeting a transnational criminal organisation behind a 195 million euro VAT fraud scheme involving the sale of smartphones, small electronic devices and protective face masks.

(Archive photo: Interior Ministry)

World.title: Major Airlines Are Leaving Zagreb. The Airport Has Announced New Plans
World.content:
November the 24th, 2026 – With major airlines like British Airways and Austrian Airlines leaving Zagreb, the airport has announced new plans.

Zagreb Airport has issued another statement today following the announced withdrawals of British Airways and Austrian Airlines, as well as flight reductions by other carriers. Index reports that they state that the departure of individual airlines isn’t good news, but they have still emphasised that the airport will not lose direct connections to the destinations affected by the announced changes. They also announced the start of the next phase of airport development during 2027.

“We’re aware that the withdrawal of an individual airline or a reduction in flight frequencies is not positive news for the airport, and we take every such business decision seriously,” they stated in the press release. They emphasised that a distinction must be made between the departure of a specific carrier and the complete cancellation of a direct connection to a given destination. “According to currently published flight schedules, all markets affected by the recently announced changes remain directly connected to Zagreb,” they said.

flight cuts and reductions

In recent days, Index has written about the problems facing Zagreb Airport, which has been left without two major European carriers. British Airways removed flights between Zagreb and London Heathrow from sale for the 2027 summer season, while Austrian Airlines will cease operating its route to Vienna at the beginning of next year. At the same time, Iberia, Qatar Airways, and several other carriers have reduced the number of flights or abandoned planned capacity increases. Despite this, Zagreb still has direct flights to London and Vienna. Croatia Airlines continues to fly to Heathrow and Vienna, while Ryanair connects Zagreb with London Stansted.

traffic growth has almost stalled

Zagreb Airport achieved a record 4.72 million passengers last year, but growth has slowed significantly this year. In the first ten months, only 0.6 percent more passengers were recorded compared to the same period last year, and every month from July to October was weaker than in 2025. However, the airport emphasized today that after the pandemic, they achieved one of the strongest recoveries among comparable European airports. Passenger numbers grew from approximately 3.4 million before the coronavirus pandemic to an expected 4.8 million by the end of this year, representing a growth of nearly 40 percent. They state that airlines adjust their operations due to demand, the profitability of individual routes, aircraft availability, and their own strategic priorities. They add that the European aviation industry is suffering the consequences of rising fuel prices and operating costs, delays in the delivery of new aircraft, and geopolitical uncertainty.

no drop in passenger numbers is expected in 2027

Despite the announced departures and flight reductions, Zagreb Airport does not expect a drop in total passenger numbers in 2027. “Based on currently available information, we do not expect the number of passengers in 2027 to be lower than the level achieved in 2026,” they stated. They admit, however, that flight schedules for the 2027 summer season have not yet been finalised and that the final picture of capacity will only be known once airlines finish their planning. They also claim that while some carriers are reducing the number of flights, others are increasing capacities and expanding their presence in Zagreb.

is the terminal expansion happening?

This latest statement also comes after reports circulated about a possible postponement of investments in expanding the passenger terminal. As a reminder, the airport is managed by a private concessionaire, the international consortium ZAIC. According to the concession agreement, when annual traffic reaches five million passengers, the concessionaire is obligated to initiate the expansion of the western part of the existing terminal, including three new departure lounges and an expansion of the apron. The final contractual deadline for the start of works is January the 1st, 2032.

It was previously reported that the concessionaire is asking the government for the possibility of reopening the old Pleso passenger terminal, to which it would transfer the traffic of low-cost carriers. According to unofficial information obtained by the media, the proposal also includes counting passenger numbers separately at the old and new terminals, which could delay the obligation to expand the new terminal. Such a calculation method is not foreseen in the existing concession agreement.

development plans remain unaltered

“The next phase of the airport’s development program begins during 2027 and will include preparatory, technical, and planning activities necessary for further increasing passenger and operational capacities,” they stated. This, however, does not mean that construction work on the terminal expansion will begin next year. The statement refers to preparatory activities, with no concrete deadline for the start of construction. Zagreb Airport did not directly comment on the possible reopening of the old Pleso terminal or the proposal to change the way passenger numbers are counted.

not a single word about fee increases…

This larest statement also made no mention of the increase in airport fees that took effect on June the 1st of this year. As was previously reported, certain fees for airlines were increased by between 10 and 24 percent. According to fee comparisons, Zagreb is more expensive than most competing airports in the region, with the exception of Budapest.

So far, there is no proof that the fee increase was the decisive reason for the departure of individual airlines. Zagreb Airport states that it continues negotiations with existing and potential carriers regarding new routes, the return of certain flights, and increased frequencies. They announce that any new destinations and carriers will be made public only after official confirmation from the airlines.

World.title: the Gap Between Europe’s Rich and Poor – Croatia is Below the Average
World.content:
November the 24th, 2026 – The gap between the rich and the poor across the European Union narrowed slightly last year, with Croatia being below the average.

Despite the aforementioned narrowing, significant differences remain among countries. Poslovni reports that Croatia is below the European average, while among the major economies, Germany, France, Spain, and Italy are more unequal than the EU as a whole, according to Euronews. According to the latest Eurostat data, the Gini coefficient for the EU back in 2025 stood at 29.2, down from 29.4 the year before. This is the lowest value in the current European data series, which began in 2010.

Croatia finished at 28.5, below the European Union average, after recording a coefficient of 29.8 in 2024. The Gini coefficient is one of the most commonly used indicators of income inequality. A value of zero would represent complete equality, meaning a situation where everyone has the exact same income. A value of 100 would represent the opposite extreme, where all income belongs to a single person.

In its calculations, Eurostat uses disposable household income after taxes and social contributions, adjusted for household size and composition. The lower the number, the more evenly income is distributed.

the highest level of inequality in the eu is in bulgaria

Among European Union countries, Bulgaria had the highest income inequality in 2025 with a Gini coefficient of 37.7. It is followed by Latvia at 35.6 and Lithuania at 35.5. If non-EU European countries are included, Turkey stands out by far with a coefficient of 43.9. Also near the top are Greece at 31.6 and Italy at 31.0, while Switzerland is also at 31.0 according to the latest available data. Eurostat emphasises that differences between countries cannot be explained by wages alone, as they depend on a combination of the labour market, tax system, social transfers, unemployment, and economic structure.

slovakia is home to the most equal income distribution

At the other end of the scale is Slovakia with a coefficient of 23.0, the lowest in the EU. It is followed by Belgium at 23.4, the Czech Republic at 24.0, Slovenia at 24.6, and Poland at 24.9. In Slovakia, low inequality is not only the result of strong redistribution through taxes and social benefits, but also of relatively small differences in pre-tax market incomes. Belgium’s result, on the other hand, is strongly tied to a well-developed system of taxes, social transfers, and institutionalised social dialogue.

croatia is below the european union average

Croatia’s Gini coefficient in 2025 was 28.5, which is 0.7 points below the EU average. One year earlier, Croatia stood at 29.8, marking a drop of 1.3 points in just one year. In the longer term, Croatian inequality has also decreased. In 2010, the Gini coefficient was 31.6, and in 2015 it was 30.4. However, the trajectory has not been linear. Croatia was at 28.3 in 2020, after which the coefficient rose again to reach 29.8 in 2024 before last year’s drop. This means that, according to this indicator, Croatia has a more even distribution of disposable income than the EU average, though this alone does not indicate how high those incomes actually are. A country can have relatively low inequality while simultaneously having lower average incomes than wealthier member states.

major economies are above the eu average

Interestingly, all four of the EU’s largest economies are above the Union average. Germany has a Gini coefficient of 30.1, France 30.4, Spain 30.8, and Italy 31.0. In other words, disposable incomes in those countries are distributed more unequally than in Croatia and the EU as a whole. Differences also exist among Nordic countries, which are traditionally associated with relatively equal income distribution. Norway remains among the most equal at 23.7, but Denmark at 28.2 and Sweden at 28.6 are now more unequal than Poland, while Finland stands at 27.1.

poland and romania narrow the gap

A comparison with the average of the previous 15 years shows that income distribution has changed significantly in some countries. The greatest progress among EU members was recorded by Romania, whose Gini coefficient in 2025 was 27.3, a full 6.4 points below its 2010–2024 average. Poland is four points below its own long-term average, Spain 2.5, Portugal 2.3, and Belgium 2.2 points. Economists link part of this reduction in Poland and Romania to strong economic growth and convergence toward the European average.

Between 2015 and 2025, Poland’s GDP per capita adjusted for purchasing power rose from 70 to 81 percent of the EU average, while Romania’s rose from 56 to 78 percent of the European average. Rising minimum wages, the expansion of social programmes, and European Union funds also played an important role.

inequality in hungary and in some nordic nations

The opposite trend is visible in neighbouring Hungary. There, the Gini coefficient in 2025 was 29.5, which is 1.9 points higher than the country’s average over the previous 15 years. Sweden is 1.6 points above its long-term average, and Finland is 1.3 points higher. Denmark also recorded slightly higher inequality than in previous years. This shows that historically even income distributions are not guaranteed and can shift depending on the labour market, unemployment, tax policy, and economic structure.

World.title: Over 80% of Americans Say They Would Visit Croatia After Malkovich Film
World.content:
November the 24th, 2026 – Over 80% of Americans state that they would visit Croatia after watching the hit John Malkovich film.

The first day of the Croatian Tourism Days in Poreč was marked by rain and an awards ceremony, while on Friday the sun shone over the city and the sea in front of Pical. Marina Knezevic-Petkovic reports for Slobodna Dalmacija that the day before at the famed Pical Resort, discussions focused on the competitiveness of European tourism and what reforms and investments mean for the people working in the tourism sector.

The Croatian National Tourist Board (HTZ) programme opened with the now very well known six-minute film CROATIA – I hear it’s beautiful. In it, the one and only John Malkovich receives a call from his agent telling him they have discovered where his ancestors are from. When he hears it is Croatia, he responds roughly the way someone who knows just enough about it to be intrigued would: he has heard it is beautiful.

malkovich’s appearance wins over swathes of americans

Dalibor Šumiga, an expert in neuromarketing and consumer psychology and founder of the Promosapiens agency, spoke about what happens after audiences watch those six minutes. How much is a famous face worth in a tourism campaign? And how much of Croatia actually needs to fit into a single film to make someone want to visit? Šumiga discussed how story and emotion can capture an audience’s attention even when a film does not try to cover every landmark that could possibly fit into the frame.

According to the results of an American market study he presented in Poreč, more than 80 percent of respondents said they would visit Croatia after watching the film. During the presentation, this result was described as a 20 percent increase compared to the travel intent expressed before watching. More than 88 percent of respondents rated the film with John Malkovich as standing out from other promotional materials.

how did john malkovich end up promoting croatia?

The journey from the initial idea to filming was shared by Pete Radovich, an American television and sports producer of Croatian roots and the film’s creative director. The winner of 45 Emmys across 18 categories spoke about his own connection to Croatia, why he took on the project, and what it was like working with Malkovich. The talk also covered how the actor reacted to the film and opened up the question of where the story might go next. At the end, behind-the-scenes footage was shown, giving a glimpse into what work on set looked like.

HTZ Director Kristjan Staničić recalled that Croatia has already brought together famous names in previous campaigns, from Luka Modrić and 2Cellos to Zrinka Cvitešić and Maksim Mrvica. Regarding the campaign with Malkovich, he highlighted its multi-million reach and the City Nation Place Award, which HTZ won in London for the best promotional strategy in tourism. Viewership results to date and a selection of domestic and foreign media coverage were also presented in Poreč. Minister of Tourism and Sport Tonči Glavina emphasized that through such campaigns, Croatia aims to build recognition in international markets even after the initial wave of attention surrounding the film passes.

World.title: Croatia Will Deport Bangladeshi National Who Assaulted a Minor
World.content:
November the 24th, 2026 – Croatia will deport a Bangladeshi national who sexually assaulted a minor. The 14 year old girl was assaulted in Istria.

A 31-year-old Bangladeshi citizen, whom the County Court in Pula non-finally sentenced to three years and three months in prison for the sexual abuse of a 14-year-old girl and for enabling the consumption of drugs, will be deported from Croatia once the verdict becomes final, the Ministry of the Interior (MUP) has confirmed to Index.

The man is currently in investigative detention, where he will remain until the verdict becomes final. MUP confirmed that the decision on his deportation will be issued during the serving of the prison sentence. “The Bangladeshi citizen is in investigative detention until the verdict becomes final, and the decision on deportation will be issued when the verdict becomes final, during the serving of the prison sentence,” MUP revealed.

convicted for the sexual abuse of a minor

As a reminder, back on the 7th of October, the County Court in Pula handed down a non-final judgement sentencing the 31-year-old to three years and three months in prison. The court established that in November last year he sexually abused a 14-year-old girl in the apartment where she was staying and that same night gave her marijuana. The girl had spent the night at an acquaintance’s place. The man took advantage of the moment when the others had gone to sleep. According to the judgement, he began to touch her inappropriately, and when she tried to move away he followed her into the room and there sexually abused her with the use of force. The girl managed to push him away and escape, then locked herself in another room.

he contacted her via snapshat asking her to keep what happened a secret

The next morning the man sent her a message via Snapchat: “What happened last night, please, can that be a secret between us?? Please.” The girl saved the message, and the court considered it one of the key pieces of evidence. After she reported what had happened, the man and his girlfriend tried to prevent the filing of a criminal complaint. According to the judgement, they pleaded with the girl’s family not to report the case to the police. The defendant denied guilt during the trial. He claimed that he had not abused the girl, but that she had tried to make physical contact with him while he was sleeping. He also denied giving her marijuana. The court did not accept his defence. It particularly highlighted the girl’s statement, which it assessed as detailed and credible, as well as the messages exchanged after the incident.

he remains in custody

For the sexual abuse of a child under the age of 15, the court imposed a sentence of three years in prison, and for enabling the consumption of drugs one year. It imposed a single sentence of three years and three months in prison. As a mitigating circumstance the court took into account his previous clean criminal record, while it assessed as aggravating the fact that he had exploited the girl’s trust and the circumstances in which she found herself. The man has been in investigative detention since the 27th of November 2025, and this time will be counted towards the sentence. The court also ordered a three-year protective supervision after his release from prison if he serves the sentence in full, without conditional release.

The verdict is not yet final, and a possible appeal will be decided by the High Criminal Court. MUP has now confirmed that, after the verdict becomes final, during the serving of the sentence it will issue a decision on his deportation from Croatia.

World.title: Over 300 Italian Companies With Over 20,000 Employees Operate in Croatia
World.content:
November the 23rd, 2026 – Over 300 Italian companies with over 20,000 employees operate across Croatia, with economic ties between Croatia and Italy constantly strengthening.

In crucial sectors of the Croatian economy, more than 300 companies with Italian or mixed capital operate today, and according to estimates by the Italian-Croatian Chamber of Commerce (THGK), they employ more than 20,000 people. Marin Penavic reports for Poslovni that Croatian-Italian economic ties are strengthening further this year, given that over the first seven months of 2026, goods trade grew by as much as 13.4 percent.

Last year, good trade reached almost €8.5 billion, representative of 3.2 percent more than the year before, meaning that Italy remains Croatia’s second trading partner and one of the leading foreign investors. These figures were presented by representatives of the Chamber and Italian diplomacy at a ceremonial awards ceremony at the Sheraton Hotel in Zagreb, which brought together the Croatian-Italian business and diplomatic community. Prime Minister Andrej Plenković addressed the guests via video message.

Speakers also included THGK President Aldo Di Biagio, Italian Ambassador Paolo Trichilo and Director General of the Assocamerestero association Domenico Mauriello. The ceremony was also attended by State Secretaries Goran Romek and Zdenko Lucić, as well as Member of Parliament of the Italian national minority Marin Corva.

Di Biagio emphasised that behind the economic indicators stand concrete people. “Twenty thousand employees means twenty thousand families who look to the future with peace and security. For Italian companies, investing in Croatia means creating concrete opportunities, developing skills and returning value to the community,” the Chamber President said.

At the ninth ITA CRO Business Awards, Valamar Riviera, Carel Adriatic, WAM Adria and Bora Nera Specialty Coffee were awarded. A special recognition went to the Consul General of the Republic of Croatia in Milan, Stjepan Ribić, while Andrea Perkov received an Italian state decoration.

World.title: Claude Can Now Send SMS and Viber Messages via Croatia’s Infobip
World.content:
November the 23rd, 2026 – A Croatian company and the country’s first unicorn has taken things to new heights. Claude can now send SMS and Viber messages through Infobip.

In the shadow of largest public share offering in history announced recently, that of Anthropic, one important piece of information remained that positions Croatia even more strongly on the global AI map. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that Infobip is a partner of Anthropic, the company behind Claude, which has just completed the largest IPO in history. The collaboration with the Croatian technology company brings new capabilities to Claude: through Infobip’s platform, AI agents can send SMS and Viber messages and track their delivery.

This is a concrete example of Infobip’s role in the global AI ecosystem. The new integration enables sending messages via SMS, RCS, MMS and Viber through a single connector. It uses Infobip’s send and check_status tools, which allow AI agents to initiate message sending and check their delivery status. In this way, communication with users can be directly included in automated business processes.

For companies developing applications based on agent artificial intelligence (agent AI), the connector enables use in various business scenarios, from sending order confirmations and delivery notifications to reminders for scheduled appointments. Instead of developing and maintaining separate integrations for each communication channel, users can now simply include Infobip’s communication services in their Claude workflows.

Infobip was founded back in 2006 in the Istrian town of Vodnjan as a small startup. It has grown into Croatia’s first unicorn (a private startup valued at more than one billion US dollars) and one of the largest technology hubs in the region. Today it operates on six continents through over 70 offices and employs more than 3,500 experts. It develops globally recognised products and services for many world brands and technology platforms, including Nvidia, Anthropic, SpaceX, OpenAI, WhatsApp, Microsoft, Oracle, Adobe, Meta, Viber, Deutsche Telekom, Virgin Atlantic and Nissan.

World.title: Zadar and Munich to Remain Connected Throughout Winter
World.content:
November the 23rd, 2026 – Zadar and Munich will remain directly connected throughout the winter schedule thanks to Croatia Airlines.

Croatia Airlines will continue to connect Zadar and Munich during its winter timetable. Karlobag.eu reports that this popular route is being co-financed by the tourist boards of the City of Zadar and Zadar County, and enables passengers to travel directly to Bavaria as well as make connections via Munich Airport.

options for onward travel through munich as a global hub

Croatia Airlines is maintaining its direct air link between Zadar and Munich during the winter 2026/2027 timetable, thereby continuing the connection of Zadar Airport with one of the more important European traffic hubs. According to the official schedule of the national airline, flights are planned from the 26th of October 2026 to the 26th of March 2027, on Mondays and Fridays. The route is jointly co-financed by the Tourist Board of the City of Zadar and the Tourist Board of Zadar County. Maintaining it during the winter months is important for Zadar’s transport accessibility outside the main tourist season, as well as for passengers who use Munich as a starting point for onward international travel.

two weekly departures during the winter schedule

The winter schedule provides for two weekly flights, enabling passengers to plan travel between the two cities even during the period of reduced tourist traffic. It is particularly significant that the direct connection is maintained after the end of the summer season, when the air transport offer from some regional airports is usually different than during the busiest tourist months. As stated above, the Zadar route is listed in the winter timetable starting on the 16th of October 2026 and ending on the 26th of March 2027. In the display of the summer 2027 timetable, this route is not listed. The Tourist Board of the City of Zadar presented the service in its announcement as year-round connectivity, but the carrier’s official table currently confirms operations during the winter period. For travel planning it is therefore important to check the availability of flights for a specific date, especially for bookings that cover different seasonal periods.

an important winter link between a coastal croatian airport and a major travel hub

One of the most important advantages of this air link is the possibility of onward travel via Munich. Munich Airport is one of the significant European aviation hubs through which passengers can arrange connections to numerous international destinations. The Tourist Board of the City of Zadar highlights precisely this transport role of Munich as an important reason for maintaining the direct connection. This possibility is particularly useful for passengers whose final destination is not Germany but other European or world cities accessible by connecting air routes. Instead of organising a separate arrival at a larger airport, passengers can start their journey from Zadar and continue it via the Munich hub. Direct flights also enable arrival in Bavaria without an additional transfer at the beginning of the journey.

joint tourist board funding

Maintaining the route is part of activities aimed at improving the transport accessibility of the Zadar area throughout the year. The Tourist Board of the City of Zadar and the Tourist Board of Zadar County participate in its co-financing, thereby supporting air connectivity with an important European market.

According to the announcement of the Zadar Tourist Board, this air link is important for extending the tourist season and the accessibility of the destination outside the summer months. Maintaining international flights during the winter can be significant for different forms of travel, including business arrivals, shorter city breaks and travel related to international events. The availability of a direct route is one of the elements that influence the possibility of organising travel in a period when tourist traffic is traditionally weaker. The co-financing also shows the role of tourist boards in the development of the destination’s transport connectivity. Their cooperation with the airline is part of a broader effort to ensure that Zadar is not viewed exclusively as a summer air destination, but as a city accessible to visitors during other parts of the year as well.

zadar airport’s new passenger terminal

In addition to maintaining international air connectivity, an important part of the development of Zadar’s airport infrastructure is the modernisation of passenger capacity. According to information from the Tourist Board of the City of Zadar, the new departure terminal at Zadar Airport was put into operation in June 2026 as part of a larger investment cycle. The improvement of airport infrastructure and the maintenance of international routes are two connected elements of air traffic development. The new terminal represents an infrastructural change in the passenger part of the airport, while the winter connection with Munich expands travel possibilities outside the main part of the tourist year. For passengers planning a trip it is important to follow the current Croatia Airlines schedule because the times and availability of individual flights may change. The confirmed winter schedule currently provides for traffic on Mondays and Fridays, and the possibility of onward travel via Munich remains one of the main advantages of this international connection.

World.title: Forest the Size of 3,740 Football Pitches Has Disappeared in 3 Croatian Nature Parks
World.content:
November the 23rd, 2026 – Forest the size of 3,740 football pitches has completely disappeared across three Croatian nature parks.

Zagreb-based programmer and entrepreneur Lada Kovjanić, who attracted public attention in early October with an interactive map of the disappearance of forest cover on Medvednica, has expanded her research to several other large forest areas in Croatia. Slobodan Muftic reports for Index that according to her new analyses published on the portal šume.eco, in the nature parks Lonjsko polje, Papuk and Kopački rit alone over the past decade or so, a reduction in tree crowns has been recorded on almost 2,700 hectares – an area corresponding to approximately 3,740 football pitches.

a new portal tracks changes to forested areas across croatia

“As I announced, I’ve opened a special portal that will over time enable insight into all larger forest areas throughout Croatia, with a particular emphasis on protected areas such as nature parks,” Kovjanić explained, adding that the changes indicated by her research are not necessarily the result of illegal logging. “I didn’t deal with questions of legality and justification, but exclusively with the change, i.e. the disappearance of forest cover for any reason over the past decade or so. I analyse satellite photographs during spring, when vegetation is at its densest, and compare them with previous years.”

The largest changes were recorded in Lonjsko polje Nature Park, where analysis of satellite images from the period from 2016 to 2026 established the complete or partial removal of tree crowns on as much as 1,246.09 hectares, or an area corresponding to 1,745 football pitches. This is an area known for valuable floodplain forests of pedunculate oak, ash and alder, which are among the most important natural assets of Lonjsko polje. Worrying proportions are also shown by the map of Papuk Nature Park, where between 2017 and 2026 a reduction in tree crowns was recorded on 914.68 hectares. In Kopački rit the analysis records 509 hectares, or 713 football pitches, fewer high tree crowns than back in 2017.

According to the data published by Kovjanić, in the area of Lonjsko polje, Papuk and Kopački rit alone a reduction in tree crowns was recorded on a total of 2,669.85 hectares, which corresponds to an area of approximately 3,740 football pitches.

“lonjsko polje has suffered the most”

“The purpose of this tool is to show on which cadastral parcels the greatest changes have occurred and to determine who manages that forest. Lonjsko polje has suffered the most. There is quite a lot of clear-cutting, areas where there is no longer any forest, in Kopački rit and Papuk. A lot was damaged in storms and due to disease, but logging is not negligible either,” Kovjanić explains. Her analysis is based on images from the European Sentinel-2 satellites, and only zones larger than 0.3 hectares (one hectare has 10,000 square metres) are included in the published total areas. Smaller changes and selective felling of individual trees therefore remain outside the display.

croatian forests claims there are serious shortcomings in interpreting the data

In their response to an enquiry sent to them about the mapping of Medvednica, where according to Lada Kovjanić’s analysis around 150 hectares of forest – an area larger than 206 football pitches – disappeared over nine years, Hrvatske šume (Croatian Forests) stated that there are “serious shortcomings in the interpretation of the published data.”

“Areas that were already arable land, agricultural land, urban areas or infrastructure facilities before 2000 have also been marked as lost forest. Likewise, the areas marked in red include parts of the surface where young forest is located, which is poorly visible on satellite images,” Hrvatske šume emphasise, adding that individual displays of open areas cannot automatically be interpreted as permanent forest loss. “I believe that transparency is in everyone’s interest and that is why I invite Hrvatske šume and all interested parties to cooperate. I think this technology could help introduce order into forest management, both of state and private forests,” says Kovjanić.

“old forests disappearing is particularly concerning”

“The trend of disappearance of forest cover, especially old forest with trees higher than 20 metres that takes more than a hundred years to regenerate, is quite worrying. Since 2001 Croatia has lost 85,983 hectares of old forest, or almost six percent of its total area. These are forests that will not regenerate in our lifetimes and this affects the entire ecosystem.” Official data shows that forest areas across Croatia are increasing. According to the results of the Second National Forest Inventory, presented in June this year, the area of forest land increased from 2.378 to 2.431 million hectares compared with the previous inventory, while the total growing stock decreased slightly, from 552 to 548 million cubic metres.

However, an increase in the area under forest does not necessarily mean that the area of old and ecologically valuable forests is also growing. Abandoned agricultural areas can grow into young forest or scrub, while the restoration of old forest habitats can take decades, and sometimes significantly longer.

might a third of mature croatian forest vanish?

Old trees have hollows, thick cracked bark and dead wood on which woodpeckers, owls, bats and rare insects such as the stag beetle and the oak longhorn beetle depend. Old and mature forest also protects soil and water and holds the most carbon. Such habitats form only after a hundred or more years, according to the šume.eco website.

It is important to emphasise that the recorded reduction in tree crowns does not automatically mean that the forest has disappeared forever on all those areas. Changes can be the result of regular forest management, storms, drought, disease, natural processes or other interventions. The maps primarily show where the forests have changed and enable the competent institutions and citizens to check what actually happened in those areas. If the felling of old forest continues at the same pace as in the past five years, by the end of the century a third of such forest that existed back in the year 2000 will disappear. According to Kovjanić’s additional analysis, on around 40 percent of the areas where a loss of high forest cover was recorded between 2001 and 2005, the tree crowns had still not reached a height of ten metres by 2020. This shows how long the recovery of high forest cover can take.

World.title: Winter heating compensation will have a big impact, says economist
World.content:
Luminor Bank's Chief Economist Lenno Uusküla said the government's decision to ease the cost of district heating and network fees during the upcoming heating season will have a "very significant impact" on consumers.

In addition to eliminating Elering's transmission network fee and compensating electricity and gas network charges, the government will reimburse household consumers for 80 percent of district heating costs above €110 per megawatt-hour.

"Relatively few people are affected, but the sums involved are actually quite substantial," Uusküla told Tuesday's "Aktuaalne kaamera."

"Heating can cost €150 per megawatt-hour, whereas the average in Tallinn is €80. So people in these areas may be paying €200 to heat a two-room apartment, which would normally cost €100. And if 80 percent of that difference is now covered, then it really will have a very significant impact in these areas," he explained.

Uusküla disagrees with Minister of Finance Jürgen Ligi's (Reform) comments that the support measure will accelerate inflation.

"It is rather the opposite. If it is done in such a way that people's heating bills decrease, Statistics Estonia will also measure it in such a way that heating bills for these people rise less or are even lower than last year, meaning that inflation will be lower. This means that all indexation adjustments linked to consumer prices will be smaller. So government expenditure will ultimately also be lower. And the overall inflationary environment will actually be calmer," Uusküla said.

The economist estimates that a support measure to ease heating bills in Narva, for example, could cost the government a few million euros.

Speaking about the high price of district heating this winter compared with last winter, he said the reason was the price of gas.

"What has driven prices up is the price of gas, which this year is once again three times higher than it was before the coronavirus pandemic and even a year ago," Uusküla said

World.title: Tartu City's budget to rise by 4 percent in 2027
World.content:
Tartu City Government submitted the city's €365.5 million draft budget for next year to the city council, an increase of 4 percent from this year. Child benefits will also rise.

Of Tartu's €365.5 million budget, operating revenues account for €276.3 million, while operating expenditure totals €257 million.

The city's largest source of revenue continues to be personal income tax. According to forecasts, income tax revenue will be 3 percent higher than this year.

The city government also plans to raise land tax next year, which is expected to bring €7.5 million into the city's coffers instead of the current €5 million, said Tartu Deputy Mayor Martin Bek.

"We are continuing with the same plan, under which [land tax] is 1 percent for residential land and 2 percent for commercial and other land. Year on year, [land tax] can increase by up to 50 percent," Bek said.

A total of €71.4 million has been earmarked for investments. For example, the city will renovate Miina Härma High School at a cost of €4.9 million. A further €1 million each has been earmarked for the construction of the Ujula tänav extension and the reconstruction of the pedestrian and cycle path on Väike kaar.

Tartu's Downtown Cultural Center "Siuru." Source: 3+1 Architects

Some €900,000 will go toward improving shelters and €19 million toward the construction of the Siuru cultural center, of which €14 million will come from a grant from the Cultural Endowment of Estonia, Bek said.

"The focus continues to be on schools, kindergartens and access to education, both in terms of content and infrastructure. The living environment, roads, streets and public spaces. We will certainly also place greater emphasis on crisis resilience," he said.

Of the total investment sum, €17.4 million will come from borrowing. This is twice as much as in this year's budget. However, the debt burden will remain within the temporarily permitted limits, rising to 66 percent of operating revenues, Bek noted.

"If we want to undertake additional projects in the city, there is no other option than to cover the shortfall in the investment budget through borrowing. In my opinion, that in itself is not a problem – we are not covering current operating expenses with borrowed money, but building facilities with a long service life," he said.

Budget 'concerning' and 'optimistic'

However, Daniel Kõiv, a Social Democrat and deputy chair of the Tartu City Council Finance Committee, said the continued increase in the debt burden was concerning.

"While five years ago we paid €2,500 in interest, today the City of Tartu pays €20,000 every day to banks in interest alone. Despite spending more and borrowing more, investment in urban space – cycle paths and other infrastructure used by pedestrians – has actually been reduced," he said.

Anneli Ott, chair of the Center Party group on Tartu City Council, said the budget appeared overly optimistic.

"Given the economic forecast, this budget is overly optimistic in terms of increasing revenues to balance the budget. Considering the currently changing economic forecasts, we could take a more conservative approach. The current approach of increasing the debt burden will limit our budgetary options for many years to come," Ott said.

Child benefits rise

For the first time in several years, the city will also raise its school allowance for children entering first grade from €50 to €100.

The childbirth allowance will also increase, from €512 to €800 for the first and second child and from €640 to €1,000 for the third and each subsequent child.

The opposition, however, considers these to be pre-election moves.

Bek said the increases in allowances had nothing to do with elections and were instead important steps that would yield returns in the longer term.

World.title: Central bank: People in Estonia taking on larger home loans relative to income
World.content:
Average loan amounts and incomes have risen, but debt burdens are growing faster, showing people are borrowing more relative to their incomes, the Bank of Estonia (Eesti Pank) said.

Although the number of housing market transactions has changed little over the past year, mortgage lending has grown more rapidly as banks have signed more loan agreements and property prices have risen, the central bank said in a review published Tuesday.

Figures show that banks signed nearly 6 percent more loan agreements in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period last year, while the total value of the loans was 13 percent higher. In the second quarter of 2026, the average mortgage was nearly €152,000, up 7 percent from a year earlier. That was broadly in line with the 6 percent rise in the housing price index over the same period, the central bank added.

Almost as many apartments have changed hands this year as did a year earlier, and nearly 10 percent more than in 2023 and in 2024. Sales of new apartments have fallen sharply, with around 30 percent fewer transactions in the first nine months than in the same period last year. On the resale market, slightly more apartments changed hands than a year earlier, the review revealed.

Buyers are relying more on bank loans to purchase apartments and houses, as mortgage lending has grown faster in recent years than the combined value of apartment and house sales. While incomes have also risen, more borrowers face a heavier repayment burden. With average loan terms holding roughly steady and interest rates only beginning to rise more sharply this year, the figures suggest people are borrowing more relative to their incomes than they did a few years ago, the Bank of Estonia said.

The rise in both the number and value of mortgages shows that borrowers have been having little difficulty obtaining loans. Banks are actively making loan offers, and growing competition among them is making loans easier to obtain, the central bank said.

Banks' lending practices also suggest they attach less importance than in the past to differences in borrowers' risk profiles. Over the past five years, the interest rate margins on new loans have been more uniform, and banks have been making exceptions to the Bank of Estonia's mortgage lending requirements considerably more often.

Rising interest rates have yet to slow mortgage growth, although the Bank of Estonia said optimism may be short-lived.

"Economic shocks arising from potential geopolitical risks could alter the course of both economic growth and interest rates," the review said. "If interest rates continue to rise, demand for mortgages could eventually begin to fall."

In its broader financial stability review published Tuesday, the Bank of Estonia warned that risks to Estonia's financial system have risen due to higher energy prices, climbing interest rates, and rapid real estate lending growth, which could make borrowing more expensive and complicate loan repayments for households and businesses. While problem loans currently account for just 0.5 percent of bank portfolios, the central bank noted that housing appears somewhat overvalued, commercial property vacancies are rising, and cross-border branch structures at banks like Luminor and SEB leave Estonian balance sheets exposed to lending risks in Latvia and Lithuania. Even so, the Bank of Estonia said Estonia's banking sector remains well-capitalized and resilient, maintaining the counter-cyclical capital buffer requirement at 1.5 percent to ensure lenders can absorb potential losses.

World.title: MPs draft legislation to stop tax breaks for online casinos
World.content:
New legislation drafted by the Riigikogu's Finance Committee will cancel future reductions in gambling tax rates, and set the limit at 5.5 percent.

The aim of the legislation adopted by the Riigikogu last December, spearheaded primarily by Eesti 200, was to attract more online casinos to register in Estonia by lowering the tax rate, thereby increasing tax revenue for the state.

Instead of generating additional revenue, however, the measure resulted in a state budget revenue shortfall of several million euros.

Under the legislation adopted, the remote gambling tax rate is to fall by 0.5 percentage points annually: it fell to 5.5 percent in 2026 and is scheduled to fall to 5 percent in 2027, 4.5 percent in 2028 and 4 percent in 2029.

The new bill ensures that the current rate will apply from July 1, 2027, and that further reductions are repealed.

Annely Akkermann Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

Finance Committee Chair Annely Akkermann (Reform) said on Tuesday: "The bill sets the tax rate for these types of gambling at 5.5 percent from July 1, 2027. Under the current law, the tax rate would fall to 4.5 percent in 2028 and to 4 percent in 2029."

She added that this would prevent some of the revenue loss in 2027 associated with lowering the tax rate from 5.5 percent to 5 percent and increase state budget revenues between 2028 and 2030.

Akkermann noted that, given the six months required for amendments to tax laws to enter into force, the 5 percent tax rate set under the current law will still apply in the first half of 2027. "The bill does not raise the tax rate above its current level or restore the previous rate of 6 percent," she said.

In late October, Minister of Finance Jürgen Ligi (Reform) said that although he considered the tax cut for online casinos to be bad policy, the government would not reverse the tax decision.

"We did not initiate it and we will not reverse the Riigikogu's decision either. But if the Riigikogu does so itself, we will be understanding," he said.
