World.title: Expanded voucher program to help sustain private schools — COCOPEA
World.content:
COCOPEA. Irineo Alvaro Jr., chairperson of the Coordinating Council of Private Educational Associations, speaks to media ahead of the 10th COCOPEA National Congress in Taguig City on November 24, 2026.

‘We really need to sustain our existence.... And this RA 12327 is a good start,’ says COCOPEA chairperson Irineo Alvaro Jr., as private schools also feel the effects of a sluggish economy

MANILA, Philippines – The newly passed law that expanded the voucher program for poor students in private K to 12 schools is seen to help sustain operations of private institutions amid declining enrollment and economic pressures, the Coordinating Council of Private Educational Associations (COCOPEA) said on Tuesday, November 24.

Republic Act (RA) No. 12327 or the Basic Education Voucher Assistance Act broadened the Expanded Government Assistance to Students and Teachers in Private Education (E-GASTPE) Act to include kindergarten and elementary school.

Currently, the decades-old E-GASTPE Act only provides tuition aid to students in private junior and senior high schools.

COCOPEA chairperson Irineo Alvaro Jr. said the reform would help decongest public schools, and affirms the inherent right and responsibility of parents to choose the best education setting for their children.

“By subsidizing a significant portion of tuition in recognized private schools, the government can alleviate financial burdens on families,” Alvaro said in a press conference.

“The voucher program is a real game changer in re-centering our education policy around the Filipino family, not just decongestion.”

Alvaro noted that enrollment rates in private schools, particularly small institutions, declined by 6% to 10% compared to last year, as they cannot match subsidized institutions and the level of teachers’ salary in public schools. Some have already closed this year, he added, without providing further details.

“We really need to sustain our existence despite all of these. And this RA 12327 is a good start. I hope this is a work in progress that could extend up to the tertiary [level],” Alvaro said.

To prevent “ghost students,” COCOPEA said it is coordinating with the Department of Education (DepEd) in pushing transparency for all transactions.

The group will also collaborate with the DepEd as the agency crafts the implementing rules and regulations of the new law.

COCOPEA legal counsel Joseph Noel Estrada wants a stronger role for the Private Education Assistance Committee (PEAC), which is the co-implementer of the tuition aid for junior high and senior high school students.

The new law does not mention PEAC, but it mandates the creation of the Bureau of Private Education under the DepEd.

“We will continue to help PEAC and explore systems to ensure that there will be no leakage, no corruption, no anomalies and irregularities,” Estrada said.

‘Stagflation’ among considerations for tuition hike

COCOPEA also called for urgent action to help schools survive economic pressures.

“Like every Filipino household, private educational institutions are hit hard by rising inflation, surging electricity and operating costs, and frequent calamities. These pressures threaten the survival of many schools and make life harder for their students, faculty, and staff,” Alvaro said.

He said sustainability of private schools would be ensured if there are policy changes promoting freedom to use flexible learning and training setups, fair and timely tuition adjustments, prompt release of government subsidies, less red tape, and respect for academic freedom.

Particularly, COCOPEA is pushing for a review of existing tuition policies so that private institutions can sustain fair compensation and support for faculty, invest in modern facilities, and continuously improve the quality of instruction.

Father Karel San Juan, president of Ateneo de Davao University and the Catholic Educational Association of the Philippines, said private schools are “very sensitive” to economic forecasts as they are tuition-dependent.

“The inflation rate in the Philippines is really escalating…the economists are projecting stagflation in the Philippines. [At the] macro level, we’re considering that. At the micro level, in our respective cities, towns where we operate all over the country, we’re considering local inflation as well,” San Juan said in the same press conference.

Stagflation refers to the combination of weak economic growth and high inflation.

Other considerations cited by COCOPEA were climate disruptions, including the impact of El Niño, adjustments in minimum wage, and competition.

San Juan said consultations with parents, students, and faculty must also be done before proposing tuition increases. – Rappler.com

World.title: Playwright, filmmaker Dustin Celestino inducted into Palanca Hall of Fame
World.content:
Dustin Celestino enters the Palanca Awards’ prestigious roster after winning first prize in the full-length play category five times

MANILA, Philippines – Multi-awarded Filipino playwright and filmmaker Dustin Edward Celestino — whose work has been recognized across theater, film, and literature — was inducted into the Hall of Fame of the Carlos Palanca Memorial Awards for Literature on Tuesday, November 24, in Makati City.

Celestino’s full-length Filipino play, Kritisismo, earned him his fifth first-place honor, solidifying his place in the prestigious Hall of Fame of the Palanca Awards, widely regarded as the local equivalent of the Pulitzer Prize.

“It’s such an honor to be included among writers I have the greatest respect for. I’m also very happy to be part of a club that includes good friends and writing peers Mikael Co, Guelan Luarca, and Joshua So,” Celestino told Rappler. All three became Hall of Famers in 2024.

Elmer Gatchalian, a member of the board of judges for Dulang Ganap na Haba (Filipino Division), said, “We were all impressed by Kritisismo because of its dramatic structure and metatheatrical form. The full-length play stands out for its intellectual depth and sharp dialogue that examines power, class divide, and systemic oppression.”

Celestino’s other entry, Seen, won second place in the Full-Length Play category, English Division, this year.

Since 2017, Celestino has received four other Palanca first-prize awards in the full-length play category:

Fidelity (English), 2025

Ang Duyan ng Magiting (The Cradle of the Brave) (Filipino), 2019

The Story of This Father (English), 2017

Ang Pangahas na si Pepe Rodriguez (The Malevolent Pepe Rodriguez) (Filipino), 2017

His other Palanca wins include second prize for the full-length English play Birdie in 2024; second prize for the one-act Filipino play Elehiya in 2025; third prize for the full-length English play The Lost Filipino Patriots of America in 2022; third prize for the one-act Filipino play Fermata in 2023; and third prize for the full-length Filipino play A.Ni.Mal in 2025.

The Palanca Awards is the longest-running and most prestigious literary competition in the country. Established in 1950 and named after philanthropist and businessman Don Carlos Palanca Sr., it is sponsored by the Carlos Palanca Foundation, Inc., and is considered the gold standard in Philippine writing excellence.

Screenwriter

In 2026, Celestino won Indie Movie Screenwriter of the Year at the 42nd PMPC Star Awards for Movies for Habang Nilalamon ng Hydra ang Kasaysayan (As Hydra Devours History). He was also nominated for Best Original Screenplay at the Luna Awards and Best Screenplay at The Eddys.

Celestino’s films Habang Nilalamon ng Hydra ang Kasaysayan and A.Ni.Mál were both nominated for Best Film at the Cinemalaya Independent Film Festival in 2025 and 2026, respectively.

In 2023, Ang Duyan ng Magiting won the Special Jury Prize at Cinemalaya, earned seven Gawad Urian nominations including Best Picture, and was one of seven films shortlisted as the Philippines’ official entry to the 96th Academy Awards.

Strange Frequencies: Taiwan Killer Hospital, which he co-wrote, competed at the 2024 Metro Manila Film Festival.

Meanwhile, Utopia won the Special Jury Prize at the 2019 Cinema One Originals Film Festival and earned Celestino nominations for Best Director and Best Screenplay.

Over seven years, Celestino staged four one-act plays at the Cultural Center of the Philippines’ Virgin Labfest (VLF): Mga Eksena sa Buhay ng Kontrabida (Scenes from the Life of an Antagonist), Doggy, Ang Munting Liwanag sa Madilim na Sulok ng Isang Serbeserya sa Maynila (The Glimmer of Light in a Dark Corner of a Beerhouse in Manila), and Fermata.

The VLF also “opened more doors” for Celestino. Those doors included writing for the series Unconditional (later streamed on Netflix) and the Viva series Di Na Muli on TV5.

Video rental shop

Celestino was born in 1983 as the eldest of four children — three boys and a girl — to entrepreneur Edgardo Celestino and teacher and preschool owner Rocelyn Domingo.

Only English books lined their bookshelves while growing up in a two-bedroom bungalow in Quezon City, making English his first language.

“I couldn’t write in Filipino well until I was in college,” he said.

Celestino’s father — who also worked as a sales representative for pharmaceutical company Unilab — owned a chain of video rental shops, and Dustin helped curate the titles they acquired.

“I watched movies as a kid, because we had video shops. At age 11 or 12, I was already asked to curate our video shop’s library because I loved watching movies,” he recalled.

Name it — Betamax, VHS, 4+1 rental promos — he watched them all and read the covers of the VHS tapes. His father favored action flicks starring Bruce Willis, Sylvester Stallone, and Mark Dacascos, while Dustin was drawn to horror.

Celestino initially took Film at De La Salle University in Manila before shifting to Philosophy with a minor in Translation. He was part of the Malate Literary Folio from 2000 to 2004.

He began joining writing competitions in 2003 and 2004, winning four times.

“I was initially into writing English fiction,” he said. It’s a path that led him to writers’ workshops organized by Iyas, Ateneo de Manila University, and Silliman University in Dumaguete.

Mythology

Celestino loved Greek mythology as a child. Aside from watching Jason and the Argonauts on Channel 9 — which “started my initial interest in mythology” — the idea of using myths as metaphors for contemporary struggles came from The Myth of Sisyphus by French philosopher and novelist Albert Camus.

What appealed to him most were the stories of mortals because they were “more relatable: Pygmalion, Icarus, Orpheus, Cassandra.”

Among his favorite foreign authors are European existentialists Camus, French philosopher and playwright Jean-Paul Sartre, and Russian novelist Fyodor Dostoevsky.

He also admires Russian-American novelist Vladimir Nabokov, Czech-French novelist Milan Kundera, Czech writer Franz Kafka, German-Swiss poet and novelist Hermann Hesse, German novelist and poet Günter Grass, and American fictionists Philip Roth and Ernest Hemingway.

“They were very good with narratives,” he said.

Among Filipino writers, the one Celestino deems closest to them is Gregorio Brillantes.

“I think Gregorio Brillantes was the best Filipino writer,” Celestino said.

Teacher

Celestino has always been a teacher, just like his mother. As a speed reader, he easily handled one of the hardest parts of the job: grading papers.

He began teaching high school at St. Scholastica’s College. Later, while he was teaching college freshmen and sophomores at Asia Pacific College, the Philippines’ shift to the K-12 curriculum left him without work in the mid-2010s.

“Walang mabigay na workload sa akin (No workload could be given to me). I was demoralized. I had to take on another job,” he shared.

He was grateful for a role as creative director, where he also handled corporate social responsibility, at an internal communications company owned by a La Salle batchmate, though he struggled with the daily commute from Fairview.

He eventually resigned to focus on writing. He devoted the first 100 days of 2017 to studying playwriting formats and reading past Palanca winners.

“I had nine entries that year,” he recalled. Both of his full-length plays (in Filipino and English) won first prize.

“I had a knack for writing screenplays,” he said. “I started writing more.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Here’s what to expect at the opening of Rodrigo Duterte’s ICC trial
World.content:
DUTERTE. Former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte attends the fourth status conference at the Trial Chamber III of the International Criminal Court in The Hague, Netherlands, on October 13, 2026.

More than 500 victims of extrajudicial killings in Duterte's drug war are authorized to participate in the trial through their team of legal representatives

THE HAGUE, Netherlands – On Monday, November 30, former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte is set to begin trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) over alleged crimes against humanity relating to his bloody drug war in the Philippines.

The much-anticipated trial phase is when the parties in the case, namely, the ICC prosecutor, the common legal representatives of the victims (CLRV), and Duterte’s defense team, will present evidence and witness testimonies.

Unlike the confirmation of charges hearing last February, when the pre-trial chamber’s goal was to determine whether there was sufficient evidence in the prosecution’s case to proceed to trial, the judges in Trial Chamber III will now determine whether Duterte is guilty beyond reasonable doubt of the crimes against humanity of murder and attempted murder.

The crimes were alleged to have been committed during Duterte’s anti-illegal drug operations as Davao City mayor and vice mayor, utilizing his so-called Davao Death Squad, as well as when he replicated the Davao model on a nationwide scale upon assuming the presidency in 2016.

Here’s what to expect when trial begins.

Plea entering

When trial opens, the judges will ask Duterte whether he understands the charges filed against him and ask him to enter a plea of guilty or not guilty.

The equivalent of this in the Philippine legal process is called an arraignment.

Opening statements

The ICC prosecutor and the victims’ representatives are expected to deliver opening statements after Duterte enters a plea. These are expected to take several hours each.

The defense will deliver a short introduction of its case, but a longer opening statement is expected later in the trial.

Witness testimonies

After the opening statements, the prosecution will begin presenting its witnesses. In the first weeks of the trial, that is, before the court goes on its winter recess on December 18, the prosecution is expected to present five witnesses.

The prosecution expects to present around 100 witnesses over the course of the trial.

“As with other complex cases involving allegations of crimes against humanity, these proceedings are expected to take some time. The exact duration of the trial will depend on a number of factors, including the volume of evidence, the number of witnesses, and any procedural matters that may arise during the trial,” said ICC spokesperson Oriane Huber Maillet in a briefing with reporters on Tuesday, November 24.

Only after the prosecution presents its case will the defense have the opportunity to present theirs.

‘Fair trial’

The ICC presumes Duterte to be innocent unless and until proven guilty before the court.

“He is represented by counsel of his choosing and is entitled to all fair trial guarantees provided under the Rome Statute, including adequate time and facilities to prepare his defense, the ability to challenge the Prosecution’s evidence, and the opportunity to present evidence and witnesses on his own behalf,” said Maillet.

Victims’ participation

More than 500 victims of extrajudicial killings in Duterte’s drug war are authorized to participate in the trial through their team of legal representatives.

The ICC said it was taking steps to protect victims and witnesses from threats against their well-being.

How to follow the hearings

ICC hearings are public and can be followed in two ways: in person, by attending the hearings at the ICC’s headquarters in The Hague, or online via its Facebook and YouTube channels.

Those who wish to attend the hearings in person may queue outside the court and are served on a first-come, first-served basis. There will be four sessions per day once trial begins, at the following schedule in local time at The Hague:

10:00 – 11:00 am

11:30 am to 12:30 pm

1:30 – 2:30 pm

3:00 – 4:00 pm

Viewers in the public gallery can watch the proceedings live, while online streams will have a 30-minute delay to allow for redactions in the event that confidential information is divulged during open session. The judges will occasionally call for a closed session to protect confidential information or participants.

“The Court remains committed to ensuring that these proceedings are conducted fairly, independently and transparently, in accordance with the Rome Statute and the Court’s legal framework,” said Maillet.

Demonstrations around the court

Both the pro- and anti-Duterte camps are expected to stage their own events and demonstrations in the days leading up to trial and when it begins.

On November 30, the Duterte Panagutin Network will hold a march and protest on ICC grounds, just before trial starts at 9 am. From 10 am onwards, Duterte’s supporters are expected to occupy the area in front of the ICC to stage their demonstration.

The ICC is set to begin Duterte’s trial amid a sharp delegitimization campaign from the former president’s supporters and global superpowers like the United States.

“The Court’s role is not to pursue any political objective. Rather, its role is to determine, through independent and impartial judicial proceedings, whether the charges have been proven according to the law,” said Maillet. – Rappler.com

World.title: BuCor flags low number of applicants for vacant prison officer posts
World.content:
Bureau of Corrections Director General Gregorio Pio Catapang Jr. —Voltaire F. Domingo/Senate PRIB

MANILA, Philippines — The Bureau of Corrections (BuCor) is struggling to attract applicants for hundreds of vacant supervisory and senior officer positions, prompting its chief to urge uniformed personnel to undergo mandatory career and leadership training to qualify for promotion.

BuCor Director General Gregorio Pio Catapang Jr. said the bureau needed more qualified personnel to fill its vacancies, particularly in higher-ranking positions.

“We need qualified personnel to be promoted so that we can fill up the vacant positions,” Catapang said in a statement dated Nov. 22.

Article continues after this 

Of the 42 vacant positions for Corrections Chief Inspector, only six personnel have applied. The bureau also recorded just four applicants for 67 vacant Corrections Senior Inspector positions.

The shortage of applicants extends to other ranks. Only 23 personnel have applied for 124 vacant Corrections Senior Officer 4 (CSO4) positions, while 34 have applied for 90 vacant CSO3 posts.

READ: BuCor chief orders armed personnel to keep guns out of children’s reach

The bureau has received only one application for a vacant CSO2 position. The CSO1 rank, meanwhile, has 82 applicants for 88 available posts.

Catapang urged personnel to take advantage of the mandatory career courses and leadership development programs conducted by the Corrections National Training Institute, saying these would improve their qualifications and readiness for promotion.

Article continues after this 

The training programs are intended to develop the bureau’s workforce and ensure that qualified personnel are available to assume leadership and supervisory responsibilities.

BuCor’s shortage of senior corrections officers came amid a revised rank structure among its more than 8,500 personnel that took effect on Aug. 1.

Article continues after this 

The revised distribution created a pyramidal hierarchy, with only four positions allotted for Corrections Chief Superintendent, 11 for Corrections Senior Superintendent and 31 for Corrections Superintendent. It also provided for 52 Corrections Chief Inspectors, 90 Senior Inspectors and 130 Inspectors, among other ranks.

READ: 7 CIW officials, personnel face charges over missing trust fund

Despite the redistribution, more than 71 percent of BuCor’s uniformed personnel remain at the entry-level Corrections Officer I rank, underscoring the limited number of higher-ranking positions available for promotion.

Under Republic Act No. 10575, or the Bureau of Corrections Act of 2013, BuCor is required to maintain a ratio of one custodial personnel for every seven PDLs across three shifts. It must also maintain one reformation personnel for every 24 PDLs during one shift to ensure adequate staffing for prison security, inmate supervision and rehabilitation.

World.title: Bill allowing homes generate power filed to address high electric rates
World.content:
Parañaque Rep. Brian Raymund Yamsuan

MANILA, Philippines — A bill was filed to allow and encourage residents to install electric generation and storage systems in order to address high power rates in the country, Parañaque Rep. Brian Raymund Yamsuan said on Tuesday.

Yamsuan in a statement said that these forms of renewable energy setups, which allow users to generate their own electric power while ensuring that these does not seep through lines going toward the power grid, will be institutionalized by House Bill (HB) No. 11459 and other measures seeking a proposed Sariling Kuryente Act.

According to the lawmaker, who authored HB No. 11459, the bills seek to promote the installation of these setups by removing unnecessary requirements.

Article continues after this 

“We now have the highest residential electricity rates in Southeast Asia, surpassing even Singapore. Dagdag pasanin ang mataas na bayad sa kuryente sa maraming pamilya at negosyo na kinakaharap pa ang mataas na presyo ng mga bilihin,” Yamsuan said.

(We now have the highest residential electricity rates in Southeast Asia, surpassing even Singapore. Higher expenses due to electricity are an additional burden to families and businesses who are already struggling with rising prices of basic commodities.)

READ: PH has plenty of sun – so why isn’t solar booming yet?

“Making solar power and other sources of clean, sustainable energy more accessible by removing unnecessary requirements in installing them will help ease their financial woes,” he added.

The Philippines has long been regarded as one of the countries with high power rates—if not the highest—in Southeast Asia. For example, power rates can be as high as $0.20 (around P11.50) per kilowatt-hour (kWh) on average, while neighbors Vietnam has $0.08 (P4.50) per kWh; and Malaysia with $0.06 (P3.50) per kWh.

Article continues after this 

According to Yamsuan, it is good that two House committees—the committee on ways and means and the committee on energy—have approved a substitute bill consolidating all measures related to the proposed Sariling Kuryente Act as it will do away with tedious application processes.

READ: ERC, Meralco vow faster net-metering approvals for solar power users

Article continues after this 

Yamsuan said the committee approval of the substitute bill to HB No. 11459 and 18 other similar measures, including the one filed by House Speaker Faustino “Bojie” Dy III and Majority Leader Ferdinand Alexander Marcos, moves the measure closer to second and third reading approval.

“We thank the Committee on Energy chaired by (Palawan) Rep. (Jose) Pepito Alvarez and the committee on ways and means headed by (Marikina) Rep. Miro Quimbo for expediting the approval of the Sariling Kuryente bill,” he said.

“We are optimistic that the bill will gain overwhelming support from our fellow lawmakers when it reaches the plenary,” he added.

If HB No. 11459 and the other bills are enacted, it will amend Republic Act No. 9136 or the Electric Power Industry Reform Act of 2001 (Epira) by adding several new sections regarding renewable energy.

“An end-user that installs and operates a behind-the-meter electricity generation or energy storage system for its own use shall not, by reason thereof, be considered a generation company,” a proposed additional paragraph to Section 6 of Epira, under Yamsuan’s HB No. 11459, stated.

“A system using equipment certified under standards recognized by the ERC (Energy Regulatory Commission) to prevent the export of electricity to the distribution system shall not require a certificate of compliance or other prior authorization from the ERC,” it added.

There have been calls for the government to utilize more of the country’s renewable energy sources, like solar energy, considering that it is mostly sunny in the Philippines.

However, several obstacles regarding the adoption of solar power were pointed out. Aside from high costs of installation, power companies frown on “guerilla” solar energy setups or those built by end-users alone.

Last May 2026, University of the Philippines Diliman professor and Inquirer data scientist Dr. Rogelio Alicor Panao said that there is a friction between “monopoly control and energy democratization” as exhibited in calls for Congress to investigate guerilla setups.

Just this September, both the ERC and the Manila Electric Co. (Meralco) have vowed to speed up the approval and energization of rooftop solar power systems, as complaints of delays were raised during a Senate committee hearing.

The complaints were aired by Senate committee on energy chair Sen. Erwin Tulfo, who said that he knew people who wanted to install rooftop solar power panels but were discouraged by reports of lengthy approval periods for net-metering from Meralco.

World.title: 2027 rocket launch to benefit agriculture, environment, security – Aquino
World.content:
Sen. Bam Aquino —Inquirer photo/Niño Jesus Orbeta

MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Bam Aquino explained early Wednesday morning that the expected Philippine rocket launch in early 2027 is to collect beneficial data for various sectors, including agriculture, environment, disaster monitoring, and national security.

Aquino, who authored the Republic Act No. 11363, known as the Philippine Space Act, explained as he defended the P1 billion budget of the Philippine Space Agency (PhilSA).

“[Space data] can be beneficial… To be specific, meron siyang application sa agriculture, environmental protection and monitoring, natural resource management, disaster risk reduction, national security among others,” Aquino explained.

Article continues after this 

([Space data] can be beneficial… To be specific, it has applications in agriculture, environmental protection and monitoring, natural resource management, disaster risk reduction, national security among others.)

READ: PH prepares for 1st rocket test launch next year

Sen. Imee Marcos probed into the purpose of the rocket launch announced by her brother, President Marcos, during his fifth state of the nation address earlier this year.

“What’s its purpose? Why are we involved in these rocket launches given that we have so little budget to spare?” Sen. Marcos questioned.

According to Aquino, PhilSA has had smaller and simpler rocket launches, and the upcoming launch in 2027 would be the first “liquid rocket launch” to develop the country’s space research.

Article continues after this 

“It’s to build the technology, regulatory framework, safety procedures, and infrastructure that will eventually allow the Philippines to develop its own launch capability,” Aquino replied.

But Marcos pointed out that some satellite capabilities may be acquired via the National Aeronautics and Space Administration for free.

Article continues after this 

To this, Aquino highlighted that relying on foreign satellites gives the Philippines “very limited control and we have to pay for it.”

The launching of the Philippines’ own satellite systems, Aquino added, is under the mandate of the Philippine Space Agency to “develop our own local infrastructure and expertise.” /cb

World.title: 4 nabbed in Navotas, Caloocan for ‘offering’ minors to foreigners
World.content:
INQUIRER.net file photo

MANILA, Philippines — Four individuals were arrested in two separate operations in Navotas and Caloocan City for allegedly offering Filipino minors to foreign nationals for sexual services through online platforms.

In an interview on Tuesday, NBI Human Trafficking Division Chief SA Rosalie Laguardia said the apprehensions were conducted at a resort in Navotas and in Caloocan City.

“May bagong modus itong mga local facilitator natin. Hindi na ginagawa sa bahay nila ’yung online service. Nagre-renta sila ng either sa hotel or ’yung Airbnb para hindi ma-identify ’yung location nila, o ’yung bahay nila,” Laguardia said.

Article continues after this 

(Our local facilitators have a new modus operandi. They no longer do the online service in their homes. They rent either a hotel or Airbnb so that their location or their home cannot be identified.)

The case in Navotas stemmed from a referral from a non-governmental organization regarding a supposed offering of minors to conduct online sexual services to foreigners, including American nationals.

READ: NBI to subpoena comedian over ‘sexual’ playground post

“Sa una, online sexual abuse pa lang. Then kapag regular customer ka na, ayun i-offer na sayo yung physical meet-up. At ’yung customer, pupunta na sa Pilipinas at pisikal nang gagawin ’yung pag-aabuso sa ating mga kabataan,” Laguardia said.

(At first, it was just online sexual abuse. Then when you were a regular customer, they would offer you a physical meet-up. And the customer would go to the Philippines and physically abuse our youth.)

Article continues after this 

Laguardia said the two Filipino suspects usually charge foreign customers P1,000 or more for online sexual services and P10,000 or more for in-person meet-ups.

During the entrapment operation at the resort in the first week of November, NBI agents rescued eight individuals supposedly being offered to foreigners—four male minors and four adults.

Article continues after this 

Laguardia also said initial information revealed that the suspects were offering female minors, but upon verification, the victims were actually males.

READ: NBI chief’s Christmas wishlist: Arrest of high-profile fugitives

Meanwhile, the entrapment operation in a hotel in Caloocan City was conducted on Nov. 12.

The case originated from the bureau’s operation in October last year, wherein electronic devices were confiscated.

Upon conducting a forensic examination of the gadgets recovered during the earlier operation, NBI agents identified a Canadian customer and suspected local facilitator of a supposed human trafficking scheme.

Laguardia said this information was turned over to the NBI’s counterpart in Canada, which conducted a separate investigation and later arrested the Canadian customer within its jurisdiction.

Meanwhile, the NBI traced the local facilitator, who turned out to be offering her own children and her neighbor’s children to foreign customers.

“Nahuli rin natin ’yung nanay ng mga batang ito (neighbor) na kasama doon sa entrapment operation,” the bureau’s Human Trafficking Division chief said.

(We also caught the mother of these children (neighbor) who was involved in the entrapment operation.)

Operatives rescued four female minors during the operation.

Laguardia said the rescued individuals in Navotas and Caloocan are already undergoing counseling and intervention.

Meanwhile, the four suspects were charged with complaints for alleged violations of the Anti-Trafficking in Persons Act and laws against online sexual abuse or exploitation of children and child sexual abuse or exploitation of materials. /cb

World.title: Dela Rosa’s counsel ‘concerned’ about SC’s Duterte writ ruling
World.content:
Inquirer photo

MANILA, Philippines — A legal counsel for Sen. Bato Dela Rosa on Tuesday expressed concern over the Supreme Court’s (SC) dismissal of the consolidated petitions for a writ of habeas corpus following the International Criminal Court (ICC) arrest of former President Rodrigo Duterte, saying the move could be seen as a “guide” to future scenarios.

Dela Rosa also faces an ICC warrant.

The senator’s lawyer Israelito Torreon made the remark after the High Court voted 9-4 to deny the consolidated petitions filed by Duterte’s children—Sebastian, Veronica, and Paolo Duterte—on behalf of their father to challenge his March 2025 arrest and turn him over to the International Criminal Court (ICC).

Article continues after this 

In a decision penned by Associate Justice Japar Dimaampao and released Tuesday, the SC said issuing the writ, a strictly domestic remedy that is enforceable only within the country, “would serve no practical purpose” since Duterte is already under ICC’s jurisdiction.

READ: Future ICC warrants of arrest to be enforced immediately – Palace

“We respect the Supreme Court,” Torreon, who is also a lawyer of the former president, said in a statement. “With equal candor, we respectfully disagree with the majority ruling dismissing the habeas corpus petitions as moot.”

READ: SC asks Senate, House to comment on Sara Duterte impeachment vote rule

Torreon noted that the petitions were not only about where Duterte is detained, but to challenge the arrest, the detention at Villamor Air Base, and the transfer out of the country within hours which was done without a Philippine warrant.

Article continues after this 

“The legality of those acts is a separate question from the custody he is now under at The Hague,” Torreon said. “It remains a question that only our Supreme Court can answer.”

Torreon said: “We are also concerned that this ruling may be read as a guide for the future.”

Article continues after this 

READ: Jonvic Remulla: Arresting Sen. dela Rosa could lead to 10,000 deaths

“If liberty can be taken and carried beyond our borders in a single day, and the speed of the removal is then enough to put it beyond judicial review, the Bill of Rights becomes a promise that depends on how quickly the government moves,” he added.

At least 6,000 people were killed during the war on drugs under Duterte’s administration, according to official government data, but human rights watchdogs and the ICC prosecutors estimate the death toll to be between 12,000 and 30,000 from 2016 to 2019.

Dela Rosa was the PNP chief from 2016 to 2018, when he enforced the Duterte administration’s deadly anti-drug campaign before becoming a senator.

Arresting Dela Rosa could lead to “10,000 deaths” prompting the government to negotiate for his surrender, according to Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla.

World.title: 60 writers bag 2026 Palanca honors; Inquirer editor judges anew
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines — Philippine literature feted its finest voices as 60 standout writers received honors during the 76th Carlos Palanca Memorial Awards for Literature on Tuesday in Makati City.

Philippine Daily Inquirer executive editor Voltaire Contreras was among the 63 judges of this year’s Palanca awards. Contreras, who also judged submissions in 2025, evaluated entries in the Kabataan division.

The country’s longest-running literary competition received 3,040 submissions this year, the highest in the competition’s history. Of 60 honorees, 36 were first-time winners, with the youngest awardee at only 11 years old.

Article continues after this 

Playwright Dustin Edward Celestino is the latest inductee into the Palanca Hall of Fame, which recognizes writers who have earned first prize five times across any of the contest’s regular writing categories.

Celestino netted his fifth first prize this year for “Kritisismo” under the Dulang Ganap ang Haba category. He had already won the top honors in this category twice in 2017 and 2019, and another two times in the Full-Length Play category in 2017 and 2025.

Meanwhile, writer-lawyer Nicolas Pichay graced the awards night as Guest of Honor and Gawad Dangal ng Lahi awardee. Pichay was a 2007 inductee into the competition’s hall of fame, with award-winning works spanning plays, poetry collections and musicals that champion cultural heritage and human rights.

In his speech, Pichay questioned the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) among writers.

“AI beckons us with the promise of convenience and speed. But what happens to us when we no longer have to struggle for words?” he said.

Article continues after this 

“A large part of me resists AI because I am addicted to the pain of writing. But more precisely, I feel that giving up that painful struggle with words will take away that which makes me most human. And in so doing, I would surrender the very ability to create literature,” Pichay added.

Named after philanthropist Don Carlos Palanca Sr., the annual Palanca awards is considered the “gold standard” in Philippine literature excellence.

World.title: UK Sanctions 5 Regime Generals Following ICJ Rohingya Genocide Ruling
World.content:
The United Kingdom on Monday sanctioned five more senior Myanmar military officers after the United Nations’ top court ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya community in 2017.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) announced its ruling in the case on November 19.

The UK stated on Monday that it formally recognized the ICJ ruling and announced a major package of measures in response, imposing sanctions against five Myanmar military officers for atrocities against civilians since the 2021 coup.

The new UK sanctions target Brigadier General Myo Htut Hlaing, Major General Myo Min Tun, Major General Myat Thet Oo, Major General Kyaw Soe and Major General Kyaw Swar Oo.

The UK announced asset freezes, travel bans and director disqualifications in response to ongoing violence and repression against civilians across the country.

“Today, we are imposing new sanctions on those suspected of involvement in repression of the civilian population and other serious abuses of human rights in Myanmar,” UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said.

The UK claimed that Brig-Gen Myo Htut Hlaing, deputy commander of Northwestern Regional Command, is responsible for serious cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment of detainees in Chin State.

Maj-Gen Myo Min Tun, Eastern Military Command chief in Shan and Karenni states, was involved in repression of the civilian and threatens the peace, stability and security of Myanmar, it said.

Former head of the Northern Command in Kachin State and ex-ambassador to Laos Major General Myat Thet Oo, who was reportedly removed and jailed in 2024, was sanctioned for his role in enabling military authorities to repress civilians.

Maj-Gen Kyaw Soe, commander of the Western Command in Rakhine State, was sanctioned for involvement in airstrikes on civilians and medical infrastructure.

The UK said Maj-Gen Kyaw Swar Oo, former head of the Western Command, was responsible for repression of civilians including through an airstrike on Mrauk-U General Hospital that killed 33 civilians, including a baby, and left many others injured.

London also intends to introduce legislation targeting the export and supply of aviation fuel to Myanmar.

Alongside the sanctions, the UK is providing £5 million (US$6.53 million) in new aid for about 350,000 people, including Rohingya and other communities in Rakhine State, while a further £3 million will go towards strengthening accountability and justice for survivors of human rights abuses across Myanmar.

The United Kingdom has already imposed sanctions on 42 individuals and 39 entities, including individuals responsible for atrocities against the Rohingya, since the 2021 coup.

The UK earlier welcomed the ICJ ruling and ordered the expulsion of Myanmar’s defense attaché, Captain Soe Aung, from London.

World.title: 2 More Chinese Scam Syndicates Raided on Military-Linked Land in Yangon
World.content:
The Myanmar regime has raided two more Chinese scam syndicates operating at sites on military-owned land or believed to have military-linked ownership in the commercial capital Yangon.

The regime raided two residential houses in Mayangone Township and a Golden City Condo in Yankin Township on November 20 and November 22 respectively, arresting over 120 people, according to regime reports.

Observers believed the series of scam raids was prompted by tip-offs provided by Beijing.

On Sunday night, the regime raided Golden City Condo in Yankin Township and arrested 16 people on suspicion of involvement in an online gambling scam, the regime reported on Monday.

During raids on four condo rooms, the regime seized 15 laptops, 26 smartphones and three Wi-Fi routers. All four units were linked to Chinese national Jiang Hong Feng, who allegedly operated online casino and sports betting platform Zaw Play.Com.

Golden City condo sits on military-owned land leased in 2013 under a long-term Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT) agreement with the military’s Office of the Quartermaster General.

In 2016, Singapore-based Emerging Towns & Cities Singapore (ETC) entered the development by taking a 70-percent stake. The other 30 percent is held by a military-linked local partner, Nature Link. The project generates revenue for the Myanmar military through land-use premiums and ongoing lease payments.

In 2023, two years after the coup, ETC took steps to sell its stake in a subsidiary linked to the project to Grand Ally Pte Ltd, which is owned by Li Bo, a Chinese citizen who is the vice president of sales and marketing for ETC, and the company’s regional sales and marketing director for Myanmar.

Justice For Myanmar (JFM), a rights watchdog, pointed out that ETC’s related-party sales risk maintaining ties to the military through personnel and stakeholders.

Nature Link belongs to Yangon-based Jewellery Luck, a group owned by regime crony Kyaw Sein with interests in real estate, hospitality, mining and forestry.

This scam syndicate not only sits on military-owned land, but is also just 500 meters from police housing compounds, a local resident told The Irrawaddy. The condo sheltering the scam center also shares a compound with the military-owned Myawaddy Media Center, formerly the Military Records Department. It is also located 600 meters from the regime’s No. 2 Police Security Command Headquarters located at the corner of No. 1 Industrial Road and Sayar San Road.

Following Sunday night’s raid, word spread in real estate circles, with agents warning other agents who had rented properties to Chinese nationals to flee the area, a local resident noted.

Real estate agents have a lot of incentive to rent to Chinese nationals in the Golden City condo, she added.

“To enter the condo, you have to pass a security gate and do a face scan,” she said.

Prior to Sunday’s raid, some media—citing resident accounts—had reported a previous regime raid on the condo on November 13, in which suspected scammers were also detained. But the regime has not made any public announcement about the earlier raid.

On the night of November 20, the regime raided suspected Chinese scam syndicates based in two residential buildings in Mayangone Township’s Ward No. 5, arresting 33 Chinese, two Thai and 70 Myanmar nationals.

The two compounds at 19/A and 43/1 Ma Soe Yein Street were just under 1 km from military bases including Military Intelligence Assistant Unit 1. Military defectors claimed the land housing the scam centers is linked to retired military officers and others in military circles.

A Chinese analyst claimed this raid, too, came in response to a tip-off from China.

Although the regime has pledged to keep fighting scam operations and act in accordance with the law, online critics are widely questioning how authorities could remain unaware of large numbers of people living in such compounds while Myanmar nationals face strict overnight guest registration rules and constant surveillance.

“When we register overnight guests, we have to provide the regime ward administrators with portrait photos of guests with their personal identities,” a Yangon resident said.

“Why don’t the ward administrators and authorities know about that?” he said.

Online critics urged authorities to check the many other places in Yangon where Chinese nationals live or rent together, alleging they could be running online scams.

On the night of November 12, the regime raided nine rooms at Golden River Residence condo in Thaketa Township and arrested 52 Chinese nationals, including Su Fu Quan, who was wanted by China, along with eight Vietnamese and 46 Myanmar nationals.

According to the regime’s reports, the syndicates targeted Chinese, Japanese, South Korean and Indian nationals with romance and investment scams.

The regime reported the arrest of 323 people—302 Chinese nationals and 21 Myanmar women—during a raid on a makeshift online scam and gambling compound in southern Shan State’s Kyethi Township on Monday morning.

In a January 2026 report, the Institute for Strategy and Policy-Myanmar (ISP-Myanmar) said scam syndicates in Shan State were relocating from the China-Myanmar border to central Shan State and major urban centers such as Yangon and Mandalay.

ISP-Myanmar also said crackdowns on scam compounds in Karen State had pushed syndicates to relocate to other areas.

On November 19, the U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctioned the Democratic Karen Benevolent Army’s Commander-in-Chief General Saw Shwe Wah and Phaya Thonezu town commander Colonel Saw A One, accusing them of operating and facilitating cyber-scam centers on the Myanmar-Thailand border.

World.title: After the Genocide Verdict, Myanmar’s ‘Foreign Intruder’ Scare Returns
World.content:
Since November 3, when the International Court of Justice (ICJ) announced the date for its judgment in Myanmar’s Rohingya genocide case, one word has surged across Burmese-language social media: “khoe win”, meaning “illegal entrant.” It is routinely paired with “Bengali,” the label Myanmar’s military establishment uses to deny the Rohingya their chosen identity. Sometimes it comes with “kalar,” a slur against Muslims and people of South Asian descent.

The message is familiar. The timing should worry anyone who remembers where it led.

On November 19, the ICJ ruled, by nine votes to six, that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya during the military’s 2017 operations in northern Rakhine State.

Rather than reckon with that finding, pro-military nationalist circles are again urging Myanmar people to look for “Muslim outsiders” in their own neighborhoods.

Over the past three weeks, I have been monitoring Facebook and TikTok, Myanmar’s most-used social media platforms, and found hundreds of posts demanding that “Bengali intruders” be expelled, questioning Muslim businesspeople’s identity cards or calling for household members’ lists or guests’ lists inspections.

Some propose an Operasi-style campaign, borrowing the Malay term for enforcement operations against undocumented migrants, including Myanmar workers. An old video of former spy chief Khin Nyunt denying Rohingya identity has resurfaced on TikTok. None offers evidence of an influx from Bangladesh.

From social media to parliament

The posts are not all anonymous. On Facebook, veteran pro-military journalist Myat Khine encouraged guest-list checks, suggesting they would expose intruders.

Since November 19, the day of the ruling, Ashin Agga Dhamma, a famous nationalist Buddhist monk, has posted at least 12 interview videos featuring two Muslim businessmen. One of them, Htay Aung, claims Yangon is seeing an influx of illegal Muslim immigrants and rejects Rohingya identity. The monk and Htay Aung are widely seen as close to Ma Ba Tha, the ultranationalist Buddhist movement, and have previously appeared at anti-Rohingya rallies.

On November 15, the Burma Human Rights Network warned that Ma Ba Tha-backed groups were reportedly preparing nationwide protests against the ICJ ruling. It documented threats demanding that Myanmar Islamic organizations deny Rohingya identity, backed by calls to boycott Muslim-owned businesses if they refused.

Separately, UN Special Rapporteur on Myanmar Kelley Currie warned on October 29 that groups behind earlier anti-Muslim agitation were becoming more active online and in political spaces under military control. On November 18, citing reports from inside Myanmar, she told journalists in Dhaka that authorities in Naypyitaw were acting alongside Ma Ba Tha and other Buddhist nationalist organizations previously involved in spreading hatred and inciting violence.

On November 10, before the judgment, the inflammatory language reached the military-controlled parliament. Lawmaker Hla Swe accused the Arakan Army of letting undocumented entrants cross from Bangladesh. Deputy Immigration Minister Lin Zaw Tun outlined plans for inspections and arrests of people described as undocumented “Bengali” migrants. No independently verified evidence of the alleged influx was presented, but online demands to “check papers” had acquired an official counterpart. On November 20, the regime rejected the judgment and again called Rohingya “Bengalis.”

The road to 2017

This same deadly playbook has unfolded before. A UN fact-finding mission cited a government inquiry recording 192 deaths during the 2012 Rakhine violence, which displaced more than 140,000, mostly Rohingya. Anti-Muslim mobs killed at least 44 in Meiktila in 2013, according to Human Rights Watch. False online rape allegations helped ignite Mandalay riots that killed two in 2014, according to the US State Department.

These attacks occurred under former General Thein Sein’s military-backed government. Military hardliners and nationalists exploited religious fears during the political opening, presenting the army as the country’s protector. They used the same message against Aung San Suu Kyi’s National League for Democracy before its 2015 landslide.

The violence of 2012–2014 was part of a broader campaign of hatred and discrimination that culminated in the military’s far larger assault on the Rohingya in 2017. By then, Aung San Suu Kyi led a civilian government, but the military still controlled security operations. The generals carried out the atrocities while her government bore much of the international backlash. That outcome also served the military’s political interests.

The ICJ’s judgment now shows how far the military took this approach. Citing UN investigators, it noted that 36 military-linked Facebook pages posted 10,485 anti-Rohingya hate-speech items, including repeated material, during six months of 2017.

Why revive the rhetoric now?

Min Aung Hlaing, president since April after a military-dominated election, faces pressure on several fronts. On the battlefield, while Chinese pressure helped Naypyitaw secure fragile ceasefires in parts of northern Shan State, major regime counteroffensives in Rakhine and Kachin states have stalled against fierce ethnic and resistance forces.

Diplomatically, ASEAN still bars the junta’s political representatives from summits, while Ambassador Kyaw Moe Tun, who is loyal to the pro-democracy parallel government, still holds Myanmar’s UN seat. At home, the economy is in deep distress, with the kyat plunging toward 5,000 to the U.S. dollar and driving severe inflation.

The ICJ judgment brings another humiliation for a military establishment that has long portrayed itself as the sole defender of Myanmar’s sovereignty. Inciting public anger toward supposed foreign infiltrators is a tactic used by successive generations of generals. But repeating it today carries a far deadlier risk. Myanmar is far more heavily armed than during the communal riots a decade ago. Since the 2021 coup, the military has equipped and mobilized local militias, including Pyithu Sit and Pyu Saw Htee groups, to fight the resistance. In Meiktila in 2013, mobs carried machetes and petrol bombs. Today, the same crowd has access to guns and grenades. Another massacre is not inevitable, but hatred in a country with so many armed groups could be harder to contain.

The opposition has responsibilities too. The National Unity Government and Karen National Union welcomed the ruling. Yet some democracy supporters still reject Rohingya identity. Opposing military rule is not enough if we still deny the minorities’ rights and identity.

Rohingya civilians are not the enemies of Rakhine Buddhists, nor are Rakhine civilians the enemies of the Rohingya. Neither community is the enemy of Myanmar’s people. Their grievances and rights cannot be settled by another campaign of suspicion and hatred.

Myanmar’s generals have spent decades teaching people to fear one another, and those divisions have repeatedly helped the military justify its grip on power. Myanmar’s people have seen where campaigns against supposed outsiders can lead. The genocide judgment should be a reason to confront that history, not repeat it. A demand to inspect someone’s identity card must not become the first step toward another burning village.

Nyein Chan Aye is a Burmese journalist based in Washington, D.C., who previously worked for the BBC and Voice of America. He writes on Myanmar, U.S. policy, China and regional affairs.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Battles Resistance on Irrawaddy’s Northern Banks
World.content:
Resistance forces led by the Kachin Independence Army (KIA) have captured three regime outposts on the Twin Nge–Mongmit road in northern Shan State while regime troops are busy with their offensives across the river in Sagaing.

The combined forces of the KIA, heartland People’s Defense Forces (PDF) and All Burma Students’ Democratic Front seized regime positions in three villages on the road leading from Twin Nge on the east bank of the Irrawaddy River to northern Shan State’s Mongmit, according to resistance sources.

The outposts were reportedly crucial to the defense of Mongmit, which is held by the central military regime under an uneasy truce with ethnic armed forces.

At least five regime soldiers were killed and 20 others wounded in the attacks, resistance sources said. The Irrawaddy could not independently verify the casualties.

The towns of Mogoke and Mongmit were captured during Operation 1027 by the Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA), which returned them to the regime under Chinese pressure last November. But the KIA and allied resistance forces retain a presence in rural parts of the two townships.

The military has now fortified Baw Dae village in Mongmit Township at one end and is airlifting reinforcements to a military training school in Twin Nge at the other.

Just across the river in northern Sagaing, meanwhile, regime troops have taken control of the road stretch between Kantbalu and Indaw townships after fighting since early October. Twenty-five resistance fighters were reportedly killed in the clashes.

More than 700 troops from 33rd Light Infantry Division are deployed in Kawlin and Kantbalu, according to resistance forces.

Military defector Zin Yaw said the regime has recaptured northern Kantbalu and is preparing to advance on the southern part of the township.

“Troops from 33rd have reached the Armored Battalion 6006, so their objective for northern Kantbalu has been achieved,” he said.

Battles have also been raging since April in three villages opposite Katha town further upriver, where more than 300 troops from Northeastern Command previously based in Lashio are conducting an offensive.

World.title: 14 Countries ‘Acknowledge’ ICJ Ruling on Rohingya Genocide
World.content:
LONDON—The UK and 13 other countries on Monday “acknowledged” the top UN court’s ruling that Myanmar perpetrated genocide against its Rohingya minority as London announced new sanctions.

The foreign ministers of Australia, Belgium, Canada, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Estonia, Iceland, Latvia, Luxembourg, New Zealand, Portugal, Spain, the Gambia and the United Kingdom said Myanmar had “violated its obligations under the Genocide Convention.”

“We underscore that the Court’s judgment is binding upon Myanmar and call on Myanmar to comply fully with its obligations under international law, including the Court’s decision,” they said in a joint statement.

The UK separately said it “formally recognizes” genocide against the Rohingya and announced sanctions on five senior military figures.

“The horrific violence and persecution inflicted on the Rohingya cannot go unanswered,” UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said.

The sanctions include asset freezes and travel bans, a Foreign Office statement said, adding that London “also intends to introduce legislation targeting the export and supply of aviation fuel to Myanmar”.

“The UK is providing an additional £5 million [US$6.5 million] in new funding to support Rohingya and other communities with essential lifesaving and life-affirming services to approximately 350,000 people who need it most in Rakhine State, where humanitarian need is most acute,” the statement added.

It said a further £3 million would “go towards strengthening accountability and justice for survivors of human rights abuses across Myanmar.”

On November 19 in a historic verdict, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority during a 2017 crackdown in Rakhine State.

The ruling was the first time in the ICJ’s 80-year history that it has determined that a state committed genocide.

Myanmar’s government called the ruling unfair and a “great disappointment.”

Shortly after the verdict, Britain announced it would expel Myanmar’s defence attache.

World.title: Inside the Shadow Networks Helping Min Aung Hlaing Consolidate Power
World.content:
With the help of a Russian-trained military network led by a key aide-de-camp, a team of old spooks and the military’s security and intelligence apparatus, junta boss Min Aung Hlaing now runs Myanmar with an extraordinary degree of personal authority.

Diplomats, Naypyitaw insiders and regional security specialists say the regime’s system of governance has shifted from institutionalized military junta rule toward a highly personalistic system centered on Min Aung Hlaing.

While formal cabinet ministries, the diplomatic corps and conventional military command structures remain intact on paper, The Irrawaddy has learned that substantive authority is increasingly concentrated within a narrow circle of trusted military, intelligence and informal advisers. Sources said Min Aung Hlaing has consolidated personal control since the 2021 coup, while creating three primary networks that have sidelined formal institutions and now exercise substantial influence over state and military policy.

From institutionalized junta to personalistic rule

Historically, successive Myanmar military regimes—notably the State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) and the State Peace and Development Council (SPDC)—operated through a degree of collective leadership among senior generals and powerful regional commanders. Since the February 2021 coup, however, sources close to the military say Min Aung Hlaing has systematically dismantled those consultative norms, concentrating executive, legislative and operational authority in his own hands.

According to insiders familiar with decision-making in Naypyitaw, major political, economic and battlefield directives now originate directly from the Commander-in-Chief’s Office rather than through cabinet deliberations or collective military council meetings. They said internal mechanisms for debate and peer review among senior generals have steadily hollowed out, leaving top brass with little room to challenge or shape core regime strategy.

At the same time, cabinet ministers and senior bureaucrats have been subordinated to the role of administrative implementers tasked with executing orders rather than formulating policy, according to people familiar with the regime’s current governance in Naypyitaw.

Within this centralized structure, access to the junta chief depends heavily on personal trust, household proximity and demonstrated loyalty, which frequently outweigh seniority or formal military rank. Insiders note that Min Aung Hlaing routinely prioritizes his own strategic instincts and the counsel of trusted informal circles over professional or technocratic assessments. They said that rather than governing through the military’s established institutional machinery, Min Aung Hlaing increasingly relies on bespoke personal networks, reducing formal state organs to instruments of execution.

Who has his ear? The three circles of influence

Sources within and close to the regime point to three distinct yet overlapping circles that exercise disproportionate sway over Min Aung Hlaing’s thinking across defense technology, foreign outreach and internal security.

Influence Circle Key Figures & Entities Primary Domain Mechanism of Influence Circle 1: Technical & Russian-Trained Network Lt-Col Kyaw Zaw Ye, aide-de-camp, DSA Intakes 46 & 47 graduates Defense procurement, drone warfare, Russia ties, strategic messaging Proximity to the leadership’s household; technical specialization bypassing general staff Circle 2: Former Intelligence Network Thein Swe, Hla Min; Paragon Institute Informal political advice, discreet foreign outreach (especially China) Reactivation of legacy Khin Nyunt-era intelligence networks; track-two diplomacy Circle 3: Security-Intelligence Core Office of the Chief of Military Security Affairs (OCMSA) Regime security, internal surveillance, political & battlefield intelligence Direct institutional control over intelligence filtering; constant personal access

Circle 1: Kyaw Zaw Ye and the Russian-trained military network

One of the most striking shifts inside Min Aung Hlaing’s inner circle is the ascent of younger, technically specialized officers educated in Russia—particularly graduates of Defense Services Academy (DSA) Intakes 46 and 47. Some 21 personnel from the two intakes form a key part of the inner circle. Multiple sources told The Irrawaddy that Lieutenant Colonel Kyaw Zaw Ye, a DSA Intake 47 graduate, has emerged as an influential figure with direct access to the junta chief. He was appointed as Min Aung Hlaing’s aide-de-camp last year. Trained in Russia, Kyaw Zaw Ye belongs to a cohort of officers versed in Russian defense hardware, procurement pipelines and emerging military technologies.

Insiders say Kyaw Zaw Ye’s clout stems less from his mid-level rank than from close personal ties to Min Aung Hlaing and the leadership’s immediate household, giving him direct channels to the top that bypass senior commanders. The Irrawaddy has learned that this network plays an active role in bilateral defense dealings with Moscow, specialized arms acquisitions, and efforts to source and deploy unmanned aerial vehicles (drones) to counter resistance forces. Sources also link Kyaw Zaw Ye to military propaganda and strategic communications, reflecting the regime’s push to overhaul its information operations. By elevating Russian-educated technical officers through personal access, Min Aung Hlaing has cultivated an alternative source of military-strategic advice that routinely sidesteps conventional general staff hierarchies, people familiar with the matter said.

Circle 2: Thein Swe and the former military intelligence network

Facing severe diplomatic isolation and institutional deficits after 2021, the regime has turned to veteran operatives from Myanmar’s dismantled military intelligence apparatus—specifically figures formerly aligned with ousted prime minister and spy chief General Khin Nyunt. Both Thein Swe and Hla Min, prominent intelligence officers in the former military intelligence establishment under the previous regime, were arrested during the 2004 purge of Khin Nyunt’s faction and later released. Following the 2021 coup, they quietly returned to advise and assist Min Aung Hlaing’s regime.

The Irrawaddy has learned that the Paragon Institute, a policy and research platform run by Thein Swe and Hla Min, serves as an informal hub for former operatives. In 2024, they travelled to China ahead of Min Aung Hlaing’s trip to meet with organizations that promote Chinese foreign policy and work for policy research projects commissioned by major Chinese government departments.

Sources familiar with the group’s activities indicate operational overlap between Paragon-linked figures and the Office of the Chief of Military Security Affairs (OCMSA), particularly in managing discreet international contacts and backchannel outreach to key regional powers, most notably China. Through Thein Swe and platforms like the Paragon Institute, sources said, Min Aung Hlaing has effectively reactivated legacy intelligence networks to conduct sensitive political groundwork and foreign engagement beyond the constraints of formal diplomacy.

Circle 3: OCMSA and the security-intelligence apparatus

While informal advisers provide specialized channels, the OCMSA serves as the regime’s primary institutional pillar of control. Although the agency is now led by Lieutenant General Kyaw Ko Htike, its former chief—current Commander-in-Chief of Defense Services General Ye Win Oo—is widely regarded by insiders as Min Aung Hlaing’s closest confidant and principal gatekeeper, with a steady rise through the military hierarchy that reflects decades of close personal and professional alignment with the junta chief.

Since February 2021, the OCMSA’s reach has expanded dramatically. Sources say the agency oversees surveillance of resistance networks, monitors civilian political actors, vets state officials and conducts intensive counterintelligence policing inside the military itself to preempt defections and internal dissent. They said OCMSA has operated not merely as a counterintelligence service, but as the primary informational filter shaping Min Aung Hlaing’s political and strategic decisions.

The sidelining of ministers and formal institutions

As power has consolidated around these three circles, formal state institutions and cabinet ministries have seen their policymaking authority sharply curtailed. Sources in Naypyitaw say senior ministers and economic officials have repeatedly seen their warnings—particularly regarding foreign exchange controls, trade restrictions and diplomatic isolation—overruled whenever they clash with Min Aung Hlaing’s immediate political or security priorities.

Consequently, key ministries have been hollowed out of strategic influence. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has been largely reduced to handling protocol and consular affairs and defending the regime in multilateral forums, while substantive negotiations take place through intelligence and military channels. Economic ministries, meanwhile, operate primarily as enforcement arms for ad hoc directives rather than architects of coherent macroeconomic policy. Even within the armed forces, operational decision-making has become heavily centralized, limiting the autonomy of regional commanders and traditional staff departments while elevating security and procurement insiders.

While formal ministries no longer shape major strategic decisions, insiders note they remain useful to the regime for bureaucratic execution, day-to-day administration and projecting the outward appearance of state continuity.

Min Aung Hlaing’s reliance on the three circles described above has taken its toll on the country, analysts and diplomats said.

On the economic front, he has failed to listen to experts. Instead, he relies on advisers with military backgrounds, leading to misguided decisions and restrictive measures that have further undermined the economy.

As a result, Myanmar’s economic crisis has reached an extremely critical, if not its worst, point, sources said.

In foreign relations, Min Aung Hlaing appears to be counterbalancing China by leaning toward the United States, while also moving noticeably closer to Russia. He appears to be openly snubbing China, failing to recognize that antagonizing Beijing serves neither his own interests nor Myanmar’s efforts to resolve its ongoing crisis, some diplomats said.

His foreign trips have also failed to deliver tangible results. Despite reaching agreements and making commitments with international partners, few have translated into concrete action.

This likely reflects the limited capacity of those advising him, who appear to lack the understanding and expertise needed to turn diplomatic agreements into practical outcomes that serve the country’s interests, insiders said.

World.title: Myanmar Migrant Workers Have a Weapon Against Junta Abuses – Here’s How to Use It
World.content:
Representatives of the International Labor Organization (ILO) Workers’ Group for Asia-Pacific and Arab States met on the sidelines of the Governing Body’s 358th Session on Nov. 14 to discuss the junta’s demand that Myanmar migrant workers remit 25 percent of their salaries through official channels.

Among those attending the Geneva meet was Phyo Sandar Soe, Assistant General Secretary of the Confederation of Trade Unions Myanmar (CTUM), who represented Myanmar’s labor movement.

In addition to the remittance issue, participants discussed strengthening trade unions, challenges facing workers across the region, and the hardships confronting Myanmar migrant workers in the Middle East, Asia and the Pacific.

The ILO adopted its strongest constitutional enforcement measure (Article 33) against Myanmar in June 2025 following mass arrests of labor leaders and the dismantling of independent unions. At the latest meeting, member states were urged to enforce Article 33 measures demanding an end to violence, forced labor and conscription, and the restoration of union freedoms. The article also gives countries UN backing to impose trade sanctions while opening a UN channel for workers and unions to submit complaints of junta abuses, including passport extortion, forced remittance rules, and conscription threats.

Myanmar’s regime responded by dismissing the enforcement decision and rejecting the ILO’s monitoring mechanism.

Phyo Sandar Soe spoke to The Irrawaddy about the meeting, the junta’s labor policies, and recent developments at the ILO.

What were the key issues raised at the meeting?

The regime’s remittance rule is not only affecting workers in Thailand and Malaysia but worldwide.

We told ILO regional directors for Asia-Pacific and the Middle East that Myanmar migrant workers are facing serious rights violations and requested an emergency meeting on the issue. The ILO agreed to convene a meeting with experts in attendance.

Junta labor minister Maung Myint has dismissed the ILO’s concerns about migrant workers as exaggerated and misleading. What is your response?

Looking at his social media posts, it’s clear that despite holding the post of labor minister he has no desire to defend workers.

His comments reflect a dictatorship’s mindset. They don’t care how much suffering is endured by workers. Their repression never stops even as people sink deeper into misery.

A labor ministry is supposed to protect the grassroots, the working class of the country. The situation is quite the opposite in Myanmar, which is a shame for the country.

Normally, a country that sends out migrant workers asks the receiving countries to protect its citizens. But in this case, Thailand had to ask the ILO to help protect Myanmar migrant workers. That is deeply embarrassing. The generals should reflect on their own position.

Has the situation for both migrant and domestic workers worsened under the new labor minister?

The regime faces a severe shortage of foreign currency and needs money to fund its military and purchase weapons. So, it has imposed import-license restrictions, tightened access to foreign currency, and is now milking even more from migrant workers through exchange-rate controls and remittance requirements. Regime leaders do not see migrant workers as fellow Myanmar citizens – which is not strange given that they are already killing their own people. What we are seeing is an attempt to squeeze more money from workers to finance further repression.

What decisions were made on Myanmar during the 358th session of the ILO Governing Body in Geneva on Nov. 17?

A follow-up decision on the Article 33 resolution for Myanmar was adopted by the Governing Body. It calls for an immediate end to violence, arbitrary arrests of labor leaders, and forced military recruitment. It also demands the unconditional release of political prisoners, the repeal of laws and orders restricting freedom of association, safe access for ILO missions to Myanmar, and the establishment of a mechanism to monitor labor-rights violations.

The decision further urges member states to review their relations with Myanmar authorities and calls on governments not to forcibly return refugees to Myanmar.

We will urge the ILO to enforce these by January 2027. The ILO Director-General is expected to present an update on Myanmar and progress in implementing the recommendations of the Commission of Inquiry at the 359th session of the Governing Body in March 2027.

What message do you have for Myanmar workers inside and outside the country?

Some people think ILO mechanisms achieve nothing, but a mechanism is only effective if people use it. A knife becomes sharp only when properly sharpened. The same is true of international mechanisms: the more workers make use of them, the more effective they become in protecting Myanmar workers.

Many ask why the international community fails to act despite widely publicized abuses. The reason is simple: without complaints from victims and affected workers, cases cannot move forward.

So, if workers want action and accountability, they need to file complaints and use these mechanisms. I encourage workers to make full use of them.

World.title: Dimash Qudaibergen Holds First Solo Concert in Colombia
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakh singer Dimash Qudaibergen held his first solo concert in Colombia on Nov. 22, performing before thousands of fans at Bogotá’s Movistar Arena as part of his DIMENSIONS world tour.

The concert marked the continuation of the Latin American leg of the tour following five performances in Mexico. Colombian fans welcomed the singer with prolonged applause and chants, including “¡Se vive, se siente, Dimash está presente!” (You live it, you feel it, Dimash is here!) and “¡Dimash querido, aquí eres bienvenido!” (Dear Dimash, you are welcome here!).

Throughout the performance, the audience sang along to familiar songs and applauded the artist, creating an enthusiastic atmosphere at one of the capital’s major concert venues, reported the Dimash News agency.

One of the highlights of the program was Vocalize, an original composition by Qudaibergen performed without lyrics. The piece showcases his vocal range and interpretation, allowing the voice itself to convey the musical expression without words.

The performance featured minimalist stage design, with a live image of the singer displayed on a large screen. Without dancers or elaborate visual effects, the arrangement placed the focus on his vocal performance.

Addressing the audience, Qudaibergen thanked Colombian fans for their years of support and for making his first solo concert in the country possible.

“Thank you so much, Colombia! After 27 years of studying, many years of work, and thanks to the support of my family and friends, our meeting has finally happened! Thank you all!” he said.

The Bogotá concert was another stop on the Latin American leg of the DIMENSIONS world tour. His next performance is scheduled for Nov. 24 in Santiago, Chile.

Earlier, a photo exhibition dedicated to Qudaibergen’s artistic career opened in Mexico City.

World.title: Kazakhstan Explores New Air Routes to India, Airline Cooperation With Canada
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is exploring opportunities to expand air connectivity with India and Canada, including potential new flights to Indian cities and codeshare agreements with Canadian airlines, following aviation talks held during the 7th ICAO World Air Transport Conference.

Kazakhstan’s Vice Minister of Transport Talgat Lastayev met with Samir Kumar Sinha, head of the Indian delegation and secretary of India’s Ministry of Civil Aviation, to discuss expanding bilateral cooperation, international routes and coordination between aviation authorities, reported the Civil Aviation Committee on Nov. 23.

Kazakh airlines have expressed interest in launching flights to Hyderabad and Ahmedabad. India has preliminarily confirmed its readiness to expand flights to Hyderabad, with the two sides agreeing to hold further negotiations on air connectivity.

Currently, Kazakhstan and India operate 18 flights per week. The Almaty–Delhi route accounts for 12 weekly flights, seven operated by Air Astana. Almaty–Mumbai has three weekly flights, two operated by Air Astana. SCAT operates one weekly flight between Astana and Goa, while Almaty–Goa is served by SCAT and FlyArystan, with two flights per week.

Kazakhstan and Canada consider codeshare agreements

Separately, Kazakhstan and Canada discussed expanding aviation cooperation through codeshare agreements that could provide passengers with more route options and convenient connections between the two countries.

The talks involved Kazakhstan’s Civil Aviation Committee Chair Saltanat Tompiyeva and Deputy Director of the Office of Canada’s Chief Air Negotiator Patrick Cuenso. The sides examined opportunities to improve air connectivity to support tourism, business ties and transportation accessibility.

Agreements would allow airlines to sell tickets on flights operated by partner carriers, potentially expanding travel options without necessarily introducing new direct services.

The sides also discussed preparations for a bilateral air services agreement, exchanging updates on domestic procedures and steps required to finalize the document.

No direct flights between Kazakhstan and Canada have been agreed upon so far, and neither side has announced specific routes, airlines or launch dates. Both sides confirmed their interest in expanding cooperation and agreed to continue negotiations on air connectivity.

World.title: Independence Remains Kazakh Citizens’ Most Important Value Across Generations, Survey Finds
World.content:
ASTANA – Independence remains one of the most important personal values for Kazakhstanis across generations, reflecting its significance not only as a milestone in the country’s history but also as a cornerstone of its present-day development, according to a survey commissioned by the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies (KazISS) under Kazakhstan’s President.

Respondents across all age groups identified independence as their most important personal value, the survey of 8,105 people found.

The findings also indicate broad public optimism about the country’s development, with 93% of respondents saying Kazakhstan is moving in the right direction. Support was highest among young people aged 18-29, at 95.1%.

Public perceptions of reforms

Respondents gave the highest positive assessments to government efforts to strengthen national unity and the rule of law, as well as to developments in culture, education and science.
