The survey also found a strong correlation between public perceptions of the country’s development and whether citizens believe the government listens to them and addresses their concerns.

Overall, 82.4% of respondents rated the implementation of the Listening State concept positively. Support was highest among young people aged 18-29, at 89.6%, while respondents aged 61 and older recorded 77.6%.

The survey was conducted from Oct. 5 to Nov. 5 among 8,105 respondents aged 18 and older across 17 regions and the cities of Astana, Almaty and Shymkent.

World.title: Almaty Ranks 12th Globally in UN Digital Services Survey 2026
World.content:
ASTANA – Almaty climbed 15 places to rank 12th among 194 cities worldwide in the United Nations’ 2026 digital services ranking, reflecting improvements in the city’s online public services, according to the UN E-Government Survey 2026.

The city’s Local Online Services Index (LOSI) score increased from 0.8021 in 2024 to 0.9604 out of a maximum of 1, placing Almaty alongside Copenhagen, London, Tokyo, Shanghai and other major cities.

According to the UN assessment, the index evaluates how accessible and convenient digital services are for residents. It examines official city websites, online government and municipal services, access to urban information, feedback mechanisms and opportunities for public participation in city governance across six key areas.

Digital infrastructure development also benefits visitors by making it easier to access information, navigate the city, plan trips and use urban services.

In October 2025, Almaty received the Special Recognition for Tourism Innovation and Urban Transformation award at the Global Tourism Forum in Brussels for its tourism innovations and efforts to transform the urban environment.

The city’s improved ranking and international recognition reflect its ongoing efforts to expand digital services, modernize urban infrastructure and improve the quality of life for residents and visitors.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Japan Discuss Expanding Strategic Partnership
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Japan discussed strengthening bilateral cooperation, including trade, investment and regional engagement, during a meeting between Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi and Japan’s Special Representative for Central Asia Tomoaki Ishigaki.

The meeting focused on implementing agreements reached during Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s official visit to Japan in December 2025, as well as prospects for expanding trade, economic and investment cooperation.

The sides also discussed cooperation within the Central Asia–Japan framework and reaffirmed their commitment to further strengthening the countries’ expanded strategic partnership.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Singapore Explore Investment Opportunities at Business Forum
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan and Singapore are seeking to expand economic cooperation in trade, investment, logistics and digitalization, as businesses from both countries explored new opportunities at a bilateral business forum in Singapore on Nov. 23.

The Kazakhstan-Singapore End-of-the-Year Networking Event was organized by the Kazakh Embassy in Singapore in partnership with Kazakh Invest, bringing together executives from Singaporean and international companies, investment funds and business organizations, including Meta, Changi Airports International, Singapore Cooperation Enterprise, Surbana Jurong, Food Empire Holdings, Gotion Singapore, PhillipCapital and Quest Ventures.

Opening the forum, Kazakh Ambassador to Singapore Askar Kuttykadam said bilateral relations had entered a phase of practical implementation following Singapore Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong’s official visit to Kazakhstan in August.

Bilateral trade reached $1.3 billion in the first eight months of 2026, surpassing the total recorded for the whole of 2025. Singapore’s foreign direct investment in Kazakhstan reached nearly $1.5 billion in 2025. The bilateral agreement on trade in services and investment, which has entered into force, also provides businesses with preferential market access.

Cooperation is advancing in logistics and digitalization, including SCAT Airlines’ launch of flights to Singapore, an agreement with Changi Airports International on developing Astana’s airports, and efforts to digitalize the Middle Corridor in partnership with Singapore’s PSA International.

Kazakhstan presents investment and economic priorities

Kazakh representatives presented the country’s economic outlook and investment priorities against the backdrop of the new Constitution entering into force and economic growth of 4.5% recorded during the first 10 months of 2026.

The presentations highlighted priorities outlined in President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s Oct. 28 State of the Nation Address, including the $13 billion People’s Construction program, the planned International Financial and Commercial Center in Alatau City operating under English common law principles in coordination with the Astana International Financial Centre, projects under the Digital Qazaqstan program and plans to commission 13.3 gigawatts of power generation capacity by 2029.

World.title: Kazakhstan Pushes Ahead With Digital Infrastructure Projects Worth $731 Million
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan is advancing digital infrastructure projects worth approximately 333 billion tenge (US$731 million), as the government seeks to accelerate data center development, secure necessary power and network connections, and ensure facilities are ready to operate, Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov said at a Nov. 24 government meeting.

Bektenov instructed the ministries of artificial intelligence and digital development and energy, together with investors, to approve a schedule within two months for launching key and planned data centers, including provisions for energy capacity, engineering infrastructure and demand for computing services.

“Digital economy development and the widespread adoption of artificial intelligence require significant computing power. Large data center construction projects are underway in the country. However, it is important not only to build them but also to ensure the conditions for their full operation,” Bektenov said.

“We must not allow facilities to remain idle because of a lack of necessary infrastructure or insufficient demand for their services,” he added.

Data center development

The AKASHI data center campus is under construction in Astana as part of the country’s digital infrastructure expansion. The project has a planned capacity of 100 megawatts.

Kazakhstan currently has seven data centers, with three more under construction. Its fiber-optic network spans approximately 15,000 kilometers, Aslan Zhusupov, chief executive officer of Freedom Cloud Holding, said at the meeting.

“AKASHI campus in Astana holds a special place among our projects. It is a Tier IV data center, the highest reliability category, and the first and only of its kind in Central Asia. The project is already underway. The first building is 81% complete, and we expect it to launch in the fourth quarter of 2027,” Zhusupov said.

Bektenov said the government supports such projects, including through the Baiterek holding, and stressed the importance of completing digital infrastructure projects on schedule and ensuring the timely repayment of funds provided.

Tier IV is the highest data center reliability classification, designed to allow continuous operations during equipment failures and maintenance.

Digital infrastructure as a priority

Bektenov said reliable telecommunications networks and internet access are essential to the modern economy, supporting businesses, government services, healthcare, education and financial systems.

“The development and resilience of communication networks and the internet are fundamental infrastructure for the modern economy. Their availability and stability determine the operation of businesses, government services, healthcare, education and financial systems,” he said.

He stressed that service quality, rather than the number of infrastructure facilities built, should be the main measure of progress.

“For citizens and businesses, reports on the number of base stations built are not what matters. What matters is being able to use uninterrupted internet at work, on the road and at home. The quality and accessibility of connectivity should be the main criteria for evaluating the industry’s development,” Bektenov said.

The Digital Qazaqstan strategy envisages large-scale digitalization, he said, adding that artificial intelligence, cloud platforms and digital government services require increasingly powerful infrastructure.

The government is also working to improve investment conditions in the telecommunications sector. Bektenov said network development requires significant capital and takes years to build and recoup, making stable and predictable regulations essential for long-term planning.

He instructed the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development and relevant government agencies to develop measures to remove administrative barriers to investment and establish equal competitive conditions for telecom operators by the end of the first quarter of 2027.

He added that government support should be accompanied by commitments from operators to expand coverage, improve service quality and keep connectivity affordable.

World.title: Kazakhstan to Become Central Asia’s First Country to Host Four Satellite Operators
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan expects to become the first country in Central Asia to host ground stations for four satellite internet operators as it expands connectivity infrastructure and strengthens its role in international data transit, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev said at a Nov. 24 government meeting.

Shanghai Spacecom Satellite Technology and Amazon LEO are expected to enter the Kazakh market next year, joining OneWeb and Starlink, which have already received licenses to operate in the country. The expansion is expected to improve internet access in remote areas and strengthen Kazakhstan’s telecommunications infrastructure.

The country is also developing satellite connectivity for mobile devices through Direct-to-Cell technology, launched in partnership with Beeline and Starlink Mobile. The service enables messaging and basic internet access directly to smartphones via satellites. Android support is already available, while iOS integration is under development.

Expanding connectivity across the country

Satellite internet is being introduced in remote settlements where laying fiber-optic cables is difficult, as well as on transport and at tourist destinations.

Air Astana has equipped one aircraft with OneWeb connectivity, with plans to extend the service to 20 more aircraft next year. Starlink Wi-Fi is already available in 1,500 passenger train cars operated by Kazakhstan Temir Zholy (KTZ).

Internet access has also been installed at 10 popular tourist destinations this year, with another 50 planned for next year. All border crossing points are connected through fiber-optic and satellite networks.

Kazakhstan is also strengthening its position as a data transit hub between Europe and Asia.

“The Trans-Caspian fiber-optic communication line has been launched in Kazakhstan, creating an additional route for internet traffic between Europe and Asia. To improve its resilience, a backup channel along the Caspian seabed must be built,” Madiyev said.

Meanwhile, construction of the West-East backbone network connecting Khorgos and Aktau is 87% complete, with work expected to finish next year. The infrastructure is expected to increase transit capacity, reduce data transmission delays and support efforts to attract international companies to Kazakhstan’s Data Center Valley.

Telecom investments exceed $2.8 billion

Kazakhstan plans to invest more than 1.3 trillion tenge (US$2.86 billion) in telecommunications over three years as the country expands mobile coverage, satellite connectivity and international data transit infrastructure.

Average mobile internet speeds increased from 73.6 to 93.4 megabits per second over the past two years, while internet traffic is expected to more than double this year compared with 2024.

Kazakhstan ranked seventh among 55 countries with high-speed internet in terms of mobile internet affordability in November, according to Madiyev. The average monthly mobile tariff is about $10, compared with the global average of $27.

As data consumption continues to rise, telecom operators will need to invest in network expansion to improve speeds and extend 5G coverage. Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov stressed that telecom tariffs should remain affordable while the sector stays attractive to investors.

“The development of 5G networks should yield a tangible economic benefit, rather than being limited to merely increasing the speed of mobile internet,” he said.

Cybersecurity and digital services

“As digitalization advances, cybersecurity becomes an increasingly pressing issue. Protecting data is extremely important. I urge you to pay attention to this,” Bektenov said.

According to Madiyev, telecom operators monitor network infrastructure around the clock, address vulnerabilities, use protection against distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks and maintain data backups. Backup communication channels and power sources are also in place to ensure continuity of services.

In the event of large-scale cyberattacks, operators coordinate with relevant agencies to protect infrastructure and restore operations. Work is also underway to establish a comprehensive system for protecting telecommunications networks against cyber threats.

Bektenov also called for wider adoption of the national messaging platform Aitu, particularly among government agencies, saying official communications should increasingly move to the platform.

“Aitu is not just a messenger. We need to build a national ecosystem and step up our efforts. Government employees, in particular, should use Aitu daily, and official information should be sent exclusively through this national messenger,” he said.

Aitu has about seven million registered users, with approximately 350,000 people using it daily, Madiyev said. Mobile internet usage on the platform is not charged. Aitu also integrates eGov GPT and provides access to 55 government services.

By the end of the year, integration is expected to expand to cover 75-80% of services available through the eGov system. Government agencies and Samruk Kazyna, Kazakhstan’s sovereign wealth fund, already use Aitu Workspace in their daily operations.

World.title: Georgian Dream propaganda network ran coordinated campaign against Metropolitan Iov – ISFED
World.content:
Campaign against Metropolitan Iov in Georgia

Following a sermon that included criticism of the Georgian government, a coordinated disinformation campaign against Metropolitan Iov was launched on social media. Dozens of social media pages published posts with identical content at almost exactly the same time.

As part of the campaign, at least 20 paid s appeared on Meta platforms, generating between 77,600 and 107,180 views in total.

Pro-government media outlets, Facebook pages and individuals affiliated with Georgian Dream’s propaganda network stepped up the campaign against Metropolitan Iov following his critical sermon.

The campaign was investigated by the International Society for Fair Elections and Democracy (ISFED).

The organisation analysed how identical quotes targeting the metropolitan spread across dozens of pages within minutes of each other; how videos from previous years were used in a new context; and how paid advertising complemented the campaign’s organic reach.

What Iov said and why it led to a confrontation with the authorities

The confrontation followed a sermon that Metropolitan Iov delivered at Urbnisi Cathedral on 10 November. He called government officials “non-believers” and “alien to the Church”, saying that the government had exhausted its potential and that the Georgian people should choose more worthy leaders in the future.

The metropolitan criticised the Church’s dependence on state funding, saying that the authorities were trying to merge Church and state.

He also raised issues such as corruption, the prevalence of drug addiction among young people and the widespread popularity of gambling. In addition, he referred to information allegedly leaked from the State Security Service in 2021, which contained details of surveillance of members of the clergy.

In his sermon, Iov also mentioned Bidzina Ivanishvili, the founder of the Georgian Dream party. He also referred to the previous administration, saying: “We know what the previous government was doing; everything is obvious – the people voted against it.”

Metropolitan Iov’s remarks attracted particular attention because he had previously supported Georgian Dream.

On 21 November, during another sermon, he explained that although he had supported the ruling party, he believed it had since changed course, making criticism necessary.

“I supported Georgian Dream and stood by them, but I saw that they had gone astray. The situation had changed, and it became necessary to speak out against such actions. If they put things right, take these remarks into account and bring about change in Georgia – if they change the course of these developments – I may support them again,” he said.

Metropolitan Iov was also among the candidates for the post of patriarch in May 2026. Metropolitan Shio Mujiri was elected patriarch.

Identical posts and quotes from ‘experts’

According to ISFED’s monitoring, representatives of Georgian Dream were the first to react to Metropolitan Iov’s sermon.

MP Levan Machavariani called it “irresponsible”, saying that a senior clergyman should not use the pulpit to make political statements. Meanwhile, MP Mariam Lashkhi, responding to journalists’ questions, remarked: “May God forgive him.”

Meanwhile, pro-government figures began posting their views on social media.

On 11 November, news agencies and television channels linked to Georgian Dream published the same quote from a Facebook post by Gia Abashidze. He claimed that Bishop Iov was using the church pulpit to call for a change of government.

Screenshots of the posts. Source: ISFED

Thirteen minutes after Abashidze’s statement, a quote from Davit Kartvelishvili was circulated. He accused the metropolitan of having links to Saakashvili’s political forces, referred to criminal cases involving the metropolitan’s diocese and raised the issue of the seizure of agricultural land.

According to ISFED, these allegations came without references to specific sources or any particular case. Nevertheless, the text appeared on 14 pages within a few hours.

Screenshots of the posts. Source: ISFED

Tamta Megrelishvili, Davit Chikhelidze and Zaal Anjaparidze also joined the campaign. In their posts, they accused Metropolitan Iov of making political statements against the government, supporting Saakashvili and taking a position that ran counter to the country’s interests.

Davit Chikhelidze even linked the metropolitan’s diocese to harbouring criminals and “gangland-style disputes”.

A fake Facebook profile also took part in the campaign

The campaign also involved a Facebook profile that Myth Detector had previously identified as fake. The account, registered under the name Ketevan Mikiashvili, published two posts targeting Bishop Iov, just a few hours apart.

In her first post, Mikiashvili addressed the metropolitan ironically, referring to the election of the new patriarch. She remarked that Bishop Iov had “dropped his mask” after Shio became patriarch. The post included an archive television report captioned “Call to release Saakashvili”.

In her second post, she shared a video recorded on 25 September 2019, titled “Bishop Iov on Petre Tsaava”, implying that the footage revealed the metropolitan’s true motives.

These posts highlighted another narrative promoted by the campaign: Bishop Iov’s criticism of the authorities was presented not as a political or ecclesiastical disagreement, but as a personal grievance stemming from his defeat in the patriarchal election.

Mikiashvili later published another post portraying Bishop Iov’s sermon as yet another attempt to stage a revolution.

Personal attacks also appeared in posts by other figures.

On 11 November, Lasha Natsvlishvili, a Georgian Dream supporter and propagandist, published a Facebook post containing insults directed at Metropolitan Iov. [Fact-checkers say Lasha Natsvlishvili is behind the fake “Ketevan Mikiashvili” profile – JAMnews].

The post prompted a strong reaction, including from members of the clergy.

In 2012, Lasha Natsvlishvili became an MP on the Georgian Dream party list. He later served as first deputy interior minister and deputy chief prosecutor, before working as a public relations adviser to Georgian Dream.

The Interior Ministry launched administrative proceedings against Lasha Natsvlishvili over the post containing insults directed at Metropolitan Iov. On 16 November, Judge Manuchar Tsatsua fined Natsvlishvili 2,500 lari.

20 adverts and nearly 107,000 views

According to ISFED, part of the campaign was paid for. Data from the Meta Ad Library as of 17 November showed that at least 20 adverts targeting Metropolitan Iov’s reputation had appeared on five Facebook pages.

All the adverts ran between 11 and 14 November, with up to $100 spent on each. ISFED estimated that they generated between 77,600 and 107,180 views in total.

The adverts published on an anonymous page called Ganulebuli Opozitsia (“Cancelled Opposition”) attracted the most views – between 47,000 and 60,094. The same page also shared a post about Metropolitan Iov’s “vast wealth”.

Screenshots of the posts. Source: ISFED

Advertising materials also appeared on the pages Fact • ფაქტი, Ustari, Akhla • ახლა and Saerto Gazeti.

According to ISFED’s research, Jaba Khubua, the head of Fact • ფაქტი, is a presenter on the pro-government Imedi TV channel. Shako Kuchashvili, the owner of Ustari, is a Georgian Dream supporter and one of the presenters of the Fake Control programme on the same channel.

ISFED notes that the Fact and Ustari pages were created in 2026 and that the people behind them have links to the pro-government Imedi TV channel and Georgian Dream.

ISFED says this is significant because, following sanctions imposed by the UK, the main pages of the pro-government Imedi and POSTV channels faced restrictions on placing s. This forced them to use new pages to distribute their content.

The disinformation campaign also circulated footage from previous years. One advert used a recording of a sermon delivered by Metropolitan Iov in 2024, in which he discussed the release of Mikheil Saakashvili from prison. The video was accompanied by footage from Saakashvili’s time in power showing police storming a church in Gldani. However, the post did not mention that the sermon had been recorded two years earlier.

Government response and reaction within the Church

The campaign against Metropolitan Iov extended beyond social media. On 15 November, Imedi TV broadcast a 17-minute report as part of its Imedis Kvira (“Imedi Week”) programme, titled “A political manifesto from the pulpit”.

On the same day, Goga Khaindrava, a film director and Georgian Dream supporter, described the sermons delivered by Metropolitan Iov and the clergy who supported him as political statements.

Other members of the clergy, including Metropolitan Ilarion of Svaneti, expressed support for Metropolitan Iov. They criticised the ruling party’s policies and drew attention to issues such as the demographic crisis, gambling and drug addiction.

On 16 November, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze commented on the dispute. He said that public arguments between the clergy and the authorities harmed both the Church and the country, adding that the government had no intention of joining the dispute.

Campaign against Metropolitan Iov in Georgia

World.title: Seven people detained during protests in Georgia released: What do we know about them?
World.content:
Pardoning of protesters in Georgia

Seven people detained during the 2024 protests have been released from custody. They were among 232 people pardoned by President Mikheil Kavelashvili to mark St George’s Day.

Those released include Giorgi Okmelashvili, Irakli Metvinetukhutsesi, Giorgi Mindadze, Anri Kvaratskhelia, Nikoloz Javakhishvili, Davit Lomidze and Temur Zasokhashvili.

News of the pardons emerged late on Sunday, 22 November. The full list was not initially made public, but some of the names became known.

It also remained unclear exactly when those pardoned would be released. Some relatives and friends spent the entire night outside detention facilities, waiting for their release.

The prisoners were freed in the morning, shortly after 11:00. Footage of the moment shows highly emotional scenes.

Over the past two years, a period marked by protests in Georgia, more than 100 protesters have been arrested and prosecuted. All but three were sentenced to prison.

None of those detained admitted guilt during their trials.

Who was released and what were they accused of?

Two of the seven, Irakli Megvinetukhutsesi and Giorgi Okmelashvili, were arrested in May 2024 during protests against the so-called “Russian law” (the law on “foreign agents”).

The other five were arrested during pro-European protests that began in November-December 2024, after Irakli Kobakhidze announced the suspension of EU accession talks.

Giorgi Okmelashvili – 922 days in prison

Giorgi Okmelashvili reunites with his family. Photo: Publika, Mindia Gabadze

Giorgi Okmelashvili is a film director and producer who works in marketing. He is the founder of Limoni, an advertising and video production company.

He was detained on 15 May 2024 while on his way to work. At the time, protesters were holding demonstrations outside the Georgian parliament against the “Russian law” on “foreign agents”.

His arrest stemmed from an incident during a protest outside parliament on 13 May. The day before the legal affairs committee was due to hold a third-reading vote on the “Russian law”, protesters spent the night outside the parliament building under the slogan: “We will stay awake all night for Georgia”.

According to the prosecutor’s office, Okmelashvili struck a police officer in the face with his elbow during the protest. After his arrest, the Interior Ministry released video footage in an attempt to substantiate the charge. Okmelashvili and his lawyers insisted that his actions were an instinctive response to defend himself: at the time, riot police were trying to push protesters back.

On 3 February 2025, Giorgi Okmelashvili was sentenced to five years in prison.

“Rock’n’roll goes on. It wasn’t easy – that’s all I can say. Greetings to cell 414. I’m pretty much the same person I was before. Nothing has changed, except that I’ve read a lot of books and thought about many things,” Okmelashvili said after his release.

His young wife, their child, who is in the first year of primary school, and his parents were waiting for him at home.

🟥 Giorgi Okmelashvili spent 922 days in detention, from 15 May 2024 to 23 November 2026. That is 2 years, 6 months and 8 days.

Irakli Megvinetukhutsesi – 928 days in prison

Irakli Megvinetukhutsesi was arrested in the spring of 2024 during protests against the “foreign agents” law. He was taken into custody on 9 May 2024.

Little information about Megvinetukhutsesi’s background is publicly available. His family rarely speaks to the media. It is known that he was over 21 at the time of his arrest.

Megvinetukhutsesi faced two charges: assaulting a police officer and illegally acquiring and possessing marijuana. According to the prosecution, he threatened police officers with a knife during the protest. The prosecution claimed that one officer was injured while disarming him.

The defence insisted that Megvinetukhutsesi had no intention of harming the officer and had merely raised the knife in a demonstrative gesture.

On 30 December 2024, Tbilisi City Court found Megvinetukhutsesi guilty on both charges. He was sentenced to five years in prison.

🟥 Irakli Megvinetukhutsesi spent 928 days in prison – 2 years, 6 months and 14 days.

Giorgi Mindadze – 722 days in prison

Giorgi Mindadze reunites with his adoptive mother, Nani Tsulaia. Photo: MO SE

Giorgi Mindadze is a student who was arrested during the pro-European protests in November–December 2024. He was 21 at the time of his arrest and was in his third year at medical university.

On the evening of 1 December 2024, police arrived at his relatives’ home in the village of Tsilkani, where Mindadze was staying at the time, and detained him. They gave no explanation for his arrest at the scene.

It later emerged that investigators had accused him of setting off pyrotechnics during a protest on 29 November. He faced a criminal charge of assaulting a police officer. According to the prosecution, a firework launched by Mindadze struck a police officer, injuring his leg.

The defence lawyer noted that the case file contained no direct evidence that the officer had been injured by pyrotechnics launched by Mindadze. The prosecution presented a photograph taken on 29 November showing Mindadze holding a pyrotechnic device, as well as testimony from the police officer.

On 3 July 2025, the court found Mindadze guilty and sentenced him to five years in prison.

Giorgi has no mother – she died when he was very young. His neighbour, Nani Tsulaia, adopted him and raised him as her own son. Nani was with Giorgi when police arrested him. Officers took him away without telling her where they were taking him.

She went from one police station to another, trying to find out where they were holding her adopted son.

Nani Tsulaia has become one of the prominent figures in the protest movement. Since Giorgi’s arrest, she has taken part in street protests without fail. Along with other parents, she travelled across Georgia to tell the public the truth about those detained.

“I really want to go home… Freedom for everyone!” were Giorgi’s first words after his release from prison.

🟥 Giorgi Mindadze spent 722 days in detention, from 1 December 2024 to 23 November 2026. That is 1 year, 11 months and 22 days.

Anri (Anzor) Kvaratskhelia – 718 days in prison

Anri Kvaratskhelia after his release from prison. Photo: MO SE

Anri (Anzor) Kvaratskhelia also took part in the pro-European protests in November and December 2024. He was among those charged with assaulting a police officer.

Anri was arrested at his home on 5 December 2024. He was 25 at the time. According to the prosecution, during a protest on Rustaveli Avenue on the night of 1 December, Kvaratskhelia threw a Molotov cocktail towards riot police officers.

His defence lawyers stressed that no law enforcement officers were injured in the incident. They argued that there was no actual victim who had sustained physical injuries and that the bottle had not reached the police cordon.

On 18 July 2025, Tbilisi City Court found him guilty and sentenced him to four years and six months in prison.

Anri was born on 20 January 1999 to a family of internally displaced people from Abkhazia. His mother is an emigrant.

“I’ll visit the guys. I hope they’ll be released soon. They’re great guys – they know what they’re doing!” he said after his release.

🟥 Anri Kvaratskhelia spent 718 days in detention, from 5 December 2024 to 23 November 2026. That is 1 year, 11 months and 18 days.

Nikoloz Javakhishvili – 723 days in prison

Nikoloz Javakhishvili after his release from prison. Photo: MO SE

Nikoloz Javakhishvili was arrested on 30 November 2024. He also took part in the autumn protests. He was 20 at the time of his arrest and worked as a DJ before his detention.

Javakhishvili, along with seven other protesters, was charged with participating in group violence. The case became known in the media as the “case of the eight”.

Javakhishvili was accused of throwing pyrotechnics at police during a protest. As part of its evidence, the prosecution presented video footage showing a young man with a Georgian flag draped over his shoulders and a brown blanket thrown over it. The footage shows him throwing pyrotechnic devices. Investigators claimed that the person in the video was Javakhishvili.

The defence challenged this identification from the outset, arguing that the person could not be identified from the footage. Lawyers also insisted that the protesters had formed neither an organised group nor a prior conspiracy.

On 2 September 2025, the court sentenced Nikoloz Javakhishvili to two years in prison. He had been in custody since 30 November 2024. His sentence was due to end on 4 December 2026. The pardon secured his release 11 days before the end of his sentence.

🟥 Nikoloz Javakhishvili spent 723 days in prison – 1 year, 11 months and 23 days.

Davit Lomidze – 722 days in prison

Davit Lomidze and Temur Zasokhashvili after their release from prison. Photo: MO SE

Davit Lomidze was 53 when police arrested him on 1 December 2024 during a pro-European protest on Rustaveli Avenue.

Police initially detained him on an administrative offence charge. However, just as he was due to be released, they took him into custody again, this time as part of a criminal case opened against him.

According to the prosecution, on the night of 1 December, during a protest outside parliament, Lomidze threw a Molotov cocktail towards riot police officers and a water cannon. Investigators claim that the water cannon caught fire as a result.

According to Lomidze’s lawyer, the case file contained two video recordings and a police report. The footage did not show who had thrown the Molotov cocktail, making it impossible to identify Lomidze as the perpetrator.

Moreover, riot police officers brutally beat and mistreated Lomidze during his arrest.

On 8 August 2025, Tbilisi City Court found Davit Lomidze guilty of assaulting a police officer. It sentenced him to four years and six months in prison.

🟥 Davit Lomidze spent 722 days in prison – 1 year, 11 months and 22 days.

Temur Zasokhashvili – 722 days in prison

Temur Zasokhashvili was arrested on 1 December 2024 alongside Davit Lomidze. The court heard their cases together.

He was 39 at the time of his arrest. He lived in Tbilisi with his father; his mother and brother had been living abroad for many years. He previously worked for the State Security Service and, before his arrest, was employed in the technical department of a hotel.

Zasokhashvili faced the same charge as Lomidze: setting fire to a water cannon using a Molotov cocktail. He denied the charges. His defence also questioned whether investigators could identify the person in the video footage.

His lawyer, Dimitri Vardiashvili, said he saw Zasokhashvili after his arrest at the detention centre. He had been beaten, his eyes were swollen and guards had to support him to prevent him from falling.

On 8 August 2025, the court sentenced him to four years and six months in prison.

🟥 Temur Zasokhashvili spent 722 days in detention – 1 year, 11 months and 22 days.

The pardon process

Under Georgia’s Constitution, granting pardons is the exclusive prerogative of the president and constitutes an individual act of clemency.

The president may exercise this power at any time. Traditionally, pardons are granted to mark significant religious holidays.

The president’s power to grant pardons allows them to:

Grant a full pardon;

Reduce a sentence;

Remove a criminal conviction.

A pardon is not the same as an amnesty. A pardon is an individual decision by the president concerning specific people, while an amnesty involves the mass release of certain categories of convicted people and is granted by parliament.

When making a decision, the president may consult relevant government agencies or experts, although this is not mandatory.

Representatives of the Georgian Dream party have repeatedly raised the possibility of pardoning people arrested during protests. The ruling party has set a condition: those seeking a pardon must admit their guilt and express remorse.

In December 2025, Mikheil Kavelashvili said that people described as “prisoners of conscience” were in fact guilty and should admit their mistakes.

In May 2026, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze also said that “repentance, remorse and admission of guilt” were essential conditions for receiving a pardon.

In June, he urged prisoners to admit their guilt and submit pardon applications to the president.

In September, Kobakhidze again stressed that there were no “prisoners of conscience” in Georgia. Nevertheless, the authorities said they were willing to grant pardons on condition that prisoners admitted their guilt and expressed remorse.

Some prisoners rejected this demand. They insist they have committed no crimes and refuse to admit guilt in exchange for their freedom. Some continue to hold this position. They include journalist Mzia Amaglobeli, actor Andro Chichinadze, 19-year-old Mate Davitdze, doctor Irakli Kerashvili and many others.

Dozens of people arrested during the protests remain in Georgian prisons. Some are due to complete their sentences by the end of this year, while others are scheduled for release in early 2027. However, some have received prison terms of four years or more.

“We all need to be free now. None of us belongs in prison. I would advise them to take this opportunity [for a pardon] and get out. The situation in the country is such that we – young people – are needed here,” pardoned protester Nikoloz Javakhishvili said, addressing those who remain behind bars.

Pardoning of protesters in Georgia

World.title: ‘Jewish question’ sparks first major criticism of South Ossetia’s new president
World.content:
The new president of South Ossetia, Marat Kambolov, has faced his first serious criticism since taking office. The controversy stems from talks with Akiva Avshalom Khudainatov, the rabbi of Kislovodsk and head of the city’s Jewish Historical and Cultural Centre, about setting up an international investment fund in Tskhinval.

Representatives of Kislovodsk’s Jewish community also proposed restoring a synagogue and a Jewish cemetery in the South Ossetian capital. This proposal has also met with strong public opposition.

Opponents of these initiatives stress that their objections are not directed at Jews as a group. Rather, they argue that these particular Jewish representatives and their projects have no connection to South Ossetia.

The meeting between Kambolov and Khudainatov took place in Tskhinval on 13 November, but neither the presidential press service nor official media reported it. Details of the talks emerged through posts by a local Telegram channel that receives inside information from the presidential administration.

Only three days later, on 16 November, Kambolov’s press service issued a statement saying:

“Another initiative put forward by the Jewish community was to establish a financial and investment centre in South Ossetia. Representatives of Jewish communities from around the world could take part in its work. The initiators believe this would help develop Tskhinval and the republic.”

South Ossetian society reacted very negatively to the proposal. However, the criticism was directed not at the Jewish community, but at the president himself.

“If Israel, like most countries in the world, does not recognise South Ossetia’s sovereignty, how does Rabbi Khudainatov intend to attract finance and investment from around the world to Tskhinval?” local bloggers and ordinary residents of South Ossetia have asked. They oppose what they see as “unrealistic” projects.

They also point out that Rabbi Akiva Khudainatov has no ties to South Ossetia or its local Jewish community. Blogger and political analyst Alan Mamiyev also notes that the Kislovodsk rabbi follows Chabad-Lubavitch Hasidism, a religious movement that Tskhinval’s Jews have never followed.

“The local Jews of Tskhinval were never followers of Chabad. Accordingly, the Kislovodsk Jewish community has no right to claim the city’s synagogue,” he argues. Many others share this view.

Social media users have also reminded Kambolov and Khudainatov that Georgian-South Ossetian conflict destroyed Tskhinval’s Jewish Quarter, which had existed during the Soviet era. At the height of the fighting, members of the Jewish community had to leave South Ossetia.

The only Jewish woman who remained there was Rybka Dzhindzhikhashvili, who died alone in April 2025. Her Ossetian neighbours supported her as best they could, while the Kislovodsk Jewish community showed no interest in her plight. Now, however, its representatives have suddenly appeared with their projects.

The ruined synagogue in Tskhinval

Under a barrage of criticism, Kambolov was forced to defend himself. His press service published a post explaining the president’s position. It turned out that he had been surprised by the public reaction.

“These people came to clean up the cemetery and asked for a meeting, expressing their intention to invest in the development of our republic. I listened to them. What is there to condemn?” Kambolov said, shrugging.

He added that listening to someone does not mean agreeing with their proposals or making any commitments. The president insisted that “all decisions will be made exclusively in the interests of South Ossetia and the Ossetian people”, saying he had no other priorities.

However, Kambolov’s belated statements failed to dispel public concerns entirely. Former president Eduard Kokoity stepped in to try to resolve the dispute. In a video address, he urged people not to politicise the issue. He stressed that the Ossetian people were known for their tolerance, that Tskhinval had been a multi-ethnic city and that local Jews had never faced persecution.

“Today, it is particularly important to distinguish reality from the information noise, assess what is happening soberly and avoid panic and rumours based on speculation and assumptions.

We should not imitate various radical movements seeking to infiltrate our society, including under external influence. Radicalism in any form is alien to the Ossetian people.”

Kokoity also advised the new government leadership, made up largely of Russian officials, to pay greater attention to the republic’s history, its armed conflict with Georgia and the consequences of that conflict. He urged them to take account of the local population’s mentality and its deeply emotional attachment to its land.

“We have shed too much blood for our land and our capital for anyone to seriously suggest today that we are ready to ‘surrender’ or ‘sell’ it, as some short-sighted fellow citizens are trying to portray it.

At the same time, attracting investment must under no circumstances run counter to national interests, let alone infringe on the rights and interests of our people – which is precisely what President Marat Kambolov has said,” Kokoity said.

The last major debate over South Ossetia’s Jewish community erupted when the previous authorities decided to demolish the ruins of Tskhinval’s Jewish Quarter, which they deemed beyond restoration.

Opinions were then divided between supporters and opponents of the demolition. But the proposal to establish an investment fund has met with unanimous rejection.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website

World.title: ‘My last hope has died’: Georgia plans to ban surrogacy, prompting backlash
World.content:
Surrogacy ban in Georgia

The ruling Georgian Dream party plans to ban surrogacy completely in Georgia. Irakli Kirtskhalia, one of the leaders of the parliamentary majority, announced the initiative on Sunday, 22 November, following a meeting of the majority.

He said the party was actively discussing the issue with the Patriarchate. He also said lawmakers would submit the relevant bill in the near future.

The initiative has drawn strong criticism on social media, including from members of the medical community. Reproductive medicine specialists say that although the sector clearly needs regulation, authorities should not ban it outright.

Many believe the government is trying to win the Patriarchate’s favour. These suspicions have been fuelled by recent tensions between Georgian Dream and the Patriarchate over a debate on gambling. The Patriarchate itself has yet to issue a public statement.

How the ruling party explains its decision

Georgian Dream says it wants to ban surrogacy because of the ethical and legal risks involved. The ruling party points to threats such as human trafficking, the possible exploitation of women and violations of children’s rights.

At a special briefing, Irakli Kirtskhalia said a ban on surrogacy could have economic consequences. However, he stressed that no economic benefit could outweigh these risks:

“We fully understand that banning surrogacy could have some economic impact. However, we believe that economic benefits cannot outweigh these risks and ethical concerns.”

The parliamentary majority leader stressed that 98% of people who use surrogacy services are not Georgian citizens. As for the remaining 2%, “they will certainly understand the decision”.

“Believe me, given the specific nature of our society, our mentality, and our shared values and views, even these 2% or 1.5% [of the population] will fully understand the risks we are talking about,” Kirtskhalia added.

One of Kirtskhalia’s main arguments is that children born in Georgia are taken abroad to various destinations, after which the state loses control over their fate.

The ruling party says only five or six post-Soviet countries still allow surrogacy, and Georgia is one of them. Kirtskhalia also said the surrogacy “market” had grown significantly since 2023:

“Even in European Union member states, surrogacy is either banned or subject to very strict regulation. As for commercialisation – a problem that already existed in 2023 – the situation has unfortunately reached enormous proportions. In fact, the market is growing by 100% every year.”

He also said that although the authorities planned to ban surrogacy completely, in vitro fertilisation (IVF) procedures would not fall under the restrictions. However, they would remain subject to strict oversight.

“My last hope has died”

News of the initiative sparked an outpouring of anger on social media.

“Instead of improving the legislation, protecting the rights of surrogate mothers and punishing those who commit crimes in this sector, they are simply banning surrogacy! My last hope has died!

I want everyone – including the descendants of those who came up with this ban, those who are now pushing for it, approving it and signing the relevant law – to go through the same experience I have endured over the past seven years, both psychologically and financially,” journalist Nino Kapanadze wrote.

She published several posts on the subject.

“I wonder who the lawmakers consulted before deciding to ban surrogacy. Reproductive medicine specialists? Doctors? Agencies that organise surrogacy arrangements? Specialist clinics? And what right – or expertise – does a religious organisation have to interfere in a decision to ban surrogacy?” she asked.

Nino Tarkhnishvili, a journalist with Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, has been covering surrogacy since 2022 and has published numerous reports on the subject.

In her reports on foreign women who travelled to Georgia to become surrogate mothers, she documented numerous cases of violations of women’s rights. Following the publication of these reports, Georgian authorities launched an investigation and arrested the heads of several agencies.

“I did not write these articles to call for any bans. Quite the opposite: my only aim was to ensure that Georgia introduced legislation that would properly protect surrogate mothers, children and prospective parents, leaving no loopholes for human trafficking or other serious crimes.

Banning something is the easiest option. Proper regulation, sound legislation and bringing standards into line with international norms are much harder. But the authorities have chosen the easy way – the way of bans,” the journalist wrote on social media.

Reproductive medicine specialists: “We need regulation, not a ban”

Reproductive medicine specialists have also spoken out against the proposed ban on surrogacy. They acknowledge that abuses in the sector need to be addressed. However, they argue that an outright ban, rather than proper regulation, would deprive people for whom surrogacy is the only option of the chance to become parents.

“Surrogacy is not simply a commercial activity. It is part of assisted reproductive technology and people often turn to it for strict medical reasons. For many people who cannot conceive a child themselves because of health conditions, surrogacy remains the only realistic path to parenthood,” says Professor Nino Museridze, founder of the Association of Oncofertility.

She says authorities should address the risks through clear regulations, oversight of clinics and intermediary organisations, and safeguards to protect the rights of everyone involved. Museridze hopes that the government will eventually include assisted reproductive technologies in state-funded programmes, making infertility treatment accessible to more families.

“The state should tackle the root causes of existing problems rather than trying to ban a medical option itself.”

Keti Gotsiridze, an obstetrician-gynaecologist and reproductive medicine specialist, sees surrogacy as more than just a medical procedure.

“Surrogacy is first and foremost a human story. Behind every such story lies a simple but profound dream – the dream of becoming a mother,” she says.

According to reproductive medicine specialist Nana Janelidze, work to regulate the surrogacy sector was already under way. She says experts from the International Organization for Migration had developed 33 recommendations aimed at improving the regulation of assisted reproductive technologies.

Janelidze believes the authorities should hold public consultations on these recommendations before deciding whether to ban surrogacy. Surrogate mothers, families, doctors, lawyers and government agencies should all take part. “Why should we move towards a ban without publicly discussing the recommendations that have already been developed?” she asks.

“The ruling party wants to win the Patriarchate’s favour”: reactions to the proposed changes

Tensions have recently emerged between Georgian Dream and the Patriarchate. One source of disagreement has been the regulation of gambling. In October, the parliamentary majority fast-tracked amendments allowing casinos to host international gambling tournaments and benefit from certain tax breaks.

The Patriarchate strongly criticised the decision, saying the authorities had not consulted it. Shio, the locum tenens of the patriarchal throne, also commented on the issue. He said that promoting gambling was as grave a sin as making a direct profit from the activity itself.

Against this backdrop, many have interpreted the government’s announcement of a surrogacy ban as an attempt to ease tensions with the Church.

“A shameful and disgraceful decision! In an attempt to ‘smooth things over’ with the Patriarchate, they are depriving thousands of women of the chance to become mothers. Just imagine how many children will now never be born! And this is happening in a country facing a total demographic catastrophe!” wrote Nika Gvaramia, leader of the opposition Coalition for Change.

The Georgian Orthodox Church’s opposition to surrogacy is not new. In its official statements, the Patriarchate has repeatedly described the practice as a “grave crime”.

In its 2014 Christmas message, for example, the Patriarchate asked: “Can a family truly be happy if it raises a child born to a surrogate mother?” It added that “such a child may be condemned to a life without love and in loneliness”.

These remarks sparked public criticism at the time, prompting the Patriarchate to issue a clarification.

Tamta Mikeladze, head of the Social Justice Centre, argues in a lengthy social media post that the surrogacy sector does face systemic problems and needs regulation.

However, she questions whether the government can be expected to pursue consistent policies that protect women’s rights when it has removed the concepts of “gender” and “gender equality” from its legislation:

“The timing of this decision and its political context give legitimate grounds to suspect that political interests have driven it. For years, even when various civil society groups and the Church called for surrogacy regulation, the government failed to take any effective steps in that direction.”

The surrogacy industry in Georgia

The surrogacy market in Georgia has expanded significantly, particularly since 2022. Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, several international agencies operating in the sector moved their operations from Ukraine and Russia to Georgia.

A detailed article published by Deutsche Welle cites figures from Georgia’s Public Service Development Agency.

According to the data, more than 3,000 surrogate mothers were registered in the country in 2023. Since 2012, they have given birth to more than 5,000 children.

The article notes that surrogate mothers gave birth to around 300 children in 2021, but the figure exceeded 1,100 in 2023. According to Deutsche Welle, around 19 clinics in Georgia offer these services.

In Georgia, surrogacy is not simply a medical service or a reproductive option for foreign couples. It also raises serious questions about protecting the rights of women who take part in these programmes, particularly those who come from other countries.

For years, specialists in surrogacy and egg donation have highlighted the same problem. Their main recommendation is that Georgia needs a legal framework in line with European standards. It should clearly define the rights and responsibilities of surrogate mothers, couples struggling with infertility, clinics, doctors and intermediary agencies.

Previous attempt to ban surrogacy

The government has previously raised the issue of restricting surrogacy. In 2023, the cabinet submitted a bill to parliament that aimed to restrict foreign nationals’ access to assisted reproductive technologies, including surrogacy.

Irakli Garibashvili, who was prime minister at the time and is now in prison, announced the initiative:

“Our female citizens are being offered what is presented as a ‘profitable business’. Afterwards, nobody knows who takes the child born here or which couple takes the child. There are reports that same-sex couples may take these children. This could lead to a host of problems,” Garibashvili said.

Parliament officially registered the bill, but it never became law.

Surrogacy ban in Georgia

World.title: Anti-Annexation Platform: Minsk meeting between Georgian and Russian officials threatens to undermine Geneva talks
World.content:
The Anti-Annexation Platform has called on the Georgian authorities to explain a meeting in Minsk between Giorgi Zurabashvili, the prime minister’s special representative for relations with Russia, and Mikhail Galuzin, Russia’s deputy foreign minister.

The platform says the meeting, which took place on 19 November, does not continue the informal dialogue with Russia that existed previously. Instead, it creates a new, direct high-level political channel that could undermine the Geneva International Discussions.

What does the platform’s statement say?

The platform points out that the meeting took place in an official setting, with the two countries’ national flags on display.

It says the Russian side presented the meeting as an official contact between the foreign ministries of the two countries, and the Georgian side did not object.

“This raises the question: are the authorities laying the groundwork for normalising Russian-Georgian relations in a way that no longer makes de-occupation a precondition?” the statement says.

The Anti-Annexation Platform is a non-partisan civic association founded in Georgia on 27 August 2026. It aims to oppose Russia’s occupation and annexation policies and defend Georgia’s territorial integrity and sovereignty.

Its founders include politicians, former military personnel, diplomats, security experts and journalists.

The Anti-Annexation Platform also focuses on the location of the meeting and the issues discussed.

It says Minsk was not chosen by chance: Russia openly stated in 2024 that it wanted to move the Geneva International Discussions to Minsk.

The platform therefore warns of a risk that Minsk could become the centre of a political channel running parallel to the Geneva format.

The statement stresses that the Geneva International Discussions remain the only active international negotiating format involving the European Union, the United Nations and the OSCE. The talks address the situation in the occupied territories, Russia’s responsibility, security and humanitarian issues.

The platform believes that moving these issues into a bilateral format with Russia would weaken international involvement and Georgia’s negotiating position.

19 ноября в вечернем эфире проправительственного грузинского телеканала «Имеди» министр On 19 November, Georgian Foreign Minister Maka Bochorishvili said on the evening news programme of the pro-government Imedi TV channel that “there is nothing wrong with dialogue with Russia”.

“In recent years, whenever it comes to our relations with Russia or our attitude towards it, there have been attempts to instil fear of dialogue and talks, and to reject them outright. This is the country with which we have the most problems, and they are the biggest ones. We cannot resolve any problems without talks and dialogue if our goal is to find solutions or settle disputes,” the minister said.

The Anti-Annexation Platform says Bochorishvili’s remarks the previous day about fear of talking to Russia miss the point:

“Georgian society is not afraid of dialogue. The key question is on what terms this dialogue takes place, what agenda it follows and whose interests it serves.”

The Anti-Annexation Platform has called on the authorities to answer the following questions:

Why did the Georgian side agree to hold the meeting in Minsk?

Why did it not explore the possibility of holding a meeting under the new format in Geneva rather than Minsk?

What do the “practical arrangements” mentioned by Russia involve?

How will the authorities distinguish this new format from the Geneva International Discussions?

What guarantees are there that this process will not undermine the Geneva format and lead to the normalisation of diplomatic relations without de-occupation?

The meeting and its political context

According to statements by the Georgian government and the Russian Foreign Ministry, the two sides discussed trade and economic cooperation, cultural and humanitarian ties, regional security and the importance of the Geneva International Discussions.

Both sides said they had reached certain practical arrangements and agreed to maintain contact. However, they did not disclose the details of these arrangements.

This was the first meeting of its kind since Zurabashvili became the prime minister’s special representative. His mandate covers not only trade, economic and humanitarian issues but also the peaceful settlement of the conflict with Russia.

Since 2012, direct dialogue with Russia had taken place under the so-called Karasin-Abashidze format. The meetings were held mainly in Prague and focused on trade, transport and humanitarian issues.

The new format, the choice of Minsk as the venue and Zurabashvili’s broader mandate have prompted criticism in Tbilisi.

Former diplomats and experts have expressed concern that the meeting could mark a step towards direct political dialogue with Russia and the restoration of diplomatic relations.

World.title: Armenian authorities urge opposition not to ‘obstruct a referendum on the new Constitution’
World.content:
Pashinyan offers the opposition a “deal”

Armenian parliament speaker Ruben Rubinyan has urged the parliamentary opposition to accept the “deal” proposed by the prime minister and not obstruct a referendum on the new Constitution.

“If your only goal is to remove Pashinyan, you have a 100% chance of doing so,” he stressed.

Nikol Pashinyan has offered the opposition a “deal” several times in recent days. It concerns holding a constitutional referendum. He promises to resign if voters reject the new Constitution. If they approve it, he will seek another term as prime minister. In other words, the Civil Contract party would not nominate him in the next election.

The Armenia faction immediately rejected Pashinyan’s proposal. MP Kristine Vardanyan said the opposition could not discuss a change of power with the very people currently in power. She added that opposition members had no confidence in the authorities’ sincerity.

Tigran Abrahamyan, secretary of the Strong Armenia opposition faction, said they also rejected the prime minister’s offer.

However, Nikol Pashinyan does not consider the matter closed and expects his opponents to change their position.

Both opposition factions in parliament call the new Constitution “Aliyev’s Constitution”, although the authorities have not yet published its text. They claim that Armenia is changing its Constitution at the request of Azerbaijan. The reason is that Azerbaijan refuses to sign a peace treaty with Armenia until the country amends its Constitution. Baku considers references to the Declaration of Independence in the preamble to the current Constitution particularly problematic. The declaration calls for the reunification of Armenia and Nagorno-Karabakh. Although the authorities have not yet published the text of the new Constitution, Pashinyan has repeatedly said it will not refer to the declaration. Representatives of the ruling party stress that adopting a new Constitution is an internal matter for Armenia and that they do not discuss it with external actors. Parliament must approve the initiative before Armenia can hold a referendum on the new Constitution. The ruling Civil Contract party does not have enough seats to pass it on its own. Two-thirds of MPs must vote in favour, and the party is six votes short. The Ministry of Justice will publish the draft Constitution on 23 November. The prime minister will address the nation on the same day.

“Go ahead, remove me from office”: Pashinyan’s offer to the opposition

Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has urged the opposition not to obstruct the referendum, making the following proposal:

“I propose that the opposition provide the six votes we need to hold a referendum on the new Constitution,” the prime minister said.

He said he would resign within a week if voters rejected the new Constitution. If they approved it, the Civil Contract party would not nominate him for prime minister in the next election.

He also told journalists the previous day that giving up the post of prime minister would not mean leaving politics.

Pashinyan said the adoption of the Constitution would usher in “institutional and irreversible peace”, as guarantees existed that the peace agreement would be signed and ratified. He cited his entire “political capital” as one such guarantee:

“I will consider my mission complete once we sign and ratify the peace agreement and establish fundamental institutional peace. But I will step down in either case [whether voters approve or reject the new Constitution in the referendum]. So go ahead, remove me from office.”

The prime minister believes the new Constitution will allow Armenia to “turn the page on conflicts”. He is confident that an overwhelming majority will vote in favour of the new Constitution in the referendum.

The ruling party’s position

Pashinyan offers to step down without a “secret plan”

Sargis Khandanyan, an MP from the ruling Civil Contract faction, has urged the Strong Armenia opposition faction to respond to Pashinyan’s “open plan” to remove him from office:

“Given the current circumstances, you are the largest opposition force in Armenia. Society expects you to respond to a plan that would achieve two very important results: Nikol Pashinyan would no longer be Armenia’s prime minister, and peace would become institutionalised and irreversible.”

Samvel Karapetyan, leader of the pro-Russian opposition Strong Armenia party, has frequently spoken about a “secret plan” to change the government in Armenia in recent weeks. He made these remarks in response to questions about what steps the opposition intended to take to oust the current authorities.

Pashinyan believes the plan aims to prevent Armenia from continuing its path of economic development. “I do not want to conceal the fact that this plan also enjoys support in certain circles within the Eurasian Economic Union, led by Russia, and in the Russian Federation,” the prime minister said.*

“Obstructing peace matters more than removing Pashinyan”

Parliament speaker Ruben Rubinyan said he had the impression that opposition members had failed to notice the prime minister’s offer:

“There are two possible outcomes of the referendum: either ‘yes’ wins or ‘no’ wins. In both cases, he steps down. If ‘no’ wins, he resigns immediately; if ‘yes’ wins, he leaves after the next election. Why don’t you accept this offer?”

Rubinyan said the only logical explanation was that, for the opposition, “obstructing peace matters more than removing Pashinyan”.

He stressed that the people would decide on the Constitution, while the opposition could present its arguments for why voters should reject it.

The opposition’s response

“We are avoiding Pashinyan’s trap”

Kristine Vardanyan, an MP from the Armenia faction, said any proposal from Pashinyan was unacceptable.

“By refusing the deal, we are avoiding the trap Pashinyan has set. I cannot imagine a scenario in which Pashinyan offers a deal with the genuine intention of leaving power. It would be downright foolish to trust his words,” she said.

Vardanyan does not believe that rejecting Pashinyan’s offer means the opposition is missing an opportunity to remove him from office:

“There is an opportunity to remove Pashinyan wherever there is no deal with him. I rule that out if we make a deal with him.”

“He will leave no matter what”

Tigran Abrahamyan, secretary of the Strong Armenia faction, told journalists that after discussing the prime minister’s proposal, the faction had decided not to support changes to the Constitution:

“Our position is that Armenia’s Constitution must not be changed at the request of Azerbaijan or Aliyev.”

Abrahamyan also believes that rejecting the offer does not mean the opposition is missing an opportunity to remove Pashinyan. He is convinced that the prime minister will leave office regardless:

“We are consistently moving towards our goal, following the roadmap we have set out. This applies both to our institutional struggle and to the street protests, which, as we have said, will take place once and bring victory.”

Asked about the possibility of early elections, Abrahamyan rejected the suggestion that they could strengthen the ruling party’s position:

“We are ready for early elections at any moment. We are confident that the opposition will strengthen its position even further if new elections take place.”

Pashinyan offers the opposition a “deal”

World.title: Abkhazia investigates fraud in small business support programme
World.content:
Small business support in Abkhazia

In Abkhazia, a government programme to support small and medium-sized businesses has been affected by fraud.

The Investigative Department of the Prosecutor General’s Office has launched preliminary checks into 34 cases of suspected fraud under the “Support for Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises in the Republic of Abkhazia for 2025” programme.

Under the programme, the government provided non-repayable funding for selected projects aimed at developing small-scale production facilities and farms. Beneficiaries were selected by the Ministry of Economy, the Ministry of Agriculture and specially established commissions operating under the two ministries.

Some of the approved projects have already received full funding. However, an inspection ordered by President Badra Gunba revealed that, in a number of cases, the money had been spent but the work for which it was allocated had not been carried out. A total of 34 such projects were identified.

The authorities have not disclosed the amount of financial damage pending the conclusion of the investigation. However, it is known that a total of 261m roubles [$3.5m] was allocated to the programme from the budget in 2025, while 265 applicants were approved as participants. This means that one in eight approved projects turned out to be fraudulent.

The president has now instructed the prosecutor’s office to recover the stolen funds and return them to the budget. The further progress of the criminal cases, including whether they proceed to trial, will depend on this.

“A state programme backed by such substantial budgetary resources must under no circumstances be perceived by citizens as ordinary financial assistance or a subsidy. This is a clear instruction from the country’s president, which we will strictly follow.

These state programmes serve an entirely different purpose. Their key objective is not simply to distribute resources, but to create sustainable jobs, stimulate production and develop a real economic foundation at the local level,” Deputy Prime Minister Jansukh Nanba said.

Meanwhile, the very fact that the president personally ordered an inspection of the business support programme prompted journalists to question how the programme was being implemented.

“If the president instructs law enforcement agencies to establish an interdepartmental group to oversee the implementation of state support programmes, it can only mean one thing: something is clearly wrong with these programmes. It seems that someone has already decided to make a tidy profit from state support for entrepreneurs.

Now law enforcement agencies have several options: simply scare those involved into stopping further theft; investigate what has already been stolen; or get a cut of the money themselves,” the Respublika Telegram channel wrote.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Gas explosion in Tbilisi: Neighbours mourn victims and salvage belongings from ruins
World.content:
Explosion in Fonichala

Six people were killed in a gas explosion in a residential building in Ponichala, a district in Tbilisi. Two of the victims were young children who died alongside their mothers.

One of the five people injured in the explosion remains in critical condition. Two minors are also still receiving hospital treatment.

The destruction left 28 families homeless. They are currently staying in hotels.

Photographs of the six victims at a small park next to the building. Neighbours have set up an impromptu memorial here.

What is happening near the site of the explosion

In Lower Ponichala, where a gas explosion on the morning of November 19 caused two stairwells of a residential building to collapse, the area remains cordoned off with yellow tape. Rescue workers are still at the scene.

Trucks loaded with construction debris stand in the courtyard. Rescue teams are clearing the collapsed building of concrete rubble.

A makeshift memorial has been set up in a small park near the building. It is covered with photographs of the victims, flowers, candles and colourful stuffed toys. Little girls are tying black ribbons around the memorial.

The small park next to the building where the explosion occurred. Photo: Interpressnews

It has been raining in Tbilisi for several days. To protect the photographs, flowers and candles from the rain, the memorial has been covered with a tarpaulin.

Relatives of the victims, neighbours and acquaintances keep coming to the park. No one seems able to talk about what happened. People are still struggling to hold back their tears.

The victims’ classmates and friends also come to pay their respects, bringing dozens of large stuffed toys.

With the help of rescue workers, survivors are returning to their damaged apartments to retrieve whatever personal belongings remain intact. They carry them out in plastic bags.

“There was a terrible noise and everything shook – we thought it was an earthquake.” What happened in Ponichala

At around 9 a.m. on November 19, a powerful explosion rocked Lower Ponichala, at 16 Rustavi Highway. People were getting ready to leave for school and work. Some were already out on the street.

The explosion was caused by a build-up of natural gas on the fifth floor of a five-storey residential building. The blast wave destroyed part of the building, brought down the floor slabs and turned two stairwells into a pile of concrete within seconds.

People jumped from windows in an attempt to escape.

The blast wave threw a young man out of the fifth-floor apartment where the explosion occurred. He was the owner of the apartment. He is now in hospital with severe burns.

“There was a terrible noise and everything shook. At first, we thought it was an earthquake,” survivors who narrowly escaped the building recall.

Seven people were trapped under the rubble.

Neighbours say that in the first minutes after the explosion, they could hear several people screaming for help from beneath the debris. They were trapped under enormous concrete slabs, and it was impossible to reach them.

Of the seven people trapped, only one — three-year-old Taiya — was rescued alive. The other six were found dead. The rescue operation ended around midnight.

November 22 was declared a national day of mourning in Georgia.

Survivors: children remain in hospital, 31-year-old man in critical condition

Five people were taken to hospital following the explosion. Four were admitted in the morning, immediately after the incident. The fifth, a three-year-old girl, was brought to hospital later.

Three of the five injured people remain in hospital. They include two minors — 11-year-old Andria and three-year-old Taiya.

As of November 20, both children’s conditions were stable and satisfactory. According to doctors, a psychologist is also working with them. The three-year-old girl is expected to be discharged before the 11-year-old boy.

The third patient, a 31-year-old man, remains in critical condition.

The other two injured people sustained minor injuries and have already been discharged from hospital.

Three-year-old Taiya – eight hours under the rubble

Footage of the rescue of three-year-old Taiya.

Three-year-old Taiya was the only person rescued alive from the devastating collapse. She spent eight hours trapped beneath the rubble.

Firefighter and rescue worker Gaga Gigashvili describes the operation to save her:

“There were what amounted to three floors of debris on top of her – concrete slabs, blocks and wooden materials. When we reached her, only one leg was visible. When we touched it, she moved her leg slightly. Then we managed to reach her hand. She was holding a toy, as well as a hair clip, which she had kept clenched in her fist for all eight hours. When we opened her hand and took the clip, we held her hand and asked her to squeeze ours if she could hear us. When she squeezed our hand, we realised she was conscious and responding to us.”

The footage of the girl’s rescue is deeply moving. She is wearing a blue sweater covered in dirt and white tights. Her face is also smeared with soil and concrete dust. Rescuers carry her out of the rubble in their arms.

“Bless you, my dear,” one of the rescuers can be heard saying. It is Gaga Gigashvili. His face is contorted with emotion and exhaustion.

Gaga hands the little girl to another rescuer, who holds her close and runs towards the ambulance.

A huge crowd has gathered outside the building. People greet Taiya’s emergence with applause and tears. Her rescue gives those gathered hope that the other six people might also be found alive.

By this point, it is already known that Taiya’s mother and her seven-year-old sister are among those trapped beneath the rubble.

11-year-old Andria sustained serious injuries

Eleven-year-old Andria remains in hospital. He was admitted together with his mother, a 38-year-old woman.

According to Gia Bibilashvili, a doctor at Ingorokva Clinic, the boy was brought to hospital with more serious injuries than his mother.

Andria sustained focal brain injuries, several areas of bruising, a lung contusion, skull bone injuries, damage to his outer ear, and multiple injuries to his skin and soft tissues. He also required plastic surgery to repair the damage to his ear.

His condition is now relatively stable. Doctors plan to transfer him from intensive care to a regular hospital ward soon.

Andria’s mother suffered a concussion. She was discharged from hospital shortly afterwards.

31-year-old Ilia Isaev – the man whose apartment was the site of the explosion

The most seriously injured of all the survivors is 31-year-old Ilia Isaev. He was admitted to hospital with burns covering 87% of his body. According to doctors at the burns centre, his respiratory tract was also damaged.

Ilia was initially conscious. Before being taken to hospital, he managed to describe how the explosion happened.

He did not live in the apartment permanently. He had returned to Tbilisi from Batumi just one day before the incident. According to his account, he had tried to switch on the gas heater during the night but was unable to do so.

In the morning, he tried again. A powerful explosion followed. The blast wave threw Ilia out of the apartment.

He is now in hospital in extremely serious condition and is on a ventilator. Doctors continue to describe his condition as critical.

Who were the victims of the Ponichala explosion?

Six people died in the explosion: two young mothers and their young daughters, a 54-year-old woman and a 28-year-old man.

Nino Chelidze and her seven-year-old daughter Nutsa

Nino and seven-year-old Nutsa

Nino Chelidze was the mother of three-year-old Taiya. She was raising five children and worked at a clothing store.

At the time of the explosion, Nino was at home with two of her children — three-year-old Taiya and seven-year-old Nutsa. Her husband had taken their other three children to school shortly before the blast.

Nino’s body was found shortly after rescuers managed to pull Taiya out of the rubble. Nutsa was found much later, after hours of searching.

“Nino and her husband were raising five wonderful children. They were very happy – cheerful, good people. And suddenly, everything came crashing down on them. I have no words. When Taiya was found, I truly hoped the others would also be found alive, but unfortunately, that did not happen,” a family friend, still shaken by the tragedy, says.

Veriko Vanishvili and first-grader Ariana

Veriko Vanishvili and Ariana
