Veriko Vanishvili lived on the second floor of the apartment building in Fonichala with her six-year-old daughter, Ariana Ristich. Both mother and daughter were at home that morning.

Veriko worked as the head of marketing at Grand Bellagio casino.

“Her smile, sincerity and dedication to her work will remain with our team forever,” the casino wrote in a Facebook post.

Ariana is remembered by staff at Tbilisi Kindergarten No. 58 and by her classmates.

“You will forever remain a tremendous pain, an irreplaceable loss, an emptiness and an unhealed wound for us, our bright, lively, warm and sweet girl,” kindergarten staff wrote.

“Ariana, you were and will always remain a little part of our school. It is difficult to come to terms with the fact that your childhood smile will no longer light up the classroom,” the administration of Helios private school wrote.

Lali Shishmanashvili — “the mother of the twins”

Lali Shishmanashvili

Lali Shishmanashvili, 54, lived on the first floor. Her twin daughters were also at home when the explosion occurred.

According to neighbours, when the building began to collapse, Lali managed to shout to her daughters to jump out of the window. This helped save their lives.

“The mother managed to shout: ‘Jump!’” one neighbour recalls. The neighbours called Lali “the mother of the twins”.

According to the neighbour, Lali was calling for help and pleading to be rescued. She said she was afraid of the dark.

“Her bedroom door was blocked by concrete slabs, and a slab had also collapsed inside the room. There was nothing anyone could do to help her. I kept telling her: ‘The rescuers are already here. They will get you out soon,’” the neighbour recalls.

Lali was a philologist and also tutored students at home.

“She was a mother who lived for her children. She did everything she could to give them a good life,” recalls a friend of Lali. She spent the entire night outside the building, hoping her friend would be rescued.

Jaba Sakevarashvili — a 28-year-old courier

Jaba Sakevarashvili

Another victim of the Fonichala explosion was 28-year-old Jaba Sakevarashvili. He worked as a courier for Georgian Post.

His colleagues remember him as a responsible, hardworking employee who was dedicated to his job.

According to someone close to Jaba, the young man had only recently moved into the apartment.

28 families left homeless, while 62 remain in the same building

The building where the explosion occurred is a multi-apartment residential block with six entrances. According to Tbilisi City Hall, 90 families lived in the building. All residents were evacuated immediately after the explosion.

Initially, Tbilisi City Hall said it was ready to accommodate all evacuated residents in hotels. On the same day, a municipal service inspected the building. Following the inspection, Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze said that only two entrances were affected – the one where the explosion occurred and the adjacent one. The remaining four entrances were considered safe for residents to return to.

The 28 families who lived in the two collapsed entrances – a total of 143 people – are currently staying in hotels.

According to the mayor, the municipality will offer these families a housing replacement programme. Until new apartments are built for them, they will be accommodated in rented housing, with the rent covered by the city.

Remains of family photo albums near the collapsed building. Photo: Georgian Public Broadcaster.



Late in the evening on November 20, the ruling Georgian Dream party released a condolence letter from Bidzina and Eka Ivanishvili. The letter stated that the Ivanishvilis would purchase apartments for the 28 families left homeless.

The announcement followed an earlier statement by the Tbilisi mayor. It is not yet known where the Ivanishvilis will purchase the apartments, when the families will receive their new homes, or how the assistance will be distributed. It has also not been clarified how this initiative will be coordinated with the housing replacement programme proposed by the municipality.

According to Tbilisi City Hall, residents of the building’s four surviving entrances will also be offered the opportunity to participate in the housing replacement programme. These are the 62 families who are still living in the building.

Could the tragedy have been prevented? The investigation must establish the facts

Giorgi Lefsveridze, deputy technical director of the gas distribution company Tbilisi Energy, said that the apartment where the explosion occurred was listed in the company’s database as disconnected from the gas supply.

According to him, no gas consumption had been recorded at the address from December 2025 until the day of the explosion, and the subscriber had received zero-balance bills every month. The company also said it had received no reports of a smell of gas from this address over the previous two years.

Lefsveridze said that scheduled inspections of the building had been carried out in January 2025 and January 2026. However, in January 2026, company employees were unable to enter the apartment where the explosion later occurred. With the help of neighbours, they contacted the owner, who said he was outside Tbilisi and would allow the inspection once he returned.

The investigation must establish what exactly caused the explosion and who bears responsibility for what happened.

A criminal investigation has been launched under Article 240 of Georgia’s Criminal Code, which concerns violations of safety regulations during construction work.

In parallel, the Energy Ombudsman’s Office has also launched its own examination of the incident. On the day of the tragedy, the office requested relevant information from Tbilisi Energy.

One-off incident or systemic problem? Tbilisi has seen similar tragedies before

The explosion in Ponichala is not the first incident of its kind. Gas explosions have occurred periodically in Tbilisi for years. Some have claimed lives, while others have caused such extensive damage that dozens of families have been temporarily left homeless.

In 2019, the organisation FactCheck published statistics based on data from the gas distribution company KazTransGaz.

“According to KazTransGaz data, between 2016 and the first quarter of 2019, 101 people died and another 285 were poisoned in Tbilisi as a result of explosions caused by natural gas leaks and gas-related intoxication.”

Every such tragedy reignites the debate over responsibility: who is accountable for these incidents? Who should inspect the structural integrity of residential buildings and ensure that gas distribution networks are functioning properly and safely?

Now, new questions have emerged: what happens when gas company employees cannot gain access to an apartment? Does zero gas consumption mean that an apartment is safe? What mechanisms are in place when a property owner is away for an extended period and a technical inspection cannot be carried out?

Engineer and professor Temur Mikiashvili, speaking to Netgazeti, says that the absence of gas consumption does not guarantee safety. According to him, a meter may fail to register a small leak, while gas can gradually accumulate inside an unoccupied apartment.

He also points to the deterioration of plastic pipes and rubber hoses connected to gas appliances, which can cause leaks that go unnoticed.

According to the expert, gas detectors are an important preventive measure. These devices sound an alarm or send a notification when they detect a leak. Some models can also automatically shut off the gas supply.

Another problem in Tbilisi: ageing residential buildings

Faulty gas systems are not the only problem facing Tbilisi. The residential building in Fonichala collapsed so rapidly that the tragedy has once again raised questions about the lifespan and structural safety of residential buildings.

Tbilisi has numerous old and deteriorating apartment blocks. Many buildings constructed decades ago no longer meet modern safety standards.

Tbilisi City Hall has a dedicated programme and budget for addressing the problem of unsafe residential buildings.

According to data published by corruption researcher Irakli Abesadze, two main municipal budget programmes are being implemented in this area:

Reinforcement of unsafe buildings – between 2018 and 2025, during Kakha Kaladze’s tenure as mayor, a total of GEL 87,742,800 was spent on the programme. A total of 269 buildings were fully or partially reinforced.



– between 2018 and 2025, during Kakha Kaladze’s tenure as mayor, a total of GEL 87,742,800 was spent on the programme. A total of 269 buildings were fully or partially reinforced. Replacement of unsafe buildings – launched in 2022, the programme received a total of GEL 19,081,700 in funding between 2022 and 2025.

Abesadze compares the funding allocated to these programmes with sums allegedly misappropriated through suspected corruption schemes.

According to him, the GEL 41,105,298 allegedly embezzled from the Tbilisi metro carriage modernisation project alone would have been enough to increase funding for the building reinforcement programme by 50%.

Abesadze estimates that this additional funding could have enabled the reinforcement of around 100 more buildings. The same amount, he says, would also have made it possible to triple the budget of the unsafe building replacement programme.

Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association: The state’s responsibility does not end with launching an investigation

The Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA) also points to the scale and systemic nature of the problems. According to the organisation, the state’s obligations do not end with launching an investigation. It is necessary to establish whether inspection requirements under the gas distribution network regulations are being properly enforced and what measures are taken when access to a consumer’s apartment cannot be secured.

GYLA refers to the regulations approved by Resolution No. 80 of the Georgian National Energy and Water Supply Regulatory Commission (GNERC), dated December 31, 2021. Under these rules, the system operator is required to regularly inspect the gas supply system within a consumer’s property. If violations are identified, the consumer must be notified in writing and appropriate measures must be taken.

This issue is particularly important in older residential buildings, where infrastructure installed decades ago, modified pipes, outdated heating appliances and inadequate ventilation systems remain in use.

World.title: Former Turkish parliament speaker Hikmet Cetin dies at 89
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 24. Hikmet Cetin, former Speaker of the Grand National Assembly of Türkiye (TBMM), former foreign minister and former leader of the Republican People's Party (CHP), has died at the age of 89.

His death has been met with sadness in political circles, given his long-standing role in Turkish politics.

Born in 1937 in the Lice district of Diyarbakir, Hikmet Cetin graduated from Ankara University's Faculty of Political Sciences.

After holding various positions at the State Planning Organization, Cetin entered politics and went on to serve as Deputy Prime Minister, Minister of Foreign Affairs and Speaker of the Grand National Assembly of Türkiye.

Cetin served as leader of the Republican People's Party (CHP) from February 18 to September 9, 1995.

World.title: Azerbaijan welcomes TRIPP project, hopes for its swift implementation - FM
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 24. We welcome the TRIPP project and hope it will be implemented soon, Azerbaijan’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Jeyhun Bayramov, said during a joint press conference with Georgia’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs, Maka Botchorishvili, Trend's correspondent reports.

According to the minister, since the corridor’s entry and exit points are located on the border with Azerbaijan, the Azerbaijani side has been regularly briefed on the progress of the process to facilitate the project’s implementation and coordinate efforts accordingly.

“The significance of this initiative for Azerbaijan can be assessed in two main areas. The first aspect relates to the domestic context and creates additional opportunities for unimpeded communication between the main part of Azerbaijan and the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic. The second aspect, however, encompasses a broader regional context. Thus, this route, serving as a new branch and direction of the East–West Middle Corridor, will bring additional opportunities and benefits not only to Armenia but also to all countries in the region, including the states of the South Caucasus,” he noted.

The minister added that other infrastructure projects being implemented in parallel also complement this process. In particular, work is scheduled to be completed on increasing the capacity of the Baku–Tbilisi–Kars railway.

“At the same time, Türkiye has begun construction on the 224-kilometer Kars-Iğdır-Aralık-Dilucu Railway Project. Azerbaijan is also extending new railway lines currently under construction to the Azerbaijani-Armenian border and, in addition, is working to improve the quality of the existing line in the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic and integrate it with projects in Türkiye.

Taken together, all these lines—in addition to the East–West Corridor—form a single, broad corridor and a new link for the South Caucasus itself. This link allows for the flexible rerouting of freight routes in various directions, depending on needs,” the foreign minister said.

World.title: Georgia, Azerbaijan continue border delimitation, demarcation efforts - FM
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 24. Georgia and Azerbaijan are engaged in certain efforts regarding the delimitation and demarcation of their borders, the country’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister, Maka Botchorishvili, said during a joint press conference with Azerbaijan’s Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov, Trend's correspondent reports.

The Georgian minister noted that this process is being conducted on the basis of mutual respect.

“A special commission is in place to address these issues. It operates on a regular basis: the parties gather, meet, cooperate with one another, and discuss matters related to this process. Naturally, both sides must work to advance the process, and, of course, if progress is made in this direction, we will welcome it.

This is a fairly important process that is proceeding on the basis of taking each other's interests into account as much as possible and mutual respect,” she said.

World.title: Azerbaijan outlines two green energy export routes to Europe, FM says
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 24. As part of a new development initiative in accordance with the agreement reached with the European Union in 2022, work is underway in the field of alternative energy, Azerbaijan’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Jeyhun Bayramov, said during a joint press conference with Georgia’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs, Maka Botchorishvili, Trend's correspondent reports.

The minister noted that this initiative involves the production of alternative energy and its transmission via cable to the European market via various routes.

“One of them is a route passing through Azerbaijan, Georgia, Türkiye, and Hungary based on a four-party agreement. Another route involves laying a cable across the Caspian and Black Seas, including along the seabed of the Black Sea to the coast of Romania, and from there to Hungary and other countries.

Work on the technical and financial-technical feasibility study for this project has been completed. Experts note that the project is technically feasible, as well as financially sound and practical. It is expected that this will become one of the new main routes in the future,” he said.

World.title: EPA investigates after thousands of fish found dead in irrigation channels
World.content:
The NSW Environment Protection Authority (EPA) is investigating Murrumbidgee Irrigation over a possible breach of the Pesticides Act after 2,800 fish were found dead in Leeton Shire channels over the past week.

The discovery came after Murrumbidgee Irrigation conducted weed spraying along the area's channel systems between the Riverina towns of Leeton, Stanbridge and Wamoon to improve flow rates for irrigators.

The EPA has released a statement, confirming it was informed about the situation last week.

"The EPA is investigating to see whether there has been a breach of the Pesticides Act," a spokesperson said,

"Murrumbidgee Irrigation are [sic] working to clean up the channel, and we have directed them to undertake further sampling.

"We are advised an estimated 2,800 fish are deceased, predominantly European Carp, with some native fish also impacted."

The Leeton Shire Council said there were no concerns for residential drinking water, but some residents remained concerned about the impact on native species.

In a statement, Murrumbidgee Irrigation said 95 per cent of the fish killed were European carp.

But Leeton resident and avid fisherman Josh Higgins has disputed that.

Josh Higgins feels more could be done to protect the channel's ecosystems. (ABC Riverina: Nicola Ceccato)

"I've not ever seen fish dead like this before," he said.

"There were certainly hundreds of Murray cod there and ranging from all sizes.

"Some quite small, but there was quite a few that were upwards of that 60 and 70-centimetre mark up to that metre and over the metre mark, which is pretty devastating."

Murrumbidgee Irrigation says the majority of fish affected in the recent fish kill were European carp. (ABC Riverina: Nicola Ceccato)

Mr Higgins said he was worried that the weed treatment happened at a time when Murray cod were breeding.

"Your average recreational fisherman is unable to go and target a Murray cod this time of the year because it's their breeding time," he said.

"There's no denying there is quite a bit of weed through that area and it would affect flow rates for the farmers and obviously they need to get water.

"So that's completely understood, but there has to be better ways to go about it."

Yabbies and other crustaceans were also impacted in the recent fish kill. (Supplied)

Chemical concerns

The product used by Murrumbidgee Irrigation in its spraying program is called Magnacide H, which has a general biocide called Acrolein as its active ingredient.

It is used to treat submerged aquatic weeds like pondweed and ribbon weed.

Magnacide H is currently the only product approved by the Australian Pesticide and Veterinary Medicines Authority to treat weeds in irrigation channels.

On Murrumbidgee Irrigation's website, the company states that it expects all fish in the channels where Magnacide H is used will die, but previous cases showed it was mainly European carp impacted.

Director of the University of NSW Centre for Ecosystem Science Richard Kingsford said to understand the full impact on the channel's ecosystem, every species killed by the chemical should be tracked.

Richard Kingsford says Acrolein is a very toxic chemical for aquatic species. (Supplied: Richard Kingsford)

"Even though this chemical doesn't hang around for very long, if it kills a lot of things like yabbies and shrimps," Professor Kingsford said.

" It can have impacts longer term on the whole food web that's dependent on that system. "

Professor Kingsford said finding a solution to the weed problem could be difficult, with no other approved APVMA treatment for irrigation weeds and the high cost and effort of manually clearing long stretches of channel.

"It could also be about how do you make sure your timing of using herbicides doesn't coincide with when native fish are migrating and in big numbers in those channels," he said.

"The problem with herbicides and pesticides … there are also chronic effects where [they] can build up in the tissues and affect the way these animals survive and breed."

Murrumbidgee Irrigation says only 5 per cent of the fish kill were native fish. (Supplied)

In a statement, Murrumbidgee Irrigation said weeds needed to be treated at different times of the year depending on growing cycles.

"Our channels are private infrastructure used to deliver irrigation water and for reasons of safety, at all times of the year we recommend that people do not use our channels for recreational purposes, including fishing," it said.

The company said the recent spraying was a "controlled and purposeful activity" and said it was working with the EPA to "identify any lessons that can inform future weed management activities".

World.title: Republican China hawks challenge Trump over Huang's Nvidia return
World.content:
Republicans in the US Congress are pressing for sweeping investigations into the Nvidia scandal, mounting a rare challenge to Donald Trump as their hawkish stance on China puts them at odds with his support for the AI chip giant's reinstated chief executive.

The return of Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang this week, 11 days after he resigned over extramarital affairs, reportedly including a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, has intensified demands for answers and tougher controls on the sale of powerful artificial intelligence chips.

Jensen Huang a 'protected species' Jensen Huang is back as CEO of Nvidia and US President Donald Trump is taking credit for the move. For Congress and experts alike, that is raising some flags.

Mr Trump personally intervened to secure Huang's reinstatement, telling CNBC: "I made the deal."

Nvidia's board said it had received input from senior US government officials and was confident Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk, even though its own independent investigation remained unfinished.

Republican Senator John Curtis demanded to know who had provided those assurances and why the board had reversed its earlier decision not to reinstate Huang.

"Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board?" he wrote on X.

"I'd like to know what changed."

Senate Intelligence Committee chairman Tom Cotton warned that Mr Huang's reinstatement did not resolve the underlying concerns.

"Congress has much to investigate," the Republican senator said.

Congressional grilling

Public criticism of Mr Trump is rare among Senate Republicans, and the objections raised by at least six of them over Mr Huang's reinstatement represent an unusually strong show of dissent.

Most, however, have directed their criticism at Nvidia or questioned the administration's assurances rather than attacking the president personally.

Mr Huang is already scheduled to face questioning behind closed doors on December 1 by three Republican-led House committees: Foreign Affairs, Intelligence and the select committee on China.

The three committee chairmen said his reinstatement and Nvidia's "brief internal investigation" did not erase the national security questions facing the company.

Jensen Huang has acknowledged having extramarital affairs. (Reuters: Ann Wang)

Mr Huang will also testify publicly before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3, while Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to appear before the committee on December 10, CBS News reported.

At the heart of the scandal are allegations that Nvidia's advanced chips were diverted to China through Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company formerly led by Alice Huang, whom US intelligence suspects of working for Beijing.

Reports have identified her as a woman with whom Jensen Huang had an affair, although he did not name her when acknowledging his infidelity.

Mr Lutnick's commerce department faces scrutiny over its handling of Megaspeed, which had been under investigation over suspected violations of export restrictions.

'Sold out'

Last week Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that several government agencies had supported blacklisting the company for months, but Commerce had delayed taking action.

The department finally added Megaspeed to its trade blacklist Monday, the day Mr Huang returned to Nvidia.

Nebraska conservative Pete Ricketts said reinstatement did not absolve Mr Huang of answering questions about national security and potentially unaccounted-for chips.

Other Senate Republicans have demanded fuller explanations of the company's activities and the administration's involvement.

Huang's return not the end of Nvidia saga The shock return of Jensen Huang, heralded by US President Donald Trump, does not mean the Nvidia co-founder is out of the woods.

The controversy is also strengthening calls for legislation to restrict access to cutting-edge American technology.

Mr Cotton has promised to push ahead with bipartisan chip export-control legislation, while Senate Republican leader John Thune has pledged support for stronger restrictions.

Mr Trump's own financial interests are also attracting scrutiny.

According to a Washington Post review of financial disclosures, his Nvidia holdings were valued at between US$13 million ($19.5 million) and US$62 million as of late August. The White House says independent managers make his investment decisions.

A spectacular rebound in Nvidia's share price after Huang's return may have added as much as US$15 million to Mr Trump's holdings in the stock on Monday, according to calculations by The Financial Times.

Democrats, meanwhile, say they are are preparing to wield their new congressional majorities from January to investigate potential corruption involving Nvidia and senior Trump officials.

World.title: Bumper harvest 'a blessing' for SA after years of crippling drought
World.content:
South Australian farmers are seeing a spectacular change in fortune as they reap what is potentially one of the biggest harvests in history.

The recovery from consecutive years of crippling drought has culminated in millions of tonnes of grain rolling out across the state.

While last week's storm on the Eyre Peninsula potentially wiped out millions of dollars worth of crops across several farms, expectations are still high that yields statewide will reach record-breaking levels.

With so much grain expected to flow into grain handling sites in the coming weeks, the state government has allowed companies to hastily install extra storage infrastructure without planning approval to ensure none of it goes to waste.

SA farmers still face many long weeks to get their crops harvested. (ABC News: Trent Murphy)

With many more weeks and long hours of harvest ahead, many farmers remain cautiously optimistic.

Grain grower Brenton Vanstone, from Wandearah in SA's mid-north, is out harvesting good yields of lentils, wheat and barley — although a little less than what the season had earlier promised.

"Because we had 60 to 70 millimetres [of rain] in August but none in September, we had a bulk of growth and we thought yields were going to be a lot better than what they are," Mr Vanstone said.

Millions of tonnes of grain will be trucked to receival sites across SA this harvest. (ABC News: Trent Murphy)

"It was mainly [due to the] transition from a very wet winter to a dry spring.

"But we are happy with the yields and it's going to be a lot better than 2024; that was a bane and this year's a blessing."

Scramble for extra storage

SA is forecast to produce around 13 million tonnes of grain this summer, representing an increase of about 46 per cent to last year.

Concerned the state's existing storage infrastructure may not cope with that volume, the SA government announced temporary measures removing the need for planning approval to build additional bunkers and silos.

Storage has been at the top of some people's minds this harvest. (ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly)

It said this was to avoid up to $70 million worth of grain going to waste.

Grain handler Bunge has already received more than 2 million tonnes of grain as harvest hits full swing.

Bunge's Tailem Bend site director of industrial management Gavin Cavanagh said that represents close to a quarter of what the company expects to receive in total.

Bunge director of industrial management Gavin Cavanagh and Grain Producers SA CEO Brad Perry. (ABC News: Trent Murphy)

"It will be one of the biggest and potentially the biggest crop that we've had on record, which is really exciting time for farmers, the communities they're operating in, and ourselves as well," Mr Cavanagh said.

Bunge has installed around half a million tonnes of extra storage capacity across its SA sites this season, 200,000 tonnes of that under the government's emergency measures.

'Extraordinary' record crop

Grain Producers SA chief executive Brad Perry was confident the state was heading for an "extraordinary" record crop, despite recent storm damage and some farmers reporting mixed results.

"Some crops aren't as big yield-wise as expected, but then others are even bigger than expected, so depends on where you are in the state," Mr Perry said.

"We've never seen anything like this on the Eyre Peninsula; the crop size is phenomenal and there's places that have been so dry for a couple of years that have got really big crops, it's fantastic to see.

Bunge has installed extra grain storage at a number of sites, including this one at Tailem Bend. (ABC News: Trent Murphy)

" Farmers have got a smile on their face, which is the most important thing. "

Grain receiver T-Ports anticipated the need for extra storage early on, having already gone through the red tape of approval prior to the government's announcement.

T-Ports grower relations officer Hayley Lewis said that involved extra bunkers at its sites on the Yorke Peninsula.

She said farmers she spoke to were feeling "quietly confident" of a large and lengthy harvest.

T-Ports grower relations officer Hayley Lewis. (ABC Rural: Brooke Neindorf)

"You can't really count your chickens until they hatch, and they are just waiting to get it off the paddock and in the bunkers before they celebrate too much," she said.

"It is definitely a much bigger year than the previous couple, and probably on par or even bigger than the 2022 season, which was quite a big year.

"I think it will definitely be a big and long one and there will be a lot of people looking forward to a holiday at the end of it, me included."

World.title: Scathing report finds years of poor management of Tasmania's ports
World.content:
The auditor-general has issued a scathing report about Tasmania's port infrastructure, warning of significant future costs and potentially severe service disruptions.

The government-owned company TasPorts operates 10 ports across the island state, including major ones in Hobart, Devonport, Burnie and Bell Bay.

But in his report, Auditor-General Martin Thompson said the state's port infrastructure had not been managed well "for a long period of time".

While noting "high-profile failures", including the delayed and over budget Spirit of Tasmania facilities in Devonport, he warned of potentially bigger problems in the future.

"There is a much broader, and potentially far more significant risk of failure in relation to managing the strategic and operational aspects of Tasmania's entire port infrastructure network," he said.

The delay in building the new deeper water Devonport berth for Tasmania's new ferries contributed to a blowout of the project cost. (Supplied: Tasmanian government)

Mr Thompson described current planning by TasPorts and Building Tasmania, formerly known as the Department of State Growth, as "inadequate".

Martin Thompson says TasPorts has not been providing a full picture of its situation to the government. (Supplied: Audit Tasmania)

"The result is that Tasmania is left with port infrastructure that is rapidly approaching end of life, likely to require significant increases in maintenance costs and experience more frequent and severe service disruptions and no clear pathway to funding the cost of replacement."

He said the cost of maintaining existing infrastructure, or expanding it as TasPorts planned, would be "very expensive" and likely unachievable within its existing business model.

"The current condition of Tasmania's port infrastructure presents a significant risk for the state," he said.

"Decision makers need to consider all options for its mitigation, including rationalisation, decommissioning, renewal or replacement."

The report says Tasmania's ports have not been managed effectively for "a long period of time". (Supplied: TasPorts)

Lack of whole-of-state transport strategy criticised

The report said an independent assessment valued TasPorts's assets at $477 million in 2025.

But it found the cost of replacing the infrastructure would be closer to $1.29 billion.

TasPorts's wharves, which were rated as being in a "poor" condition, accounted for almost half of the estimated replacement cost.

But if TasPorts proceeded with plans to expand its commercial wharves, including climate change adaptation and electrification, the report said it could require an investment of $2.2 billion.

Mr Thompson said the situation had partly arisen because there was no whole-of-state transport strategy to guide strategic decision-making.

"Without such a strategy, Tasmania risks continuing to make port infrastructure decisions in isolation of other forms of transport infrastructure such as road, rail and air.

" This may result in fragmented investment, delayed resolution of structural network constraints and continued inefficiencies across the Tasmanian supply chain. "

He also said TasPorts had not been providing sufficient information about the condition of its assets and funding gaps to its shareholding ministers.

"This is particularly critical given the current poor condition of wharf infrastructure and the level of future investment required," he said.

"If ministers are not receiving advice on the key risks related to deterioration in asset condition, that can delay recognising the need and providing for asset renewal."

The report noted the "high-profile" debacle of failing to construct the new port for the new Spirit ferries. (Supplied: TT-Line)

Required investment 'may exceed' TasPorts' funds

Mr Thompson made four recommendations, including:

A whole-of-state multi-modal transport strategy

A strategy outlining how TasPorts will implement and fund its plans

A reporting and escalation framework covering asset condition, renewal needs, and funding gaps

Improved record keeping of all meetings between TasPorts and its ministers

Building Tasmania accepted the transport strategy recommendation in principle, with expected completion by December 2027.

The other recommendations were accepted in full, with similar completion deadlines.

The current condition of Tasmania's port infrastructure "presents a significant risk", the report says. (Supplied: TasPorts)

Spirit IV docks late again after 'technical issue' It's the second time this month that the new Spirit of Tasmania ferry has dropped passengers off hours behind schedule. Tracking shows the new vessel spent hours performing loops in Port Philip Bay before being escorted by a tugboat into Geelong.

In a response included in the report, TasPorts chair Greg McCann said significant changes had already been made to its asset management, project governance and risk management.

He said a port master planning process would be undertaken next year to determine whether infrastructure should be maintained, renewed, expanded or retired.

This would include considering opportunities to "consolidate assets and freight activities", he said.

However, Mr McCann said that funding and delivery remained a challenge.

" The investment required over coming decades may exceed what TasPorts can fund from its own balance sheet while remaining financially stable. "

Mr McCann said TasPorts would work with its shareholding ministers on a "sustainable approach" to funding and sequencing its renewal program, including for community ports, which provide regional benefits but earn limited commercial returns.

"Addressing the long-term investment challenge is likely to require alternative funding sources and models," he said.

He said that options may include government co-investment, customer contributions, third-party investment or other funding mechanisms.

In a statement released on Tuesday night, TasPorts CEO Allan Gray said the auditor-general's recommendations had been accepted in full.

"We have made no secret of the challenges presented by Tasmania's aging port infrastructure and the significance of the asset renewal program that will be required in coming years," he said.

World.title: Powderfinger secure all-star Australian support acts for reunion tour
World.content:
It's the hottest reunion ticket in town. Powderfinger are playing 36 outdoor shows around the country in late 2027, their first tour since splitting in 2010.

Today, the Brisbane band have fulfilled their promise to book an all-Australian line-up for their marathon comeback, unveiling the full list of support acts.

Inside Powderfinger's reunion For Powderfinger, reuniting wasn't about cashing in on nostalgia, but creating a cultural moment to bring some joy back to the band, and to a divided world.

It's an impressive bill, bringing together established and emerging artists, and in many cases giving them a massive hometown stage.

Joining Powderfinger in their native Brisbane will be Ball Park Music, DZ Deathrays, The Jungle Giants, Radium Dolls, Nice Biscuit, Beddy Rays, Vlads and Shag Rock.

Playing both shows in Cairns are King Stingray, Dune Rats, Tullara and The Bluebottles.

Perth will feature Jebediah, Old Mervs, The Southern River Band, Smol Fish, GRUB and Rowena Wise.

The Sydney bill is stacked with the likes of recent two-time ARIA winners DMA'S, reunited rockers The Preatures, Middle Kids, The Buoys, The Lazy Eyes, Jem Cassar-Daley and William Crighton.

Adelaide will host John Butler Trio, King Stingray, The Tullamarines and Any Young Mechanic.

Melbourne is packed with Jet, Sarah Blasko, Grace Cummings, Gordi, Floodlights, Creature Fear, Sleepazoid and Loose Content. And Canberra will get to see Ball Park Music and Emma Donovan.

Supporting the next generation

Three of Powderfinger's 52 support slots have been reserved for triple j Unearthed acts, giving one young up-and-comer in Brisbane, Sydney and Melbourne a platform to play to tens of thousands of people.

Forget My Happiness, these are Powderfinger's essential songs Powderfinger are back! What better time for fans old and new to revisit the legacy of the Brisbane rock icons?

Unearthed will open a competition in early 2027, with any artist with a triplejunearthed.com profile eligible to enter for a chance to play alongside the 'Finger.

"I remember when we played with The Angels in 1992," frontman Bernard Fanning told ABC's Zan Rowe.

"We had no idea what we were doing. But just going and being inside the tent and seeing how everything operates, it's another step up from the local venue.

" Hopefully that rubs off on some of these Unearthed guys. It'd be great if they see it as a chance to step up. "

Using their popularity to spotlight contemporary bands and showcase the "incredible wealth" of Australian talent has been a key part of Powderfinger's booking strategy, explains bassist John "JC" Collins.

"It's a tough time to be a musician, or anyone working in the creative arts," he says.

"Support slots give emerging acts the chance to play to bigger audiences and grow their fanbase.

" We're really happy to pass it on to the next wave of Aussie artists. "

During Powderfinger's hiatus, Collins has operated multiple music venues and was appointed Queensland's nightlife commissioner. (ABC News: Liz Pickering)

In the spirit of giving back, Powderfinger are also partnering with the Australian Music Venue Foundation (AMVF), donating $100,000 to the organisation.

Launched last year and modelled after the UK's Music Venue Trust initiative, the AMVF aims to protect, support and sustain grassroots music venues around the country.

"Kids aren't going out as much to see live bands, so those venues are closing, so then the opportunity closes down for bands," Fanning told Zan Rowe.

Listen to Powderfinger's reunion interview Bernard Fanning and Darren Middleton joined Zan Rowe to talk about what prompted Powderfinger's reunion, adding extra shows, and more.

He said the combination of declining live attendance, festival cancellations and Australians streaming less Australian music than ever has created "this domino effect" that threatens the entire ecosystem.

Collins, who sits on the AMVF board and is Queensland's nightlife commissioner, says: “Grassroots music venues are essential to the future of Australian music."

"They provide the first gigs, the first audiences and the first opportunities for artists starting out, but right now, all across the country they're under enormous pressure.

"When I think about where it all began for Powderfinger, it was small venues like The Orient in Brisbane that backed us in those early years.

"Those rooms gave us the chance to learn, experiment, fail, improve and ultimately become the band we wanted to be. They're the breeding ground for our next generation of artists."

World.title: Weight-loss drug boom could leave Aussies facing falls and fractures
World.content:
The weight-loss drug boom could leave Australians facing bone fractures and lost independence from unchecked muscle loss, according to the peak exercise physiology body.

Exercise and Sports Science Australia (ESSA) is sounding the alarm about the risk of muscle strength loss during GLP-1 treatment, unveiling new clinical resources for GPs overseeing patients on the medication.

The use of GLP-1-based medications such as Ozempic or Mounjaro has been rising rapidly in Australia, with an estimated 500,000 people using the injections.

New GLP-1 pills have also hit the market, making the drug more accessible.

GLP-1 is now available in pill form. (Reuters: Hollie Adams)

ESSA chief executive Katie Lyndon said without appropriate oversight, patients might enter retirement struggling to stand, walk or live independently, which could push already strained health and aged care systems "beyond breaking point".

"If GLP-1 weight-management treatment strips away the muscle strength, keeping us steady on our feet, a simple stumble could mean fractures, a hospital bed or lost independence," Ms Lyndon said.

TGA clear Australia's first weight-loss tablet for use The first oral weight-loss tablet has been cleared for use in Australia. It is the first GLP-1 approved by the Therapeutic Goods Administration in oral form.

GLP-1 drugs mimic the activity of a natural hormone, helping people feel full for longer, which can assist with weight loss.

They are also considered an important medication to help treat conditions like type 2 diabetes by controlling blood glucose levels.

However, weight loss, including through the use of GLP-1 medication, can involve the loss of lean tissue such as muscle as well as fat.

Ms Lyndon said while GLP-1s were "transforming lives and improving health outcomes", it was important that patients were aware of the risks and received appropriate support.

Katie Lyndon says people need to be made aware of all the risks associated with taking weight-loss drugs. (Supplied)

ESSA's new screening tools prompt doctors to look for risk factors including faster-than-expected weight loss, older age, previous falls and low or declining physical activity.

"Resistance training, proper nutrition and regular strength and mobility checks cannot be optional. They must be treated as essential to weight-management treatment, or we risk leaving patients lighter on the scales but weaker on their feet," Ms Lyndon said.

Resistance training should be 'part of the prescription'

For more than three years, construction worker Rob Fleeton has been on GLP-1 medication to help address pre-diabetes.

But when he moved to light duties after a shoulder injury, his strength and muscle mass deteriorated significantly.

"I went from being able to carry things around, swing a sledgehammer at work, no dramas, to not being able to do anything … I could feel myself losing muscle mass, and I could feel myself losing strength," he said.

Rob Fleeton says his muscle mass deteriorated significantly on GLP-1 until he started resistance training. (Supplied)

After shoulder surgery, he started a program written by his wife Jen, an exercise physiologist.

"I'm actually stronger now than I was in high school and I'm 44, which sounds ridiculous, but the resistance training was so good. It just did so much for me," he said.

A recent study of 120 people by University of Western Australia researchers found people who did resistance training while taking the GLP-1 tirzepatide lost about 25 per cent less lean tissue than those who did not.

That prompted the lead researcher to say resistance exercise should be "part of the prescription" for patients on the medication.

Royal Australian College of GPs spokesman Tim Jones welcomed the new clinical resources to help ensure "a high standard of care".

GLP-1 drugs and heart health A large study suggests people with type 2 diabetes who start and then stop GLP-1 drugs may have poorer health outcomes.

He said the medication was a very useful tool when prescribed and overseen appropriately, and he already advised those taking the medication to take part in exercise programs that support bone health, strength, and overall fitness.

"If we have patients who are already experiencing a sedentary lifestyle, they are at high risk of de-conditioning and ending up with serious complications, such as falls and fractures," Dr Jones said.

Tim Jones says patients who are already experiencing a sedentary lifestyle are at high risk of serious complications. (ABC News: Jordan Young)

He also raised concerns that patients who have sourced GLP-1 medication through telehealth companies or who were self-injecting unapproved drugs like retatrutide may not be getting thorough advice.

"[One patient] came in deeply concerned because … they could no longer leave the couch without some assistance," he said.

"No-one had really counselled them about the importance of exercise in maintaining good health through their treatment, and to me that's a cautionary tale about the risks."

World.title: Why Harry Styles isn't coming to your city on his Australian tour
World.content:
Play all the time, tour occasionally. That's the approach Harry Styles has taken to live performance throughout 2026.

Originally, the 32-year-old pop star's Together, Together tour consisted of 50 gigs in seven cities. The centrepiece was to be a marathon, 30-show run at New York's Madison Square Garden, followed by consecutive dates in Sydney and Melbourne.

Hear and read more from triple j triple j brings you the best new music from Australia and around the world. Discover your next favourite artist here.

It's not the same as it was. Styles told fans in September that he would supplement the residency shows with conventional concerts in 12 cities — but until 2027, the One Direction alumni will occupy single venues on repeat and on purpose.

Like a growing list of international touring artists, Styles is prioritising quality over quantity, self-compassion over exertional malaise.

Could this explain the rise of concert residencies?

The perks of being a resident: mental health and creative control

Life on the road often means mental and physical exhaustion. While jet lag, sickness and low morale are occupational hazards for touring musicians, residents can conserve their energy.

"[Concert residencies] allow me to stay in my life while I'm doing it," Styles told Apple Music's Zane Lowe back in March.

" I think it allows me to take care of myself better, which I think makes me better at doing the thing. "

"Treat people with kindness" isn't just the mantra behind one of Styles's best-known songs — it's an ethos that extends to himself as well as his crew.

For his recent New York dates, he took Manhattan three times a week for 10 weeks, accommodating personnel unwilling or unable to uproot their young children.

Here, Harry followed a path already worn by Celine Dion, Usher, Lady Gaga and Adele, artists who've used Vegas residencies to stay closer to home.

The Weekends With Adele concert series saw the UK star perform two shows per week at a Las Vegas casino from 2022 to 2024. (Getty Images: Kevin Mazur)

During Elvis Presley's infamous Vegas tenure, playing show after show in a row signalled creative stagnation. But, unlike Elvis, these contemporary residents appear to be calling the shots themselves.

Weekends with Adele conjured spectacle, intimacy and magical moments that, when disseminated on social media, kept the distant superstar in the public eye from 2022–2024.

Together, Together lands in Australia this week, with Styles playing Sydney and Melbourne. But multi-night residencies are nothing new here: they're already a drawcard at the Sydney Opera House.

"The artist is definitely doing us and the city a favour, and we're here to help realise their art in the best possible way for their audience," Sydney Opera House head of contemporary music Ben Marshall says.

Recently, the Opera House has welcomed Solange, Sufjan Stevens and Mitski. Soon, iconic Britpop outfit Suede will bring their unique vision to life on its stages.

"You can see the joy of it from an artist's perspective," Marshall says.

"They get to settle into the room; they're not having to schlep between cities … There's just a beautiful way, if it's an exclusive residency, of having the country come to them."

Rather than touring capital cities, Mitski drew fans to Sydney for a run of four sold-out Opera House performances in 2026. (Supplied: Jordan Munns)

Similarly, where Styles praises the model for combating malaise and producing better shows, a smaller-scale residency can push Opera House artists to experiment.

As Marshall says of the Redstar Wu's Neighbourhood Jams that award-winning Genesis Owusu conducted in September 2025: "That was a brilliant Australian artist prepared to do something really different."

"He wanted to try out the show in a round that was a model for much bigger rooms, and the [Opera House] Studio is a great place to do that."

Logistics in a post-pandemic world: Who pays the price?

Concert residencies big and small are a sign of the times.

"It's not like I'm saying I'll never travel again," Styles told Zane Lowe.

"But I want to see what it looks like if you do it a different way."

From Styles's perspective, it could look cost-effective. Ticketek Entertainment Group (TEG) told a 2024 parliamentary inquiry that touring expenses had increased by 30–40 per cent following the onset of COVID-19.

Jayden Roy, a promoter and booking agent at Australian live music promoter Destroy All Lines, witnesses these challenges firsthand.

More than one-third of Australian music festivals are not profitable, according to new data Just over half of Australian music festivals are actually turning a profit, according to new research from Creative Australia.

In a country known for its vast land mass and fragmented population, touring acts must consider inflation, travel, marketing, insurance, labour and venue hire.

"By the time you start adding all these things up, you're talking tens of thousands of dollars, and that's even just on a small-scale tour," Roy says.

Destroy All Lines promotes all manner of events, from Good Things Festival to Suede's upcoming residency. They've partnered with homegrown up-and-comers and acclaimed international acts like Deftones, Kesha and Interpol.

"As everything gets bigger, there are more challenges that also come with that, and that's where the gamble becomes more and more risky over time," Roy says.

" We've seen the rise of ticket pricing as well to meet with this demand. "

Roy is concerned that young people may miss out on live music amid a cost-of-living crisis.

According to industry body Live Performance Australia, average ticket prices have surged in recent years. Fans shouldered costs when Styles moved into Madison Square Garden.

The British entertainer has an estimated net worth of £235 million, around $462 million Aussie. Meanwhile, everyday punters were compelled to shell out for flights, accommodation and stadium seats — valued between $72.20 and $1,706.86 before dynamic and resale pricing was applied.

"You shouldn't have to give your whole paycheck [sic] to an artist just to see them live," one disgruntled fan posted on Reddit.

Harry Styles fans travelled from around the world to Wembley Stadium, where the pop star played a record-breaking 12 sold-out shows in June. (Getty Images: Carlo Paloni)

Musicians may have to toe a fine line, coordinating residencies alongside typical tours to avoid alienating fans.

Styles has already course-corrected, confirming a standard second leg of Together, Together with Kylie Minogue as one of the openers. Fatboy Slim and Rufus Wainwright have also scheduled tour-residency hybrids for 2027.

Bad Bunny implemented this same strategy 16 months ago.

The Latin trap king played 31 hometown shows in San Juan — shielding Spanish-speaking fans from ICE and injecting hundreds of millions of dollars into Puerto Rico's economy — before entertaining a further 3.1 million ticketholders worldwide.

"He's not only providing an amazing show for people; he's servicing his country," Roy says of the residency — perhaps a means of doing good while funding Bad Bunny's world tour.

"These acts need to find more ways to continue to be able to perform and still pay the bills, which is the same with a lot of older artists as well."

Whether it's Styles filling Madison Square Garden or Owusu testing new songs in a 600-seat studio, the logic is the same: stay still long enough, and the audience will come to you.

Harry Styles starts his Australian tour in Melbourne this Friday night.

World.title: Brisbane council racks up $2.5m on studies for bikeway promised 13 years ago
World.content:
PoliticsQueenslandCity life Brisbane council racks up $2.5m on studies for bikeway promised 13 years ago Felicity Caldwell November 25, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Brisbane City Council’s bill for planning a bikeway that was promised 13 years ago and is yet to be delivered has risen to almost $2.5 million. Under an agreement signed in 2013, the Queensland government delivered stages one to four of the North Brisbane Bikeway, from Herston to Wooloowin, completing those sections by early 2021. The council was responsible for stage five, which, when completed, would connect 40 kilometres of protected paths from the Brisbane CBD to Redcliffe. A section of the North Brisbane Bikeway delivered by the Queensland government. Felicity Caldwell But this final bikeway link has repeatedly stalled.



Figures released via a question on notice showed the council spent $2.49 million on consultation and design work for the North Brisbane Bikeway from 2017 to 2025. Related Article Exclusive

City life One-way traffic and 40km/h limits planned for notorious Toowong black spot However, early in 2025, the council dumped its plan for bike lanes north, on Dickson Street from Price Street, connecting via Keith, Sydney and Jackson streets before joining the Kedron Brook Bikeway. The council instead said it preferred a route that travelled west, including on Kent Road. This Kent Road alignment was the original route proposed in 2018, but rejected amid complaints about a loss of on-street parking.



In February 2025, when dumping the Dickson Street route, the council said it would seek funding from the state government to progress the Kent Road plan. At the time, Hamilton Councillor Julia Dixon said the bikeway was a “complex matter with varying opinions” and she was supportive, “along with the majority of residents, of Kent Road as the preferred alignment”. Twenty-one months later, the council has not secured state funding for the back-to-the-future Kent Road route. Following questions from this masthead, a council spokesman said the proposed Dickson Street alignment raised concerns among residents about traffic, parking and safety.



“We listened to those concerns and are backing the alternative Kent Road alignment,” he said. “We’ll also be seeking Queensland government funding to progress the Kent Road alignment of the North Brisbane Bikeway.” Instead of continuing the North Brisbane Bikeway along Dickson Street from Price Street, the Brisbane City Council plans to progress the bikeway west and onto Kent Road. Felicity Caldwell Community consultation in 2021 showed 60 per cent of the more than 1000 people who provided feedback supported the Dickson Street route. A Right to Information request for council documents, submitted by a bicycle user group, showed about 70 per cent of members of a community working group in 2024 also supported the Dickson Street route.



However, a minority of working group members did not support the alignment, arguing it would impact businesses and properties. “This minority were residents living on the alignment or immediately adjacent to, who are concerned about specific project elements that they perceive will impact their street and private properties, including worsening congestion, aesthetics of traffic-calming devices, the right-turn ban at Keith Street, and parking loss,” said a report prepared by staff conducting the consultation. Several fences along the proposed Dickson Street route have signs opposing the bikeway, and there has been fierce opposition to the route from some community members. Felicity Caldwell “Feedback was also received from members living on the alignment who supported the reference alignment and proposed design options, indicating a variety of views in the local community.” The community working group included seven residents from Clayfield, Wooloowin, Kalinga and Nundah, one businessperson, five people from community organisations, five active transport users, and two visitors to the area who travelled via private car or public transport.



Under a section of “Community engagement questions” in the working group documents from 2024, it said the Kent Road route previously proposed in 2018 did not progress because “it had significant impacts to parking on lower order residential streets and was not considered direct, accessible and legible to get to the Kedron Brook Bikeway”. The now-scrapped Dickson Street route for stage five of the North Brisbane Bikeway also included “green streets” and traffic-calming measures in streets such as Clayfield’s Jackson Street. Felicity Caldwell Labor council opposition leader Jared Cassidy was critical of the delay in the bikeway’s delivery. “Each day that active transport investment is stalled, ratepayers pay the price with more dollars spent on designs and more time lost stuck in congestion,” he said. World.title: ASX set to slip as Wall Street falls; Anthropic tumbles below IPO price, Nvidia slumps
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slip as Wall Street falls; Anthropic tumbles below IPO price, Nvidia slumps Stan Choe November 25, 2026 — 5:26am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Stocks tied to the artificial intelligence industry are dragging the US market lower after their surge from the day before quickly fizzled. That’s even though much of the rest of Wall Street is rising, along with confidence among Americans in the economy. The S&P 500 fell 0.3 per cent and is heading toward its eighth loss in the last nine days. Tech stocks once again led the way lower and dragged the Nasdaq composite down a market-leading 1.3 per cent, in early afternoon trade. Stocks outside of AI held up much better, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 441 points, or 0.9 per cent. AI stocks weighed down Wall Street on Tuesday after Monday’s Nvidia-driven surge. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to slip, with futures at 5.04am AEDT pointing to a loss 0f 6 points, or 0.1 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 1.8 per cent on Tuesday. The Australian dollar was stronger at US66.44¢. They’re the latest swings for a market that’s been mostly sinking since setting its all-time high last month. The primary worry is that prices for AI-related stocks shot too high into a possible bubble and need to deflate. That carries immense consequences for the broader market and workers’ retirement accounts because AI companies have grown into Wall Street’s most influential stocks.



While the surprise return of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO announced does bring back a charismatic leader who championed and helped build the entire AI industry, it does not settle the deep concerns dogging it. For one, doubts remain about whether AI can possibly produce enough profit and productivity to make the massive investments underway in data centres worth it. Related Article Opinion

AI Murky business: Batting for Jensen Huang’s return could backfire on Trump Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist At the same time, high interest rates make it more difficult to borrow money to pay for the industry’s growth. Sweeping victories for Democrats earlier this month in the US midterm elections, meanwhile, have raised concerns about more regulation for AI, including possible halts to further construction of data centres. To be sure, AI stocks and the broader US market have been prone to extreme reversals since the summer, not only week to week but even hour to hour. For now, at least, the momentum is back downward.



Nvidia fell 7.1 per cent a day after soaring 31.5 per cent to its biggest gain in more than two decades. Other stocks around the AI industry fell by similar amounts. CoreWeave, which buys Nvidia chips and rents out access to them over the cloud, sank 11.6 per cent. GE Vernova, which is helping to power AI data centres, dropped 4.6 per cent. And Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI chatbot, tumbled 7.4 per cent to drop below $US83. That’s how much Anthropic first sold its stock for in its initial public offering last week. The stock had briefly jumped as high as $US115 in its first day of trading amid a frenzy of hype. Such drops were powerful enough to drag the S&P 500 index lower even though the majority of stocks within the index climbed. They rose following the latest report to say confidence among US consumers is improving by more than economists expected. Confidence jumped sharply for Democrats and independents following the midterm election results, according to the Conference Board. That narrowed the wide gap between them and Republicans, whose confidence fell slightly. The results echo a preliminary report from the University of Michigan released earlier in the month, which also showed a jump in sentiment following the midterm elections and a drop in oil prices from late October.



Related Article Analysis

AI Jobs, Zuckerberg, now Huang. Tech still can’t quit its founder worship Companies in industries across the economy, meanwhile, continue to report strong growth in profits for the summer. Dollar Tree climbed 12.5 per cent after reporting better earnings for the latest quarter than analysts expected. The average shopper spent slightly more in its stores during the three months than a year earlier, and more of them came in than last year. Kohl’s rallied 18.9 per cent after reporting a profit for the latest quarter, when analysts were expecting basically zero. It also gave forecasts for revenue for the final three months of its fiscal year that were better than expected. Businesses in the S&P 500 are on pace to report overall growth in earnings per share of more than 25 per cent for a third straight quarter, according to FactSet. That’s a big deal because stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate profits and interest rates over the long term. But emotions of investors can also overwhelm them in the short term, as the last few weeks have demonstrated.



In the bond market, Treasury yields slipped as investors moved into investments seen as safer bets. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.91 per cent from 4.92 per cent late on Monday. That was despite a rise in oil prices, which tend to push upward on inflation and on bond yields. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 1.7 per cent to $US88.14. It’s been yo-yoing between $US72 and $US114 since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed across Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi jumped 6.3 per cent, and Japan’s Nikkei 225 rallied 3.9 per cent for two of the world’s bigger moves, as they caught up to Monday’s surge from Wall Street. World.title: Trump and Vance are clenched in a bear hug. It’s looking like a death roll
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Opinion Trump and Vance are clenched in a bear hug. It’s looking like a death roll Cory Alpert Former White House staffer November 25, 2026 — 5:05am

November 25, 2026 — 5:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

In the most recent lurch in the scandal surrounding Jensen Huang, Donald Trump did something unusual: he gave credit to someone else. According to Trump, JD Vance had been instrumental in getting the CEO of the world’s most valuable company back in his office, thereby restoring trillions of dollars to the sharemarket that the US president has spent two years prioritising over cost of living concerns for ordinary people. Donald Trump and JD Vance already appear at odds. Marija Ercegovac The vice president called out those affordability concerns in his midterm postmortem on social media site X, catching attention for his candour in blaming the election results on the administration’s prolonged war in Iran. Trump, who has rarely taken well to criticism, has been remarkably accommodating to Vance’s analysis so far, calling his initial post “largely true”.



Vance is caught up in the same bear hug with Trump that dragged a generation of Republican politicians to their party’s worst defeat since Watergate. For much of the past two years the vice president has been the frontrunner for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination, but polling shows his standing has plummeted since the midterms. Related Article Opinion

Billionaires I’ve spent time with tech oligarchs – you have no idea just how weird they are Cory Alpert Former White House staffer Now, Vance must try to build a new layer to Trump’s politics that will allow the MAGA movement to live beyond Trump. His midterm postmortem conceded that Trump had deviated from the politics that bear his name. The political movement that Vance is seeking to inherit began in earnest in 2008, when Sarah Palin emerged as the Republican nominee for vice president, harnessing a brand of ignorance as a virtue, where distance from elite institutions became evidence of authenticity. That strain of conservative populism became the Tea Party in 2010, a movement later harnessed by Trump.



MAGA has never had a coherent ideology beyond Trump’s moveable instincts. Vance’s attempts to articulate a post-Trump vision of MAGA means setting principles that, almost by definition, Trump will violate. Vance is the first Republican to be able to make a credible attempt at this. He has the necessary combination of intelligence, demonstrated loyalty, visible leadership, and a credible path to be elected president when Trump steps aside. Photo: Matt Golding Trump chose Vance as his running mate because presidential candidates need balance on their ticket. Institutionalists pick firebrands. Trump, the firebrand, picked Mike Pence in 2016 to court the evangelical voters nervous about Trump’s irreligious history. Vance brought with him a constituency of power rather than a constituency of voters. His relationships with Silicon Valley run deep, securing the merger between Trump’s political project and the power ambitions of the world’s most valuable companies.





Jensen Huang’s ouster from Nvidia and the accompanying share sell-off were an existential crisis for Trump, given his focus on the performance of a handful of technology companies. Vance is having to weigh the interests of the power base that sent him to Washington with those of the voters whose trust he will need to earn. Which is all without mentioning the very real possibility that Trump was protecting his own assets, given that he traded as much as $US97.5 million ($147 million) in Nvidia stock since his return to the White House. That includes a sale of up to $US1 million in the days after Trump was told about Huang’s relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. The performance by Trump and Vance is getting louder and more frantic. If Vance strikes out to define the structure of MAGA they might enter a death roll.



If Vance is unable to escape the bear hug and create enough distance to win over voters who have soured on Trump, he will suffer the same fate as the Republicans mauled in the midterms. In the race to succeed Trump and to lead his movement, Trump may yet give Vance the space he needs to define the new rules. But that may not be enough to hold onto the voters who gave them power in the first place. Cory Alpert is a PhD researcher at the University of Melbourne looking at the impact of AI on democracy. He previously served in the Biden-Harris administration. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: ASIC following up on more allegations of misconduct by consulting giants
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesConsulting ASIC following up on more allegations of misconduct by consulting giants Colin Kruger November 25, 2026 — 5:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The corporate regulator is investigating 35 allegations of serious misconduct following a probe of Australia’s audit giants, and is referring other complaints to professional bodies for further investigation. The action comes after the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) uncovered 558 audit-related complaints earlier this year, having used its compulsory information gathering powers to access internal complaints at consultants KPMG, EY, Deloitte and PwC staff in the three years from July 2023. ASIC has stepped up its surveillance of the Big Four audit firms after KPMG’s whistleblower scandal. Paul Rovere “ASIC has identified 35 complaints involving potential statutory audit conduct issues or misuse of audit client information from a review of internal complaints at Australia’s four largest audit firms,” the regulator said. “Some complaints contained serious allegations of misconduct that ASIC is examining through enforcement and targeted industry surveillance work.”



The surveillance was conducted by ASIC in response to the KPMG scandal this year, where a whistleblower alleged senior partners misused confidential client information to win new audit business. Some of the allegations have now been substantiated, senior KPMG executives have been forced to resign and hundreds of jobs have been slashed as lucrative clients like Macquarie Group walked away from the firm. Related Article Whistleblowers KPMG consultant admits to ‘gaps’ in its whistleblower report ASIC did not say whether the latest complaints related to all four audit firms dominating Australia’s corporate landscape and boardrooms. ASIC’s report said there have also been other issues identified which relate to matters it is already investigating, including “several matters which have been referred for consideration as part of our existing investigations into KPMG about misstatements in transparency reporting”.



This relates to KPMG allegedly failing to report internal whistleblower complaints. ASIC highlighted the seriousness of the latest allegations, given these four firms audit more than 94 per cent of Australia’s listed companies by market valuation, and 85 per cent of registrable superannuation entities. “Auditors are gatekeepers to Australia’s financial markets. Investors, businesses and superannuation members rely on them to scrutinise financial information with independence, integrity and professional scepticism,” ASIC Commissioner Kate O’Rourke said. ASIC Commissioner Kate O’Rourke during a Senate estimates hearing at Parliament House in Canberra. Alex Ellinghausen O’Rourke said some of the issues identified from the internal complaints include directions to not escalate audit concerns, failure to escalate material audit issues, breaches of confidentiality and victimisation of employees who reported issues.



“Internal complaints can provide valuable intelligence regarding deficiencies with how statutory audits are conducted. Audit firms should carefully and thoroughly interrogate complaints to identify and address these issues,” O’Rourke said. ASIC noted there are no regulatory provisions directly governing how audit firms handle internal complaints and said it did not investigate every complaint in detail, or reach findings about every person mentioned in the complaints. Related Article Updated

Consulting KPMG set to slash hundreds more jobs before Christmas Most of the 558 complaints fell outside ASIC’s regulatory powers. It said some of the allegations, which include bullying and sexual harassment, have been referred to other regulators – including Chartered Accountants ANZ, CPA Australia and the Tax Practitioners Board for possible breaches of professional and ethical standards. ASIC said it has already released information in relation to a number of individuals, and is continuing to engage with these other regulators around additional matters of potential interest.



The corporate watchdog said its work is ongoing, and it will continue to communicate the outcomes of any further regulatory action. Just last week, KPMG said it is cutting 230 jobs as the fallout from the whistleblower scandal continues. The job cuts are mostly in its consulting division, with smaller cuts in supporting areas and the team that advises companies on corporate deals. “We must align our business with client demand. This is a necessary step towards renewing and rebuilding our firm,” KPMG’s recently appointed chief executive John Sams said. State and federal governments have banned KPMG from winning new work since the full scale of the whistleblower scandal became clear.
