World.title: Should I pay extra off my mortgage, or put it in an offset account?
World.content:
MoneyBorrowingAsk an expert Opinion Should I pay extra off my mortgage, or put it in an offset account? Noel Whittaker Money columnist November 25, 2026 — 5:01am

November 25, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

I have a home mortgage and am fortunate enough to have some spare money each month. I am wondering whether I would be better off making additional repayments directly into the mortgage or depositing the money into a mortgage offset account. My main aim is to reduce the interest I pay and get the loan paid off as quickly as possible. Is one option more effective than the other, or do they achieve essentially the same result? Provided you have a 100 per cent offset account, both options generally produce the same interest savings, assuming the mortgage interest rate is identical. The main difference is how easily you can access your money. Paying more off your mortgage directly may reduce the amount owed, but it can keep your money frozen for longer. Simon Letch An offset account is a separate bank account linked to your mortgage, and every dollar in it reduces the loan balance on which interest is calculated. The money remains yours and can generally be withdrawn whenever you wish, just like an ordinary bank account. By contrast, additional repayments go directly into your mortgage, reducing the amount owing. Many loans offer a redraw facility that allows you to withdraw those extra repayments if needed, but access is subject to the lender’s terms and conditions.



The lender may impose minimum withdrawal amounts, fees or restrictions, and in some circumstances may reduce or suspend access to redraw funds. This makes redraw less flexible than having the money sitting in your own offset account. The other consideration is cost. Lenders often charge higher interest rates or additional fees for loans with offset facilities. It may be worthwhile talking to a mortgage broker to see whether you could refinance to a cheaper loan without an offset account. The savings from a lower interest rate could outweigh the convenience of an offset facility. Whichever option you choose, keeping your regular repayments unchanged while reducing the interest charged will help you pay off the mortgage faster. We are a married couple and all our bank accounts, credit cards, debit cards and other assets are held jointly. We are both authorised signatories on the accounts. If my husband dies, will I be able to continue operating the accounts and using the cards as normal, or will the bank freeze them until his estate is finalised? I would like to understand what happens in practice and whether there is anything we should arrange now to avoid problems for the surviving spouse. The good news is that genuinely joint bank accounts are generally not frozen when one account holder dies. The surviving spouse can usually continue operating the account, and the deceased’s interest in the money normally passes automatically to the survivor.



However, the bank will need to be notified of the death and may require a death certificate before changing the account into the survivor’s sole name. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert I’m retired with two super funds. Should I move both into pension mode? Paul Benson Money contributor Credit cards are a different matter. Many couples believe they have joint credit cards when, in fact, one spouse is the primary cardholder and the other is merely an additional cardholder. If the primary cardholder dies, the account will generally be closed and the additional card will cease to operate. Debit cards issued in the deceased’s name will also be cancelled, although the surviving spouse should be able to continue using their own debit card linked to a joint account. Other jointly owned assets, such as the family home, will generally pass automatically to the survivor if held as joint tenants. However, assets held as tenants in common are treated differently and the deceased’s share forms part of their estate.



My advice is to check with your bank now that your accounts are genuinely joint, establish who is the primary holder of each credit card, and make sure each spouse has access to sufficient funds independently. A little preparation now could save a great deal of inconvenience at an already difficult time. I am retired and turn 65 in December. I have approximately $1.8 million in accumulation-phase superannuation, and I am considering converting as much as possible into an account-based pension to provide a regular income stream. I also receive a defined benefit pension of approximately $40,000 a year. My concern is how this existing pension will affect the amount I can transfer into retirement phase, given the current transfer balance cap of $2.1 million. How is my defined benefit pension assessed against the cap, and what options do I have to maximise the amount I can hold in retirement phase? Your defined benefit pension counts towards your transfer balance cap, generally at a “special value” of 16 times the annual pension entitlement at commencement. The general transfer balance cap is currently $2.1 million, but your personal cap may be lower because your pension has already commenced. Before starting an account-based pension, check your transfer balance account on the ATO portal to confirm how much cap space you have available.



I am 81 and have approximately $80,000 in superannuation. I recently read an article stating that superannuation does not automatically form part of a deceased person’s estate, which has made me concerned about what will happen to my money when I die. My will clearly sets out who should inherit my assets, and I want to make sure my remaining superannuation goes to those beneficiaries. Editor's pick Opinion

Gender pay gap Women are retiring with $51,000 less in super. Here’s how to fight back Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor Would it be safer to withdraw the $80,000 from superannuation now and deposit it into my bank account so it forms part of my estate, or is there a way to ensure my superannuation is distributed according to my wishes without withdrawing it? It is the trustee of your superannuation fund who has the final say as to where the proceeds are distributed. You can take some control over this process by lodging a binding death benefit nomination with your fund. But considering the relatively small amount you have in super and your age, it may be simpler to withdraw the whole sum tax-free now and place that in an interest-bearing account.



Also bear in mind that the taxable component of your superannuation left to a non-dependent, and at your age, I would imagine your beneficiary would be non-dependents, has a death tax of 17 per cent. But drawing the money now means your beneficiaries don’t suffer that tax. Noel Whittaker is the author of Retirement Made Simple and other books on personal finance. Email: noel@noelwhittaker.com.au. World.title: Paying for aged care just got a lot fairer – but crunch the numbers carefully
World.content:
MoneySuper & retirementAged care Opinion Paying for aged care just got a lot fairer – but crunch the numbers carefully Rachel Lane Money contributor November 25, 2026 — 5:01am

November 25, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The 2025 aged care reforms removed an important choice for new residents: how they pay for their accommodation. Those who were yet to complete a means assessment or declare themselves as ‘means not disclosed’ were unable to pay a lump sum refundable accommodation deposit (RAD). Instead, they were forced to pay a daily accommodation payment (DAP). The DAP is calculated using a government-set interest rate, currently 8.51 per cent, on any unpaid RAD. For someone with a $750,000 RAD, that means paying around $175 a day – or $5300 a month – pending their means assessment. How you pay for your aged care accommodation is a big financial decision. Getty It created an expensive dilemma. Residents could either pay thousands of dollars in daily payments or declare themselves ‘means not disclosed’ so they could pay the RAD. But being means not disclosed makes you liable for the maximum means-tested fees, the hotelling fee and non-clinical care contribution, totalling $132 a day. For many residents, the problem wasn’t confined to just the cost of aged care. The inability to pay the RAD was also negatively affecting their pension payments.



Consider a couple, one moving into aged care, with $750,000 in the bank, ready to pay a RAD. While waiting for their means assessment, they are paying $175 a day in daily accommodation payments. Editor's pick Opinion

Aged care No room at the inn: The Christmas aged care shortage stressing families Rachel Lane Money contributor The money in the bank is also reducing their age pension by $2250 a fortnight. Once their assessment is completed, the means-tested hotelling and non-clinical care contributions will be $39 a day. If they declare themselves means not disclosed, they can pay the RAD and avoid the DAPs and the reduction in their age pension – saving almost $10,200 a month. But there is a catch: they have to pay the maximum means-tested fees of $132 a day, rather than $39. If they can crunch all the numbers they will see that they are still better off by about $3000 a month. The situation was both complex and costly. But finally, sense has prevailed. From 1 November, residents can again choose to pay their accommodation by lump sum, daily payment or a combination of both while waiting for their means assessment.



Of course, paying a RAD is not the right decision for everyone. The money is tied up in the aged care home while you live there, and a retention fee of 2 per cent a year applies for up to five years. If you are selling the family home to pay the RAD, there is a lot more that you need to consider, including the pension and aged care means test concessions you are giving up. How you pay for your aged care accommodation is a big financial decision. It is a decision that can affect your pension, other aged care fees, cash flow and your estate planning wishes. Now that choice has been restored, choose wisely. Rachel Lane is the author of Downsizing Made Simple, a book and website aimed at demystifying downsizing. World.title: I’m legally blind and can’t seem to land a job. How can I increase my chances?
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsGot a Minute? I’m legally blind and can’t seem to land a job. How can I increase my chances? Kirstin Ferguson November 25, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Each week, Dr Kirstin Ferguson tackles questions about workplace, career and leadership in her advice column Got a Minute? This week: concerns about a growing CV gap, accusing a colleague of lying and an early morning meeting. There is no need to turn a job interview into a recount of your medical history. Dionne Gain I’m in my early 40s and am legally blind due to a progressive eye condition. I’ve worked in teaching and administration, and loved my job at a not-for-profit until restructures and changes to my role meant I needed to leave. A later role wasn’t the right fit, partly because I was still learning what workplace adjustments I needed. I’ve been job hunting since January and applying seriously since April. I tailor every application, have approached employers and recruiters directly, and have sought specialist support. So far, four interviews have led nowhere. I’m worried about the growing gap on my CV and my references getting stale. Should I apply for more jobs, retrain or change my approach entirely? While it may not feel like it, achieving four interviews shows that employers can find value in your experience. The job now is to consider whether something else is impacting your ability to get the role. Have you asked the interviewers for specific feedback? Was it the examples of experience you provided, a missing skill they needed or how the role would work with adjustments? Some will not respond, but even one useful answer beats guessing or making assumptions. You might like to ask someone you trust to review one application and practise an interview with you. Prepare a concise explanation of your employment gap and a clear account of the tools or adjustments that help you do the job. You need not turn an interview into a recount of your medical history.



Related Article Got a Minute? Should I tell my boss’s wife he’s having an affair with a colleague? You might like to also search JobAccess for an Inclusive Employment Australia provider with experience in vision loss, and ask a JobAccess adviser about recruitment adjustments and equipment funding. For suitable Federal public service vacancies, check whether RecruitAbility applies and request accessible assessment methods where needed. These routes do not guarantee a job, but they may remove barriers unrelated to your vision loss. To avoid feeling your former referees are going stale, keep them updated on the progress of your job search with a short update. This way as time gets further away from when you last worked together, they will understand your job search remains an active process. I think my colleague’s “miscarriage” may have been a lie. My colleague took extended compassionate leave after telling our manager she had suffered a miscarriage. I later overheard her laughing with a friend about the overseas holiday she took during the same period. I may have misunderstood what I heard, but our exhausted team carried her workload and donated money for meals. Is it cruel to question her story — or dishonest to say nothing?



Related Article Got a Minute? I overheard two execs making fun of employees’ accents and weight. What do I do? Looks like another question where I have no choice but to shout. YES, IT IS CRUEL TO QUESTION HER STORY. MIND YOUR OWN BUSINESS. Just because a woman has a miscarriage doesn’t mean they can’t laugh with friends, travel overseas or do anything else they may choose to do to overcome their loss. How a woman deals with anything that happens to her body is entirely her business. None of it – not one bit – needs to be explained to you. I am sure she was grateful that your team helped manage her workload and helped with meals while she was gone. Next time, when it is you who may need support, I am sure it will be you who will be grateful when she returns the favour. I am sure you will also be pleased to not have her question whether the support is warranted.



Our manager has decided that our twice-weekly team meetings, formerly held at 10am, will now start at 8am. Everyone else is delighted, as it means leaving work an hour earlier at the end of the day, but I am not an early morning person and really struggle to make it in on time. While my co-workers are bright-eyed and bushy-tailed around the table, I am sluggish and find it difficult to keep up. I am worried it is going to impact my career. What should I do? If your only argument is you are “not a morning person” then you probably have a slim chance of persuading your manager to alter an arrangement that seems to suit everyone else. Instead of fighting against the change, I think you will need to find ways to make it work for you. That might mean you need to prepare your updates or questions the afternoon before, to help you be your best in the meeting itself. I would try a month of these earlier times and see how you go. Your body is bound to adjust. To submit a question about work, careers or leadership, visit kirstinferguson.com/ask. You will not be asked to provide your name or any identifying information. World.title: Footnotes, villains and a redacted donkey: Is this book about to save literature?
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

If there’s one place you should be safe from audience participation, it’s when reading a book. Not any more. Early on in Jasper Fforde’s Dark Reading Matter the author makes a request of his readers – no matter where you are, or what you are doing, if you see text appear in a certain font, could you please read it aloud. The first time I see this I’m at home, and despite being the sort of person who strategically positions herself in comedy shows for minimal interaction, or who got through school choir by half-heartedly miming, I find myself gingerly speaking the words aloud: “Oh my goodness, they’ve trodden on the gibbon.” Dark Reading Matter is the eighth and final book in the Thursday Next series. It started in 2001 with Fforde’s debut novel, The Eyre Affair, and tracks the titular Thursday Next, a detective, as she fights battles of varying surreality against corporations, corruption and, on occasion, Enid Blyton characters. “I think that the real jumping-off point for this book was that I dedicated it to readers,” says Fforde. “If you’ve been reading my series for the last 25 years, this is for us … and we’re going to have some fun.” Author Jasper Fforde Mari Fforde The series has always been meta – the main character lives in an alternate version of our world, and within her world she discovers that books aren’t simply objects containing words; they’re the output of the BookWorld, where all the characters are real and performing books kind of like a play. Beyond that they have their own society and lives and, yes, a police force, which is there to stop things going off the rails. In the final novel, however, Fforde takes the opportunity to shake off all shackles and see what truly is possible with the written word. Our world is suddenly a new layer on top of things, we the reader have a role to play – thus the speaking aloud – and Fforde himself turns up in the book – well, sort of. “He’s awful!” says Fforde with a laugh. “I mean, he’s a terrible human being.”



The techniques Fforde uses in all his books push at the boundaries of what we expect. His novels throw you in the deep end, with their seemingly chaotic blend of wordplay, adventure and hard truths – but it’s at 3am, when you realise you haven’t been able to put the book down, that you realise how intricately put together it all is. There’s a reason for the seemingly random illustration at the front. That isn’t just any donkey on the cover. And the gibbon is important. Under all the fun and the wordplay his books all take on deeper themes; they’re about free will, they fight against unchecked authority and they advocate for what is fair and right. Here is no different – what on the surface may seem like silliness is actually a battle cry. Dark Reading Matter is first and foremost a joy to read and a love letter to the readers who have come on this decades-long journey with Fforde and his fictional detective Thursday Next – but at its core it’s a fight for the future of literature. Dark Reading Matter comes at an existential moment for literature; at a time when physical stories are being literally cut up and fed into machines to teach AI how to write. Photo: The key antagonist of the story, Roger Thatt, is trying to gain access to the “dark reading matter” – not the BookWorld but all the bits from around the edge. It’s the place where all ideas and potential ideas go; memories, thoughts, discarded drafts. Thatt wants to harvest it all, to monetise it, to control inspiration. This novel manages to explore the threat of AI without being preachy or dull – a miraculous achievement in a saturated conversation – and manages to do it through both plot and structure. “I was out to write a book that AI could not scrape. It could not scrape this. It could not understand it,” he says. It’s true – what would artificial intelligence make of conversations that happen purely in the footnotes, which in the book are used as a communication system? How would it navigate the narrative impact of font changes? Or, stepping back, would the character names – including Landen Parke-Laine, Acheron Hades and Jack Schitt – and the entire blend of pop culture, history and puns that go into creating them even be a possibility? “It can’t think up new stuff. It can only take old stuff and repackage it,” he says.



Before he was an author, Fforde was in the film industry, working as a focus puller. He started at age 19, and across a 20-year career worked on films including GoldenEye, Entrapment and The Mask of Zorro, but it was a volatile industry. “The jobs could dry up literally any moment.” He started writing short stories at the age of 27, and across the next 12 years “I had five books written and [none published]. No one interested at all.” He found a strange freedom in the rejection, however, and started writing The Eyre Affair. “I thought, well, it doesn’t matter what I write because I’m not going to be published. So I’m just writing for fun.” The manuscript was “fun and silly, and it just mixes everything together – literary theory and vampires and werewolves and everything else”. The resulting book deal was enough that Fforde could stop work. His final project was an ad featuring Leonardo DiCaprio – “and the following week I was an author”. The Eyre Affair was an instant hit and became a New York Times bestseller. Though Fforde is still a keen photographer and still working in the creative industries, there is both a wistfulness and an edge of concern when he talks about the film industry. “I miss it a lot,” he says. The threat of AI is looming, though. “If I was in the film industry now, I would be thinking it’s all over for us,” he reflects. “If I was an actor or a filmmaker I would be terrified.” He pauses. “Or, alternatively, I would be thinking I need to start a theatre troupe. You know – this could be the greatest resurgence of theatre that the world may ever see.” Fforde has been pushing boundaries, subverting expectations and challenging himself with every book he writes. The Constant Rabbit is a novel that takes on nationalism and Brexit specifically while also being about anthropomorphised rabbits. His first standalone novel Early Riser imagines a world where the human race hibernates for months each year. The Shades of Grey novels take on discrimination and class through a society that ranks people based on what colours they can perceive. There is another, quieter thread that laces through the latter half of Dark Reading Matter, in a non-fiction detour where a version of Fforde himself is the protagonist. He reflects on articles he’s read, on his writing, and in one section recalls drives with his mother “during her latter years when the Alzheimer’s became momentarily not the debilitation that it was, but a gift that could keep on giving: I could take her on these drives each week and every time she would enjoy it as though the first”, he writes.

World.title: Brisbane council racks up $2.5m on studies for bikeway promised 13 years ago
World.content:
PoliticsQueenslandCity life Brisbane council racks up $2.5m on studies for bikeway promised 13 years ago Felicity Caldwell November 25, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Brisbane City Council’s bill for planning a bikeway that was promised 13 years ago and is yet to be delivered has risen to almost $2.5 million. Under an agreement signed in 2013, the Queensland government delivered stages one to four of the North Brisbane Bikeway, from Herston to Wooloowin, completing those sections by early 2021. The council was responsible for stage five, which, when completed, would connect 40 kilometres of protected paths from the Brisbane CBD to Redcliffe. A section of the North Brisbane Bikeway delivered by the Queensland government. Felicity Caldwell But this final bikeway link has repeatedly stalled.



Figures released via a question on notice showed the council spent $2.49 million on consultation and design work for the North Brisbane Bikeway from 2017 to 2025. Related Article Exclusive

City life One-way traffic and 40km/h limits planned for notorious Toowong black spot However, early in 2025, the council dumped its plan for bike lanes north, on Dickson Street from Price Street, connecting via Keith, Sydney and Jackson streets before joining the Kedron Brook Bikeway. The council instead said it preferred a route that travelled west, including on Kent Road. This Kent Road alignment was the original route proposed in 2018, but rejected amid complaints about a loss of on-street parking.



In February 2025, when dumping the Dickson Street route, the council said it would seek funding from the state government to progress the Kent Road plan. At the time, Hamilton Councillor Julia Dixon said the bikeway was a “complex matter with varying opinions” and she was supportive, “along with the majority of residents, of Kent Road as the preferred alignment”. Twenty-one months later, the council has not secured state funding for the back-to-the-future Kent Road route. Following questions from this masthead, a council spokesman said the proposed Dickson Street alignment raised concerns among residents about traffic, parking and safety.



“We listened to those concerns and are backing the alternative Kent Road alignment,” he said. “We’ll also be seeking Queensland government funding to progress the Kent Road alignment of the North Brisbane Bikeway.” Instead of continuing the North Brisbane Bikeway along Dickson Street from Price Street, the Brisbane City Council plans to progress the bikeway west and onto Kent Road. Felicity Caldwell Community consultation in 2021 showed 60 per cent of the more than 1000 people who provided feedback supported the Dickson Street route. A Right to Information request for council documents, submitted by a bicycle user group, showed about 70 per cent of members of a community working group in 2024 also supported the Dickson Street route.



However, a minority of working group members did not support the alignment, arguing it would impact businesses and properties. “This minority were residents living on the alignment or immediately adjacent to, who are concerned about specific project elements that they perceive will impact their street and private properties, including worsening congestion, aesthetics of traffic-calming devices, the right-turn ban at Keith Street, and parking loss,” said a report prepared by staff conducting the consultation. Several fences along the proposed Dickson Street route have signs opposing the bikeway, and there has been fierce opposition to the route from some community members. Felicity Caldwell “Feedback was also received from members living on the alignment who supported the reference alignment and proposed design options, indicating a variety of views in the local community.” The community working group included seven residents from Clayfield, Wooloowin, Kalinga and Nundah, one businessperson, five people from community organisations, five active transport users, and two visitors to the area who travelled via private car or public transport.



Under a section of “Community engagement questions” in the working group documents from 2024, it said the Kent Road route previously proposed in 2018 did not progress because “it had significant impacts to parking on lower order residential streets and was not considered direct, accessible and legible to get to the Kedron Brook Bikeway”. The now-scrapped Dickson Street route for stage five of the North Brisbane Bikeway also included “green streets” and traffic-calming measures in streets such as Clayfield’s Jackson Street. Felicity Caldwell Labor council opposition leader Jared Cassidy was critical of the delay in the bikeway’s delivery. “Each day that active transport investment is stalled, ratepayers pay the price with more dollars spent on designs and more time lost stuck in congestion,” he said. World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slip as Wall Street falls; Anthropic tumbles below IPO price, Nvidia slumps Stan Choe November 25, 2026 — 5:26am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Stocks tied to the artificial intelligence industry are dragging the US market lower after their surge from the day before quickly fizzled. That’s even though much of the rest of Wall Street is rising, along with confidence among Americans in the economy. The S&P 500 fell 0.3 per cent and is heading toward its eighth loss in the last nine days. Tech stocks once again led the way lower and dragged the Nasdaq composite down a market-leading 1.3 per cent, in early afternoon trade. Stocks outside of AI held up much better, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 441 points, or 0.9 per cent. AI stocks weighed down Wall Street on Tuesday after Monday’s Nvidia-driven surge. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to slip, with futures at 5.04am AEDT pointing to a loss 0f 6 points, or 0.1 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 1.8 per cent on Tuesday. The Australian dollar was stronger at US66.44¢. They’re the latest swings for a market that’s been mostly sinking since setting its all-time high last month. The primary worry is that prices for AI-related stocks shot too high into a possible bubble and need to deflate. That carries immense consequences for the broader market and workers’ retirement accounts because AI companies have grown into Wall Street’s most influential stocks.



While the surprise return of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO announced does bring back a charismatic leader who championed and helped build the entire AI industry, it does not settle the deep concerns dogging it. For one, doubts remain about whether AI can possibly produce enough profit and productivity to make the massive investments underway in data centres worth it. Related Article Opinion

AI Murky business: Batting for Jensen Huang’s return could backfire on Trump Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist At the same time, high interest rates make it more difficult to borrow money to pay for the industry’s growth. Sweeping victories for Democrats earlier this month in the US midterm elections, meanwhile, have raised concerns about more regulation for AI, including possible halts to further construction of data centres. To be sure, AI stocks and the broader US market have been prone to extreme reversals since the summer, not only week to week but even hour to hour. For now, at least, the momentum is back downward.



Nvidia fell 7.1 per cent a day after soaring 31.5 per cent to its biggest gain in more than two decades. Other stocks around the AI industry fell by similar amounts. CoreWeave, which buys Nvidia chips and rents out access to them over the cloud, sank 11.6 per cent. GE Vernova, which is helping to power AI data centres, dropped 4.6 per cent. And Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI chatbot, tumbled 7.4 per cent to drop below $US83. That’s how much Anthropic first sold its stock for in its initial public offering last week. The stock had briefly jumped as high as $US115 in its first day of trading amid a frenzy of hype. Such drops were powerful enough to drag the S&P 500 index lower even though the majority of stocks within the index climbed. They rose following the latest report to say confidence among US consumers is improving by more than economists expected. Confidence jumped sharply for Democrats and independents following the midterm election results, according to the Conference Board. That narrowed the wide gap between them and Republicans, whose confidence fell slightly. The results echo a preliminary report from the University of Michigan released earlier in the month, which also showed a jump in sentiment following the midterm elections and a drop in oil prices from late October.



Related Article Analysis

AI Jobs, Zuckerberg, now Huang. Tech still can’t quit its founder worship Companies in industries across the economy, meanwhile, continue to report strong growth in profits for the summer. Dollar Tree climbed 12.5 per cent after reporting better earnings for the latest quarter than analysts expected. The average shopper spent slightly more in its stores during the three months than a year earlier, and more of them came in than last year. Kohl’s rallied 18.9 per cent after reporting a profit for the latest quarter, when analysts were expecting basically zero. It also gave forecasts for revenue for the final three months of its fiscal year that were better than expected. Businesses in the S&P 500 are on pace to report overall growth in earnings per share of more than 25 per cent for a third straight quarter, according to FactSet. That’s a big deal because stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate profits and interest rates over the long term. But emotions of investors can also overwhelm them in the short term, as the last few weeks have demonstrated.



In the bond market, Treasury yields slipped as investors moved into investments seen as safer bets. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.91 per cent from 4.92 per cent late on Monday. That was despite a rise in oil prices, which tend to push upward on inflation and on bond yields. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 1.7 per cent to $US88.14. It’s been yo-yoing between $US72 and $US114 since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed across Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi jumped 6.3 per cent, and Japan’s Nikkei 225 rallied 3.9 per cent for two of the world’s bigger moves, as they caught up to Monday’s surge from Wall Street. World.title: Trump and Vance are clenched in a bear hug. It’s looking like a death roll
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Opinion Trump and Vance are clenched in a bear hug. It’s looking like a death roll Cory Alpert Former White House staffer November 25, 2026 — 5:05am

November 25, 2026 — 5:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

In the most recent lurch in the scandal surrounding Jensen Huang, Donald Trump did something unusual: he gave credit to someone else. According to Trump, JD Vance had been instrumental in getting the CEO of the world’s most valuable company back in his office, thereby restoring trillions of dollars to the sharemarket that the US president has spent two years prioritising over cost of living concerns for ordinary people. Donald Trump and JD Vance already appear at odds. Marija Ercegovac The vice president called out those affordability concerns in his midterm postmortem on social media site X, catching attention for his candour in blaming the election results on the administration’s prolonged war in Iran. Trump, who has rarely taken well to criticism, has been remarkably accommodating to Vance’s analysis so far, calling his initial post “largely true”.



Vance is caught up in the same bear hug with Trump that dragged a generation of Republican politicians to their party’s worst defeat since Watergate. For much of the past two years the vice president has been the frontrunner for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination, but polling shows his standing has plummeted since the midterms. Related Article Opinion

Billionaires I’ve spent time with tech oligarchs – you have no idea just how weird they are Cory Alpert Former White House staffer Now, Vance must try to build a new layer to Trump’s politics that will allow the MAGA movement to live beyond Trump. His midterm postmortem conceded that Trump had deviated from the politics that bear his name. The political movement that Vance is seeking to inherit began in earnest in 2008, when Sarah Palin emerged as the Republican nominee for vice president, harnessing a brand of ignorance as a virtue, where distance from elite institutions became evidence of authenticity. That strain of conservative populism became the Tea Party in 2010, a movement later harnessed by Trump.



MAGA has never had a coherent ideology beyond Trump’s moveable instincts. Vance’s attempts to articulate a post-Trump vision of MAGA means setting principles that, almost by definition, Trump will violate. Vance is the first Republican to be able to make a credible attempt at this. He has the necessary combination of intelligence, demonstrated loyalty, visible leadership, and a credible path to be elected president when Trump steps aside. Photo: Matt Golding Trump chose Vance as his running mate because presidential candidates need balance on their ticket. Institutionalists pick firebrands. Trump, the firebrand, picked Mike Pence in 2016 to court the evangelical voters nervous about Trump’s irreligious history. Vance brought with him a constituency of power rather than a constituency of voters. His relationships with Silicon Valley run deep, securing the merger between Trump’s political project and the power ambitions of the world’s most valuable companies.





Jensen Huang’s ouster from Nvidia and the accompanying share sell-off were an existential crisis for Trump, given his focus on the performance of a handful of technology companies. Vance is having to weigh the interests of the power base that sent him to Washington with those of the voters whose trust he will need to earn. Which is all without mentioning the very real possibility that Trump was protecting his own assets, given that he traded as much as $US97.5 million ($147 million) in Nvidia stock since his return to the White House. That includes a sale of up to $US1 million in the days after Trump was told about Huang’s relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. The performance by Trump and Vance is getting louder and more frantic. If Vance strikes out to define the structure of MAGA they might enter a death roll.



If Vance is unable to escape the bear hug and create enough distance to win over voters who have soured on Trump, he will suffer the same fate as the Republicans mauled in the midterms. In the race to succeed Trump and to lead his movement, Trump may yet give Vance the space he needs to define the new rules. But that may not be enough to hold onto the voters who gave them power in the first place. Cory Alpert is a PhD researcher at the University of Melbourne looking at the impact of AI on democracy. He previously served in the Biden-Harris administration. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: ASIC following up on more allegations of misconduct by consulting giants
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesConsulting ASIC following up on more allegations of misconduct by consulting giants Colin Kruger November 25, 2026 — 5:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The corporate regulator is investigating 35 allegations of serious misconduct following a probe of Australia’s audit giants, and is referring other complaints to professional bodies for further investigation. The action comes after the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) uncovered 558 audit-related complaints earlier this year, having used its compulsory information gathering powers to access internal complaints at consultants KPMG, EY, Deloitte and PwC staff in the three years from July 2023. ASIC has stepped up its surveillance of the Big Four audit firms after KPMG’s whistleblower scandal. Paul Rovere “ASIC has identified 35 complaints involving potential statutory audit conduct issues or misuse of audit client information from a review of internal complaints at Australia’s four largest audit firms,” the regulator said. “Some complaints contained serious allegations of misconduct that ASIC is examining through enforcement and targeted industry surveillance work.”



The surveillance was conducted by ASIC in response to the KPMG scandal this year, where a whistleblower alleged senior partners misused confidential client information to win new audit business. Some of the allegations have now been substantiated, senior KPMG executives have been forced to resign and hundreds of jobs have been slashed as lucrative clients like Macquarie Group walked away from the firm. Related Article Whistleblowers KPMG consultant admits to ‘gaps’ in its whistleblower report ASIC did not say whether the latest complaints related to all four audit firms dominating Australia’s corporate landscape and boardrooms. ASIC’s report said there have also been other issues identified which relate to matters it is already investigating, including “several matters which have been referred for consideration as part of our existing investigations into KPMG about misstatements in transparency reporting”.



This relates to KPMG allegedly failing to report internal whistleblower complaints. ASIC highlighted the seriousness of the latest allegations, given these four firms audit more than 94 per cent of Australia’s listed companies by market valuation, and 85 per cent of registrable superannuation entities. “Auditors are gatekeepers to Australia’s financial markets. Investors, businesses and superannuation members rely on them to scrutinise financial information with independence, integrity and professional scepticism,” ASIC Commissioner Kate O’Rourke said. ASIC Commissioner Kate O’Rourke during a Senate estimates hearing at Parliament House in Canberra. Alex Ellinghausen O’Rourke said some of the issues identified from the internal complaints include directions to not escalate audit concerns, failure to escalate material audit issues, breaches of confidentiality and victimisation of employees who reported issues.



“Internal complaints can provide valuable intelligence regarding deficiencies with how statutory audits are conducted. Audit firms should carefully and thoroughly interrogate complaints to identify and address these issues,” O’Rourke said. ASIC noted there are no regulatory provisions directly governing how audit firms handle internal complaints and said it did not investigate every complaint in detail, or reach findings about every person mentioned in the complaints. Related Article Updated

Consulting KPMG set to slash hundreds more jobs before Christmas Most of the 558 complaints fell outside ASIC’s regulatory powers. It said some of the allegations, which include bullying and sexual harassment, have been referred to other regulators – including Chartered Accountants ANZ, CPA Australia and the Tax Practitioners Board for possible breaches of professional and ethical standards. ASIC said it has already released information in relation to a number of individuals, and is continuing to engage with these other regulators around additional matters of potential interest.



The corporate watchdog said its work is ongoing, and it will continue to communicate the outcomes of any further regulatory action. Just last week, KPMG said it is cutting 230 jobs as the fallout from the whistleblower scandal continues. The job cuts are mostly in its consulting division, with smaller cuts in supporting areas and the team that advises companies on corporate deals. “We must align our business with client demand. This is a necessary step towards renewing and rebuilding our firm,” KPMG’s recently appointed chief executive John Sams said. State and federal governments have banned KPMG from winning new work since the full scale of the whistleblower scandal became clear. World.title: Should I pay extra off my mortgage, or put it in an offset account?
World.content:
MoneyBorrowingAsk an expert Opinion Should I pay extra off my mortgage, or put it in an offset account? Noel Whittaker Money columnist November 25, 2026 — 5:01am

November 25, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

I have a home mortgage and am fortunate enough to have some spare money each month. I am wondering whether I would be better off making additional repayments directly into the mortgage or depositing the money into a mortgage offset account. My main aim is to reduce the interest I pay and get the loan paid off as quickly as possible. Is one option more effective than the other, or do they achieve essentially the same result? Provided you have a 100 per cent offset account, both options generally produce the same interest savings, assuming the mortgage interest rate is identical. The main difference is how easily you can access your money. Paying more off your mortgage directly may reduce the amount owed, but it can keep your money frozen for longer. Simon Letch An offset account is a separate bank account linked to your mortgage, and every dollar in it reduces the loan balance on which interest is calculated. The money remains yours and can generally be withdrawn whenever you wish, just like an ordinary bank account. By contrast, additional repayments go directly into your mortgage, reducing the amount owing. Many loans offer a redraw facility that allows you to withdraw those extra repayments if needed, but access is subject to the lender’s terms and conditions.



The lender may impose minimum withdrawal amounts, fees or restrictions, and in some circumstances may reduce or suspend access to redraw funds. This makes redraw less flexible than having the money sitting in your own offset account. The other consideration is cost. Lenders often charge higher interest rates or additional fees for loans with offset facilities. It may be worthwhile talking to a mortgage broker to see whether you could refinance to a cheaper loan without an offset account. The savings from a lower interest rate could outweigh the convenience of an offset facility. Whichever option you choose, keeping your regular repayments unchanged while reducing the interest charged will help you pay off the mortgage faster. We are a married couple and all our bank accounts, credit cards, debit cards and other assets are held jointly. We are both authorised signatories on the accounts. If my husband dies, will I be able to continue operating the accounts and using the cards as normal, or will the bank freeze them until his estate is finalised? I would like to understand what happens in practice and whether there is anything we should arrange now to avoid problems for the surviving spouse. The good news is that genuinely joint bank accounts are generally not frozen when one account holder dies. The surviving spouse can usually continue operating the account, and the deceased’s interest in the money normally passes automatically to the survivor.



However, the bank will need to be notified of the death and may require a death certificate before changing the account into the survivor’s sole name. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert I’m retired with two super funds. Should I move both into pension mode? Paul Benson Money contributor Credit cards are a different matter. Many couples believe they have joint credit cards when, in fact, one spouse is the primary cardholder and the other is merely an additional cardholder. If the primary cardholder dies, the account will generally be closed and the additional card will cease to operate. Debit cards issued in the deceased’s name will also be cancelled, although the surviving spouse should be able to continue using their own debit card linked to a joint account. Other jointly owned assets, such as the family home, will generally pass automatically to the survivor if held as joint tenants. However, assets held as tenants in common are treated differently and the deceased’s share forms part of their estate.



My advice is to check with your bank now that your accounts are genuinely joint, establish who is the primary holder of each credit card, and make sure each spouse has access to sufficient funds independently. A little preparation now could save a great deal of inconvenience at an already difficult time. I am retired and turn 65 in December. I have approximately $1.8 million in accumulation-phase superannuation, and I am considering converting as much as possible into an account-based pension to provide a regular income stream. I also receive a defined benefit pension of approximately $40,000 a year. My concern is how this existing pension will affect the amount I can transfer into retirement phase, given the current transfer balance cap of $2.1 million. How is my defined benefit pension assessed against the cap, and what options do I have to maximise the amount I can hold in retirement phase? Your defined benefit pension counts towards your transfer balance cap, generally at a “special value” of 16 times the annual pension entitlement at commencement. The general transfer balance cap is currently $2.1 million, but your personal cap may be lower because your pension has already commenced. Before starting an account-based pension, check your transfer balance account on the ATO portal to confirm how much cap space you have available.



I am 81 and have approximately $80,000 in superannuation. I recently read an article stating that superannuation does not automatically form part of a deceased person’s estate, which has made me concerned about what will happen to my money when I die. My will clearly sets out who should inherit my assets, and I want to make sure my remaining superannuation goes to those beneficiaries. Editor's pick Opinion

Gender pay gap Women are retiring with $51,000 less in super. Here’s how to fight back Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor Would it be safer to withdraw the $80,000 from superannuation now and deposit it into my bank account so it forms part of my estate, or is there a way to ensure my superannuation is distributed according to my wishes without withdrawing it? It is the trustee of your superannuation fund who has the final say as to where the proceeds are distributed. You can take some control over this process by lodging a binding death benefit nomination with your fund. But considering the relatively small amount you have in super and your age, it may be simpler to withdraw the whole sum tax-free now and place that in an interest-bearing account.



Also bear in mind that the taxable component of your superannuation left to a non-dependent, and at your age, I would imagine your beneficiary would be non-dependents, has a death tax of 17 per cent. But drawing the money now means your beneficiaries don’t suffer that tax. Noel Whittaker is the author of Retirement Made Simple and other books on personal finance. Email: noel@noelwhittaker.com.au. World.title: Paying for aged care just got a lot fairer – but crunch the numbers carefully
World.content:
MoneySuper & retirementAged care Opinion Paying for aged care just got a lot fairer – but crunch the numbers carefully Rachel Lane Money contributor November 25, 2026 — 5:01am

November 25, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The 2025 aged care reforms removed an important choice for new residents: how they pay for their accommodation. Those who were yet to complete a means assessment or declare themselves as ‘means not disclosed’ were unable to pay a lump sum refundable accommodation deposit (RAD). Instead, they were forced to pay a daily accommodation payment (DAP). The DAP is calculated using a government-set interest rate, currently 8.51 per cent, on any unpaid RAD. For someone with a $750,000 RAD, that means paying around $175 a day – or $5300 a month – pending their means assessment. How you pay for your aged care accommodation is a big financial decision. Getty It created an expensive dilemma. Residents could either pay thousands of dollars in daily payments or declare themselves ‘means not disclosed’ so they could pay the RAD. But being means not disclosed makes you liable for the maximum means-tested fees, the hotelling fee and non-clinical care contribution, totalling $132 a day. For many residents, the problem wasn’t confined to just the cost of aged care. The inability to pay the RAD was also negatively affecting their pension payments.



Consider a couple, one moving into aged care, with $750,000 in the bank, ready to pay a RAD. While waiting for their means assessment, they are paying $175 a day in daily accommodation payments. Editor's pick Opinion

Aged care No room at the inn: The Christmas aged care shortage stressing families Rachel Lane Money contributor The money in the bank is also reducing their age pension by $2250 a fortnight. Once their assessment is completed, the means-tested hotelling and non-clinical care contributions will be $39 a day. If they declare themselves means not disclosed, they can pay the RAD and avoid the DAPs and the reduction in their age pension – saving almost $10,200 a month. But there is a catch: they have to pay the maximum means-tested fees of $132 a day, rather than $39. If they can crunch all the numbers they will see that they are still better off by about $3000 a month. The situation was both complex and costly. But finally, sense has prevailed. From 1 November, residents can again choose to pay their accommodation by lump sum, daily payment or a combination of both while waiting for their means assessment.



Of course, paying a RAD is not the right decision for everyone. The money is tied up in the aged care home while you live there, and a retention fee of 2 per cent a year applies for up to five years. If you are selling the family home to pay the RAD, there is a lot more that you need to consider, including the pension and aged care means test concessions you are giving up. How you pay for your aged care accommodation is a big financial decision. It is a decision that can affect your pension, other aged care fees, cash flow and your estate planning wishes. Now that choice has been restored, choose wisely. Rachel Lane is the author of Downsizing Made Simple, a book and website aimed at demystifying downsizing. World.title: I’m legally blind and can’t seem to land a job. How can I increase my chances?
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsGot a Minute? I’m legally blind and can’t seem to land a job. How can I increase my chances? Kirstin Ferguson November 25, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Each week, Dr Kirstin Ferguson tackles questions about workplace, career and leadership in her advice column Got a Minute? This week: concerns about a growing CV gap, accusing a colleague of lying and an early morning meeting. There is no need to turn a job interview into a recount of your medical history. Dionne Gain I’m in my early 40s and am legally blind due to a progressive eye condition. I’ve worked in teaching and administration, and loved my job at a not-for-profit until restructures and changes to my role meant I needed to leave. A later role wasn’t the right fit, partly because I was still learning what workplace adjustments I needed. I’ve been job hunting since January and applying seriously since April. I tailor every application, have approached employers and recruiters directly, and have sought specialist support. So far, four interviews have led nowhere. I’m worried about the growing gap on my CV and my references getting stale. Should I apply for more jobs, retrain or change my approach entirely? While it may not feel like it, achieving four interviews shows that employers can find value in your experience. The job now is to consider whether something else is impacting your ability to get the role. Have you asked the interviewers for specific feedback? Was it the examples of experience you provided, a missing skill they needed or how the role would work with adjustments? Some will not respond, but even one useful answer beats guessing or making assumptions. You might like to ask someone you trust to review one application and practise an interview with you. Prepare a concise explanation of your employment gap and a clear account of the tools or adjustments that help you do the job. You need not turn an interview into a recount of your medical history.



Related Article Got a Minute? Should I tell my boss’s wife he’s having an affair with a colleague? You might like to also search JobAccess for an Inclusive Employment Australia provider with experience in vision loss, and ask a JobAccess adviser about recruitment adjustments and equipment funding. For suitable Federal public service vacancies, check whether RecruitAbility applies and request accessible assessment methods where needed. These routes do not guarantee a job, but they may remove barriers unrelated to your vision loss. To avoid feeling your former referees are going stale, keep them updated on the progress of your job search with a short update. This way as time gets further away from when you last worked together, they will understand your job search remains an active process. I think my colleague’s “miscarriage” may have been a lie. My colleague took extended compassionate leave after telling our manager she had suffered a miscarriage. I later overheard her laughing with a friend about the overseas holiday she took during the same period. I may have misunderstood what I heard, but our exhausted team carried her workload and donated money for meals. Is it cruel to question her story — or dishonest to say nothing?



Related Article Got a Minute? I overheard two execs making fun of employees’ accents and weight. What do I do? Looks like another question where I have no choice but to shout. YES, IT IS CRUEL TO QUESTION HER STORY. MIND YOUR OWN BUSINESS. Just because a woman has a miscarriage doesn’t mean they can’t laugh with friends, travel overseas or do anything else they may choose to do to overcome their loss. How a woman deals with anything that happens to her body is entirely her business. None of it – not one bit – needs to be explained to you. I am sure she was grateful that your team helped manage her workload and helped with meals while she was gone. Next time, when it is you who may need support, I am sure it will be you who will be grateful when she returns the favour. I am sure you will also be pleased to not have her question whether the support is warranted.



Our manager has decided that our twice-weekly team meetings, formerly held at 10am, will now start at 8am. Everyone else is delighted, as it means leaving work an hour earlier at the end of the day, but I am not an early morning person and really struggle to make it in on time. While my co-workers are bright-eyed and bushy-tailed around the table, I am sluggish and find it difficult to keep up. I am worried it is going to impact my career. What should I do? If your only argument is you are “not a morning person” then you probably have a slim chance of persuading your manager to alter an arrangement that seems to suit everyone else. Instead of fighting against the change, I think you will need to find ways to make it work for you. That might mean you need to prepare your updates or questions the afternoon before, to help you be your best in the meeting itself. I would try a month of these earlier times and see how you go. Your body is bound to adjust. To submit a question about work, careers or leadership, visit kirstinferguson.com/ask. You will not be asked to provide your name or any identifying information.
