World.title: Footnotes, villains and a redacted donkey: Is this book about to save literature?
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

If there’s one place you should be safe from audience participation, it’s when reading a book. Not any more. Early on in Jasper Fforde’s Dark Reading Matter the author makes a request of his readers – no matter where you are, or what you are doing, if you see text appear in a certain font, could you please read it aloud. The first time I see this I’m at home, and despite being the sort of person who strategically positions herself in comedy shows for minimal interaction, or who got through school choir by half-heartedly miming, I find myself gingerly speaking the words aloud: “Oh my goodness, they’ve trodden on the gibbon.” Dark Reading Matter is the eighth and final book in the Thursday Next series. It started in 2001 with Fforde’s debut novel, The Eyre Affair, and tracks the titular Thursday Next, a detective, as she fights battles of varying surreality against corporations, corruption and, on occasion, Enid Blyton characters. “I think that the real jumping-off point for this book was that I dedicated it to readers,” says Fforde. “If you’ve been reading my series for the last 25 years, this is for us … and we’re going to have some fun.” Author Jasper Fforde Mari Fforde The series has always been meta – the main character lives in an alternate version of our world, and within her world she discovers that books aren’t simply objects containing words; they’re the output of the BookWorld, where all the characters are real and performing books kind of like a play. Beyond that they have their own society and lives and, yes, a police force, which is there to stop things going off the rails. In the final novel, however, Fforde takes the opportunity to shake off all shackles and see what truly is possible with the written word. Our world is suddenly a new layer on top of things, we the reader have a role to play – thus the speaking aloud – and Fforde himself turns up in the book – well, sort of. “He’s awful!” says Fforde with a laugh. “I mean, he’s a terrible human being.”



The techniques Fforde uses in all his books push at the boundaries of what we expect. His novels throw you in the deep end, with their seemingly chaotic blend of wordplay, adventure and hard truths – but it’s at 3am, when you realise you haven’t been able to put the book down, that you realise how intricately put together it all is. There’s a reason for the seemingly random illustration at the front. That isn’t just any donkey on the cover. And the gibbon is important. Under all the fun and the wordplay his books all take on deeper themes; they’re about free will, they fight against unchecked authority and they advocate for what is fair and right. Here is no different – what on the surface may seem like silliness is actually a battle cry. Dark Reading Matter is first and foremost a joy to read and a love letter to the readers who have come on this decades-long journey with Fforde and his fictional detective Thursday Next – but at its core it’s a fight for the future of literature. Dark Reading Matter comes at an existential moment for literature; at a time when physical stories are being literally cut up and fed into machines to teach AI how to write. Photo: The key antagonist of the story, Roger Thatt, is trying to gain access to the “dark reading matter” – not the BookWorld but all the bits from around the edge. It’s the place where all ideas and potential ideas go; memories, thoughts, discarded drafts. Thatt wants to harvest it all, to monetise it, to control inspiration. This novel manages to explore the threat of AI without being preachy or dull – a miraculous achievement in a saturated conversation – and manages to do it through both plot and structure. “I was out to write a book that AI could not scrape. It could not scrape this. It could not understand it,” he says. It’s true – what would artificial intelligence make of conversations that happen purely in the footnotes, which in the book are used as a communication system? How would it navigate the narrative impact of font changes? Or, stepping back, would the character names – including Landen Parke-Laine, Acheron Hades and Jack Schitt – and the entire blend of pop culture, history and puns that go into creating them even be a possibility? “It can’t think up new stuff. It can only take old stuff and repackage it,” he says.



Before he was an author, Fforde was in the film industry, working as a focus puller. He started at age 19, and across a 20-year career worked on films including GoldenEye, Entrapment and The Mask of Zorro, but it was a volatile industry. “The jobs could dry up literally any moment.” He started writing short stories at the age of 27, and across the next 12 years “I had five books written and [none published]. No one interested at all.” He found a strange freedom in the rejection, however, and started writing The Eyre Affair. “I thought, well, it doesn’t matter what I write because I’m not going to be published. So I’m just writing for fun.” The manuscript was “fun and silly, and it just mixes everything together – literary theory and vampires and werewolves and everything else”. The resulting book deal was enough that Fforde could stop work. His final project was an ad featuring Leonardo DiCaprio – “and the following week I was an author”. The Eyre Affair was an instant hit and became a New York Times bestseller. Though Fforde is still a keen photographer and still working in the creative industries, there is both a wistfulness and an edge of concern when he talks about the film industry. “I miss it a lot,” he says. The threat of AI is looming, though. “If I was in the film industry now, I would be thinking it’s all over for us,” he reflects. “If I was an actor or a filmmaker I would be terrified.” He pauses. “Or, alternatively, I would be thinking I need to start a theatre troupe. You know – this could be the greatest resurgence of theatre that the world may ever see.” Fforde has been pushing boundaries, subverting expectations and challenging himself with every book he writes. The Constant Rabbit is a novel that takes on nationalism and Brexit specifically while also being about anthropomorphised rabbits. His first standalone novel Early Riser imagines a world where the human race hibernates for months each year. The Shades of Grey novels take on discrimination and class through a society that ranks people based on what colours they can perceive. There is another, quieter thread that laces through the latter half of Dark Reading Matter, in a non-fiction detour where a version of Fforde himself is the protagonist. He reflects on articles he’s read, on his writing, and in one section recalls drives with his mother “during her latter years when the Alzheimer’s became momentarily not the debilitation that it was, but a gift that could keep on giving: I could take her on these drives each week and every time she would enjoy it as though the first”, he writes.

World.title: How does your salary compare - here and in Australia?
World.content:
Audio player for " How do I tell a scam from a real bank call? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/business/2767586%2Fhow-does-your-salary-compare-here-and-in-australia

How do I tell a scam from a real bank call? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 15m

Australian employers are still paying a premium over New Zealand - but the gap might not be as large as you think in some cases.

Recruiter Robert Half has released its latest salary guide, which shows what a number of corporate roles across finance and tech are paying on both sides of the Tasman.

An Auckland finance manager is earning an average NZ$160,000 a year according to the survey, while the equivalent in New South Wales earns A$165,000, or about NZ$200,000.

Financial controllers were getting an average NZ$210,000 in Auckland, or NZ$300,000 in New South Wales.

Some tech roles were more similar. An Auckland cloud engineer was earning NZ$160,000 according to the guide, compared to NZ$170,000 in Australia.

Data scientists were getting NZ$150,000 in Auckland and NZ$210,000 in Victoria. AI engineers also earned more in Australia.

The report showed some differences within New Zealand, too. A tax account was earning an average $135,000 in Auckland, $120,000 in Wellington and $115,000 in Christchurch.

A graduate accountant was getting $72,500 in Auckland, and $67,500 in Wellington and Christchurch.

Robert Half associate director Alyse Young said Australian employers were still generally paying more. "They're a much bigger country with different state organisations … there are a lot of different factors, versus New Zealand we're a lot smaller."

She said Australia's superannuation scheme, in which employers made a 12 percent contribution on top of employees' salary also made their remuneration more generous.

"I think a lot of organisations in New Zealand haven't necessarily moved or increased their salaries over time as much as potentially Australia has, which has also created a sort of bigger divide over time as well."

She said wage growth had slowed here although not as much as some people might have thought. "We're still seeing people get small increases in organisations but we're also seeing a greater shift of people moving roles to look for that salary increase. Where people might have stayed in roles for five to 10 years a period of time ago, their tenure in roles is shorter. A lot of the time that is partly to do with salary factors and development as well."

Robert Half's surveying showed almost 80 percent of employees said their pay was not fully keeping pace with the cost of living. More than half were thinking about changing jobs in the next year, usually for better salary or benefits.

"People feel like their income isn't increasing at the same rate.

"But I also think different things that we're seeing people start to value, maybe not quite as much as pay, but the flexibility and those sorts of things as well, we are seeing people sort of favour a little bit more than just salary increases."

More than 60 percent said they would consider leaving work or would leave if their flexibility was removed. Almost 90 percent said AI helped their work.

Young said a couple of years ago there had been a large spike in migration to Australia. "People talking about their families moving overseas and relocating kids who are in school and all those sorts of things. I think that's definitely slowed down.

"We're still seeing a lot of the grads or people who are in the first five years of their working careers making the move over there. But we are seeing the more mature workforce that we deal with a lot in our role staying put. And there's opportunities around for them more so than maybe there was a couple of years ago. I think that's also a positive thing in terms of keeping some of those skilled professionals around as well."

World.title: Consumer calls out Kmart's 'wild double standard' over asbestos sand
World.content:
Audio player for " Gemma Rasmussen on lessons from asbestos in play-sand " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/health/2767591%2Fconsumer-calls-out-kmart-s-wild-double-standard-over-asbestos-sand

Gemma Rasmussen on lessons from asbestos in play-sand Morning Report Download MP3 6m

Consumer NZ has found "serious gaps" in the country's product safety system, a year on from the discovery of asbestos in coloured sand sold at Kmart.

A new report by Consumer's investigations team found current product safety protocols had allowed more than eight tonnes of contaminated coloured play sand to be sold in the past decade, according to Ministry of Health documents.

Gemma Rasmussen, head of research and advocacy at Consumer NZ, said it was because New Zealand's product safety system ran on trust, not testing.

"I think New Zealanders shouldn't assume that products available for purchase here are as safe as they think they are."

Consumer research had found nearly one in four New Zealanders had reported a product safety issue in their household in the past two years, yet 88 percent were confident that products sold here were safe.

"Government departments aren't joined up, businesses are able to write their own recalls and say what the level of risk is, and there's no one really checking behind the scenes."

Gemma Rasmussen Supplied / Consumer NZ

By law, businesses must ensure goods are safe before they go on sale, Rasmussen said. But there was currently no compulsory asbestos testing for coloured play sand in New Zealand.

While the Commerce Commission was investigating, eight tonnes of sand had been sold and so far no business has been held to account, she told Morning Report.

There should be a lead agency, potentially MBIE, to handle the country's product safety system but it would need to be adequately resourced.

"There are examples overseas of product safety systems that have traceability, rapid recall rules, mandatory testing and rapid alert systems for when things go wrong."

The next product scandal might involve the likes of chemical burns or electrical fires, Rasmussen said.

"What we have seen with this is there's been error after error after error."

Official Information Act documents had shown Customs had carried out no investigations, prosecutions, convictions, penalties, warnings or infringement notices in the decade since the introduction of the Imports and Exports (Asbestos-containing products) Prohibition order in 2016.

There had been one intercepted consignment, of crayons in 2017, which required an EPA permit the importer did not provide. The goods were surrendered.

Customs was tasked with ensuring that asbestos-containing products, when declared, were covered by an import permit, issued by the Environmental Protection Authority (EPA).

A spokesperson said Customs did not routinely test imported consumer products for asbestos.

"The majority of imports containing play sand fall under the Toys tariff classification and, given the high volume of legitimate toy imports, introducing operational rules to identify play sand products would have a significant operational impact, including disruption to compliant trade.

"Customs is not undertaking further investigation on imports from the recalled sand products that have tested positive for asbestos. Our current focus is to operationalise the unsafe goods notice that relates to sand products by February 2027."

The risk from the Kmart play sand came to light through a chance finding by a laboratory doing a routine training exercise.

When Kmart recalled its 14-piece sandcastle building set in November 2025, it called the risk of airborne asbestos "low" and fibre release "unlikely" unless the sand was crushed or pulverised.

"Many assumed the recall wording was government advice," Rasmussen said. "It was published by MBIE [the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment] on the official product safety site, but it was written by Kmart."

Kmart recalled its 14-piece sandcastle building set in November 2025. Supplied / MBIE

MBIE said it had since introduced a new rule to ensure all notices clearly stated who - that is, the name of the business - was doing the recalling in the introduction sentence.

"This has been designed to remove any misunderstanding and make it clear that the recall and the information in the recall instructions is the businesses' decision, rather than MBIE's decision."

But behind the scenes, government health experts agreed it was impossible to quantify the risk.

On 27 November 2025, the Ministry of Health's technical advisory group agreed classifying the risk as low, medium or high was "impossible at this stage". Yet the notice calling the risk "low" stayed on a government website.

Five days after the first recall, WorkSafe told Kmart the sand did not need to be crushed to qualify as friable asbestos-containing material, and classified the sand as requiring Class A asbestos removal.

But Kmart's New Zealand notice kept the "low risk" wording until July 2026, even after Auckland University of Technology research confirmed that fibres in some craft sands - excluding the moulding sands tested - became airborne during ordinary simulated play.

And some recall notices continued to say "fibre release is unlikely unless the sand is crushed or pulverised".

Ian Caplin. Supplied / Australia and New Zealand School of Government

MBIE product safety spokesperson Ian Caplin said in a statement its role was to "work with businesses to facilitate the publication of recall notices and ensure consumers are informed about potentially unsafe products as quickly as possible".

He said MBIE had raised concerns about this wording when the original recall notice was being developed, and again during discussions on subsequent Kmart recalls.

"In this case, MBIE made its concerns known to Kmart and continued to challenge the wording. However, there was a need to balance resolving points of disagreement against the importance of ensuring recall notices were published promptly so consumers could be made aware of the potential safety risk and take appropriate action."

Neither the Ministry of Health nor Health New Zealand were involved in developing wording for product recall notices.

Consumer calls out Kmart's 'double standard'

On 20 November 2025, Kmart found loose sand in the staffroom of its Te Rapa store in Hamilton. It closed the store and brought in a licensed Class A asbestos removalist. In correspondence with WorkSafe, Kmart said, "As a business, we are keen to remove all potentially contaminated material from our sites as quickly as possible."

Meanwhile, Kmart's recall advice told households to wear gloves, double-bag the sand and contact their council about appropriate asbestos disposal.

"That's a wild double standard. Kmart took major precautions, at great expense, in its own workplace - while customers were expected to manage the potentially contaminated product themselves," Rasmussen said.

A Kmart spokesperson said they appreciated the matter had caused concern and disruption for some customers, and said product safety and maintaining customers' trust were of paramount importance.

"When the matter became known to us, we acted quickly by removing affected products from sale, issuing recall notices, providing refunds to customers and guidance on safe disposal of the products based on regulatory advice at the time."

Researchers found fibres in some craft sands became airborne during ordinary simulated play. Kmart / supplied

The report called for action from the government.

MBIE said its product safety team currently had 3.5 FTE, supported within MBIE by experts in various subjects including communications, legal and policy.

Rasmussen said that wasn't enough.

Consumer NZ wanted the current patchwork approach replaced with a coordinated, properly funded product safety system, and an end to suppliers putting unverified risk claims in recall notices.

It suggested New Zealand model its system on successful overseas product safety ecosystems, such as the European Union's baseline safety rules, traceability, mandatory testing for high-risk categories like toys, and a shared rapid-alert system.

World.title: Injuries mount for under fire All Blacks with Will Jordan heading home
World.content:
The All Blacks will be without star wing Will Jordan for this weekend's rematch with England at Twickenham, while captain Codie Taylor is in doubt.

Jordan, who returned from a hamstring strain in last weekend's record loss to the English, has reaggravated the injury and is heading home, while Taylor has a tight calf.

Chiefs hooker Samisoni Taukei'aho has recovered from a calf injury of his own and has joined the squad as cover for Taylor.

Hooker Codie Taylor is being assessed for a calf injury. Brett Phibbs / www.photosport.nz

The All Blacks are also sweating on the fitness of forward Tupou Vaa'i and back Anton Lienert-Brown, who also picked up injuries in last Sunday's defeat.

The pair are being assessed and are day-to-day prospects at this stage.

Head coach Dave Rennie said they needed to bring Taukei'aho in just in case Taylor is ruled out.

"We are hopeful that Codie may be cleared to play, but have brought Samisoni in as cover in case he is not declared fit," Rennie said.

"It is great to see Soni recovered from his calf injury and back in with the group."

The All Blacks will be desperate to win this weekend's test at Twickenham and end their season on a high following back to back defeats.

World.title: Kāinga Ora homes pitched as opportunity for land bankers
World.content:
The sale of Nuku Street's public housing in the Wellington suburb of Strathmore sparked backlash last month.

Now, almost an entire street of Kāinga Ora homes - boasting about 80 bedrooms in total - is on the market in Lower Hutt, promoted as an opportunity for investors, developers, and land bankers.

Locals and housing advocates, who say public land should stay in public ownership, are planning to protest the sale of the Manderson Grove properties ahead of the deadline on 8 December.

Kāinga Ora said the properties were no longer fit for purpose and the sales were part of its nationwide programme to renew and improve its housing portfolio.

'Big housing need'

Local Anglican priest Alison Robinson said her church, St David's, saw the reality of homelessness up close.

"Over the years, we've obviously supported people, seen people, we've had people who are sleeping on the street.

"We have someone who actually often camps outside our centre currently. So, I mean, there is without a doubt, a big housing need."

Kāinga Ora says the properties are no longer fit for purpose. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

According to the Ministry of Social Development Housing Register, 339 households were on the waitlist for public housing in Lower Hutt as at September 2026.

Robinson stressed that the number was households, not individuals, and was dismayed to see the properties on Manderson Grove on the market.

"We just feel that this is happening again and again, hard on the heels of Nuku Street.

"We want the wait list for public housing to be taken seriously," she said, and ultimately called for the sale to be halted.

"Once the land is gone, it's gone. We want to see public land kept for public homes."

Hutt Valley Public Housing Futures spokesperson Michelle Ducat wanted to know where the proceeds from the sale would go.

"Is it to rebuild houses in Lower Hutt or is it somewhere else? And does it mean that we're increasing the base level of housing overall and from what level?"

Ducat described the marketing of the properties on Manderson Grove as "interesting".

"It's asking for speculators to see if they can make a big profit off public land. It seems wrong when people are in housing need," she said.

"It feels like the privatisation of this public asset when it could be used for public good."

Houses on Manderson Grove in Lower Hutt. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

What is land banking?

Prospective buyers could acquire one property or the entire holding, according to Bayleys, with each Manderson Grove listing pointing to the potentional for investment or development.

The lisitings also highlighted the opportunity for land banking.

Bayleys has been approached for comment.

Long-time property investor Steve Goodey said the Manderson Grove properties were a prime example of "an uneconomical use of space".

Goodey said suggesting land banking was a method used by agents to get developers' attention, but said the practice itself wasn't that common in the Wellington region.

"It's kind of what we refer to, I suppose, as a cradle to grave strategy, which is where you buy something that's a bit rough, not worth really improving, and you let it in essence rot into the ground, generating the bare minimum of income to cover itself."

He said in a decades' time, give or take, the land would be close to debt free, which meant the bank was more likely to loan the money to develop it.

"That's the traditional land banking, but realistically, nobody really does it anymore because everybody wants to move faster than that," he said.

Kāinga Ora says it's comfortable with Bayleys's marketing approach. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Chief economist with the New Zealand Initiative, Eric Crampton, said there was a type of land banking that had been problematic in New Zealand.

"There can be advantage in buying land early, in advance of the infrastructure being laid out, knowing that councils have been pretty bad at sheeting the costs of infrastructure to the beneficiaries of it.

"In that case, you get an uplift in the value of your land when the infrastructure goes in, you can develop it, you can onsell it."

He said changes to the Resource Management Act should fix the issue, and said it didn't apply to Manderson Grove.

Allowing development of the Manderson Grove site wouldn't affect demand or drive up house prices, Crampton said, and had the potential to add "an awful lot more housing".

Sales proceeds to be reinvested

A spokesperson for Kāinga Ora said it was comfortable with Bayleys's marketing approach with the Manderson Grove properties.

"We want to get the best price for the properties as the proceeds will be reinvested into new social housing."

Kāinga Ora regional director Greater Wellington Sarah Willson said the Manderson Grove properties were no longer fit for purpose and the sales were part of its nationwide programme to renew and improve its housing portfolio.

World.title: 'Agents of the devil': Outrage in PNG after five women allegedly buried alive over sorcery claims
World.content:
Papua New Guinea's government says the full force of the law must be brought against those behind the killing of five women accused of sorcery in Southern Highlands Province.

The five women, including one who was pregnant, were allegedly buried alive over the weekend in Kaa village in relation to sorcery accusations.

Local media report Police Commissioner David Manning confirmed that three men suspected of involvement in the incident have been taken into custody.

An estimated 200 people are killed due to SARV in PNG every year. 123RF

A police operation to recover the deceased has also been conducted.

There has been swift condemnation from the government, not for the first time in response to an appalling sorcery accusation-related attack.

Some parts of PNG have grappled with sorcery accusation-related violence for decades - most often the violence targets women.

The low rate of prosecutions reflects how work to reduce the tolerance for this violence in some communities still has a long way to go.

Police Minister John Pundari said the nation had been sickened by the torture and killing of innocent women in Kaa village and other locations.

He said those responsible, and those who failed to prevent the offending, would be held to account.

"There is no other way to describe these vile crimes other than to say the perpetrators are agents of the devil," Pundari said.

"Sorcery-related violence is not part of our culture, it was invented by sick people to abuse women and the elderly, and it must be stamped out."

Pundari also issued a warning to elders and leaders in villages and communities: they will face the full force of the law if they fail to prevent sorcery accusation-related violence.

Meanwhile, the Minister for Community Development, Religion and Youth, Jason Peter, issued a statement with UN Women Papua New Guinea, condemning the killings "in the strongest terms".

"Everyone responsible must face thorough investigation and fair, timely prosecution.

World.title: Pacific governments step up El Niño response as drought and water crisis deepen
World.content:
Fijian Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka says he knows that families across the country are increasingly concerned about the availability of water.

This comes as more Pacific governments step up their response to ongoing El Niño droughts in their nations.

In Fiji, where a national state of natural disaster has been declared in response to the El Niño drought, 11 of the 14 water sources in the Western Division have reached critical levels.

Energy Fiji Limited has warned that its hydroelectric dams could be forced to shut down for safety reasons by the end of January 2027, or even earlier, if the prolonged dry conditions associated with El Niño persist.

The disaster declaration in Fiji led to a Ministry of Education decision that students across the country will now finish the school year four days earlier than originally planned. Classes will now finish on 27 November instead of 30 November.

Fiji drought Facebook / Fiji Government

Rabuka said the government would now intensify its response to the long dry spell in the country.

He said people were worried about the effects of prolonged dry conditions on their daily lives.

He said there would be coordinated action by all relevant authorities under the established national disaster management arrangements.

"Government has allocated FJ$20 million for the national response through a redeployment of exisiting funds within a ministry; this funding will support emergency water supplies, assistance to affected communities, support for farmers and livestock owners and other urgent interventions arising from the prolonged dry conditions."

Papua New Guinea

Papua New Guinea is preparing drought assistance for 680,000 people as El Niño impacts deepen in various parts of the large Pacific Island nation.

Papua New Guinea drought RNZ Pacific / Johnny Blades

Its government and the UN have been supplying water, food, and health services as extreme weather puts communities at risk.

A new analysis by seven UN agencies says El Niño is likely to continue over the next six months, with its peak expected in December.

The report names PNG and Tonga as countries of particular concern, while Kiribati, Naoero and Tuvalu are forecast to experience more rainfall than usual.

El Niño drought is hitting hard in Papua New Guinea's capital Port Moresby, late 2026. RNZ Pacific / Johnny Blades

Many parts of Papua New Guinea are feeling the full force of El Niño, with devastating impacts now reported from the Highlands to the coastal provinces.

NBC reports that communities from the Schouten Islands in East Sepik Province are calling for urgent government assistance as they face severe food and water shortages caused by the El Niño weather conditions.



Pastor Adrian Reim of Ruprup Island told NBC News that communities had been affected since June 2026 but had not received assistance from the national government's El Niño relief funds.

Power disruptions are also being felt in parts of the country.

The Eastern Highlands Provincial Health Authority (EHPHA) has assured the public that Goroka Provincial Specialist Hospital continues to operate despite challenges affecting the delivery of healthcare services.

EHPHA chief executive Dr Pomuso Warima has clarified the hospital's position following an earlier memo announcing a scale-down of operations due to challenges caused by El Niño, power disruptions and funding constraints.

Tonga

A state of emergency that has been declared over El Niño in Tonga applies to all the land and sea areas of the kingdom.

The 27-day state of emergency declaration last week is in

Tonga declared drought across most of its islands last month, with the effects of El Niño expected to persist until at least June next year.

World.title: Call for probe after West Papuan student leader dies weeks after alleged police assault
World.content:
A West Papuan university student leader has died, weeks after an alleged police assault in Jayapura.

Wialo Silak was the chair of the Student Consultative Council at Cenderawasih University, and died in hospital in Waena, Jayapura City, at the weekend.

Human Rights Monitor reports that seven weeks earlier, Silak was allegedly assaulted by police intelligence officers at the Jayapura City headquarters of the Indonesian Police.

The student leader reportedly sustained injuries to his face and head during the assault and subsequently experienced persistent headaches and worsening health problems.

His family, supported by the Legal Aid Institute in Papua, has demanded an independent investigation into the cause of death.

Students taken in by police

On 30 September, Wialo Silak accompanied dozens of fellow students to the Jayapura City police headquarters, where four student representatives from his university had been summoned for questioning over a demonstration held in mid-August.

According to Silak's own account relayed to Human Rights Monitor, a confrontation began when police officers brought in four students arrested during a separate Morning Star flag-raising protest at the University of Science and Technology Jayapura.

Officers reportedly accused Silak of photographing or recording the arrests with his mobile phone, before police intelligence officers allegedly assaulted him outside the investigation rooms.

Silak was repeatedly struck on his face and head, including near his right eye and ear, causing a bleeding injury.

He also described being physically restrained, interrogated and intimidated.

Deteriorating condition

Although Silak later sought medical treatment at a hospital in Abepura, efforts by police intelligence officers to engage him and his companions reportedly intimidated him, leading to his decision to leave before completing treatment.

In the days following the alleged assault, Silak reportedly suffered persistent headaches and pain around the right side of his head and ear.

By early November, his health problems came to a head, leading to a sudden deterioration in his condition before he died at Dian Harapan Hospital on 21 November.

Silak's family has noted the existence of a pre-existing ear infection, according to Human Rights Monitor.

World.title: Where New Zealanders are travelling as dollar hits 17-year low
World.content:
Audio player for " How do I tell a scam from a real bank call? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/personal-finance/2767583%2Fwhere-new-zealanders-are-travelling-as-dollar-hits-17-year-low

How do I tell a scam from a real bank call? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 15m

A weak New Zealand dollar is making holidays to places like the Cook Islands, Samoa and Vietnam more appealing than longer-distance travel.

The dollar has hit its lowest level in 17 years against the US, overing around US54c.

Heidi Walker, general manager of Flight Centre, said that was affecting holiday decisions.

"What we are seeing is that destinations like the USA, Europe, Hawaii, they are destinations where people are really having to plan that trip. It's not just a casual decision to travel that far.

"Where the Kiwi dollar is going to get its most value is where we're getting the most inquiries. Those destinations are closer to home. We've got inquiries, we're seeing peaks in places like Samoa. The Cook Islands is a great one because obviously they operate on the New Zealand dollar ... and then the other destinations that we're seeing are Vietnam, Thailand, you know, that Asia sector, we really can get great value for money and get a really good accommodation quality. And then also your food and beverage when you're on the ground goes a little bit further."

She said it had been a notable factor in the last year or so.

"Kiwi travellers are resilient to small movements, but with the cost of living challenges in New Zealand, on top of this currency change, even travelling to Australia now, you can see things are not going as far as they used to. People are becoming more and more aware of it and obviously as we talk about it more in mainstream conversation and media, it also becomes something that people are more aware about."

Flight Centre NZ general manager Heidi Walker. Supplied / Flight Centre

She said opting for a holiday package that included food or a cruise could help travellers avoid the impact of currency fluctuations.

Some people were travelling with cash that they converted before they left to provide surety about the exchange rate.

"They're not riding those highs and lows of the currency on the ground on the day when they're purchasing something as well."

House of Travel chief executive David Coombes said history would indicate that people would keep travelling no matter what happened to the currency.

"They take the trip but head somewhere like Vietnam, where meals and accommodation come at a fraction of the price, so you still get plenty of bang for your buck.

"Our forward bookings for 2027 show the top picks for our customers are closer to home. Australia is number one and the Cook Islands, with no exchange rate to factor in once you've landed, is popular right across the country and one place we expect will stay a favourite.

"A weaker dollar is good for our tourism industry making New Zealand more attractive to overseas visitors, and more inbound visitors normally means airlines add more services. High fuel prices are holding fares up for now, so I wouldn't wait for a drop, but over time I would expect Kiwi travellers could see more choice and better fares in market.

"If you're planning a trip, budget on today's exchange rate and talk to your travel consultant about destinations and all-inclusive packages that offer good value for money."

Economist Benje Patterson. Supplied

Economist Benje Patterson said he expected some people considering 2027 trips, especially during the school holidays, would think twice about going overseas and might opt for a domestic holiday instead.

"That being said, the gradual improvements we are seeing within the New Zealand economy will cushion any downside and so the net effect may be minimal.

"The big news for travel will be for inbound tourism into New Zealand. The weakening of the New Zealand dollar is like a Black Friday sale for international travellers and it means they will be able to spend up large when they are in the country, without it costing as much in their own currency. I would anticipate that many New Zealand tourism businesses exposed to international travellers, will see much improved yields this summer."

World.title: England crushes Australia to level T20 series in Gold Coast massacre
World.content:
England has hit back to level the T20I series in devastating fashion, thrashing Australia by eight wickets on the Gold Coast.

Aneurin Donald (85 off 32 balls) and Phil Salt (58 off 30) laid siege to Australia's bowlers, bludgeoning six after six after six at Carrara Stadium to make light work of Australia's 8-184.

England's blazing opening batting display was delivered with furious intent, starting fast and simply getting faster throughout the contest.

Welshman Donald excelled, reaching his maiden international century off just 16 balls.

How Salt made Joel Davies pay for dropping him on 10, belting him for 31 off a single over to reach his own half-century in just 24 balls.

The 100-run partnership came in just 44 balls amid the carnage.

Aneurin Donald hit a 16-ball 50. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Matt Roberts )

Donald eventually fell on the boundary, having plundered 85 off 32 balls, with nine sixes, after a partnership of 151, England's highest opening partnership against Australia in this format.

Ben Dwarshuis then accounted for Salt with a sensational one-handed caught-and-bowled chance.

But Harry Brook (10 off 9) and Tom Banton (26 off 8) carried on where they left off to seal victory with 41 balls remaining, with Banton fittingly hitting the winning runs with a massive six, the 16th of England's innings.

Earlier, Dwarshuis hit three massive sixes off the final three balls as Australia plundered 50 runs from the final three overs as the hosts made 8-184 at Carrara.

Ben Dwarshuis hit three massive sixes to put Australia on top. (Getty Images: Mackenzie Sweetnam)

Nikhil Chaudhary scored 45 off 35 and Joel Davis 39 off 25 for the hosts, who won the first T20I in Melbourne on Saturday night.

Aside from that, though, it was boom or bust for the Aussies at the top of the order, as England took regular wickets through the powerplay.

Mitch Marsh (15) smashed two sixes and then hit a return catch to Henry Crocombe, Jake Fraser-McGurk (27) bashed three before holing out to Brook off Sam Curran's first ball.

Chaudhary faced three dot balls before roasting Sam Harper (3) with an ill-judged run to the diving debutant James Coles at point.

Then, Tim David (6) skied a Jamie Overton delivery to Coles to give England four wickets in the powerplay, and Australia 4-58.

Middle-over maestro Adil Rashid bowled three overs unchanged for a miserly 1-13, working in tandem with left-arm spinner Liam Dawson to stymie the flow of runs.

That spell accounted for Lachlan Shaw, who laboured to a 17-ball 10 before sweeping the Rashid straight down the throat of Phil Salt.

Sam Curran bowled superbly until the final three balls. (Getty Images: Mackenzie Sweetnam)

Davies and Chaudhary built their 49-run partnership steadily, although it could have been over far earlier when Davies was dropped on 6 by Donald at deep backward square, the Welshman using a combination of both hands and his face to save a boundary.

Davies then survived an LBW review after Curran hit him square in the box.

Those near-misses looked to cost England as the 23-year-old belted Rashid for 10 in his final two balls.

Curran had Chaudhary caught at deep square leg for 45 (35), Curran holding a clenched fist towards the Delhi-born batter, a low-key addendum to their heated MCG discussion on Saturday night.

The Australians countered beautifully at the close, hitting 16 runs off Overton in the 18th over, 14 off the expensive Crocombe in the 19th, and 20 off the otherwise excellent Curran in the last.

Jack Edwards fell for an entertaining 18 off Crocombe, while Curran effected the runout of Davies (39) off his own bowling when Davis and Dwarshuis attempted a suicidal second run.

However, Dwarshuis made up for that by crushing the Englishman for three straight sixes to end the innings and set England what seemed like a more than acceptable 185 to win the match.

World.title: Marnus Labuschagne suffers bizarre Shield dismissal
World.content:
Marnus Labuschagne's frustrating run of starts has hit a bizarre new level, with the dropped Test star caught off the back of his bat against NSW in the Sheffield Shield.

Labuschagne was out for 34 before tea on day three in Sydney, with Queensland 2-106 and an 81-run lead when rain stopped play.

Ryan Hicks's fighting 92 not out for the Blues on Tuesday morning and Sydney's wet weather means a result is unlikely, with Test ramifications now the bigger factor.

But Labuschagne's dismissal was the big moment on day three, before rain washed away close to two hours of play.

After a long run of scores between 30 and 49 for Australia in the past year, Labuschagne was out for 37 and 34 in this match.

He was attempting to sweep Lyon when the ball bounced off his upper chest and onto the back of his bat before being well caught by Hicks.

Labuschagne pointed to his chest in frustration as he argued the ball had not come off his bat, but replays told a different story.

The wicket was also a notable one for Lyon (1-30), who took 1-86 in the first innings and looked largely unthreatening in Queensland's first innings on a docile SCG pitch.

National selectors have shown over the past 15 months they are no longer guaranteed to play a spinner in every Test, having gone into five of the past 11 without one.

Lyon will be in Australia's squad for the first Test against New Zealand in Perth on December 9, with his role as the side's number one spinner not up for debate.

But if it is a pace-friendly wicket, questions could be raised around his spot.

Lyon took a fourth-innings 3-51 to help NSW to victory in their last match against South Australia and more wickets on Wednesday will not hurt his cause.

NSW resumed at 7-195 in reply to Queensland's first-innings 278 on Tuesday and were 8-197 when Lyon fell early.

Hicks then put on 59 for the ninth wicket with Liam Hatcher and 47 for the last with Bryce Jackson, pulling quick Michael Neser and Tom Straker for sixes.

Hatcher then had Angus Lovell caught at midwicket for four, as the Blues eyed off running through Queensland to force a result.

But Hugo Burdon ensured Queensland kept the match under control, hitting Jackson for two sixes over the legside on his way to an unbeaten 53.

Mitchell Swepson provided the other highlight for Queensland, taking NSW's last three wickets to finish with a career-best 6-73.

Swepson has not been part of a Test squad since Australia's last tour of India, but remains the number one red-ball legspinner if required.

AAP

World.title: Lani Pallister eyes history as bullish Aussies lay down Olympic gauntlet
World.content:
Australia's swimmers are bullishly approaching the 2026 World Short Course Championships as they gear up for a massive lead-in to the 2028 LA Olympics.

The 23-strong Australian team heads to Beijing on Thursday, ahead of the short course championships getting underway on December 1.

Lani Pallister will headline the Australian team, looking to win a third consecutive women's 800-metre title, an event she also holds the world record in, beating legendary American Katie Ledecky's mark by a colossal 3.42 seconds in October last year.

"Any time I get behind the blocks I want to make history; I want to swim times that haven't been seen before," she said.

"I was super stoked last year with my 800. Breaking Katie's world record by three seconds was, I feel, the big jumping point for my career, particularly in the last 12 months."

Lani Pallister handed Katie Ledecky a rare defeat in California. (Getty Images: Maddie Meyer)

For a generation, Ledecky has been the benchmark against which all other female distance swimmers are measured — and for good reason.

The American legend has proven almost unbeatable over the 800m freestyle, claiming the last four Olympic gold medals in the distance.

And yet, at the Pan Pacific Championships earlier this year, Pallister stunned the living legend to land a remarkable psychological blow as the Olympics approaches.

"I am the kind of person who likes getting behind the blocks and racing everyone," Pallister said.

"I don't want the result to be just about beating Katie; I want it to be [that] I swam a world-class time that only two other people in history have beaten.

"That's a really important thing for me, stamping my legacy as a distance swimmer and not just someone that's racing someone else in the pool."

Pallister acknowledges that Ledecky's mantle as the greatest women's distance swimmer of all time is unlikely to be shaken in the short or even medium term, whether she claims victory in LA or not.

But that does not mean that the Sunshine Coast swimmer is overawed by her rival.

Lani Pallister is planning on getting through a mountain of work. (Getty Images: Maddie Meyer)

"Katie's held that title [greatest of all time] for the last 14 years. I think she's done absolutely tremendous things for women's distance swimming and women's sport in general," Pallister said.

"Just to be part of that story and part of that race in two years' time will be unreal, but also knowing that I'm doing it for me and because I want to swim and I want to be successful.

"To be able to have the opportunity to race in two years' time and be in Brisbane in six years' time and challenge for Olympic gold medals and be close to world records for long course and short course is all I ever dreamed of."

Pallister is a noted workaholic when it comes to racing — the day after the trials for the world short course championships she flew from Sydney to Brisbane to compete in an ocean swim hosted by her surf lifesaving club, Alex Heads. She won it, too.

As such, the 24-year-old will endure an abundance of racing over the next 12 months, which is the backbone of her strategy for success.

"Racing's the best form of training," Pallister said of her plans over the next year.

"So I'm the type of person who's happy to live out of a suitcase and travel and see friends and people overseas, but more importantly get the race practice in."

Flynn Southam has also embraced the chance to race hard and often over the past 12 months, enjoying huge success in Glasgow at the Commonwealth Games.

Flynn Southam says Australia is in a golden era for swimming. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

"I think it kind of stamped my authority," Southam said of his four golds and one silver in Glasgow.

"Not just as potential, but, 'He's here and he's arrived.'

"Our job is to go into the Americans' backyard and play some games with them."

Southam even went as far as to say Australia was in a "golden age" of swimming, a bold claim for a nation with such a tremendous history in the pool.

"This is the best team we've had in this Olympic cycle, and probably will be going into LA [the best] that we've ever had," the 21-year-old said.

Southam, the Commonwealth 100m freestyle champion, said the prospect of competing in LA was all-consuming, dominating his thoughts.

"It's all I can think about," he said.

"Most people can go down to the pub and watch a game of sport and switch off.

"But for me, it's all I think about; it's in my mind 24/7.

"That's what fuels my fire. I live for it. I breathe this stuff.

"The higher the challenge, the higher the pressure, the more I rise to the occasion.

"I think the man who's going to win the 100 free at the LA Olympic Games is the one who is going to be able to deal with the most pressure, the most adversity and still perform under any circumstances.

"And I believe with my whole heart that that's going to be me."

World.title: Hobart's new $1.23 billion stadium price tag explained
World.content:
It has become a familiar — verging on cliché — line when discussing anything regarding the Macquarie Point stadium.

The devil is in the detail.

When Premier Jeremy Rockliff revealed the updated cost of the stadium had risen from $1.13 billion to $1.23 billion via his Facebook page this morning, the number was met with a mix of relief and surprise from those who expected a much higher spike.

But here comes that devil.

A simulation of the internal concourse at the proposed Macquarie Point stadium. (Supplied: MPDC)

Hobart's stadium and precinct costs rise to $1.54b The state government blames high oil, materials and labour prices for the blowout from a $1.13 billion budget set last year.

For the stadium to actually function, it requires broader precinct works at Macquarie Point to be completed.

They are works that sit outside the core construction of the stadium but are vital to its functionality.

Energy. Water. Landscaping. For those things, an extra $132 million has been allocated by the government.

It is true that that infrastructure will serve a broader purpose — TasPorts, and future developments (hotels, restaurants, shops, housing) on the site will all draw on the energy and water upgrades that will happen as part of the stadium development.

But it is also true that for the stadium's lights to turn on and for its toilets to flush, those things must be built and therefore must be included as a cost.

Doing so sees the price lift from $1.23 billion to $1.36 billion.

The developer cited the war in Iran as a major factor behind the cost increase. (Supplied: MPDC)

Then there are the costs of facilitating that extra work, as well as costs already incurred by the Macquarie Point Development Corporation.

That spits out at $183 million.

Now we are at $1.54 billion for the stadium and the precinct works that let it operate.

And that's if everything goes to plan across the life of the build.

The roof was a condition of the contract with the AFL. (Supplied: MPDC)

One crucial number that's missing from the update is the contingency price, with the government and Macquarie Point Development Corporation opting to keep that number secret ahead of penning a building contract with construction partner BESIX Watpac.

Previous estimates included this figure, with $174 million making up part of the stadium's last cost estimate of $1.13 billion.

That is 14 per cent of the budget.

Applying this number to the new overall cost adds another $215 million to the total, for a total budget of $1.76 billion.

How much contingency the Macquarie Point Development Corporation keeps up its sleeve depends on the contract it signs with BESIX Watpac.

Jeremy Rockliff (right) says the "cost has changed, but the opportunity for Tasmania has not". (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

At a recent public accounts committee hearing, department secretary Kathrine Morgan-Wicks spoke of assurances made before the "final investment decision".

"This includes understanding the proposed relationship between MPDC and the lead contractor," she said.

" For example, the contract cost will be higher as risks are transferred to the contractor, or lower if the state accepts risks. "

The MPDC cited the war in Iran as a major factor behind the cost increase, as well as Australia's competitive infrastructure pipeline, which includes the upcoming Brisbane Olympics.

In a bid to keep costs low, the MPDC also confirmed it had "value managed" the project by $100 million, mainly through the design process and the process in which the stadium is delivered.

So, let's break down the numbers even further.

Many elements of the project have not been factored into the new cost. (Supplied: MPDC)

Included in the $1.2 billion stadium cost is the core construction of the stadium building, seats, roof, grass and fit-out.

Everything that makes a stadium a stadium.

It also includes the cricket test rig, which was constructed earlier this year, dilapidation surveys, environmental monitoring equipment and bulk excavation works currently occurring at the Macquarie Point site in anticipation of the build.

A smaller-scale roof was constructed to test if the shadows were a problem for cricket play. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

The $132 million in precinct costs will cover stormwater and water upgrades, power upgrades and landscaping.

A car park has also been included, but MPDC chief executive Anne Beach said it "absolutely wasn't required" for the stadium; rather, it would act as an "enabler" for the precinct.

The $183 million in project delivery costs are the costs to deliver the precinct — It includes paying for consultants, the Macquarie Point Development Corporation staff, incidentals like personal protective equipment, computer software, training, headworks and building insurance.

Not included? The Northern Access Road, which is priced at $78.9 million and, while necessary for the stadium to function, is a long-existing project which will be headed up, and funded by, Building Tasmania.

The cap on state funding of $875 million, agreed to by Jeremy Rockliff in exchange for support, is essentially scrapped. (Supplied: MPDC)

The updated budget also does not account for interest on the additional borrowings which will be required to cover the increased cost, which will flow through a new "funding facility" being set up for the MPDC.

In other words, the MPDC's borrowing limit will be increased in order for it to pay for the project, and $1.29 billion of the total project cost will currently be borne by the Tasmanian taxpayer through capital and borrowings.

That means the state funding cap of $875 million agreed to by Premier Jeremy Rockliff in exchange for the upper house vote of Bec Thomas is essentially scrapped.

But there does still remain the possibility for more funding from external sources, with the premier today confirming ABC reporting that conversations had begun with the federal government, AFL, cricket and private sector regarding increased financial contributions.

Jeremy Rockliff says "every generation has a couple of rare opportunities to change their future … for us, this is a golden one". (ABC News: Owain Stia James)

The new budget will be presented to cabinet by November 30 and is expected to be approved, with a construction contract to be signed in the coming weeks.

"We've had our commercial and legal team, as well as our technical team, look at the detail submitted by [BESIX] Watpac," MPDC's Anne Beach said.

"We've undertaken an analysis, and we're confident that we can deliver within that budget," she said.

World.title: Munster calls Storm contract offer 'disappointing'
World.content:
Cameron Munster has declared all options are on the table after officially rejecting a deal to stay in Melbourne and labelling the Storm's latest offer "disappointing".

With Melbourne already facing a battle to retain Harry Grant, the Storm is now officially fighting a retention war on two fronts after Munster's decision.

The Melbourne superstar admitted on Tuesday that Grant's future could play a role in his own call, as well as Craig Bellamy's impending retirement at the end of 2027.

As it stands, Munster will not take up an offer from the Storm that is understood to have been for one year with an option for a second.

"I have declined it," the Queensland State of Origin captain said.

"I am not saying I am going to leave Melbourne. Just with the terms and conditions that they put out to me, it is probably something that is a little disappointing.

"But it's a business, I am not stupid."

Munster admitted his own form had not been good enough for the Storm last season as they missed the finals for the first time in his career.

The Storm did not enjoy a good NRL season, missing the finals. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

And in turn, the 32-year-old conceded the offer may have been as a result of that.

"That [offer] just makes my job a little bit harder. But it's also a bit of a challenge saying I am not where I need to be," he said.

"Maybe I need to be a little bit better to earn that contract that we're looking for.

"And maybe it is a little bit of a kick up the bum from them. I am not too sure where we'll go from here but all options are open at the moment."

Munster's rejection comes after Grant met with Gold Coast officials last Friday and officially received an offer to join the Titans.

It is understood Melbourne's offer for the Queensland dummy-half will either be worth similar or more than the Titans.

But Gold Coast are hopeful of luring the hooker north, given his relationship with ex-Maroons assistant coach Josh Hannay and prop Tino Fa'asuamaleaui.

Harry Grant may also be moving away from the Storm. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne )

NSW prop Stefano Utoikamanu is also off contract at the end of next year and has also been linked to the Sydney Roosters.

At the same time, Bellamy's retirement at the end of next season is proving a challenge for the Storm, given he is like a father figure to Munster.

"When you look at someone like Craig as a coach, he is a great coach and I have so much respect and have admired him for such a long time," Munster said.

"It's going to be different at the club. I'm not too sure where the club wants to go with all that stuff.

"I don't know who they are going to get and I'm sure it will be a daunting job coming after him."

Munster also confirmed he will likely follow the Cameron Smith route and give away representative football at some point to focus on club duties.

"It definitely has [crossed my mind]," Munster said.

"The hard thing for me is giving up the captaincy.

"Once I start declining [I will look at it] and I thought I was declining. But after my last few games for the World Cup I am pretty confident I can get back to that."

AAP

World.title: Why there's no time to waste for Matildas ahead of World Cup
World.content:
With no time to waste as the Matildas hurtle towards next year's Women's World Cup, Mary Fowler and Kyra Cooney-Cross's respective returns cannot come quickly enough for captain Sam Kerr.

Australia play world No.19 Colombia in Canberra on Saturday, then again in Geelong next Wednesday.

Fowler missed the last window through personal reasons while Cooney-Cross returns to camp having spent time away for personal reasons since the Asian Cup.

"We only have six games left, so to play together as a team is most important," Kerr said.

Sam Kerr recently joined American club Gotham FC. (Getty Images: Dustin Satloff)

"And of course you want to see new faces and you want to see the new talent coming through.

"But you also want to build cohesion and play with the people that probably are mainstays on the team. And Mary, Kyra, all of those girls are.

"And it's obviously harder when you go into a World Cup with less minutes together.

"So we need as many minutes as we can with everyone, and while breeding the new talent."

This month's games mark the final window before the December 11 World Cup draw as the clock ticks down to next year's tournament in Brazil.

Kerr said she had not spoken to Fowler, nor many of her other teammates this window, but was keen to have her back in the fray.

Mary Fowler will return to Matildas camp after missing matches due to personal reasons. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

"Of course, Mary's an important part to the team," she said.

"Hopefully she can play well for us."

Facing Colombia, who have established themselves as the second-best South American team behind hosts Brazil, serves as crucial preparation.

"I know it sounds like six months, but we probably spend a month of that together. So we've got to make the most of every game," Kerr said.

"And Colombia is a really good team and a team that we could face at the World Cup.

"They're a different team. We don't normally face teams like this. They play hard. They play a different style of football than we're used to, similar to Brazil and those countries.

"But personally, I want to win the games."

Kerr famously missed most of the 2023 World Cup, where Australia made the semi-finals, with a calf injury.

Sam Kerr missed much of the 2023 World Cup through injury. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

A horror protracted return from a knee reconstruction wiped her out for almost two years.

"When you see the draw coming up, all of those things, the last few teams of qualifying, this camp over in Europe, it starts to feel real," Kerr said.

"Six months will go like that. The last 3.5 years has gone really quickly, so it seems crazy that 2023 was nearly four years ago, it's gone really quick.

"Just really excited but taking it day by day, kind of focusing game by game. Getting excited though."

Kerr crossed from English powerhouse Chelsea to NWSL team Gotham FC last season and is confident she is primed to deliver for the Matildas.

"I feel good. Obviously, would have liked to have scored a few goals in the play-offs recently, but it didn't work out like that.

"But I've been going for 18 months, so I'm looking forward to a break and a refresh before starting up next season, but two more games to go.

"And I feel confident every time I play for the Matildas because it feels like a really comfortable space for me to come and perform."

AAP

World.title: Cameron Smith keen on PGA return following LIV collapse
World.content:
Moving quickly on after LIV Golf's demise, Cameron Smith has revealed a burning desire to return to the PGA Tour as his Australian peers welcome the end to the sport's bitter civil war.

With LIV filing for bankruptcy and being liquidated, Smith has joined the DP World Tour on an invite basis, but has no full-time status.

But for the first time since joining the Saudi-backed league a month after winning the 2022 British Open, Smith conceded he hoped to find a permanent home back on the PGA Tour.

"I guess that's the path. That's where I want to be now for sure," the one-time world number two said ahead of this week's Australian PGA Championship in Sydney.

"DP's given us a chance to kind of fulfil that. We'll see how that goes. There's plenty of good players out there and plenty of other guys that want to do the same thing, so it's going to be difficult.

"But for sure that's where I want to play."

Cam Smith is playing on the DP World Tour. (Getty Images: Hector Vivas)

Only the top 10 from the DP World Tour's season-long points race qualify for the PGA Tour.

But Smith can greatly enhance his chances of getting back to the US big time by at least gaining a full DP World Tour card by winning the PGA Championship, next week's Australian Open in Melbourne or topping the summer-long Australasian order of merit.

At the very least his intention to return to the PGA Tour is a major revelation.

In January, Smith flatly rejected an offer to come back under strict guidelines, insisting he had "no" temptation to follow Brooks Koepka and make a $5 million charity donation.

While he remains disappointed at how LIV collapsed, the 33-year-old ex-Ripper GC captain is relieved a resolution has finally come so he can open a new chapter in his decorated career.

Smith signed with LIV Golf in 2022. (Reuters: Imagn Images/Dennis Schneidler)

"There were lots of rumours floating around throughout the year. There was a lot of uncertainty and then in a way it was good to just like get the noise over and done with," Smith said, maintaining he has no regrets about ever joining LIV.

"It was a big move to go LIV at the start for sure, and I think everyone that was close to me and all my friends saw why I was doing it and why I made the decision.

"So I didn't lose many friends over it — I didn't lose any friends over it, really. I still talk to the same people, I still have the same conversations. I've always tried to do the right thing."

Compatriots Min Woo Lee and fellow major champion Adam Scott said they'd love to see Smith back excelling in the States again.

Smith is the biggest star in Australian golf. (AP: Alastair Gran)

"He's a good friend and we want to see a short-game [star] around the PGA Tour, so it'll be very exciting to see him play on the PGA Tour again," Lee said on Tuesday.

"Whenever we get Aussies on the tour, it's a good time. When we see each other, it doesn't seem like we've missed a day and it's nice.

"Hopefully the golfing world is coming back together. Even just yesterday I was in the locker room with Cam and it's just 'welcome back'.

"I don't pay attention too much to it — (the LIV rivalry) but, yeah, hopefully it all comes back together and we're all happy."

Scott dismissed the notion that Smith couldn't be a success again in America after losing his mojo on the so-called less competitive LIV league.

"Cam's incredibly talented and hell adjust to his new environment and he'll be just fine," Scott said.

"There's no doubt about it."

AAP

World.title: Teenager threatened with violent sexual assault after losing tennis match
World.content:
An 18-year-old player has been subjected to death threats and graphic abuse after losing her tennis match during an Adelaide international tournament.

Adelaide's Taylah Lessue was competing during the City of Playford Tennis International on Sunday, winning the first set 6-4 before succumbing to an ongoing illness and losing 6-4, 0-6, 0-6.

According to her mother, Rachelle Lessue, the singles player had been bed-ridden for three weeks with glandular fever before giving the tournament "everything she had".

"Only eight days ago she was in hospital on a drip and lost 6 kilograms in a week unable to eat or swallow anything," Ms Lessue wrote in a social media post.

"But what breaks my heart is, 15 minutes after walking off court, the disgusting, hurtful and sick messages she received on social media."

The online abuse arrived within 15 minutes of Taylah Lessue's match ending. (Supplied)

Lessue is number 647 in the ITF World Tennis Junior Girls Singles rankings and her match, which was streamed live, had apparently been subject to betting.

She received a torrent of violent, sexually explicit death threats shortly after her loss, even as she recovered from the "fatigue, chest tightness and muscle spasms" her mother said had affected her performance.

"These people have no idea what Tay has battled the last few weeks, and the huge amount of courage and fight she showed to play today," Ms Lessue said.

The abuse started as Lessue stood courtside after the match with City of Playford Mayor Glenn Docherty, who described it as "too graphic" to repeat.

"I know that she's a pretty resilient young lady, but she should not be putting up with this type of abuse," he told 891 ABC Adelaide.

"It's just absolutely scary.

"To see the content of those messages … I'm sickened by it.

"Hopefully this person or persons can be unmasked and can be dealt with appropriately by law enforcement."

Taylah Lessue was courtside with Glenn Docherty when the abuse started. (Facebook)

Police said they were investigating after a victim received messages of an inappropriate and offensive nature on social media.

"Northern District Police are investigating and will determine if there is evidence to sustain any criminal charges," a spokesperson said.

Tennis Australia responds

Tennis Australia head of integrity Dan Stuk said it was disgraceful that people would go online and "target individuals that they don't even know simply because of their sporting performance".

He said social media was an "overwhelmingly positive space" that gave a lot of "support and love for a number of athletes".

"But there are small numbers of abuse taking place and what we're finding is that it has, as you would imagine, very deeply personal impacts and it can have a real effect on the athletes."

Mr Stuk said the abuse could be targeted at anyone from experienced players to junior athletes, and was "circumstance-specific".

"I would say that online abuse can come from a number of different areas and it can be betting-related, but it can also be related to any other aspect of society," he said.

"Our job at Tennis Australia is to be ready to respond to that, regardless of the abuse.

He said that included educating players about social media use and their privacy settings, how to manage and report any online abuse, and options to monitor and moderate online content with a third-party provider so "they don't even see this in the first place".

It also included providing support for players and family in response to abusive content.

Taylah Lessue won the first set in her match but succumbed to illness. (Facebook)

Ms Lessue said tournament doctors examined her daughter after the match and she had been ruled out of any competition for the next seven to 10 days.

"But the way she conducted herself and fought until the end, when most other people would be bedridden or retired mid-match, fills me with immense pride," she said.

"While it's a loss on the scoreboard, it's another step in her journey and she learned many valuable lessons.

"Above all else, she can hold her head high knowing she fought her heart out and gave the match everything she had."

Tech.title: Now Firefox can select which sites use its VPN, and clear your browsing history with one click
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Mozilla released Firefox 161 on Tuesday with a new setting you can use to choose which pages automatically open with the browser’s VPN active. Using the “Manage VPN rules” option in Firefox’s VPN panel, you can set it to “always on” or “always off” for specific sites, so you don’t have to toggle it manually every time you visit certain pages.

Starting Tuesday, Mozilla is also rolling out a “Fire” button in standard Firefox windows that lets you quickly clear your browsing data directly from the toolbar. You can choose which data it deletes, including browsing history, downloads history, cookie data, site data, temporary files, saved form info, and website permissions and preferences. If you set the button to delete all of that data, clicking it will sign you out of everything and open a fresh Firefox window.

Tuesday’s Firefox update also adds an option for creating a keyboard shortcut for copying your current tab’s URL, and brings its “read aloud” option in Reader Mode to the Android version of Firefox. Alongside the update, Mozilla says Firefox is also now available directly through the Play Store on cars with Google built-in.

Tech.title: David Fincher is being dragged for suspected use of AI in his latest film
Tech.content:
is a reporter focusing on film, TV, and pop culture. Before The Verge, he wrote about comic books, labor, race, and more at io9 and Gizmodo for almost five years.

Though David Fincher’s fans had been eagerly anticipating The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, early screenings of the Once Upon a Time in Hollywood sequel starring Brad Pitt have raised questions about whether generative AI was used in the film. People have claimed that the movie is chock-full of uncanny, inconsistent visuals that make it feel more like slop than the sort of polished film you’d expect from the director of sleek productions like Fight Club and The Social Network.

Following a number of Cliff Booth critics screenings that took place last week ahead of the film’s premiere on November 25th, moviegoers rushed to social media to lament what they saw. One of the most vocal reactions came from YouTuber / director Patrick Tomasso, who said on X that he walked out of his screening feeling “completely gutted” and that the film featured “some of the most blatant and egregious AI use” he has ever seen from a major studio. Tomasso also insisted you can see AI-generated footage in Cliff Booth’s trailers that have been posted online, and he was confident that Fincher’s latest film is filled with “slop as you know and loathe it. The shit you can pump out of Higgsfield.”

Others echoed Tomasso’s sentiments, writing that “the amount of AI in the CLIFF BOOTH movie is astounding to an absurd degree” and vowing to “never watch another Fincher, Pitt or Tarintino [sic] movie again.” Yet some critics enjoyed the film and suggested that the bad AI people thought they were seeing might have actually just been bad CGI. Netflix has neither confirmed nor denied whether AI was used in any capacity to make the film, but Netflix’s heavy involvement in the film’s production and the company’s recent investments in generative AI technology left many suspicious.

It did not help that David Fincher, in a recent interview with the Los Angeles Times, responded to questions about his thoughts on AI with “I’m not a Luddite, so I don’t fear the unknown.” Fincher also reasoned that the anti-AI crowd is advocating for artists to stop iterating on their creative processes: “Is everyone satisfied that we have figured this art form out enough that what we really need to do is go back to celluloid? How long have people painted? 40,000 years? We’re talking about a thing that’s a hundred years old and everyone’s going, ‘Stop. Pencils down. No more iterating. It’s not necessary to have at your fingertips the ability to change the color of that person’s eyes.’ Well, it exists. Should we not use it?” The spiel made it sound like he might be jumping on the AI bandwagon.

Set about a decade after Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, Cliff Booth picks up in 1977 at a time when Booth (Pitt) has left his life as a stuntman behind to become a fixer who quietly deals with scandalous problems for Hollywood elites. Cliff still works a number of side gigs as a projectionist and bartender. But the movie is primarily focused on his budding romance with critic-turned-talent agent Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki) and his working relationship with Charlie Peters (Scott Caan), a TV actor who needs Booth’s services to keep his wife (Carla Gugino) from being murdered.

At least one trailer for the film features some baffling shots of what looks like people sitting backward in a horse-drawn carriage that make it seem like there might be some generative AI in the mix. It’s hard to tell from the trailers whether that’s actually the case, but in a moment when many creators have been trying to pass off AI generations as human-made art, it’s not surprising that people are suspicious.

Netflix has been incorporating AI into its movies and series for some time now, and it seemed like the company was doubling down earlier this year when it acquired Ben Affleck’s startup, InterPositive, for around $600 million. Rather than turning text into visual outputs like many commercially available AI tools, InterPositive’s AI models are designed to generate assets based on footage captured during a film’s production. According to Netflix, InterPositive’s AI was developed with the intention of making it easier to tweak details like lighting or to remove unwanted background elements. The company also made a big deal of emphasizing that InterPositive’s models were highly customizable and well suited to replicating a human director’s signature style.

Netflix buying InterPositive and absorbing the company’s development team is part of why there has been so much speculation about AI being used in Cliff Booth. If Cliff Booth actually uses AI and the visuals really are as bad as some have said, it would be a major knock against both Netflix and Fincher — a director known for his meticulous (obsessive, some might argue) attention to detail.
